Patterns: Conservation and balance; Quadratic structure; Decomposition

Name: D'Alembert's formula
Intuition: Initial displacement splits equally into left- and right-moving copies. Initial velocity contributes through the interval that can influence the point by time t.
Conditions: For the whole-line equation u_tt=c²u_xx with c>0, t≥0, f∈C²(R), g∈C¹(R), u(x,0)=f(x) and u_t(x,0)=g(x); the formula gives the classical solution.
Example: If initial velocity is zero, u(x,t) is the arithmetic mean of f(x−ct) and f(x+ct).
Prerequisites: Wave equation; Riemann integral; Arithmetic mean

Name: Conservation of wave energy
Intuition: A wave exchanges kinetic activity with stored spatial deformation. When no forcing or boundary work adds energy, their total remains constant.
Conditions: c>0; Ω is bounded with C¹ boundary; u is a sufficiently smooth real solution of u_tt=c²Δu with homogeneous Dirichlet or homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.
Example: A single standing wave alternates between maximum displacement and maximum speed while this total stays fixed.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Quadratic structure; Decomposition

Name: Constant-velocity transport
Intuition: The entire profile moves with one velocity without changing its shape. Following a point carried by that motion makes the observed value constant.
Conditions: v∈Rⁿ is constant and f∈C¹(Rⁿ); the formula is the classical whole-space solution with u(0,x)=f(x).
Example: In one dimension, f(x)=e^{−x²} and v=2 gives a Gaussian bump centered at x=2t with unchanged width.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Conservation and balance; Composition

Name: Method of characteristics
Intuition: Choose paths that move with the transport field. Along those paths, the spatial derivative and time derivative merge into one ordinary derivative.
Conditions: b is C¹ in space and time on the local region, f is continuous and u is a C¹ solution; characteristic ODEs are considered over times where their flow exists.
Example: For u_t+xu_x=0, characteristics satisfy x(t)=x₀eᵗ and u(t,x)=u(0,xe^{−t}).
Prerequisites: Multivariable chain rule; Picard iteration for an initial value problem

Name: Duhamel's principle
Intuition: Every instant of forcing launches a homogeneous response that evolves for the remaining time. Add all those responses to the freely evolved initial state.
Conditions: S(t) is a strongly continuous semigroup of bounded operators on a Banach space X with generator A, u₀∈X, and f:[0,T]→X is continuous; the vector-valued integral gives the mild solution of u′=Au+f. Additional regularity is needed for a classical time derivative.
Example: With S(t)=e^{−at}, the formula solves y′+ay=f(t) by an exponentially weighted history integral.
Prerequisites: Variation of parameters for a linear system; Convolution

Name: Poisson boundary value problem
Intuition: A source distribution determines the curvature required of an equilibrium field. Boundary values anchor the otherwise underdetermined potential.
Conditions: This entry defines the classical Dirichlet problem on a bounded domain: seek u∈C²(Ω)∩C(closure Ω) for specified interior source f and boundary data g. Existence and regularity require suitable domain and data hypotheses; the weak formulation supplies one precise alternative.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Conservation and balance; Optimization

Name: Euler–Lagrange equation
Intuition: An optimal or stationary curve must resist every small admissible deformation to first order. Integration by parts turns that global stationarity requirement into a local differential equation.
Conditions: L is C², y is C², and variations are C¹ with zero endpoint values on a finite interval. The equivalence is between the differential equation and vanishing first variation; stationarity alone does not imply a minimum.
Example: For L=½m(y′)²−V(y), the equation is my″+V′(y)=0.

Name: Beltrami identity
Intuition: If the integrand does not explicitly depend on the position along the independent variable, one combination of value and slope remains constant. This reduces a second-order variational equation to a first integral.
Conditions: L(y,v) is C² and independent of the independent variable t; y is a C² solution of the Euler–Lagrange equation on an interval.
Example: For arc length L=√(1+(y′)²), the identity gives 1/√(1+(y′)²)=C, implying a constant slope for a smooth stationary graph.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Symmetry and invariance; Decomposition

Name: Hamilton's equations
LaTeX: p=\partial_{\dot q}L,\qquad H=p\cdot\dot q-L,\qquad\dot q=\partial_pH,\quad\dot p=-\partial_qH
Intuition: Describe motion using position and momentum instead of position and velocity. One scalar Hamiltonian then generates both rates through paired derivatives with opposite signs.
Conditions: L(q,v,t) is C² for q,v∈Rⁿ and its velocity Hessian is nonsingular in the region considered, so v can be expressed locally in terms of (q,p,t); H uses that substitution and the trajectory obeys Euler–Lagrange.
Example: For H(q,p)=p²/(2m)+V(q), Hamilton's equations give q̇=p/m and ṗ=−V′(q).
Patterns: Duality; Conservation and balance; Change of coordinates

Name: Noether conservation law for a configuration symmetry
Intuition: A continuous change of coordinates that leaves the Lagrangian unchanged produces a quantity the motion cannot change. The conserved quantity pairs momentum with the infinitesimal symmetry direction.
Conditions: L(q,v,t) is C²; a smooth one-parameter configuration transformation Q_ε with generator ξ leaves L(Q_ε(q),DQ_ε(q)v,t)=L(q,v,t), with time fixed; q is a C² Euler–Lagrange solution. This version assumes exact invariance, not invariance only up to a total derivative.
Example: Translation symmetry in one coordinate gives conservation of the corresponding momentum component; rotational symmetry gives angular momentum.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Conservation and balance; Duality

Name: Second variation of a one-dimensional functional
Intuition: The first variation measures slope in the space of curves, and the second variation measures curvature there. Its sign tests whether small perturbations tend to raise or lower the functional.
Conditions: J[y]=∫_a^b L(t,y,y′)dt on a finite interval; L is C² near the curve, y,η are C¹ and η(a)=η(b)=0; all L derivatives are evaluated at (t,y(t),y′(t)). A smooth local minimum requires this quantity to be nonnegative for every admissible η, but nonnegativity alone is not sufficient.
Example: For J[y]=½∫(y′)²dt, δ²J=∫(η′)²dt, strictly positive for nonzero fixed-endpoint perturbations.
Patterns: Quadratic structure; Optimization; Geometry and distance

Name: Dirichlet Rayleigh–Ritz principle
Intuition: The lowest-frequency mode is the nonzero shape with the least gradient energy per unit squared amplitude. Restricting the search to trial shapes gives computable upper bounds on that eigenvalue.
Conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded, connected and has Lipschitz boundary; λ₁ is the first eigenvalue of −Δ with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. The minimum is attained by a first eigenfunction.
Example: On (0,L), sin(πx/L) attains the quotient (π/L)².
Patterns: Optimization; Quadratic structure; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Regular Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville problem; Sobolev norm; Poincaré inequality with zero boundary values

Name: Probability axioms
Intuition: Probability assigns a consistent amount of mass to events. Splitting an event into disjoint pieces preserves its total mass.
Conditions: Events belong to a sigma-algebra on a sample space; the A_i are pairwise disjoint.
Example: For a fair die, each of six disjoint outcomes has mass 1/6.

Name: Conditional probability
Intuition: Conditioning restricts attention to the outcomes still possible and rescales their mass to one.
Conditions: A and B are events with P(B)>0; conditioning on probability-zero events requires a different construction.
Example: Among even die rolls, the chance of rolling 6 is (1/6)/(1/2)=1/3.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Information and uncertainty

Name: Law of total probability
Intuition: Split a complicated chance calculation into cases, then average the answers using the chances of those cases.
Conditions: The B_i form a finite or countable measurable partition with P(B_i)>0; zero-mass pieces may be omitted.
Example: A machine chosen with probabilities .6 and .4 has defect rates .01 and .03, giving .018 overall.

Name: Bayes' rule
Intuition: Evidence reweights competing explanations by how well each predicts it. The denominator puts the revised weights back on a common probability scale.
Conditions: The hypotheses form a finite or countable partition, the displayed conditionals exist, and P(E)>0.
Example: With prior odds 1:1 and a likelihood ratio of 3, the posterior probability is 3/4.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Conditional probability; Law of total probability

Name: Independence of random variables
Intuition: Knowing one variable leaves the probability law of the other unchanged.
Conditions: The identity must hold for every measurable A and B; pairwise independence need not imply mutual independence of three or more variables.
Example: Two independent fair dice give P(X=1,Y=1)=1/36.

Name: Union bound
Intuition: Adding all failure probabilities gives a safe upper bound even when failures overlap.
Conditions: A_i is a finite or countable family of events; the upper bound may exceed one and may be loose.
Example: If five checks each fail with probability at most .01, any failure has probability at most .05.

Name: Expectation
Intuition: Expectation is an average whose weights are probabilities. It compresses a distribution into the balance point of its mass.
Conditions: X is measurable and integrable: E|X|<infinity; nonnegative X also admits an extended expectation.
Example: A fair six-sided die has expectation 3.5 even though no individual outcome equals 3.5.

Name: Linearity of expectation
Intuition: An average of a sum equals the sum of the averages, even when the summands depend on one another.
Conditions: The number of summands is finite, all X_i are integrable, and a_i,b are deterministic real constants.
Example: The expected number of heads in ten possibly dependent fair coin tosses is five.

Name: Probability as an indicator expectation
Intuition: Turn a yes-or-no event into a number. Counts then become sums of indicators, so expected counts become sums of probabilities.
Conditions: The second formula is for a finite family, or a countable family with nonnegative terms and possibly infinite expectation.
Example: Expected fixed points in a random permutation of n objects equal n times 1/n, hence one.

Name: Variance
Intuition: Variance measures average squared distance from the balance point. Squaring makes deviations in opposite directions reinforce rather than cancel.
Conditions: X is real and E[X^2]<infinity.
Example: A Bernoulli(p) variable has variance p(1-p).

Name: Variance under affine change
Intuition: Moving every value by the same amount preserves spread; multiplying distances by a scales squared spread by a squared.
Conditions: X has finite variance and a,b are real constants.
Example: Converting a measurement from meters to centimeters multiplies its variance by 10,000.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Variance of a sum
Intuition: Total uncertainty contains each variable's own spread and every pair's tendency to move together.
Conditions: A finite collection of real random variables with finite second moments; the covariance terms vanish for pairwise uncorrelated variables.
Example: Two unit-variance variables with correlation .5 have sum variance three.

Name: Covariance
LaTeX: \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb EX)(Y-\mathbb EY)]=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]
Intuition: Covariance detects whether two centered quantities tend to have matching signs. It measures shared linear fluctuation, not every kind of dependence.
Conditions: X and Y are real and square-integrable.
Example: If Y=2X+3, their covariance is twice Var(X).

Name: Pearson correlation
Intuition: Correlation is the cosine between centered random variables. Dividing by their lengths removes measurement units.
Conditions: Both variables have finite, strictly positive variance; the bound follows from Cauchy-Schwarz.
Example: If Y=-3X+2 and Var(X)>0, correlation is -1.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Covariance under a linear map
Intuition: A linear transformation carries an uncertainty ellipsoid into another ellipsoid. The same map acts on both sides because covariance compares pairs of directions.
Conditions: X is a finite-dimensional real random vector with finite second moments; A and b are deterministic and dimensionally compatible.
Example: For a scalar a, this reduces to Var(aX)=a^2 Var(X).

Name: Conditional expectation
LaTeX: Z=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\iff Z\text{ is }\mathcal G\text{-measurable},\quad \mathbb E[Z\mathbf1_A]=\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_A]\ \forall A\in\mathcal G
Intuition: Conditional expectation is the average compatible with the information available. It matches the original variable's averages on every event that information can distinguish.
Conditions: X is integrable; G is a sub-sigma-algebra. Z is integrable and unique almost surely. For square-integrable X it is the L2 projection onto G-measurable variables.
Example: Given a die's parity, the predicted roll is 3 for odd and 4 for even.

Name: Tower property
LaTeX: \mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal H],\quad \mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G
Intuition: Averaging first with finer information and then with coarser information gives the same answer as using the coarser information directly.
Conditions: X is integrable and H is a sub-sigma-algebra of G; equality holds almost surely.
Example: A population mean equals the weighted mean of subgroup means.

Name: Law of total variance
Intuition: Total variation splits into average variation within groups and variation between group means.
Conditions: X is square-integrable; conditioning means conditioning on the sigma-algebra generated by Y.
Example: For a two-stage experiment, separate randomness remaining after the first stage from randomness in the first-stage prediction.

Name: Jensen's inequality
Intuition: For a convex transformation, averaging before transforming costs no more than transforming first and averaging. Curvature determines how variability changes the result.
Conditions: X is integrable and takes values in an interval where phi is convex; assume phi(X) is integrable. Reverse the inequality for concave phi.
Example: Taking phi(x)=x^2 gives (E[X])^2<=E[X^2].

Name: Markov's inequality
Intuition: A nonnegative quantity cannot be large too often without making its average large.
Conditions: X>=0 almost surely, E[X]<infinity, and a>0.
Example: If a nonnegative waiting time has mean 2, the chance it exceeds 10 is at most .2.

Name: Chebyshev's inequality
Intuition: Finite variance limits how often observations can lie many standard deviations from their mean, regardless of the distribution's shape.
Conditions: X has mean mu and finite variance sigma^2; t>0.
Example: At most 1/9 of the probability can be at least three standard deviations from the mean.

Name: Exponential Chernoff bound
Intuition: Exponentials magnify large values, allowing a moment bound to detect rare tails. Optimizing the magnification makes the bound as tight as this method allows.
Conditions: X is real; optimize over positive lambda for which the moment generating function is finite. The bound is valid but can be uninformative.
Example: For a standard normal and a>0, choosing lambda=a gives P(X>=a)<=exp(-a^2/2).

Name: Hoeffding's inequality
Intuition: Independent bounded fluctuations cancel reliably: a large collective deviation becomes exponentially unlikely.
Conditions: X_i are independent and a_i<=X_i<=b_i almost surely, with finite deterministic bounds; t>0 and sum_i(b_i-a_i)^2>0.
Example: For n independent values in [0,1], the sample mean deviates by epsilon with probability at most 2 exp(-2n epsilon^2).
Prerequisites: Exponential Chernoff bound; Independence of random variables

Name: Strong law of large numbers
Intuition: Long averages stabilize around the distribution's balance point. Random observations collectively become a dependable numerical summary.
Conditions: X_1,X_2,... are iid real variables with E|X_1|<infinity; almost-sure convergence is an infinite-sequence statement, not a finite-sample error bound.
Example: The running fraction of heads converges almost surely to p for independent Bernoulli(p) trials.
Prerequisites: Expectation; Arithmetic mean; Independence of random variables

Name: Central limit theorem
Intuition: After their mean is removed and their size is standardized, sums of many iid finite-variance contributions approach one common bell shape.
Conditions: X_i are iid real variables, E[X_i]=mu, and 0<Var(X_i)=sigma^2<infinity. Convergence is in distribution; no universal sample-size threshold guarantees accuracy.
Example: For fair coin counts, (heads-n/2)/(sqrt(n)/2) approaches a standard normal distribution.
Patterns: Averaging; Scaling and homogeneity; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Strong law of large numbers; Variance of a sum; Normal distribution

Name: Moment generating function
Intuition: One function stores moments as its derivatives. Exponentials also turn independent addition into multiplication.
Conditions: For the derivative identity, M_X is finite on an open interval containing zero; k is a nonnegative integer.
Example: For X~Poisson(lambda), M_X(t)=exp(lambda(e^t-1)).

Name: Characteristic function
Intuition: A probability distribution can be encoded by how strongly its values align with each frequency. This transform always exists because the complex exponential has unit magnitude.
Conditions: X is any real random variable and t is real; the product identity requires X and Y to be independent.
Example: A centered normal with variance sigma^2 has characteristic function exp(-sigma^2 t^2/2).
Prerequisites: Expectation; Euler's formula; Independence of random variables

Name: Cumulant generating function
Intuition: Taking the logarithm extracts additive features of a law. Mean and variance are the first two of these cumulants.
Conditions: The real MGF is finite on an open interval containing zero; independent cumulant generating functions add on their common domain.
Example: For a normal law, K(t)=mu*t+sigma^2*t^2/2, so all cumulants above order two vanish.

Name: Probability generating function
Intuition: Store the probabilities of a count as coefficients of a power series. Products then describe sums of independent counts.
Conditions: N takes nonnegative integer values; the series converges absolutely for |z|<=1. The derivative at 1 is a left limit and may be infinite.
Example: For Bernoulli(p), G(z)=1-p+pz; n independent trials give (1-p+pz)^n.

Name: Bernoulli distribution
Intuition: The smallest random model records whether an event occurs. Its mean is exactly the probability of occurrence.
Conditions: 0<=p<=1, with endpoint values interpreted by their degenerate distributions; the power formula is unambiguous for 0<p<1.
Example: A random success indicator with success probability .7 has mean .7.

Name: Binomial distribution
Intuition: Count successes in independent repetitions of the same yes-or-no experiment. The binomial coefficient counts which repetitions succeeded.
Conditions: n is a nonnegative integer, k=0,...,n, and 0<=p<=1; use the degenerate interpretation at endpoints.
Example: Exactly three heads in five fair flips has probability 10/32.

Name: Poisson distribution
Intuition: Poisson counts describe events scattered independently at a fixed average intensity. The single parameter sets both mean count and variance.
Conditions: lambda>0; lambda=0 is the point mass at zero. A Poisson model is an assumption, not a consequence of merely knowing an average rate.
Example: At mean count two, the probability of no events is e^-2.

Name: Geometric waiting time
Intuition: To wait k trials for the first success, first observe k-1 failures and then one success. Repeated failure does not change the remaining waiting-time law.
Conditions: Independent Bernoulli(p) trials with 0<p<=1; T counts the successful trial, so its support begins at one.
Example: A fair coin takes two tosses on average to produce the first head.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Negative binomial distribution
Intuition: Count failures before the r-th success. The last trial must succeed, while the earlier trials can arrange the remaining successes in many ways.
Conditions: r is a positive integer, 0<p<=1, k is a nonnegative integer, and trials are independent with success probability p; K counts failures.
Example: With r=2 and p=1/2, exactly one preceding failure has probability 1/4.

Name: Hypergeometric distribution
Intuition: Sampling without replacement changes the remaining composition after each draw. Counting subsets handles this dependence exactly.
Conditions: N,K,n are integers with 0<=K,n<=N; max(0,n-(N-K))<=k<=min(n,K). Every n-subset is equally likely.
Example: In a five-object population with two marked objects, two draws contain both marked objects with probability 1/10.

Name: Continuous uniform distribution
Intuition: A uniform density assigns probability in proportion to interval length. Its balance point is the midpoint.
Conditions: a<b are finite real numbers; endpoint density values have no effect on probabilities.
Example: If X is uniform on [0,10], the chance X lies in [2,5] is .3.

Name: Exponential waiting time
LaTeX: f_T(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\mathbf1_{\{t\ge0\}},\quad P(T>s+t\mid T>s)=e^{-\lambda t}
Intuition: An exponential clock has a constant instantaneous event rate. Surviving a while gives no extra information about the remaining wait.
Conditions: lambda>0 and s,t>=0; E[T]=1/lambda.
Example: At rate two events per unit time, the chance of waiting longer than one unit is e^-2.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Recursion and iteration

Name: Normal distribution
Intuition: The bell curve weights values by an exponential penalty on squared distance from the center. Independent normal contributions remain normal when added.
Conditions: mu is real, sigma>0, and x is real; the density integrates to one.
Example: A standard normal has mu=0 and variance one.
Patterns: Quadratic structure; Symmetry and invariance; Exponentials and logarithms
Prerequisites: Variance; Exponential addition law; Gaussian integral

Name: Gamma distribution
Intuition: The gamma family extends waiting for several arrivals from integer event counts to a continuous shape parameter.
Conditions: alpha>0 and lambda>0 is the rate; Gamma(alpha)=integral_0^infinity t^(alpha-1)e^-t dt. Variance is alpha/lambda^2.
Example: The waiting time for three arrivals in a rate-two Poisson process is Gamma(3,2), with mean 1.5.

Name: Beta distribution
Intuition: Beta densities describe uncertain proportions and adapt naturally to accumulated successes and failures.
Conditions: alpha,beta>0, 0<p<1; density is zero outside [0,1]. The mean is alpha/(alpha+beta).
Example: Beta(1,1) is uniform on [0,1], while Beta(2,2) favors central proportions.
Patterns: Randomness and distribution; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Multivariate normal density
Intuition: A multivariate Gaussian replaces distance on a line with distance shaped by a covariance ellipsoid. Its contour surfaces are ellipsoids.
Conditions: x,mu in R^d and Sigma is symmetric positive definite; singular Gaussian laws exist but lack this density on all of R^d.
Example: For Sigma=I, the coordinates are independent standard normals after centering.
Prerequisites: Normal distribution; Covariance under a linear map; Determinant

Name: Density under a change of variables
Intuition: Probability mass stays constant when coordinates change; the density compensates for how the map stretches volume.
Conditions: X has a density on an open subset of R^d; g is a C1 diffeomorphism onto its image with nonzero Jacobian determinant. Formula holds almost everywhere, and density is zero outside the image.
Example: If X>0 and Y=log X, then f_Y(y)=f_X(e^y)e^y.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Conservation and balance

Name: Tail integral formula
Intuition: An average height can be computed by adding the fractions that rise above each horizontal level.
Conditions: X is a nonnegative measurable real variable and N is nonnegative integer-valued; both sides may be infinite. Tonelli's theorem justifies the interchange.
Example: For geometric waiting time T, summing its survival probabilities gives E[T]=1/p.
Prerequisites: Probability as an indicator expectation; Riemann integral

Name: Density of an independent sum
Intuition: To obtain a total z, combine every possible first contribution x with the matching second contribution z-x.
Conditions: X and Y are independent real variables with densities; the convolution gives a density almost everywhere.
Example: Adding two independent uniform [0,1] variables produces a triangular density on [0,2].
Prerequisites: Independence of random variables; Convolution; Law of total probability

Name: Markov chain transition law
Intuition: The current state carries all information needed for the next-step probability law. Each matrix row lists the possible next states and their chances.
Conditions: A finite or countable state space; the displayed version is time-homogeneous. Conditional equality holds almost surely for attainable histories.
Example: A two-state weather model can assign tomorrow's probabilities using only today's weather.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Randomness and distribution
Prerequisites: Conditional probability; Independence of random variables

Name: Chapman-Kolmogorov equation
Intuition: To cross several time steps, sum over every possible intermediate state. Matrix multiplication is weighted case-splitting.
Conditions: A time-homogeneous finite or countable Markov chain, with nonnegative integer m,n; sums over states are nonnegative and convergent.
Example: Two-step reachability is computed by multiplying the transition matrix by itself.
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Law of total probability

Name: Stationary distribution
Intuition: A stationary law is a probability distribution that looks the same after another transition. Inflow and outflow balance in aggregate.
Conditions: P is a stochastic matrix. A finite chain has at least one stationary law; a finite irreducible chain has a unique one. Convergence from every initial law also needs aperiodicity.
Example: For a symmetric two-state chain, pi=(1/2,1/2) is stationary.
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

Name: Detailed balance
Intuition: Every pair of states exchanges equal stationary probability flow. This stronger balance makes time-reversed trajectories statistically identical.
Conditions: P is stochastic and pi is a probability vector. Detailed balance implies stationarity; stationarity need not imply detailed balance.
Example: An undirected weighted random walk is reversible with pi_i proportional to the weighted degree.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Conservation and balance

Name: Discounted Markov reward equation
Intuition: Long-term value is immediate reward plus a discounted average of future value. The same equation is both a recursive forecast and a linear system.
Conditions: P is a finite stochastic matrix, r is a finite real reward vector, and 0<=gamma<1; the Neumann series converges and the inverse exists.
Example: For one state with reward two and gamma=.9, v=2/(1-.9)=20.
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Finite geometric sum

Name: Fundamental matrix of an absorbing chain
Intuition: Count every possible visit to transient states before absorption. Row sums then give the expected number of steps remaining.
Conditions: A finite chain with transient-state submatrix Q and eventual absorption with probability one from each transient state; equivalently rho(Q)<1.
Example: With one transient state that persists with probability q<1, expected time to absorption is 1/(1-q).
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Finite geometric sum; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

Name: Poisson process increments
Intuition: A Poisson process scatters events through time at constant intensity. Nonoverlapping time intervals receive independent counts.
Conditions: lambda>0, s,t>=0, N(0)=0, and the counting process has stationary independent increments with the displayed Poisson laws.
Example: At rate three per hour, a two-hour increment is Poisson(6).
Prerequisites: Poisson distribution; Independence of random variables

Name: Independent thinning of a Poisson process
Intuition: Independently labeling each arrival splits one Poisson stream into independent Poisson streams with proportionally reduced rates.
Conditions: N is a rate-lambda Poisson process; each arrival independently receives label one with probability p in [0,1], independently of N. N_2 counts the remaining arrivals.
Example: Randomly retaining one quarter of rate-eight arrivals gives a rate-two retained stream.

Name: Martingale property
Intuition: A martingale is a forecast that has no predictable one-step drift. New information may move it, but its current value already averages those possible changes.
Conditions: (F_n) is a filtration; M_n is F_n-measurable and E|M_n|<infinity for every n. A martingale need not have independent increments.
Example: A centered sum of independent integrable zero-mean increments is a martingale.

Name: Optional stopping for bounded times
Intuition: Choosing when to stop using only information already revealed cannot change a martingale's expected value when the stopping horizon is bounded.
Conditions: M_n is an integrable discrete-time martingale and T is a stopping time with 0<=T<=N almost surely for a deterministic finite N. Unbounded stopping needs additional hypotheses.
Example: Stop a fair random walk at a target or after 100 steps, whichever comes first; expected stopped position remains the initial position.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Information and uncertainty

Name: Brownian motion covariance and increments
Intuition: Brownian motion accumulates infinitesimal independent fluctuations. Two times share exactly the randomness accumulated before the earlier time.
Conditions: Standard Brownian motion starts at zero, has continuous paths, and has independent Gaussian increments; 0<=s<=t.
Example: W_4 has standard deviation two, while Cov(W_1,W_4)=1.
Prerequisites: Normal distribution; Covariance; Independence of random variables

Name: Brownian scaling
Intuition: Speeding Brownian time by a factor c stretches its typical displacement by the square root of c.
Conditions: W is standard Brownian motion and c>0; equality is in law as processes, not pathwise equality for one realization.
Example: A time interval four times longer has twice the standard deviation.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Ito isometry
Intuition: Independent infinitesimal noise increments make cross terms disappear. The variance of accumulated noise is the accumulated squared noise amplitude.
Conditions: W is Brownian relative to the filtration, H is predictable, and E[integral_0^T H_t^2 dt]<infinity for finite T.
Example: For deterministic H_t=2, the integral has variance 4T.
Prerequisites: Brownian motion covariance and increments; Riemann integral; Variance of a sum

Name: Ito's formula
Intuition: Random paths retain a second-order contribution that ordinary smooth paths lose. The extra curvature term comes from Brownian quadratic variation.
Conditions: X is a continuous Ito process with progressively measurable b,sigma and locally finite integral(|b|+sigma^2)dt; f is C^{1,2}. Derivatives are evaluated at (t,X_t), and localization gives the formula up to the process lifetime.
Example: For f(x)=x^2 and X=W, d(W_t^2)=2W_t dW_t+dt.
Prerequisites: Brownian motion covariance and increments; Chain rule; Taylor series of an analytic function

Name: Geometric Brownian motion
Intuition: Multiplicative noise becomes additive after taking logarithms. The variance correction ensures the original process has the stated mean drift.
Conditions: X_0>0 is deterministic, mu is real, sigma>=0, and W is standard Brownian motion.
Example: For mu=0, X_t has constant expectation X_0 although its log has drift -sigma^2/2.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
Intuition: A restoring force pulls the process toward a central value while noise continually perturbs it. Old disturbances fade exponentially.
Conditions: kappa>0, sigma>=0, theta and deterministic x_0 are real; W is standard Brownian motion.
Example: Its variance tends to sigma^2/(2*kappa), giving a stable noise level around theta.

Name: Fokker-Planck equation
Intuition: The random trajectory description and the evolving probability-density description encode the same diffusion. Drift transports probability and noise spreads it.
Conditions: Assume a nonexplosive Ito diffusion with coefficients for which the SDE is well-defined. The law satisfies this equation weakly against smooth compactly supported test functions; a classical density formula additionally requires the displayed derivatives to exist.
Example: With b=0 and sigma=1, this is the heat equation for a Brownian density.
Prerequisites: Ito's formula; Heat or diffusion equation; Integration by parts

Name: Empirical distribution function
Intuition: Replace an unknown population distribution by equal mass on the observed data points. The empirical CDF counts the fraction below a threshold.
Conditions: n>=1 and X_i are real observations. IID sampling is needed for the usual population-convergence interpretation, but not for the definition.
Example: For observations 1,2,2,5, the empirical probability of a value at most two is 3/4.
Prerequisites: Arithmetic mean; Probability as an indicator expectation

Name: Unbiased sample variance
Intuition: Estimating the center from the same data uses one independent direction. Dividing by n-1 compensates for the resulting downward bias.
Conditions: For unbiasedness, X_i are iid with finite variance sigma^2 and n>=2; the descriptive formula can be computed for arbitrary real observations.
Example: For observations 1 and 3, the sample variance is two.

Name: Standard error of the sample mean
Intuition: Averaging n independent equal-variance measurements divides uncertainty by the square root of n. The estimated standard error substitutes the sample spread.
Conditions: X_i are independent with common finite variance sigma^2; the first formula is exact. S/sqrt(n) is the customary plug-in estimate under iid sampling, n>=2.
Example: Quadrupling the number of independent observations halves the mean's standard error.
Prerequisites: Variance of a sum; Unbiased sample variance

Name: Bias-variance decomposition
Intuition: Squared estimation error separates into random wobble around the estimator's own mean and systematic displacement from the target.
Conditions: theta is a fixed real target and T has a finite second moment.
Example: An estimator with bias two and variance three has mean squared error seven.

Name: Least squares
Intuition: Choose the prediction vector closest to the observations in squared Euclidean distance. This turns fitting a model into a geometric projection problem.
Conditions: X is a finite real n-by-p matrix and y in R^n. A minimizer always exists; coefficients are unique exactly when X has full column rank.
Example: With only a constant predictor, the fitted value is the arithmetic mean of the observations.
Prerequisites: Norm axioms and induced norm; Orthogonal projection

Name: Least-squares normal equations
Intuition: The best fit leaves no residual component that any predictor could explain. Setting the objective's gradient to zero expresses exactly that condition.
Conditions: For any real finite X,y, the normal equations characterize all least-squares minimizers. The inverse formula requires full column rank; solving by QR or SVD is generally preferable numerically.
Example: For X equal to the all-ones column, the equation becomes n*beta_hat=sum_i y_i.

Name: Simple linear regression coefficients
LaTeX: \widehat b=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)}{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2},\qquad \widehat a=\overline y-\widehat b\,\overline x
Intuition: A best-fitting line uses shared centered movement divided by the predictor's own spread. Its intercept makes it pass through the data's center.
Conditions: Finite real data, n>=2, and the x_i are not all equal; an intercept is included and squared residuals are minimized.
Example: For points (0,1),(1,3),(2,5), the fitted line is y=1+2x.

Name: Gauss-Markov covariance bound
Intuition: Among linear unbiased fits, ordinary least squares has the smallest variance in every parameter direction when errors have equal variance and no correlation.
Conditions: y=X beta+epsilon with fixed full-column-rank X, E[epsilon]=0 and Cov(epsilon)=sigma^2 I. The competing estimator is Ay with AX=I; no normality assumption is needed.
Example: Any unbiased linear estimate of a contrast c^T beta has variance at least sigma^2 c^T(X^T X)^-1 c.
Prerequisites: Least-squares normal equations; Covariance under a linear map

Name: Weighted least squares
Intuition: Residuals are measured in a geometry that values some directions more heavily. Precision weighting gives reliable measurements greater influence.
Conditions: W is real symmetric positive definite and X has full column rank. For generalized least squares with known error covariance Sigma, choose W=Sigma^-1.
Example: For a constant model and diagonal W, the fitted constant is the weighted mean sum(w_i y_i)/sum(w_i).
Prerequisites: Least squares; Quadratic form; Weighted arithmetic mean

Name: Ridge regression
Intuition: A quadratic penalty trades some fit quality for smaller, more stable coefficients. It particularly suppresses directions the data measure weakly.
Conditions: X,y are finite real arrays and lambda>0; all displayed coefficients are penalized, so the inverse exists even if X is rank deficient.
Example: For X=I, every coefficient shrinks from y_i to y_i/(1+lambda).

Name: Lasso regression
Intuition: An absolute-value penalty makes small coefficients expensive relative to their benefit, allowing some fitted coefficients to become exactly zero.
Conditions: Finite real X,y and lambda>0; minimizers exist, but coefficient uniqueness needs further conditions. All displayed coefficients are penalized.
Example: For X=I, the solution soft-thresholds each observation at lambda.
Prerequisites: Least squares; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Maximum likelihood estimation
Intuition: Choose the model parameter that assigns the observed data the greatest probability density or mass. Taking logs converts independent contributions into an additive score.
Conditions: The sum formula assumes iid data with density or mass f_theta relative to a fixed dominating measure. The argmax may be empty or nonunique; likelihood is a function of theta, not a probability distribution over theta.
Example: For Bernoulli data with p allowed in [0,1], the MLE is the observed success fraction.
Prerequisites: Independence of random variables; Logarithm laws

Name: Maximum a posteriori estimation
Intuition: A posterior mode combines fit to the observations with a preference encoded by the prior. In log form, the prior becomes a penalty.
Conditions: A prior density or mass and likelihood are specified, the posterior is proper, and a maximizer exists. Density modes depend on the chosen parameterization.
Example: A centered Gaussian prior on regression coefficients gives a quadratic penalty and a ridge-type MAP estimate.

Name: Likelihood score
Intuition: The score measures which parameter directions would make an observation more plausible. At the true model its average directional push cancels.
Conditions: The definition needs differentiability and positive f_theta at x. The zero-mean identity additionally needs parameter-independent support and differentiation under the normalization integral, with integrable derivatives.
Example: For N(mu,sigma^2) with known sigma, the score for mu is (x-mu)/sigma^2.

Name: Fisher information
Intuition: Information is both score variability and average curvature of log likelihood. A sharply changing likelihood distinguishes nearby parameters more precisely.
Conditions: For the first expression the score exists and has finite second moments. The Hessian identity needs common parameter-independent support, twice differentiable densities, and justified first and second differentiation under the integral.
Example: For one normal observation with known variance sigma^2, information about its mean is 1/sigma^2.

Name: Cramer-Rao lower bound
Intuition: An unbiased estimator cannot fluctuate arbitrarily little if the data barely distinguish nearby parameter values.
Conditions: A scalar parameter lies in an open interval; n iid observations have differentiable densities on common support, 0<I_1(theta)<infinity, and differentiation passes under integrals of both f_theta and T f_theta. T is unbiased for theta and has finite variance.
Example: The sample mean of normal data with known variance attains the bound sigma^2/n.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Geometry and distance

Name: Method of moments
Intuition: Fit a distribution by matching a few population summaries to their empirical counterparts.
Conditions: A p-parameter model has the displayed finite moments. Solving the equations requires identifiability and may give no solution, several solutions, or a parameter outside the model.
Example: For an exponential rate lambda, matching the first moment gives lambda_hat=1/Xbar when Xbar>0.

Name: Neyman-Fisher factorization
Intuition: A sufficient statistic compresses the data while preserving everything relevant to the parameter in the likelihood.
Conditions: For a dominated statistical model, the existence of nonnegative measurable factors g_theta and parameter-independent h is equivalent to sufficiency of T, with the usual almost-everywhere conventions.
Example: For iid Bernoulli observations, the total number of successes is sufficient for p.

Name: Rao-Blackwell improvement
Intuition: Average away fluctuations that carry no additional information about the parameter. Conditioning on a sufficient summary preserves unbiasedness while reducing noise.
Conditions: U is an unbiased square-integrable estimator of theta in a dominated model; S is sufficient and the conditional expectation is taken using a parameter-independent conditional law given S.
Example: For iid Bernoulli data, conditioning the first observation on the success count produces the sample mean.
Prerequisites: Conditional expectation; Law of total variance; Neyman-Fisher factorization

Name: Beta-binomial conjugate update
Intuition: A beta prior and binomial data combine by adding evidence to two running counts. The posterior mean blends the prior mean with the observed success rate.
Conditions: p~Beta(alpha,beta), alpha,beta>0; given p, s~Binomial(n,p), n is a nonnegative integer and 0<=s<=n.
Example: Starting with Beta(1,1), three successes in four trials gives Beta(4,2) and posterior mean 2/3.
Prerequisites: Bayes' rule; Beta distribution; Binomial distribution

Name: Normal-normal conjugate update
Intuition: Independent Gaussian information combines by adding precision. The posterior center is an average weighted by how precisely each source is known.
Conditions: mu~N(mu_0,tau_0^2), tau_0^2>0; conditionally iid x_i~N(mu,sigma^2) with known sigma^2>0. The posterior is N(mu_n,tau_n^2).
Example: Equal prior and data-mean precision place the posterior mean halfway between their centers.
Prerequisites: Bayes' rule; Normal distribution; Completing the square

Name: Posterior predictive distribution
Intuition: Predict by averaging all parameter-specific predictions over the remaining parameter uncertainty.
Conditions: The posterior is proper and the new outcome is conditionally independent of observed data given theta; the displayed densities use appropriate dominating measures, with sums for discrete theta.
Example: Under a beta posterior, the next Bernoulli success probability equals the posterior mean of p.

Name: Student t pivot
Intuition: Replacing an unknown population spread by an estimated spread adds uncertainty. The t distribution accounts for that extra randomness exactly in the normal model.
Conditions: X_i are iid N(mu,sigma^2), sigma^2>0, n>=2, and S^2 uses divisor n-1.
Example: For n=10 normal observations, the standardized mean using S follows t with nine degrees of freedom.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Randomness and distribution
Prerequisites: Normal distribution; Unbiased sample variance; Standard error of the sample mean

Name: Chi-squared pivot for normal variance
Intuition: The centered sample occupies n-1 orthogonal Gaussian directions. Its squared standardized length has a chi-squared distribution.
Conditions: X_i are iid N(mu,sigma^2), sigma^2>0, n>=2, and S^2 is the unbiased sample variance; chi^2_k is the sum of k independent squared standard normals.
Example: A sample of six normal observations gives a five-degree-of-freedom reference law for variance inference.
Prerequisites: Unbiased sample variance; Normal distribution; Orthogonal projection

Name: Exact t interval for a normal mean
LaTeX: C(X)=\left[\overline X-t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\frac S{\sqrt n},\ \overline X+t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\frac S{\sqrt n}\right],\quad P_\mu(\mu\in C(X))=1-\alpha
Intuition: Invert the t pivot to obtain all mean values compatible with the observed standardized error at a chosen coverage level.
Conditions: IID normal observations with unknown mean and positive variance, n>=2, and 0<alpha<1. t_{nu,q} is the q quantile. Coverage refers to repetitions of the random interval construction.
Example: Choosing alpha=.05 produces a procedure with 95% coverage under the normal model.

Name: Delta method
LaTeX: \sqrt n(T_n-\theta)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\ \Longrightarrow\ \sqrt n(g(T_n)-g(\theta))\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,J\Sigma J^\top)
Intuition: A smooth transformation acts almost linearly on sufficiently small estimation errors. Its derivative pushes the limiting uncertainty into new coordinates.
Conditions: T_n is R^d-valued with the stated limit; g maps a neighborhood of theta to R^k and is differentiable at theta, with Jacobian J=Dg(theta). A zero derivative can give a degenerate first-order limit.
Example: For a positive mean estimator, the asymptotic variance of its logarithm is divided by the square of the true mean.
Prerequisites: Central limit theorem; Derivative; Covariance under a linear map

Name: Bootstrap estimate of standard error
Intuition: Treat the observed data as a provisional population, resample it, and measure how much the statistic varies across those simulated samples.
Conditions: For the iid nonparametric bootstrap, independently generate B>=2 samples of size n with replacement from the empirical distribution and recompute T. This estimates the conditional bootstrap spread; accuracy for population inference requires additional model and statistic assumptions.
Example: Resample a dataset repeatedly to estimate the sampling uncertainty of its median.
Patterns: Randomness and distribution; Recursion and iteration
Prerequisites: Empirical distribution function; Unbiased sample variance

Name: Neyman-Pearson likelihood-ratio test
Intuition: Spend the allowed false-positive probability on observations that favor the alternative most strongly. This maximizes power for two fully specified models.
Conditions: Simple hypotheses H0:f0 and H1:f1 use a common dominating measure; c>=0 and gamma in [0,1] are selected for the desired size when attainable. Randomization handles ties.
Example: Distinguishing two known normal means with common variance reduces to a threshold on the sample mean.

Name: Wilks' likelihood-ratio limit
Intuition: Compare the best unrestricted fit with the best fit obeying the null constraints. Locally quadratic likelihoods turn their difference into a squared projection length.
Conditions: IID observations in a regular identifiable p-dimensional smooth model; the true parameter is interior, the null is a smooth p0-dimensional embedded submodel, Fisher information is nonsingular, both MLEs are consistent, and the likelihood admits its usual local quadratic expansion. Boundary and singular cases are excluded.
Example: Testing one regular scalar restriction gives an asymptotic chi-squared law with one degree of freedom.
Prerequisites: Maximum likelihood estimation; Fisher information; Chi-squared pivot for normal variance

Name: Tail-area p-value
Intuition: A p-value measures how unusual the observed test statistic is under the specified null when larger values count as more extreme.
Conditions: A simple null law P0 and a test statistic T are fixed before observing x. The superuniform bound holds for alpha in [0,1]; discrete tests can be conservative. This is not a posterior probability of the null.
Example: Under a continuous null, a prechosen upper-tail test rejects at level .05 when p<=.05.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Information and uncertainty

Name: Pearson chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic
Intuition: Compare observed category counts with expected counts after normalizing each squared error by its expected size.
Conditions: (O_1,...,O_k) is multinomial(n,p), k is fixed, each known p_i>0, and n->infinity. Estimating probabilities from data changes the limiting degrees of freedom and requires additional analysis.
Example: For a fair die, the statistic compares six observed counts with n/6 and has five asymptotic degrees of freedom.
Prerequisites: Central limit theorem; Chi-squared pivot for normal variance

Name: ANOVA sum-of-squares decomposition
Intuition: Overall scatter equals scatter remaining inside groups plus scatter explained by different group centers.
Conditions: Finite real observations partitioned into nonempty groups of sizes n_j; ybar is the overall mean and ybar_j the group mean. The identity needs no distributional assumptions.
Example: If every observation equals its group mean, all variation lies in the between-group term.

Name: Logistic regression model
Intuition: A linear predictor becomes an unrestricted log-odds score, while the logistic function maps it to a valid probability.
Conditions: x,beta are finite real vectors and Y is binary. The formula specifies a conditional model; iid observations or conditional independence are extra assumptions for the usual summed likelihood.
Example: Increasing a predictor by one multiplies the odds by exp(beta_j), holding the other predictors fixed.

Name: Exponential family and log partition function
Intuition: Many familiar distributions share a linear score in selected data summaries, followed by exponential reweighting and normalization.
Conditions: h>=0 and T are measurable; eta lies where the normalizing integral is finite and positive. Interior natural parameters with justified differentiation satisfy grad A=E[T] and Hess A=Cov(T).
Example: Bernoulli has T(x)=x and A(eta)=log(1+exp eta).
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Information and uncertainty

Name: Expectation-maximization algorithm
Intuition: Alternate between averaging over unknown hidden variables and refitting the model to that averaged complete-data objective.
Conditions: The observed likelihood is positive and finite; conditional expectations and the selected maximizer exist, with compatible support for the EM lower-bound argument. Exact EM does not decrease observed log likelihood, but does not guarantee a global optimum.
Example: Gaussian-mixture EM alternates soft component membership weights with weighted mean and covariance updates.
Prerequisites: Conditional expectation; Maximum likelihood estimation; Jensen's inequality

Name: Kalman measurement update
Intuition: Correct a prior estimate using the part of a measurement it failed to predict. The gain balances prior uncertainty against measurement noise.
Conditions: Prior state X~N(m,P), P positive semidefinite; observation y=HX+epsilon with independent epsilon~N(0,R), R positive definite. These are exact conditional mean and covariance formulas.
Example: For a scalar with equal prior and measurement variances, the updated mean is their midpoint.
Prerequisites: Conditional expectation; Multivariate normal density; Covariance under a linear map

Name: Principal component variance maximization
Intuition: Find the direction in which a centered cloud varies most. Further orthogonal directions reveal successively less variance; principal components are uncorrelated, but need not be statistically independent.
Conditions: Sigma is a real symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance or sample-covariance matrix. A maximizing unit eigenvector exists; it is not unique if the largest eigenvalue is repeated.
Example: For covariance diag(9,1), the first principal direction is the first coordinate and explains 90% of total variance.
Prerequisites: Covariance under a linear map; Spectral theorem in finite dimensions; Quadratic form

Name: Convex function inequality
Intuition: Along every segment, a convex function stays below the chord joining its endpoint values. Mixing choices cannot cost more than mixing their costs.
Conditions: f is real-valued on a convex subset of a real vector space; x,y are in its domain and t in [0,1].
Example: The squared norm is convex; applying the formula to x and -x gives its minimum at zero.

Name: First-order characterization of convexity
Intuition: Every tangent plane of a differentiable convex function is a global lower bound. A zero gradient therefore certifies global optimality.
Conditions: f is differentiable on an open convex subset of R^n; the displayed inequality for every x,y is equivalent to convexity.
Example: For f(x)=x^2, the difference between the graph and its tangent at a is (x-a)^2.

Name: Second-order characterization of convexity
Intuition: A smooth function is convex precisely when it curves upward or stays flat in every direction.
Conditions: f is twice continuously differentiable on an open convex subset of R^n; positive semidefiniteness is required at every point in the domain.
Example: For f(x)=x^T A x with symmetric A, convexity is equivalent to A being positive semidefinite.
Prerequisites: Hessian matrix; Quadratic form; Convex function inequality

Name: Strong convexity inequality
Intuition: Strong convexity gives a uniform bowl shape. Moving away from a minimizer must raise the objective at least quadratically.
Conditions: mu>0, f is differentiable on a convex domain, and the inequality holds for all x,y there. A minimizer, if it exists, is unique.
Example: A quadratic with Hessian at least mu*I is mu-strongly convex.
Prerequisites: First-order characterization of convexity; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Descent lemma
Intuition: If the gradient cannot change too quickly, the graph cannot rise faster than a quadratic above its tangent. This supplies a safe model for choosing steps.
Conditions: f is differentiable on a convex domain and its gradient is L-Lipschitz there in Euclidean norm, L>0; the segment from x to y stays in the domain. Convexity of f is not required.
Example: For a quadratic with Hessian operator norm at most L, the bound follows directly from its expansion.
Prerequisites: Gradient; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Gradient descent
Intuition: Move against the local direction of fastest increase. The step size controls how far the local slope can safely guide the next move.
Conditions: f is differentiable and eta_k>0. For an L-Lipschitz gradient on R^n, a fixed 0<eta<2/L gives descent unless the gradient is zero; convergence to a global minimum needs further structure such as convexity.
Example: For f(x)=x^2/2, choosing eta=1 sends any starting point directly to zero.

Name: Convex gradient descent error bound
Intuition: For smooth convex objectives, repeated safe gradient steps reduce objective error at a guaranteed inverse-iteration rate.
Conditions: f:R^n->R is convex with L-Lipschitz gradient, L>0, and has a minimizer x*. Use constant step 1/L and integer k>=1.
Example: The bound guarantees that doubling the iteration budget halves this worst-case error estimate.
Prerequisites: Gradient descent; First-order characterization of convexity; Descent lemma

Name: Newton step for optimization
Intuition: Fit a local quadratic bowl and step toward its minimizer. Curvature corrects for directions with very different scales.
Conditions: f is twice differentiable and the Hessian is invertible at the current iterate; positive definiteness makes d a descent direction. A damping or line-search choice may be needed; unrestricted full steps need not converge.
Example: A full step solves any strictly convex quadratic exactly in exact arithmetic.
Prerequisites: Gradient; Hessian matrix; Newton's root-finding method

Name: Coordinate descent
Intuition: Improve one coordinate at a time while holding the others fixed. A large optimization problem becomes a sequence of one-dimensional problems.
Conditions: The selected one-dimensional minimum must exist. Cyclic or random coordinate selection and suitable smoothness or convexity assumptions are needed for convergence guarantees.
Example: For a diagonal positive quadratic, one exact coordinate sweep finds the minimizer.

Name: Stochastic gradient descent
LaTeX: x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kg_k,\quad g_k=\nabla f_{I_k}(x_k),\quad \mathbb E[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla F(x_k),\quad F=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf_i
Intuition: Use a randomly chosen contribution to estimate the full gradient. Each step is noisy but much cheaper when the objective has many terms.
Conditions: Each f_i is differentiable, I_k is uniform on {1,...,n} independently of past randomness given x_k, and eta_k>0. The formula alone gives no convergence guarantee; step sizes, variance, and objective geometry matter.
Example: Choose one observation at each step to update a large regression fit.
Prerequisites: Gradient descent; Linearity of expectation; Arithmetic mean

Name: Heavy-ball momentum
Intuition: Keep part of the previous displacement so consistent directions accumulate speed. Momentum can damp alternating motions but can also overshoot.
Conditions: f is differentiable, eta>0, and typically 0<=beta<1. These choices alone do not guarantee convergence; for a positive quadratic with largest Hessian eigenvalue L, stability holds for eta<2(1+beta)/L.
Example: On a narrow quadratic valley, memory of previous motion can reduce slow progress along the shallow direction.

Name: Lagrange multiplier stationarity
Intuition: At a constrained optimum, no feasible infinitesimal direction can improve the objective. The objective gradient must therefore lie among the normals to the constraints.
Conditions: f and h_j are C1 near a local constrained optimum x*, and the constraint gradients there are linearly independent. These equations are necessary, not generally sufficient.
Example: Optimizing a quadratic on the unit sphere produces an eigenvector equation.

Name: Lagrangian dual function
Intuition: Attach prices to constraint violations and minimize the priced objective. Each choice of nonnegative inequality prices gives a lower-bound candidate.
Conditions: The primal is min f0 subject to f_i<=0 and h_j=0; lambda_i>=0 and nu_j are free. The infimum uses the common domain, and g may equal minus infinity.
Example: For a linear program, a finite dual value forces cancellation of the free primal variable's coefficient.

Name: Weak duality
Intuition: Any valid dual bound lies below every feasible primal cost. A small gap between one of each certifies near optimality.
Conditions: The primal uses inequalities f_i<=0 and equalities h_j=0; g is the Lagrangian infimum and lambda>=0. Convexity is unnecessary; compare well-defined extended optimal values.
Example: A feasible solution of cost ten and dual bound nine proves the unknown optimal cost lies between nine and ten.

Name: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions
Intuition: Optimality balances the objective gradient with active constraint normals. A constraint receives a nonzero price only if it is tight.
Conditions: For differentiable convex f0,f_i on R^n and affine equalities, any feasible triple satisfying KKT is globally optimal. If a strict feasible point exists (Slater), KKT is also necessary at every attained finite optimum. Nonconvex necessity needs a constraint qualification and gives no global certificate.
Example: For min x^2 subject to x>=1, x=1 and multiplier two satisfy stationarity and complementary slackness.
Prerequisites: Lagrangian dual function; First-order characterization of convexity

Name: Slater's strong-duality condition
Intuition: A genuinely feasible interior point prevents a convex problem's constraints from pinching off the geometry needed for exact dual bounds.
Conditions: The f_i and f0 are finite convex functions on R^n, equalities are affine, and the primal optimal value is finite. The displayed strict-feasibility condition is sufficient; more general versions use relative interiors.
Example: A feasible convex program with strictly slack inequalities admits an attained dual optimum even if the primal infimum is approached only as a limit.
Prerequisites: Lagrangian dual function; Convex function inequality

Name: Linear programming duality
Intuition: A resource-allocation optimum can be described either by choosing activities or by assigning prices that bound their value.
Conditions: Finite real A,b,c; the displayed equality and attainment hold when the primal is feasible and its optimal value is finite. Without those assumptions, infeasibility or unboundedness must be handled separately.
Example: A primal solution and a feasible price vector with equal objectives certify optimality immediately.

Name: Convex quadratic program
LaTeX: \min_x\ \tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x\quad\text{subject to }Gx\le h,\ Ax=b,\qquad Q\succeq0
Intuition: A quadratic cost measures smooth tradeoffs while linear constraints describe allowed choices. This includes many fitting and allocation problems.
Conditions: Q is symmetric positive semidefinite and all arrays are finite real with compatible dimensions. Semidefinite Q can allow nonuniqueness or an unbounded objective; Q positive definite gives a unique optimum on any nonempty closed feasible polyhedron.
Example: Nonnegative least squares is a quadratic program with Q=2X^T X and constraints beta>=0.
Prerequisites: Quadratic form; Second-order characterization of convexity

Name: Convex subgradient
Intuition: At a corner, several slopes may support the graph from below. The subdifferential stores all of them.
Conditions: f is a proper convex function on R^n, possibly taking +infinity, and f(x) is finite; a boundary point can have an empty subdifferential.
Example: For f(x)=|x|, the subdifferential at zero is the entire interval [-1,1].

Name: Proximal operator
Intuition: Move toward lower cost while paying for distance from the current point. The quadratic tether makes many difficult updates well-defined and stable.
Conditions: g is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex on R^n; eta>0. The minimizer exists and is unique.
Example: For g the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set, the proximal operator is Euclidean projection onto that set.
Prerequisites: Convex subgradient; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Soft thresholding
Intuition: Shrink each coordinate toward zero by a fixed amount, stopping at zero. Small coordinates disappear entirely.
Conditions: v is a finite real vector, lambda>=0, and sign(0)=0; this minimizes one-half ||x-v||^2+lambda||x||_1.
Example: Thresholding (3,-.4,0) at one gives (2,0,0).

Name: Proximal gradient method
Intuition: Use a gradient step for the smooth part and a proximal step for the nonsmooth part. Each part is handled by the operation suited to its structure.
Conditions: For the standard convex convergence guarantee, f is convex with L-Lipschitz gradient on R^n, g is proper closed convex, a minimizer of f+g exists, and 0<eta<=1/L.
Example: For squared-error loss plus an L1 penalty, one iteration is a gradient step followed by soft thresholding.

Name: Projected gradient method
Intuition: Take a downhill step and then return to the nearest feasible point. Projection enforces the constraint after each update.
Conditions: C is a nonempty closed convex subset of R^n. For the standard convex convergence guarantee, f has an L-Lipschitz gradient, is convex, has a minimizer on C, and 0<eta<=1/L.
Example: For nonnegative variables, projection clips negative coordinates to zero.

Name: Log-sum-exp
Intuition: Log-sum-exp is a smooth maximum that lets several strong alternatives contribute. Subtracting the largest input computes it without unnecessarily large exponentials.
Conditions: x is a finite real vector, n>=1. It obeys max_i x_i<=LSE(x)<=max_i x_i+log n; the base is e.
Example: LSE(0,0)=log 2, reflecting two equally weighted alternatives.

Name: Softmax weights
Intuition: Turn arbitrary real scores into positive weights that sum to one. A score difference becomes a log probability ratio.
Conditions: x is a finite real vector and n>=1; the formula uses the natural exponential. Adding the same constant to every score changes no probability.
Example: Scores (0,log 3) give probabilities (1/4,3/4).

Name: Legendre-Fenchel conjugate
Intuition: Describe a function by how much a linear slope can exceed it. This switches from positions to supporting-slope information.
Conditions: f is a proper extended-real function on R^n; f* may take +infinity. The conjugate is convex and lower-semicontinuous even when f is not convex.
Example: For f(x)=||x||^2/2, the conjugate is f*(y)=||y||^2/2.

Name: Fenchel-Young inequality
Intuition: A function value and its dual value always cover the linear pairing. Equality means the primal point and dual slope support each other perfectly.
Conditions: f is proper closed convex; x is in its effective domain. The inequality uses extended-real values; equality requires finite values and is equivalent to the subgradient condition.

Name: Bregman divergence
Intuition: Measure how far the function rises above its tangent at y. Curvature creates a notion of discrepancy adapted to the chosen function.
Conditions: h is differentiable and strictly convex on an open convex domain containing x,y. D_h>=0 and vanishes only at x=y, but it is generally neither symmetric nor a metric.

Name: Mirror descent
Intuition: Choose a geometry that matches the variables, then take a local improvement step measured in that geometry. Probabilities and Euclidean coordinates can therefore use different natural updates.
Conditions: C is convex, h is differentiable and strictly convex at the evaluated interior points, eta_k>0, and the displayed minimum is attained. Boundary values can use a lower-semicontinuous extension; convergence needs additional assumptions on f, h, and steps.
Example: Negative-entropy geometry on the simplex produces multiplicative exponential-weight updates from an interior starting point.

Name: Finite-game minimax theorem
Intuition: Randomized strategies allow two opposing players to agree on one worst-case value. Neither player benefits from knowing which optimization order is used.
Conditions: A is a finite real m-by-n payoff matrix, and Delta_m,Delta_n are probability simplexes; payoff is bilinear and both players may randomize.
Example: In matching pennies, each player uses probabilities (1/2,1/2), giving value zero for the usual plus/minus-one payoff.
Prerequisites: Weighted arithmetic mean; Linear programming duality

Name: Self-information
Intuition: An unlikely outcome carries more surprise than a likely one. Logarithms make the surprise of independent outcomes add.
Conditions: x is an outcome of a discrete law with p(x)>0; natural logs give nats, and log base two gives bits. A zero-probability event has infinite formal self-information.
Example: An outcome of probability 1/8 carries three bits of self-information.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Information and uncertainty

Name: Shannon entropy
Intuition: Entropy is average surprise. It measures how uncertain a random outcome is before observing it.
Conditions: X has a finite or countable discrete law; use 0 log 0=0. Natural logs give nats; a countable law may have infinite entropy.
Example: A fair binary outcome has entropy log 2 nats, or one bit.

Name: Cross entropy
Intuition: Evaluate outcomes generated by p using probabilities supplied by q. The excess average surprise measures the mismatch between them.
Conditions: p and q are probability vectors on the same finite alphabet, with q_i>0 whenever p_i>0 for finite cross entropy; otherwise it is +infinity. Terms with p_i=0 contribute zero.
Example: A model assigning 1/2 to each of two outcomes incurs log 2 nats per observation under any binary source.

Name: Kullback-Leibler divergence
Intuition: KL divergence measures the extra expected log loss from using q when p describes the outcomes. It is directional, so reversing the arguments changes the question.
Conditions: p,q are probability vectors on the same finite alphabet; zero p_i contributes zero, while p_i>0 and q_i=0 gives +infinity. KL is not generally symmetric and is not a metric.
Example: For Bernoulli(1/2) versus Bernoulli(1/4), KL equals one-half log(4/3).
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Gibbs' inequality
Intuition: On average, a distribution assigns its own outcomes at least as well as any competing distribution under log loss.
Conditions: p,q are probability vectors on the same finite alphabet, with the usual zero-mass and infinite-divergence conventions.
Example: The cross entropy of p with q cannot be smaller than the entropy of p.

Name: Entropy chain rule
Intuition: Describe X first, then the uncertainty still remaining about Y. The two stages account for the full joint uncertainty.
Conditions: X,Y have finite alphabets; conditional distributions are used only at positive-mass x. All entropies use the same logarithm base.
Example: Two independent fair bits have joint entropy two bits, one from each stage.

Name: Mutual information
Intuition: Mutual information measures how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other. It detects dependence beyond linear correlation.
Conditions: X,Y have finite alphabets; the product law p_Xp_Y is positive on the support of the joint law. All logs use the same base.
Example: If Y=X is a fair bit, mutual information is one bit; independent variables have zero mutual information.

Name: Conditional mutual information
LaTeX: I(X;Y\mid Z)=\sum_zp(z)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{XY\mid z}\|p_{X\mid z}p_{Y\mid z}),\quad I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y\mid Z)
Intuition: Measure the dependence left between X and Y after accounting for Z. Averaging over Z makes this a conditional information quantity.
Conditions: X,Y,Z have finite alphabets; only z with p(z)>0 enter conditional distributions.
Example: Two variables can be independent marginally yet become dependent after conditioning, as in the XOR construction.

Name: Data-processing inequality
Intuition: Processing an observation cannot create new information about its source when the processor sees only that observation.
Conditions: X,Y,Z have finite alphabets and satisfy conditional independence X independent of Z given Y, equivalently the indicated Markov chain.
Example: Coarsening a recorded measurement to a rounded value cannot increase its information about the original source.
Prerequisites: Conditional mutual information; Markov chain transition law

Name: Fano's inequality
Intuition: If a decoder usually reconstructs a finite label correctly, little uncertainty can remain about that label. Conversely, large conditional entropy forces errors.
Conditions: X takes K>=2 possible values, Y has a finite alphabet, Xhat=g(Y), and P_e=P(Xhat!=X); use 0 log 0=0 and one common log base.
Example: For binary X, the bound reduces to H(X|Y)<=h(P_e).

Name: Maximum entropy on a finite alphabet
Intuition: If only the number of possible outcomes is fixed, spreading probability equally creates the most uncertainty.
Conditions: p is a probability vector on a specified alphabet of n>=1 outcomes, with natural logs and 0 log 0=0.
Example: A fair six-sided die has entropy log 6 nats, the largest possible for six outcomes.

Name: Differential entropy
Intuition: Differential entropy summarizes a density's spread in continuous coordinates. Unlike discrete entropy, its value depends on the units used.
Conditions: X has a Lebesgue density f; assume integral |f log f| is finite for a finite well-defined value, with 0 log 0=0. Differential entropy can be negative.
Example: A uniform density on an interval of length a has differential entropy log a.

Name: Gaussian maximum entropy at fixed variance
Intuition: With a fixed variance, the Gaussian spreads probability as unpredictably as possible under differential entropy.
Conditions: X is real with a density, finite variance sigma^2>0, and a well-defined finite differential entropy. Equality holds exactly for a Gaussian density with that variance, up to almost-everywhere equality.
Example: A unit-variance density has entropy at most one-half log(2*pi*e) nats.
Prerequisites: Differential entropy; Normal distribution; Gibbs' inequality

Name: Gibbs distribution
Intuition: Exponential weights balance low cost against diversity. Increasing beta concentrates mass on lower-energy choices.
Conditions: There are finitely many finite real energies E_i and beta>0. The displayed law uniquely minimizes sum_i p_i E_i-(1/beta)H(p) over the probability simplex.
Example: If two energies are equal, they receive equal weights for every beta.

Name: Entropy variational formula for log-sum-exp
Intuition: A smooth maximum is the best weighted average score plus a reward for keeping the weights spread out.
Conditions: x is a finite real vector, Delta_n is the probability simplex, and H uses natural logs with 0 log 0=0. The unique maximizing weights are softmax(x).
Example: For n equal scores a, the optimum is uniform and the value is a+log n.

Name: Evidence lower bound identity
Intuition: An approximate latent distribution creates a lower bound on log evidence. The missing amount is exactly its KL divergence from the true posterior.
Conditions: 0<p(x)<infinity; q is a probability density or mass absolutely continuous with respect to the posterior, and both displayed right-hand terms are finite. KL nonnegativity then gives L(q)<=log p(x).
Example: Choosing q equal to the exact posterior makes the bound tight.

Name: Capacity of a discrete memoryless channel
Intuition: Choose the input distribution that makes the output as informative about the input as possible. This value governs reliable long-block communication.
Conditions: A fixed finite-input, finite-output memoryless channel p(y|x), with no additional input constraint. C is the supremum of achievable rates with error tending to zero; natural-log information gives nats per use.
Example: A noiseless channel with n symbols has capacity log n nats per use.

Name: Real Gaussian channel capacity
Intuition: For additive Gaussian noise, useful information grows logarithmically with signal-to-noise ratio. A Gaussian input makes best use of the allowed average power.
Conditions: One real memoryless channel use is Y=X+Z, with independent Z~N(0,N), N>0, and E[X^2]<=P, P>=0. The formula is in nats per real use; divide by log 2 for bits.
Example: At P=N the capacity is one-half bit per real channel use.
Prerequisites: Capacity of a discrete memoryless channel; Gaussian maximum entropy at fixed variance; Variance of a sum

Name: Kraft inequality
Intuition: Each binary codeword occupies a branch of a binary tree. Prefix-free words must occupy disjoint branches, so their total tree mass cannot exceed one.
Conditions: For a finite collection of positive integer lengths ell_i, a binary prefix code with those lengths exists exactly when the inequality holds. Every uniquely decodable binary code also satisfies it.
Example: Lengths (1,2,2) satisfy equality and are realized by codewords 0,10,11.

Name: Entropy bound for binary prefix coding
Intuition: Entropy sets the ideal average description length. Integer codeword lengths cost less than one additional bit per symbol for an optimal binary prefix code.
Conditions: A finite alphabet with at least two positive-probability symbols; H(p) uses natural logs. The minimum is over binary prefix codes for single symbols, with average length measured in bits.
Example: For probabilities (1/2,1/4,1/4), lengths (1,2,2) achieve the entropy exactly at 1.5 bits.

Name: Fourier transform
Intuition: Measure how strongly a signal aligns with each oscillation. Frequency coordinates can expose structure hidden in its time or spatial values.
Conditions: f is a complex-valued Lebesgue-integrable function on R for this ordinary integral definition; xi is real. This branch consistently uses the 2-pi frequency convention.
Example: A normalized probability density has Fourier value one at frequency zero.

Name: Fourier inversion
Intuition: Reassemble a signal by adding its frequency contributions with their phases. Under suitable integrability, the frequency description loses no information.
Conditions: Assume f and its Fourier transform are in L1(R). The identity holds almost everywhere and at every continuity point of f; broader L2 inversion uses an L2 limit rather than this absolute integral.
Example: The transform and inverse transform of a Gaussian recover the original Gaussian.

Name: Fourier convolution theorem
Intuition: Convolution mixes shifted copies in the original coordinates. In frequency coordinates, each frequency is simply scaled by a multiplier.
Conditions: f,g belong to L1(R); their convolution belongs to L1 and the displayed identity holds at every real xi with the chosen Fourier convention.
Example: Convolving a signal with a smoothing kernel suppresses frequencies where the kernel's transform is small.

Name: Fourier translation rule
Intuition: Moving a signal changes the phase of each frequency while preserving its spectral magnitude.
Conditions: f in L1(R), a real, with the 2-pi Fourier convention.
Example: A delayed pulse has the same magnitude spectrum as the original pulse.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Fourier modulation rule
Intuition: Multiplying by a pure oscillation moves the whole spectrum to a new center frequency.
Conditions: f in L1(R) and nu real; the modulation uses the same 2-pi convention as the transform.
Example: A narrow baseband signal can be shifted to a carrier band by complex modulation.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Fourier scaling rule
Intuition: Compressing a signal in time spreads it in frequency. The amplitude factor compensates for the change in integration scale.
Conditions: f in L1(R) and a is a nonzero real number; negative a also reverses orientation.
Example: The signal f(2t) is twice as narrow in time and its spectrum is one-half fhat(xi/2).
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Change of coordinates

Name: Fourier differentiation rule
Intuition: Differentiation amplifies rapid oscillations more strongly than slow ones. In frequency coordinates, a derivative is multiplication by frequency.
