Conditions: For this statement assume f is a Schwartz function (smooth with all derivatives rapidly decreasing); weaker hypotheses can also justify integration by parts and vanishing boundary terms.
Example: A second derivative transforms to -(2*pi*xi)^2 fhat(xi).
Prerequisites: Fourier transform; Derivative; Integration by parts

Name: Plancherel identity
Intuition: Changing from time to frequency coordinates preserves total squared magnitude. Energy is redistributed among frequencies, not changed.
Conditions: f belongs to L2(R), and its transform is defined by the unique L2 extension of the L1-intersection-L2 transform. The 2-pi convention makes the equality have no extra factor.
Example: A filter that removes frequencies cannot increase L2 energy when its multiplier has magnitude at most one.
Prerequisites: Fourier transform; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Fourier transform of a Gaussian
Intuition: A Gaussian remains Gaussian under the Fourier transform, with reciprocal width. Its shape is balanced between localization in both domains.
Conditions: a>0 is real and the 2-pi transform convention is used.
Example: When a=1, exp(-pi*t^2) is its own Fourier transform.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Fourier transform; Gaussian integral; Fourier scaling rule

Name: Discrete Fourier transform
LaTeX: X_k=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x_ne^{-2\pi i kn/N},\qquad x_n=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_ke^{2\pi i kn/N}
Intuition: A finite vector can be represented by its alignment with N discrete oscillations. Orthogonality makes the representation exactly reversible.
Conditions: N>=1 is an integer, x in C^N, and indices n,k run from zero to N-1. The forward transform is unnormalized and the inverse uses 1/N.
Example: X_0/N is the arithmetic mean of the original vector.

Name: Parseval identity for the DFT
Intuition: The DFT redistributes squared length across orthogonal frequency directions. Its normalization determines the single factor of N.
Conditions: x in C^N with N>=1 and the unnormalized forward DFT used in discrete-fourier-transform.
Example: For the all-ones vector, the only nonzero coefficient is X_0=N; both sides equal N.
Prerequisites: Discrete Fourier transform; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Circular convolution and the DFT
Intuition: Wrap finite sequences around a circle and sum all pairs producing the same cyclic index. The DFT diagonalizes this cyclic mixing.
Conditions: x,y in C^N and N>=1; indices are taken modulo N. Ordinary linear convolution requires enough zero-padding to avoid circular wraparound.
Example: For lengths a and b, zero-padding to N>=a+b-1 allows circular convolution to reproduce their linear convolution.

Name: Radix-two FFT butterfly
Intuition: Split a transform into even-index and odd-index inputs, solve the two smaller transforms, and reuse their results to reconstruct the full transform.
Conditions: N=2^m with integer m>=1; E and O are the length-N/2 DFTs of even and odd subsequences, and 0<=k<N/2. Recursing gives O(N log N) arithmetic operations.
Example: An eight-point DFT splits into two four-point DFTs, then four two-point DFTs.
Prerequisites: Discrete Fourier transform; Exponential addition law

Name: Shannon sampling theorem
Intuition: Exact bandlimiting makes regularly spaced samples contain the whole signal. Shifted sinc functions reconstruct the continuous curve between samples.
Conditions: T>0, f in L2(R), and fhat vanishes outside [-1/(2T),1/(2T)]. Use the continuous bandlimited representative and sinc(0)=1; the full series converges in L2 and uniformly. A truncated finite reconstruction is an approximation.
Example: A signal with no frequencies above B can be reconstructed from all samples at spacing T=1/(2B), for B>0.
Prerequisites: Fourier inversion; Fourier series and Fourier coefficients

Name: Autocorrelation of a stationary process
Intuition: Compare a signal with a delayed version of itself and average the product. This reveals persistence and repeated structure across time lags.
Conditions: X is a complex second-order wide-sense stationary process, so the mean is constant and covariance depends only on lag. For zero mean, autocorrelation equals autocovariance.
Example: A stationary centered Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process has an autocorrelation that decays exponentially with lag magnitude.

Name: Wiener-Khinchin relation
Intuition: Time-lag dependence and frequency power contain the same second-order information. Integrating the power spectrum recovers the process variance in the zero-mean case.
Conditions: X is zero-mean, mean-square continuous, and wide-sense stationary with finite variance and integrable autocorrelation. Then S is a nonnegative spectral density; more general stationary processes require a spectral measure.
Example: Exponentially decaying autocorrelation corresponds to a Lorentzian-shaped power spectrum.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Autocorrelation of a stationary process; Fourier transform

Name: Fourier uncertainty principle
Intuition: A nonzero signal cannot be arbitrarily concentrated in both time and frequency. Narrowing one representation imposes a minimum spread on the other.
Conditions: For a simple sufficient hypothesis, f is a Schwartz function with ||f||_2=1. mu_t and mu_xi are the means under |f|^2 and |fhat|^2; the Fourier convention uses 2*pi. Shifted and modulated Gaussian functions attain equality.
Example: A Gaussian pulse achieves the smallest possible product of variance-defined time and frequency widths.
Prerequisites: Plancherel identity; Variance; Cauchy–Schwarz inequality; Fourier differentiation rule

Name: Linear map
Intuition: A linear map respects mixing: transforming a mixture gives the same result as mixing the transformed ingredients. This is the exact version of the local approximation used by derivatives.
Conditions: V and W are vector spaces over the same field; T:V→W; the law holds for every u,v in V and every pair of scalars a,b.
Example: Differentiation on polynomials sends 3p+2q to 3p′+2q′.

Name: Matrix multiplication
Intuition: Each output-to-input connection is the sum over possible intermediate coordinates. Multiplying matrices therefore records the composition of linear maps.
Conditions: A is m×n and B is n×p over the same field; the sum is finite.

Name: Basis and unique coordinates
Intuition: A basis is a smallest complete set of directions: every vector can be assembled from it in exactly one way. Coordinates are instructions relative to this chosen set.
Conditions: V is finite-dimensional over a field; b₁,…,bₙ is a basis precisely when the displayed existence and uniqueness hold.
Example: The polynomial 2−3t+t² has coordinates (2,−3,1) in the basis (1,t,t²).

Name: Rank–nullity theorem
Intuition: Input directions split into directions the map erases and independent directions visible at the output. These two counts exhaust the input dimension.
Conditions: T:V→W is linear over a field and V is finite-dimensional; W may be larger or infinite-dimensional.
Example: A rank-2 linear map from a five-dimensional space has a three-dimensional kernel.
Prerequisites: Linear map; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Dimension of a sum of subspaces
Intuition: Adding two spaces counts their shared directions twice. Subtracting the intersection corrects the overlap.
Conditions: U and W are finite-dimensional subspaces of one vector space over a field.
Example: Two distinct planes through the origin in three dimensions meet in a line, so their sum has dimension 2+2−1=3.

Name: Change of basis and similarity
Intuition: One matrix converts new coordinates to old, the operator acts, and the inverse converts back. Similar matrices describe the same transformation in different coordinates.
Conditions: T is an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space; P is invertible and its columns are the new basis vectors expressed in the old basis.
Example: Swapping coordinate axes conjugates diag(2,5) into diag(5,2).
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Basis and unique coordinates; Matrix multiplication

Name: Determinant
Intuition: The determinant is the signed volume multiplier of a linear map. The alternating sum removes combinations that collapse volume into lower dimensions.
Conditions: A is an n×n matrix over a commutative field or ring; signed-volume interpretation is for real Euclidean space.
Example: The diagonal matrix diag(2,3) multiplies oriented area by 6.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Multiplicativity of determinant
Intuition: Sequential transformations multiply their volume factors. A composition can preserve full dimension only if both square factors do.
Conditions: A and B are n×n matrices over the same commutative ring; the volume interpretation assumes real entries.
Example: A stretch by 3 followed by one by 4 along the same axis has volume multiplier 12.

Name: Inverse by the adjugate
Intuition: Cofactors assemble a matrix whose multiplication cancels all cross terms, leaving det(A) times the identity. Dividing by that factor reverses the transformation.
Conditions: A is square over a field with det A≠0; adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. This identity is conceptual, not the preferred numerical algorithm.
Example: For A=[[a,b],[c,d]], its inverse is [[d,−b],[−c,a]]/(ad−bc).

Name: Cramer’s rule
Intuition: Replacing one column by the target vector measures how much of that column direction the solution needs. The ratio compares the new oriented volume to the original one.
Conditions: A is an invertible n×n matrix over a field; Aᵢ(b) replaces its ith column with b.
Example: For 2x+y=5 and x−y=1, determinant ratios give x=2 and y=1.

Name: Trace
Intuition: Trace adds the self-to-self contributions of a map. Although diagonal entries depend on coordinates, their sum equals the eigenvalue sum and remains unchanged by a basis change.
Conditions: For the eigenvalue sum, A is complex square, or real with eigenvalues counted over C, including algebraic multiplicities. For cyclicity A is m×n and B is n×m over a commutative field.
Example: A=[[2,7],[0,5]] has trace 7, matching eigenvalues 2 and 5.

Name: Inner product
Intuition: An inner product measures alignment while extending the dot product to abstract vector spaces. It also supplies lengths and perpendicularity.
Conditions: Displayed formula is the standard inner product on Rⁿ or Cⁿ. Throughout these entries the first slot is conjugate-linear, the second linear; an abstract inner product is conjugate-symmetric and positive definite.
Example: For real vectors (1,2) and (3,4), the inner product is 11.

Name: Norm axioms and induced norm
Intuition: A norm is a consistent way to assign size to vectors. Scaling multiplies size, and taking a detour cannot beat a direct route.
Conditions: The axioms hold for all vectors and scalars in a real or complex vector space; the final formula is the Euclidean norm and is not the only possible norm.
Example: The Euclidean norm of (3,4) is 5, while its ℓ¹ norm is 7.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Geometry and distance

Name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
Intuition: Alignment cannot exceed the product of lengths. Equality means the two vectors contain the same direction, up to a scalar.
Conditions: x and y belong to a real or complex inner-product space; equality holds exactly when they are linearly dependent, including a zero vector.
Prerequisites: Inner product; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Parallelogram law
Intuition: The total squared lengths of a parallelogram’s diagonals equal twice the total squared lengths of adjacent sides. Cross terms cancel between the two diagonals.
Conditions: The identity holds for norms induced by real or complex inner products. Conversely, a norm satisfying it for all x,y comes from an inner product.
Example: For x=(1,0), y=(0,1), the two diagonal squares are 2+2=4.
Prerequisites: Inner product; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Polarization identity over the reals
Intuition: You can recover angles from distance measurements alone. The difference of the two diagonal squares isolates the interaction between the vectors.
Conditions: x,y lie in a real inner-product space and the norm is the induced one. Complex inner products require additional terms involving iy.
Example: For x=(1,0), y=(1,1), the formula gives (5−1)/4=1.
Prerequisites: Inner product; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Orthogonal projection
Intuition: Projection keeps the components pointing along a chosen subspace and discards perpendicular components. The retained point is the closest point of the subspace.
Conditions: q₁,…,qₖ is an orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional subspace U of a real or complex inner-product space; Q has those vectors as columns in orthonormal coordinates.
Example: Projection of (3,4) onto the x-axis is (3,0).
Prerequisites: Inner product; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Orthogonal decomposition and energy split
Intuition: A signal splits into the part a subspace can express and an unexplained perpendicular remainder. Their squared sizes add without cross terms.
Conditions: U is a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner-product space, or a closed subspace of a Hilbert space; Pᵤ is its orthogonal projection.
Example: For x=(3,4) projected onto the x-axis, 25=9+16.

Name: Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization
Intuition: Each new vector is cleaned of directions already represented. Normalizing the remainder produces a new independent unit direction.
Conditions: v₁,…,vₙ is a linearly independent finite list in an inner-product space; q₁=v₁/‖v₁‖. Independence ensures no denominator is zero.
Example: Starting from (1,0) and (1,1), the second residual is (0,1).
Prerequisites: Orthogonal projection; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: QR factorization
Intuition: A linear transformation becomes an orthonormal coordinate frame followed by triangular mixing. This separates geometry from the bookkeeping of dependent coordinates.
Conditions: A is m×n over R or C with m≥n and full column rank; the reduced Q is m×n, and R is invertible n×n. Requiring positive real diagonal entries makes this reduced factorization unique.
Example: The columns (1,0) and (1,1) yield Q=I and R=[[1,1],[0,1]].

Name: Bessel’s inequality for an orthonormal list
Intuition: Looking along only some perpendicular directions cannot reveal more energy than the vector contains. Missing directions account for the gap.
Conditions: q₁,…,qₖ is a finite orthonormal list in an inner-product space; equality holds iff x belongs to its span.
Example: For x=(3,4,12) and the first two coordinate directions, 9+16≤169.

Name: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Intuition: An eigenvector is a direction the transformation leaves on its own line. Along that direction the full transformation behaves like multiplication by a single number.
Conditions: A is a square matrix over a field; λ is in the chosen scalar field and v is nonzero. A real matrix may have no real eigenvalues.
Example: For diag(2,5), the coordinate axes are eigenvectors with eigenvalues 2 and 5.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Characteristic polynomial
Intuition: Subtracting a proposed scalar action tests whether some direction is annihilated. The determinant records exactly when that failure of invertibility occurs.
Conditions: A is n×n over a field; roots and eigenvectors are considered over that field or a stated extension. Over C the polynomial has n roots counting multiplicity.

Name: Cayley–Hamilton theorem
Intuition: Every square matrix obeys its own characteristic equation. High powers can therefore be rewritten using only finitely many lower powers.
Conditions: A is an n×n matrix over a commutative field; p_A(t)=det(tI−A), and polynomial evaluation uses matrix powers with constant term times I.
Example: If p_A(t)=t²−5t+6, then A²=5A−6I.

Name: Diagonalization
Intuition: A suitable coordinate system uncouples the transformation into separate stretch factors. Repeated application then becomes ordinary scalar exponentiation.
Conditions: A is n×n over a field and has a basis of eigenvectors; P consists of those eigenvectors. The power formula holds for integers k≥0, and for negative k if every eigenvalue is nonzero.
Example: A matrix with eigenvalues 2 and 3 and two independent eigenvectors has powers controlled by 2ᵏ and 3ᵏ.
Prerequisites: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Change of basis and similarity

Name: Spectral theorem in finite dimensions
LaTeX: A=U\Lambda U^*,\quad U^*U=I;\qquad A^*A=AA^*\iff\text{such a decomposition exists}
Intuition: A normal complex matrix has independent perpendicular modes. For Hermitian matrices these modes have real strengths, making quadratic energy especially transparent.
Conditions: A is a complex n×n matrix: unitary diagonalization is equivalent to normality. If A=A*, all eigenvalues are real; a real symmetric matrix has an orthogonal diagonalization. A general real normal matrix need not be real-diagonalizable.
Example: The symmetric matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] has orthogonal eigenvectors (1,1), (1,−1) with eigenvalues 3 and 1.
Prerequisites: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Inner product; Adjoint of a linear map

Name: Rayleigh quotient
Intuition: The Rayleigh quotient measures the strength of a Hermitian transformation in one direction. In an eigenbasis it is a weighted average of the eigenvalues.
Conditions: A is a nonempty Hermitian matrix, x≠0, and λmin, λmax are its smallest and largest eigenvalues. Equality occurs in the corresponding extreme eigenspaces.
Example: For diag(2,8) and x=(1,1), R_A(x)=5.
Prerequisites: Quadratic form; Spectral theorem in finite dimensions

Name: Courant–Fischer min–max principle
Intuition: To find the kth-smallest mode, choose the best k-dimensional space against its worst direction. Dimensional constraints force that space to encounter the kth eigenvalue.
Conditions: A is n×n Hermitian with λ₁≤…≤λₙ, and 1≤k≤n; S ranges over k-dimensional complex subspaces (real subspaces for real symmetric A).
Example: For diag(1,4,9), the best two-dimensional subspace has worst Rayleigh quotient 4.
Prerequisites: Rayleigh quotient; Dimension of a sum of subspaces

Name: Singular value decomposition
Intuition: Every finite matrix can be understood as orthogonal changes of coordinates surrounding independent nonnegative stretches. Unlike eigenvectors, the input and output directions may live in different spaces.
Conditions: A is m×n over R or C; U and V are orthogonal or unitary square matrices, and Σ is rectangular diagonal with nonnegative singular values. Include zeros with the usual dimensional padding.
Example: A rank-one matrix has one positive singular value and acts through one input direction and one output direction.
Prerequisites: Spectral theorem in finite dimensions; Adjoint of a linear map

Name: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse
Intuition: The pseudoinverse reverses the directions a map actually transmits and leaves erased directions at zero. It chooses the smallest solution among equally good fits.
Conditions: A is a finite real or complex matrix with SVD A=UΣV*; Σ⁺ has transposed shape. A⁺b is the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution.
Example: For diag(2,0), A⁺=diag(1/2,0).

Name: Eckart–Young–Mirsky low-rank approximation
Intuition: The best rank budget is spent on the largest independent stretches. No alternative k-dimensional representation can hide the next singular direction.
Conditions: A is m×n real or complex, σ₁≥…≥σmin(m,n)≥0 and 0≤k<min(m,n); ‖·‖₂ is the spectral norm. The same truncation minimizes Frobenius error, whose square is Σᵢ>kσᵢ²; minimizers need not be unique.
Example: For diag(5,2,1), the best rank-one spectral error is 2.
Prerequisites: Singular value decomposition; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Polar decomposition
Intuition: A square transformation separates into a pure nonnegative stretch followed by a length-preserving motion. This extends magnitude times phase from complex numbers to matrices.
Conditions: A is a square real or complex matrix; H is the unique positive semidefinite square root. U can be chosen orthogonal or unitary; it is unique when A is invertible, but may not be unique otherwise.
Example: For A=−2I, H=2I and U=−I.
Prerequisites: Singular value decomposition; Spectral theorem in finite dimensions

Name: Jordan normal form
Intuition: When independent eigenvectors are missing, chains of generalized eigenvectors describe the remaining coupling. The extra nilpotent pieces record how far the map is from diagonal.
Conditions: A is a finite square matrix over C, or over a field where its characteristic polynomial splits. Each Nα has ones on a block’s superdiagonal and is nilpotent; block ordering is arbitrary.
Example: The matrix [[2,1],[0,2]] is a single Jordan block and cannot be diagonalized.
Prerequisites: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Change of basis and similarity; Characteristic polynomial

Name: Quadratic form
Intuition: A quadratic form measures size or energy with direction-dependent weights and interactions. Its matrix records both individual squared contributions and pairwise cross terms.
Conditions: x is real and A is real symmetric; every real quadratic polynomial homogeneous of degree two has such a unique symmetric matrix. Complex Hermitian forms use x*Ax instead.
Example: q(x,y)=2x²+2xy+3y² has matrix [[2,1],[1,3]].

Name: Sylvester’s law of inertia
Intuition: A real quadratic form has intrinsic counts of positive, negative and flat directions. Coordinate changes can reshape the expression but cannot change those counts.
Conditions: A is real symmetric and P is invertible; the integers p,q,r are unique, although P is not. This is congruence, not similarity, so individual eigenvalue magnitudes need not be preserved.
Example: x²−y²+0z² has inertia (1,1,1) under any invertible real coordinate change.
Prerequisites: Quadratic form; Spectral theorem in finite dimensions

Name: Cholesky factorization
LaTeX: A=LL^*,\qquad L\text{ lower triangular with positive diagonal}
Intuition: A positive definite quadratic energy can be converted into an ordinary sum of squares by a triangular coordinate transform. Positivity makes each successive square root possible.
Conditions: A is Hermitian positive definite over C, or real symmetric positive definite; then L exists uniquely with positive real diagonal entries. Semidefinite matrices require qualifications and may have nonunique factors.
Prerequisites: Quadratic form; Adjoint of a linear map

Name: Schur complement
Intuition: Eliminating one block of variables changes the interactions among the remaining variables. The Schur complement is the effective matrix after that elimination.
Conditions: The block matrix is square, A is square and invertible, and all block sizes are compatible over a field. S need not be invertible for the determinant identity.
Example: Eliminating x from 2x+y=b₁ and x+3y=b₂ leaves coefficient 3−1/2=5/2 on y.
Prerequisites: Inverse by the adjugate; Matrix multiplication

Name: Matrix exponential
Intuition: The exponential turns a constant infinitesimal linear rule into its finite-time motion. Eigenvector directions evolve like ordinary scalar exponentials.
Conditions: A is a fixed finite square real or complex matrix, t is real or complex, and the series converges absolutely in every matrix norm. The ODE statement uses real time with x(0)=x₀; e^(A+B)=e^Ae^B is guaranteed when A and B commute.
Example: For A=[[0,−1],[1,0]], e^(tA) is a rotation through angle t.

Name: Kronecker product
Intuition: The Kronecker product lets two coordinate systems vary independently. Its block structure represents the product of two linear actions.
Conditions: A,B,C,D are finite matrices over one field and AC and BD are defined; the first formula defines the Kronecker product.
Example: I₂⊗B places two copies of B along the block diagonal.

Name: Tensor product universal property
Intuition: A tensor product packages two-input bilinear behavior into one-input linear behavior. It creates a space in which every bilinear operation can be treated as an ordinary linear map.
Conditions: V,W,Z are vector spaces over a common field; the displayed correspondence is natural and bijective. The induced linear map b̃ is unique for each bilinear b.
Example: A bilinear expression Σᵢⱼaᵢⱼvᵢwⱼ becomes a linear functional on the tensors eᵢ⊗fⱼ.
Prerequisites: Linear map; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Dual space and pullback of linear functionals
Intuition: A forward map of vectors pulls measurements backward. To measure the output, first apply the map and then the output measurement.
Conditions: T:V→W is linear over a field; V* and W* are algebraic dual spaces. Here T* denotes the dual map, not the Hermitian adjoint unless an inner-product identification is supplied.
Example: If T scales vectors by 3, it also multiplies every pulled-back linear measurement by 3.

Name: Adjoint of a linear map
Intuition: The adjoint transfers a linear action from one side of an inner-product measurement to the other. In orthonormal coordinates this reverses rows and columns and conjugates entries.
Conditions: T maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product spaces; matrices are expressed in orthonormal bases. The adjoint exists uniquely; infinite-dimensional unbounded operators need domain qualifications.
Example: A real column vector viewed as a map has its transpose as adjoint.

Name: Gram determinant and volume
Intuition: All lengths and pairwise angles together determine the volume spanned by a list of vectors. The volume vanishes exactly when the directions are dependent.
Conditions: v₁,…,vₖ are vectors in a real Euclidean space with k≤its dimension; Volₖ is the unsigned volume of their parallelepiped. The determinant is nonnegative.
Example: For v₁=(1,0) and v₂=(1,2), G=[[1,1],[1,5]] has determinant 4, so area is 2.

Name: Matrix geometric series
Intuition: Repeated feedback can be added one pass at a time. When repeated powers decay, all indirect effects sum to a single inverse.
Conditions: A is a finite square real or complex matrix with spectral radius ρ(A)<1. The series converges in every matrix norm; ‖A‖<1 in a submultiplicative norm is sufficient but not necessary.
Example: For A=(1/2)I, the sum is 2I.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Matrix multiplication; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Finite geometric sum

Name: Sherman–Morrison rank-one update
Intuition: Changing a matrix along one input-output interaction changes its inverse by another rank-one term. The denominator checks whether the update destroys invertibility.
Conditions: A is invertible and square over R or C; u,v have compatible dimensions and 1+v*A⁻¹u≠0. A* notation on v means conjugate transpose.
Example: For A=I and u=v=e₁, the updated inverse changes the first diagonal entry to 1/2.
Prerequisites: Inverse by the adjugate; Matrix multiplication

Name: Group axioms
Intuition: A group abstracts reversible actions that can be composed. You may regroup a sequence of actions, do nothing, and undo any action.
Conditions: G is a set with a closed binary operation; associativity holds for all a,b,c, one identity e exists, and every a has an inverse. Commutativity is not assumed.
Example: Rotations of a square form a group; all rigid symmetries of the square form a larger noncommutative group.

Name: Group homomorphism
Intuition: A homomorphism translates one system of actions into another while preserving how actions combine. It can forget distinctions, but must forget them consistently.
Conditions: G,H are groups and φ:G→H; the law holds for every a,b in G. The group operations may use different notation.
Example: det:GLₙ(R)→R× sends matrix composition to multiplication of determinants.

Name: Kernel and image of a homomorphism
Intuition: The kernel is exactly the information a map erases, while the image is exactly what it can express. Group laws make the erased information compatible with quotienting.
Conditions: φ:G→H is a group homomorphism; the kernel is normal in G, and the image is a subgroup of H.
Example: For reduction Z→Z/5Z, the kernel is 5Z and the image is all five residue classes.

Name: Quotient group
Intuition: A quotient treats certain transformations as invisible. Each new element is a whole class of old elements that differ only by an invisible action.
Conditions: N is a normal subgroup of G. Normality is essential for the displayed multiplication to be independent of the chosen representatives.
Example: Z/12Z models addition of hours on a clock.

Name: First isomorphism theorem
Intuition: Once you identify precisely the differences a homomorphism erases, what remains is a perfect copy of its output. This turns information loss into a structural description.
Conditions: φ:G→H is any group homomorphism; the quotient is by its normal kernel, and the induced map is a well-defined group isomorphism onto the image.
Example: The map Z→{1,−1}, n↦(−1)ⁿ has kernel 2Z, so Z/2Z is isomorphic to {1,−1}.
Prerequisites: Kernel and image of a homomorphism; Quotient group

Name: Lagrange’s theorem for finite groups
Intuition: A subgroup tiles its finite group with equal-size cosets. The total number of elements is the number of tiles times the size of one tile.
Conditions: G is a finite group and H is a subgroup; [G:H] counts left cosets. The converse divisibility claim is false: a divisor of |G| need not occur as a subgroup order.
Example: A subgroup of a group with 15 elements can only have order 1,3,5 or 15.

Name: Group action
Intuition: An abstract group becomes concrete by letting it move objects. The action law says the group’s multiplication agrees with doing those moves in sequence.
Conditions: G is a group, X a set, and the action is a map G×X→X satisfying both laws for all g,h,x. Each g necessarily acts by a bijection.
Example: The permutation group Sₙ acts on n coordinate positions by reordering them.

Name: Orbit–stabilizer theorem
Intuition: The number of genuinely different positions equals the number of available actions divided by the number that leave the object where it is. Stabilizers measure redundant ways to reach the same position.
Conditions: G is finite and acts on X; Gₓ={g:g·x=x}. The orbit-coset bijection remains valid for infinite groups, but the displayed numeric division is the finite version.
Example: The 8 symmetries of a square act on its 4 vertices; a chosen vertex has a stabilizer of size 2.
Prerequisites: Group action; Lagrange’s theorem for finite groups

Name: Burnside’s orbit-counting lemma
Intuition: To count objects up to symmetry, average how many objects each symmetry leaves unchanged. The average exactly removes overcounting from different stabilizer sizes.
Conditions: A finite group G acts on a finite set X; Fix(g)={x:g·x=x} and X/G is the set of orbits.
Example: Two-colorings of three labeled positions modulo all permutations have (8+3·4+2·2)/6=4 orbits, determined by the number of red positions.

Name: Class equation
Intuition: Conjugation groups elements by how they sit inside the symmetry system. Central elements are alone in their classes; every other class is counted by its centralizer.
Conditions: G is finite; gᵢ is one representative from each noncentral conjugacy class, Z(G) is the center, and C_G(g)={h:hg=gh}.
Example: For S₃, the class sizes are 1,3,2, so 6=1+3+2.

Name: Sylow theorems
LaTeX: |G|=p^a m,\quad p\nmid m:\qquad |P|=p^a,\quad n_p\equiv1\pmod p,\quad n_p\mid m
Intuition: The largest possible prime-power pieces of a finite group always exist, and symmetry makes them conjugate. Their possible number is sharply restricted by arithmetic.
Conditions: G is finite, p is prime, a≥1 and p does not divide m. A Sylow p-subgroup P exists; every p-subgroup lies in one; all Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate. nₚ counts them, and nₚ=1 iff the Sylow subgroup is normal.
Example: In a group of order 15, n₅ divides 3 and is 1 modulo 5, so the order-5 subgroup is unique and normal.
Prerequisites: Lagrange’s theorem for finite groups; Group action

Name: Cayley’s theorem for groups
Intuition: Every abstract group can be realized as actual permutations. Letting the group move its own elements gives a faithful concrete model.
Conditions: G is any group; Sym(G) is the group of all bijections of the underlying set. For finite |G|=n, this embeds G into Sₙ.
Example: A cyclic group of order 3 becomes the permutations generated by the cycle (123).

Name: Order of a power in a cyclic subgroup
Intuition: Taking k steps at a time around a cycle may visit only part of it. The greatest common divisor measures how many interlaced smaller cycles appear.
Conditions: g has finite order n≥1 in a group and k is an integer; gcd(n,0)=n.
Example: If g has order 12, then g⁸ has order 12/gcd(12,8)=3.

Name: Direct product of groups
Intuition: Two independent symmetry systems can run side by side. The paired system keeps both states and composes each component separately.
Conditions: G and H are groups; the order formula is the finite version. No commutativity of either factor is required.
Example: Two independent binary switches form Z/2Z×Z/2Z, with four states.

Name: Structure theorem for finite abelian groups
LaTeX: G\cong\mathbb Z/d_1\mathbb Z\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/d_r\mathbb Z,\qquad 1<d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_r
Intuition: Every finite commuting symmetry system can be built from independent cyclic counters. Divisibility-ordered counter lengths give a unique structural description.
Conditions: G is a finite abelian group; the integers dᵢ are uniquely determined, with an empty sum for the trivial group. General finite nonabelian groups do not admit this description.
Example: Z/2Z×Z/6Z is already in invariant-factor form.
Prerequisites: Direct product of groups; Order of a power in a cyclic subgroup

Name: Ring structure and distributivity
Intuition: A ring lets addition and multiplication cooperate. Distributivity is the rule that makes expanding, collecting and evaluating algebraic expressions consistent.
Conditions: A ring has an abelian additive group, associative multiplication, and the two displayed distributive laws. We use rings with identity; multiplication need not commute.
Example: Square matrices form a ring: multiplication distributes over addition even though AB may differ from BA.

Name: Quotient ring
Intuition: An ideal specifies algebraic differences to ignore while keeping both addition and multiplication meaningful. Quotienting can enforce equations by declaring their left-hand sides zero.
Conditions: R is a ring with identity and I is a two-sided ideal; commutative rings automatically have two-sided ideals. Operations are independent of representative choices.
Example: R[x]/(x²+1) is a way to construct complex arithmetic from real polynomials.
Prerequisites: Ring structure and distributivity; Equivalence relation

Name: Maximal ideals and fields
LaTeX: R/I\text{ is a field}\iff I\text{ is maximal}
Intuition: A maximal ideal removes just enough information that every surviving nonzero element becomes invertible. No intermediate proper quotient remains.
Conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity and I is a proper ideal. A field here has distinct zero and one.
Example: The ideal (5) is maximal in Z, giving the field Z/5Z; (6) is not maximal.

Name: Polynomial division algorithm
Intuition: Repeatedly canceling the highest power leaves a remainder too small to divide further. This is long division with degree playing the role of size.
Conditions: f,g are polynomials over a field and g≠0; q and r exist uniquely. Over a general coefficient ring, the conclusion still holds when the leading coefficient of g is a unit.
Example: Dividing x³−1 by x−1 gives q=x²+x+1 and r=0.

Name: Polynomial remainder and factor theorem
Intuition: A zero of a polynomial is exactly a removable linear factor. Evaluation tells you the remainder after dividing by that factor.
Conditions: f is a polynomial over a field and a is in that field; q is the unique quotient. The displayed statement also holds over a commutative ring with identity.
Example: Since f(2)=0 for f(x)=x²−3x+2, the factor x−2 divides f.

Name: Lagrange interpolation
Intuition: Build one polynomial for each data point that is one there and zero at all the others. Adding these selectors with the desired heights fits every point exactly.
Conditions: x₀,…,xₙ are distinct elements of a field and y₀,…,yₙ are arbitrary; p is the unique polynomial of degree at most n with p(xᵢ)=yᵢ.
Example: The data (0,1),(1,3) give p(x)=1+2x.
Prerequisites: Polynomial remainder and factor theorem; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Tower law for field extensions
Intuition: Choosing coordinates in two stages multiplies the number of independent scalar directions. A basis over an intermediate field expands into a basis over the smaller field.
Conditions: F⊆K⊆L are fields and both degrees on the right are finite. The extension degree is vector-space dimension.

Name: Finite fields
Intuition: Finite fields are arithmetic systems in which every nonzero number can be divided by. Their sizes are prime powers, and their nonzero elements cycle through powers of one generator.
Conditions: p is prime and m≥1. For each p^m a field exists uniquely up to isomorphism; every finite field has such a size. Cq−1 denotes a cyclic group of order q−1.
Example: F₄ can be built as F₂[t]/(t²+t+1), and its three nonzero elements form a cycle.
Prerequisites: Quotient ring; Maximal ideals and fields; Tower law for field extensions

Name: Frobenius homomorphism
Intuition: In prime characteristic the intermediate binomial terms disappear. Raising to the pth power unexpectedly becomes a structure-preserving operation.
Conditions: The identities hold in a commutative ring of prime characteristic p. Frobenius is injective on fields, and is an automorphism on finite fields; it need not be surjective on every infinite field.
Example: In characteristic 2, (a+b)²=a²+b² because 2ab=0.
Prerequisites: Binomial theorem; Ring structure and distributivity

Name: Fundamental theorem of Galois theory
Intuition: Adding more numbers to the fixed field leaves fewer allowed symmetries. This reverses inclusion and turns questions about polynomial roots into questions about subgroups.
Conditions: L/F is a finite Galois extension (finite, normal and separable). K ranges over intermediate fields and H over subgroups of Gal(L/F); Lᴴ is the fixed field. The maps are inverse and inclusion-reversing. K/F is Galois iff Gal(L/K) is normal, then Gal(K/F)≅Gal(L/F)/Gal(L/K).
Example: For Q(√2)/Q, the two automorphisms send √2 to ±√2; fixing √2 leaves only the identity.
Prerequisites: Tower law for field extensions; Group action; Quotient group

Name: Matrix commutator and Lie bracket
Intuition: The commutator measures how much the order of two linear actions matters. For infinitesimal symmetries, it produces the new direction generated by doing the actions in opposite orders.
Conditions: A and B are same-size square matrices over a field; the commutator is bilinear and satisfies [A,A]=0 and the Jacobi identity. Interpretation as infinitesimal flows uses real or complex matrix Lie groups.

Name: Jacobi identity
Intuition: Failures of pairwise commutation cannot vary independently. The three nested commutators balance in a cyclic relation.
Conditions: A,B,C lie in an associative algebra with the commutator bracket, or in any Lie algebra where Jacobi is an axiom. For vector fields the bracket is the commutator acting on smooth functions.
Example: For matrix commutators, expanding the six positive and six negative triple products cancels them pairwise.

Name: Permutations and falling factorials
Intuition: Choose an ordered list without replacement: every previous choice removes one option from the next step. Multiplication accounts for all successive choices.
Conditions: n,k are integers with 0≤k≤n; P(n,0)=1 counts the empty list. Objects are distinct and order matters.
Example: There are 5·4·3=60 ordered lists of three distinct objects from five.

Name: Binomial coefficient
Intuition: A binomial coefficient counts ways to choose a subset of a fixed size. Division removes the many orders that describe the same subset.
Conditions: n is a nonnegative integer and 0≤k≤n; conventionally the coefficient is zero for integer k outside this range.
Example: Choosing three people from seven gives C(7,3)=35 groups.

Name: Pascal’s rule
Intuition: A chosen subset either contains a distinguished element or it does not. These two disjoint cases cover every possibility.
Conditions: n≥1 is an integer and k is any integer; coefficients outside 0≤k≤n are interpreted as zero.

Name: Vandermonde’s identity
Intuition: Choose r objects from two populations, either all at once or by tracking how many come from each population. The two descriptions must count the same subsets.
Conditions: m,n,r are nonnegative integers; binomial coefficients outside their usual range are zero.
Example: Selecting two objects from groups of sizes 2 and 3 gives 3+6+1=10 choices.

Name: Multinomial coefficient
Intuition: When objects are assigned to several labeled groups, permutations within each group do not make a new assignment. Divide the full ordering count by each internal redundancy.
Conditions: n₁,…,nᵣ are nonnegative integers summing to n; the groups are labeled.
Example: The word BANANA has 6!/(3!2!1!)=60 distinct letter arrangements.
Prerequisites: Permutations and falling factorials; Binomial coefficient

Name: Stars and bars
Intuition: Place separators between identical items to divide them among labeled bins. Empty bins correspond to adjacent separators or separators at the ends.
Conditions: n≥0 and k≥1 are integers; the items are indistinguishable, bins are distinguishable, and empty bins are allowed.
Example: Distributing five identical tokens among three people gives C(7,2)=21 possibilities.

Name: Inclusion–exclusion principle
Intuition: First add individual counts, then remove double counts, restore triple counts, and continue. Each element’s total coefficient becomes exactly one.
Conditions: A₁,…,Aₙ are finite sets and n≥1. The identity extends to finite families of measurable sets with a finite measure in place of cardinality.
Example: For three sets, add their sizes, subtract the three pairwise intersections, then add the triple intersection.
Prerequisites: Inclusion–exclusion for two sets; Binomial theorem

Name: Pigeonhole principle
Intuition: At least one bin is no smaller than the average occupancy. Integrality rounds this simple average bound up to a guaranteed count.
Conditions: N≥0 objects are assigned to k≥1 bins; nᵢ are their nonnegative integer occupancies.
Example: Among 13 people, at least two share a birth month.

Name: Derangement count
Intuition: A derangement permutes objects so none returns to its original place. Alternating corrections remove permutations with one or more fixed positions.
Conditions: n≥0 is an integer, and D₀=1. The displayed sum is finite and exact.
Prerequisites: Inclusion–exclusion principle; Permutations and falling factorials

Name: Catalan numbers
Intuition: Many nested objects split at their first outer pair into a left part and a right part. The same recursive shape appears in balanced parentheses, triangulations and rooted binary trees.
Conditions: n≥0 is an integer. Cₙ counts balanced parenthesis strings of n pairs, or full ordered binary trees with n internal vertices.
Example: C₃=5 gives the five balanced strings of three pairs of parentheses.

Name: Stirling numbers of the second kind
Intuition: When adding the last object to a set partition, either place it in one of k existing blocks or give it a new singleton block. These are the only possibilities.
Conditions: S(n,k) counts partitions of an n-element labeled set into k nonempty unlabeled blocks; recurrence for n,k≥1. Boundary values: S(0,0)=1; S(n,0)=0 for n>0; S(0,k)=0 for k>0.

Name: Bell numbers
Intuition: Bell numbers count every way of chunking a labeled set into nonempty groups. To build the next partition, choose which old objects stay outside the block of the new object.
Conditions: n≥0, B₀=1; S(n,k) is a Stirling number of the second kind. The partitions have unlabeled nonempty blocks.
Example: A three-element set has B₃=5 partitions.

Name: Ordinary generating function
Intuition: A generating function stores an entire sequence as coefficients of one object. Manipulating that object turns recurrences and counting constructions into algebra.
Conditions: The primary interpretation is a formal power series over a specified coefficient ring, so analytic convergence is unnecessary. To evaluate it numerically, restrict z to a region where the series converges.
Example: The constant sequence aₙ=1 has generating function 1/(1−z).

Name: Product rule for ordinary generating functions
Intuition: To build a combined object of total size n, choose how much size each component receives. Every possible split contributes a product of counts.
Conditions: A and B are formal power series over a commutative ring; each coefficient sum is finite. For numerical power series the identity holds inside both radii of convergence.
Example: If aₙ=bₙ=1, the product has coefficient n+1, counting splits n=k+(n−k).

Name: Exponential generating function
Intuition: Dividing by factorials makes multiplication automatically choose which labels belong to each component. This is natural for combinatorial structures on labeled objects.
Conditions: A and B are formal series over a field of characteristic zero, with bₙ defined using the same n! normalization. Analytic evaluation requires convergence.
Example: For labeled sets with one structure on each size, A(z)=eᶻ; pairing two such structures gives coefficients 2ⁿ.

Name: Fibonacci recurrence
Intuition: The next state depends on the two previous states. The same rule counts constructions whose first choice leaves one of two possible smaller sizes.
Conditions: n≥0 is an integer; the initial conditions are part of the definition and distinguish this sequence from other solutions to the recurrence.
Example: F₂=1,F₃=2,F₄=3,F₅=5.

Name: Binet’s formula
Intuition: A coupled recurrence becomes a difference of two independent exponential modes. Irrational pieces cancel to produce exact integers.
Conditions: n≥0 is an integer and F₀=0,F₁=1 with the Fibonacci recurrence. The displayed formula is exact; replacing it by φⁿ/√5 is an approximation.
Example: At n=3, the expression equals 2 exactly.

Name: Characteristic-root solution of a linear recurrence
Intuition: A constant linear recurrence has exponential modes, just as a constant linear differential equation does. Initial values determine how much of each mode is present.
Conditions: d≥1; coefficients and initial values are complex; c₀≠0; rᵢ are the d distinct roots of rᵈ−Σⱼ₌₀ᵈ⁻¹cⱼrʲ. The simple displayed solution requires distinct roots; repeated roots need polynomial factors in n.
Example: For aₙ₊₂=3aₙ₊₁−2aₙ, every solution has the form α+β2ⁿ.
Prerequisites: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Polynomial division algorithm

Name: Integer partition generating function
Intuition: For each allowed part size, choose how many copies to include. Multiplication combines these independent choices while the exponent records their total size.
Conditions: p(n) counts unordered partitions of the nonnegative integer n into positive integers and p(0)=1. The identity is formal: each coefficient depends on only finitely many factors; it also converges for |z|<1.
Example: The five partitions of 4 are 4,3+1,2+2,2+1+1 and 1+1+1+1.
Prerequisites: Product rule for ordinary generating functions; Finite geometric sum

Name: Handshake lemma
Intuition: Every edge contributes one endpoint at each end. Counting edge endpoints by vertices or by edges gives the same total.
Conditions: G=(V,E) is a finite undirected graph. If loops are allowed, each loop contributes two to its vertex degree.
Example: A triangle has three vertices of degree 2, giving total degree 6=2·3.

Name: Adjacency powers count walks
Intuition: Matrix multiplication sums over intermediate vertices, so repeated multiplication follows every possible step sequence. The power records routes with repeated vertices allowed.
Conditions: A is the adjacency matrix of a finite graph, with Aᵢⱼ counting directed edges from i to j; k≥0 and A⁰=I. For weighted entries, powers sum products of edge weights instead of unweighted counts.
Example: In a triangle, (A²)₁₁=2 because two length-two walks return to vertex 1.

Name: Graph Laplacian
Intuition: The Laplacian compares each vertex value with its neighbors. Constant signals create no disagreement, so they lie in its kernel.
Conditions: G is a finite undirected graph with symmetric nonnegative edge weights and no self-loops; A is the weighted adjacency matrix and Dᵢᵢ=ΣⱼAᵢⱼ. Zero-weight edges may be omitted.
Example: For a single edge of weight w, L=[[w,−w],[−w,w]].

Name: Graph Dirichlet energy
Intuition: A signal’s graph energy is the total disagreement across edges. Minimizing it favors similar values at strongly connected vertices.
Conditions: x is real and L is the Laplacian of a finite undirected graph with symmetric nonnegative weights; the factor 1/2 compensates for summing both edge orientations.
Example: For one edge of weight 3 joining values 2 and 5, the energy is 3·(2−5)²=27.

Name: Matrix–tree theorem
Intuition: A determinant of local edge interactions counts global spanning trees. Deleting one row and column removes the constant direction that makes the full Laplacian singular.
Conditions: G is a finite undirected graph with n≥2 vertices and nonnegative weights; L⁽ⁱ⁾ deletes row and column i. τ is the sum over spanning trees of the product of their edge weights; it is zero if the graph is disconnected.
Example: For a triangle, a Laplacian cofactor [[2,−1],[−1,2]] has determinant 3, matching its three spanning trees.

Name: Cayley’s formula for labeled trees
Intuition: Every labeled tree can be encoded by a sequence of n−2 labels. The independent choices in that sequence explain the simple power.
Conditions: n≥2 is an integer; trees are undirected simple connected acyclic graphs on the fixed labeled vertex set.
Example: There are 4²=16 trees on four labeled vertices.

Name: Euler’s formula for connected planar graphs
Intuition: Drawing a connected graph on a sphere balances vertices, edges and regions. Refining the drawing adds pieces in ways that preserve the alternating total.
Conditions: G is a finite connected graph embedded in the plane without crossings; F counts all complementary faces including the unbounded face. A disconnected graph with c components satisfies V−E+F=1+c.
Example: A cube graph has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces: 8−12+6=2.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Edges in a finite tree
Intuition: A tree spends exactly one edge to attach each vertex after the first. Any additional edge would create a cycle.
Conditions: A finite tree is a nonempty connected undirected graph with no cycles. More generally a forest with c components has |E|=|V|−c.
Example: A tree joining eight vertices has seven edges.

Name: Hall’s marriage theorem
Intuition: Every group of requesters must collectively have enough distinct options. Remarkably, checking this shortage condition for all groups is also sufficient for a complete assignment.
Conditions: G=(U,V,E) is a finite bipartite graph; N(S) is the set of neighbors of S, and a matching uses no vertex twice. Saturating U matches every vertex in U, without requiring all of V to be matched.
Example: Three tasks can be assigned distinct workers only if every subset of tasks has at least as many qualified workers.

Name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
Intuition: Every route from source to sink must cross a separating cut. The tightest total cut capacity is exactly the largest feasible flow.
Conditions: The network is a finite directed graph with distinct s,t and finite nonnegative capacities. A feasible flow obeys 0≤f(u,v)≤c(u,v) and flow conservation at every other vertex; |f| is net flow out of s.
Example: If two edge-disjoint source-to-sink routes have capacities 2 and 3, and no smaller cut intervenes, maximum flow is 5.

Name: Chromatic polynomial deletion–contraction
Intuition: Colorings of the graph with an edge removed split into those whose endpoints differ and those whose endpoints agree. Contracting the edge counts the agreement case.
Conditions: G is a finite simple graph and e is an edge between distinct vertices; P_G(q) counts proper vertex colorings with q colors for integers q≥0. In G/e merge parallel edges. The polynomial identity holds for all q.
Example: For a triangle, deleting an edge gives a path and contracting it gives an edge, so q(q−1)²−q(q−1)=q(q−1)(q−2).

Name: Cycle rank of a finite graph
Intuition: After a spanning forest connects each component, every remaining edge creates one independent cycle. Cycles are the edge flows that have no net source at any vertex.
Conditions: G is a finite undirected graph with c connected components; orient edges arbitrarily and let B be its vertex-edge incidence matrix over R. Loops can be handled as zero columns.
Example: A connected triangle has cycle dimension 3−3+1=1.
Prerequisites: Rank–nullity theorem; Edges in a finite tree

Name: Euclidean division of integers
Intuition: Every integer has a unique whole-number quotient and a small leftover after division by a positive integer. The remainder is a canonical representative of its modular class.
Conditions: a is an integer and b is a positive integer; unique integers q,r satisfy the formula, including when a is negative.
Example: −17=5·(−4)+3, so the nonnegative remainder is 3.

Name: Euclidean algorithm
Intuition: Removing whole multiples does not change which integers divide both numbers. Repeating the operation makes the numbers smaller until the common divisor is exposed.
Conditions: a,b are nonnegative integers with b>0; iterate until the second argument is zero, using gcd(a,0)=a. At least one initial integer is nonzero.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Bézout’s identity
Intuition: The smallest positive integer combination of two integers is their greatest common divisor. Repeated addition and subtraction reach exactly the multiples of that gcd.
Conditions: a,b are integers not both zero; gcd(a,b)>0. The coefficients x,y exist but are generally not unique.

Name: GCD–LCM product formula
Intuition: For each prime, the shared part uses the smaller exponent and the combined coverage uses the larger. Together they use the same total exponent as the original two numbers.
Conditions: a,b are positive integers; gcd and lcm are taken positive.
Example: For 12 and 18, gcd=6 and lcm=36, so 6·36=12·18.

Name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic
Intuition: Every positive integer is assembled from prime building blocks in a unique way. The multiplicities turn divisibility questions into coordinatewise comparisons.
Conditions: n>1 is an integer; pᵢ are distinct primes and aᵢ≥1 integers. The factorization is unique up to ordering; n=1 is the empty product.

Name: Congruence modulo an integer
Intuition: Two numbers are equivalent when they differ by a whole number of complete cycles. Congruence forgets position along the infinite line while retaining position around the cycle.
Conditions: a,b are integers and m≥1 is an integer; congruence is an equivalence relation compatible with addition and multiplication.
Example: 17≡5 mod 12 because their difference is 12.

Name: Modular inverse criterion
Intuition: Division modulo m works exactly when a shares no prime obstruction with the modulus. Bézout coefficients construct the inverse explicitly.
Conditions: a is an integer and m≥2; when an inverse exists, its residue class modulo m is unique.
Example: 3⁻¹≡5 mod 7 because 3·5=15≡1.
Prerequisites: Bézout’s identity; Congruence modulo an integer

Name: Linear Diophantine equations
LaTeX: ax+by=c\text{ has integer solutions}\iff d\mid c,\qquad d=\gcd(a,b)
Intuition: Integer linear equations live on a grid, so ordinary real solvability is not enough. The gcd is the spacing between attainable values.
Conditions: a,b,c are integers, a,b not both zero, and d>0. If (x₀,y₀) is one solution, all are x=x₀+(b/d)t, y=y₀−(a/d)t with t∈Z.
Example: 6x+9y=12 is solvable since 3 divides 12; all solutions include x=2+3t,y=−2t.

Name: Chinese remainder theorem
LaTeX: \mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z\cong\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb Z/m_i\mathbb Z,\qquad x\equiv\sum_i a_i M_i y_i\pmod M
Intuition: Independent modular views can be recombined without losing information. Each term in the construction is tuned to affect exactly one modulus.
Conditions: mᵢ≥2 are pairwise coprime integers, M=∏ᵢmᵢ, Mᵢ=M/mᵢ and Mᵢyᵢ≡1 mod mᵢ. For any residues aᵢ, there is a unique solution modulo M to x≡aᵢ mod mᵢ; the first map is a ring isomorphism.
Example: x≡2 mod 3 and x≡3 mod 5 combine to x≡8 mod 15.
Prerequisites: Modular inverse criterion; Congruence modulo an integer

Name: Fermat’s little theorem
LaTeX: a^p\equiv a\pmod p,\qquad p\nmid a\Longrightarrow a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p
Intuition: Modulo a prime, multiplication by a nonzero residue permutes all nonzero residues. Their product reveals the periodicity of powers.
Conditions: p is prime and a is any integer; the second form additionally requires p not dividing a. Composite moduli can satisfy some Fermat congruences, so the converse is false.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Recursion and iteration

Name: Euler’s totient function
Intuition: Count the integers up to n that avoid every prime divisor of n. Each distinct prime removes its share of forbidden residues.
Conditions: n≥1 is an integer and the product runs over distinct prime divisors; φ(1)=1 via the empty product. Equivalently φ(n)=#{1≤k≤n:gcd(k,n)=1}.
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Modular inverse criterion

Name: Euler’s theorem on powers modulo n
Intuition: The invertible residues form a finite group, so repeatedly multiplying by one residue must cycle within that group. The group size is a universal exponent that returns every element to one.
Conditions: n≥2 is an integer and gcd(a,n)=1. φ(n) counts the units modulo n; it need not be the smallest exponent that works.
Example: For n=10, φ(n)=4 and 3⁴=81≡1 mod 10.
Prerequisites: Euler’s totient function; Lagrange’s theorem for finite groups

Name: Wilson’s theorem
Intuition: For a prime modulus, every nonzero residue pairs with a distinct inverse except 1 and −1. Those two leftovers determine the factorial product.
Conditions: p is an integer greater than 1. The equivalence is exact, though it is generally inefficient as a computational primality test.
Prerequisites: Modular inverse criterion; Permutations and falling factorials

Name: Legendre symbol
LaTeX: \left(\frac ap\right)=\begin{cases}0&p\mid a\\1&a\not\equiv0\text{ is a square mod }p\\-1&a\text{ is not a square mod }p\end{cases}
Intuition: The Legendre symbol compresses a square-root existence question into a sign. Multiplying signs corresponds to multiplying residue classes.
Conditions: p is an odd prime and a is an integer. On nonzero residues it is a multiplicative map to {1,−1}.
Example: Modulo 7, 2 is a square because 3²≡2, so (2/7)=1; 3 is not a square, so (3/7)=−1.

Name: Euler’s criterion
Intuition: Half the universal group exponent separates squares from nonsquares. The result is one for squares and minus one for nonsquares.
Conditions: p is an odd prime and a is any integer, including multiples of p for which both sides are zero modulo p.
Example: For a=3,p=7, 3³=27≡−1, so 3 is a nonsquare modulo 7.

Name: Quadratic reciprocity
Intuition: Whether one prime is a square modulo another is almost a symmetric question. A sign flip occurs exactly when both primes are 3 modulo 4.
Conditions: p and q are distinct odd primes. The Legendre symbols use the lower prime as modulus. The supplementary laws for −1 and 2 are separate statements.

Name: Number of positive divisors
Intuition: A divisor independently chooses how many copies of each prime to keep. Multiply the number of choices across primes.
Conditions: n≥1 is an integer; the prime factorization uses distinct primes with positive exponents. For n=1 the empty product gives τ(1)=1.
Example: 72=2³3² has (3+1)(2+1)=12 positive divisors.

Name: Sum of positive divisors
Intuition: The contribution from each prime is a short geometric series. Multiplying these series produces every divisor exactly once.
Conditions: n≥1 and n=∏ᵢpᵢᵃⁱ is its prime factorization; the empty product gives σ(1)=1. Every sum and product here is finite.
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Finite geometric sum

Name: Möbius function
LaTeX: \mu(n)=\begin{cases}1&n=1\\(-1)^r&n\text{ is a product of }r\text{ distinct primes}\\0&\text{some prime square divides }n\end{cases}
Intuition: The Möbius function assigns alternating signs to square-free prime selections. These signs undo the overcounting created by summing over divisors.
Conditions: n is a positive integer; the r=0 case corresponds to n=1. Square-free means no squared prime divides n.
Example: μ(30)=−1 because 30 has three distinct prime factors, while μ(12)=0.

Name: Möbius inversion over divisors
Intuition: A divisor sum blends contributions from all factors of a number. Möbius weights cancel the inherited contributions and recover the original one.
Conditions: f,F are arithmetic functions from positive integers to a commutative ring; all divisor sums are finite and μ is interpreted as an integer coefficient.
Example: Because Σd|n φ(d)=n, inversion gives φ(n)=Σd|n μ(d)n/d.

Name: Dirichlet convolution
Intuition: Convolution can split an index multiplicatively instead of additively. Every factorization n=d·(n/d) contributes one pair of function values.
Conditions: f,g map positive integers into a commutative ring. Here 1(n)=1, ε(1)=1 and ε(n)=0 for n>1; μ is the Möbius function. All sums are finite.
Example: For f=g=1, (1*1)(n)=τ(n), the divisor count.

Name: Prime exponent in a factorial
Intuition: Count one factor of p from every multiple of p, another from every multiple of p², and so on. Higher prime powers contribute repeatedly because they contain several copies.
Conditions: n≥0 is an integer and p is prime; vₚ is the exponent of p in the factorization. The displayed sum has only finitely many nonzero terms.
Prerequisites: Permutations and falling factorials; Fundamental theorem of arithmetic

Name: p-adic absolute value and ultrametric
Intuition: Two rational numbers are close when their difference is divisible by a high power of p. This replaces ordinary magnitude with agreement in prime-power arithmetic.
Conditions: p is prime. For nonzero rational x=pᵏa/b with p dividing neither a nor b, vₚ(x)=k; set |0|ₚ=0. The inequality holds on Q and its completion Qₚ.
Example: In 2-adic distance, 9 and 1 are only |8|₂=1/8 apart.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Congruence modulo an integer

Name: Continued-fraction convergent recurrence
Intuition: A continued fraction builds rational approximations by repeatedly inverting the leftover part. The determinant identity ensures consecutive approximations stay arithmetically adjacent.
Conditions: For a simple continued fraction [a₀;a₁,…], a₀∈Z and aₙ≥1 for n≥1. Set p₋₂=0,p₋₁=1,q₋₂=1,q₋₁=0; n≥0 in the recurrences, and n≥1 in the determinant identity. pₙ/qₙ is the nth convergent.
Example: For √2=[1;2,2,…], the convergents begin 1,3/2,7/5,17/12.

Name: Cross product in three dimensions
Intuition: The cross product packages oriented area into a perpendicular vector. Its magnitude measures how much two directions spread out instead of overlapping.
Conditions: a,b lie in oriented Euclidean R³ with the standard right-handed coordinate basis; the norm is Euclidean.
Example: (1,0,0)×(0,2,0)=(0,0,2), an area vector of magnitude 2.
Prerequisites: Inner product; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Curvature of a regular space curve
Intuition: Curvature measures how quickly the tangent direction turns per unit distance traveled. Dividing by arc length separates bending from the speed used to trace the curve.
Conditions: r is a C² regular curve in R³, so r′(t)≠0; s is arc length and T=r′/‖r′‖. A planar curve can be embedded in R³. This is nonnegative curvature.
Example: A circle of radius R>0 has constant curvature 1/R.
Prerequisites: Derivative; Cross product in three dimensions; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Torsion of a space curve
Intuition: Torsion measures how the osculating plane twists as you follow a curve. A curve may bend without twisting if it stays in one plane.
Conditions: r is C³ and regular in oriented R³, with r′×r″≠0 on the interval. The sign convention agrees with B=T×N and dB/ds=−τN.
Example: The circular helix r(t)=(a cos t,a sin t,bt), a>0, has τ=b/(a²+b²).
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Curvature of a regular space curve; Cross product in three dimensions; Derivative

Name: Frenet–Serret equations
Intuition: A curve carries its own moving orthonormal frame. Two scalar functions, curvature and torsion, describe all infinitesimal changes of that frame.
Conditions: The curve is C³, parametrized by arc length, and has κ>0. T=r′, N=T′/κ and B=T×N; derivatives are with respect to s. The formula treats T,N,B as a column of vector entries.
Example: For a plane circle, τ=0 and the tangent and normal rotate while the binormal stays fixed.
Prerequisites: Curvature of a regular space curve; Torsion of a space curve

Name: First fundamental form of a surface
LaTeX: ds^2=E\,du^2+2F\,du\,dv+G\,dv^2,\quad E=r_u\cdot r_u,\ F=r_u\cdot r_v,\ G=r_v\cdot r_v
Intuition: Surface coordinates may stretch and tilt a flat grid. The first fundamental form records the actual lengths and angles represented by coordinate changes.
Conditions: r(u,v) is a C¹ regular parametrized surface in R³, so rᵤ and rᵥ are linearly independent. The 2×2 coefficient matrix is positive definite.
Example: For a cylinder r(u,v)=(R cos u,R sin u,v), ds²=R²du²+dv².
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Change of coordinates

Name: Area of a parametrized surface
Intuition: A tiny coordinate rectangle becomes a tangent parallelogram on the surface. Adding its local area multiplier gives the total area.
Conditions: r:D→R³ is a regular C¹ patch, one-to-one except on a set of area measure zero, and the area density is integrable. Without the one-to-one qualification, the parameter integral counts multiplicity.
Example: For a graph z=f(x,y), the density is √(1+fₓ²+fᵧ²).
Prerequisites: First fundamental form of a surface; Riemann integral; Cross product in three dimensions

Name: Shape operator and second fundamental form
Intuition: The surface bends when its unit normal changes from point to point. The shape operator converts a tangent direction into that change, and the second fundamental form reads its normal bending.
Conditions: The surface is an oriented C² immersed surface in R³ with unit normal N. Identify the tangent plane of S² at N(p) with the tangent plane of the surface; S is self-adjoint for the induced metric. Our convention is S=−dN.
Example: For a sphere of radius R with outward normal, S=−I/R and both principal curvatures are −1/R.
Prerequisites: First fundamental form of a surface; Derivative; Adjoint of a linear map

Name: Gaussian curvature of a surface
Intuition: Gaussian curvature combines bending in the two principal directions. Same-sign bending is dome-like, opposite-sign bending is saddle-like, and its value is intrinsic to the surface metric.
Conditions: The oriented surface is C² and regular in R³; S=−dN. E,F,G are first-form coefficients and e=rᵤᵤ·N, f=rᵤᵥ·N, g=rᵥᵥ·N are second-form coefficients. Smoothness can be increased for differential curvature identities.
Example: A sphere of radius R has K=1/R²; a circular cylinder has K=0.
Prerequisites: Shape operator and second fundamental form; Determinant; First fundamental form of a surface

Name: Mean curvature of a surface
Intuition: Mean curvature is the average of the two principal bendings. It also equals the angular average of normal curvature across all unit tangent directions.
Conditions: The surface is an oriented C² immersed surface in R³, with S=−dN and real principal curvatures k₁,k₂. Reversing the normal reverses H; some texts use the unnormalized trace instead.
Example: An outward-oriented sphere of radius R has H=−1/R in this convention; a saddle with k₁=−k₂ has H=0.
Prerequisites: Shape operator and second fundamental form; Trace; Arithmetic mean

Name: Euler’s formula for normal curvature
Intuition: Bending in an arbitrary tangent direction mixes the two principal bendings. Squared direction components supply the weights.
Conditions: The surface is oriented and C²; e₁,e₂ are orthonormal principal directions of S=−dN, and the unit tangent direction is cosθ e₁+sinθ e₂. Normal curvature is II(v,v).
Example: If k₁=1 and k₂=3, a direction at 45° has normal curvature 2.
Prerequisites: Shape operator and second fundamental form; Spectral theorem in finite dimensions

Name: Riemannian metric
Intuition: A Riemannian metric assigns an inner product to every tangent space, varying smoothly from point to point. It tells a traveler how to measure distances and angles locally.
Conditions: M is a smooth manifold; gᵢⱼ=gⱼᵢ is a smooth positive definite matrix in each coordinate chart. Repeated indices are summed from 1 to the manifold dimension; v is a real tangent vector.
Example: Euclidean polar coordinates have ds²=dr²+r²dθ² away from r=0.

Name: Riemannian length and distance
Intuition: Add the local lengths along a path, then choose the least possible path length between endpoints. The metric turns an infinitesimal ruler into a global distance.
Conditions: (M,g) is a connected Riemannian manifold; γ is piecewise C¹ on a compact interval. The infimum ranges over such joining paths. A minimizing path need not exist unless further hypotheses, such as completeness, hold.
Example: On a circle of radius R, the distance is R times the smaller angular separation.

Name: Riemannian volume element
Intuition: The determinant measures how a coordinate box changes volume under the local metric. Its square root converts squared inner-product information into volume.
Conditions: g is a smooth positive definite metric in a coordinate chart. The expression defines a volume density on any Riemannian manifold; on an oriented manifold use the oriented form √det(g) dx¹∧…∧dxⁿ.
Example: In Euclidean spherical coordinates, the density is r² sinθ dr dθ dφ on the usual coordinate range.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Change of coordinates

Name: Christoffel symbols of the Levi-Civita connection
Intuition: The metric determines how to compare tangent directions at nearby points while preserving lengths and having no torsion. Christoffel symbols record this comparison in a chosen coordinate system.
Conditions: g is a smooth Riemannian metric, (gⁱʲ) is its inverse matrix, and repeated indices are summed. These coefficients belong to the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection; they are not tensor components under general coordinate changes.
Example: For ds²=dr²+r²dθ², Γʳθθ=−r and Γθrθ=Γθθr=1/r for r>0.
Prerequisites: Riemannian metric; Derivative; Inverse by the adjugate

Name: Covariant derivative in coordinates
Intuition: Differentiating vector components alone confuses actual change with movement of the coordinate frame. The connection correction separates those two effects.
Conditions: V is a smooth tangent vector field, Γ are the coefficients of a specified affine connection, and repeated j is summed. For Riemannian geometry we use the Levi-Civita connection.
Example: A constant Cartesian vector has nonconstant polar components, but its Euclidean covariant derivative is still zero.
Prerequisites: Christoffel symbols of the Levi-Civita connection; Derivative

Name: Geodesic equation
Intuition: A geodesic moves without turning relative to the surface’s own connection. Its coordinates may accelerate even while its intrinsic acceleration is zero.
Conditions: x(t) is a C² curve on a smooth Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita symbols; t is an affine parameter and repeated indices are summed. Geodesics locally minimize length over sufficiently short segments, not necessarily over their whole length.
Example: Great circles are geodesics on a round sphere; a sufficiently long great-circle arc is not the shortest route between its endpoints.
Prerequisites: Covariant derivative in coordinates; Riemannian length and distance

Name: Parallel transport along a curve
Intuition: Parallel transport gives a rule for carrying a direction along a path without intrinsic turning. After a loop, the direction may return rotated because the space is curved.
Conditions: γ is a smooth or piecewise smooth curve and Γ belong to a smooth connection; an initial tangent vector determines a unique transported field on the compact parameter interval. For Levi-Civita transport, inner products are preserved.
Example: Transport around a triangle on a sphere generally rotates a vector by an angle related to the enclosed curvature.

Name: Riemann curvature tensor
Intuition: Curvature measures the failure of two directional comparisons to commute after correcting for noncommuting vector fields. It detects geometry that no coordinate change can remove.
Conditions: M has a smooth connection; for geometric curvature here use the Levi-Civita connection of g, and smooth vector fields X,Y,Z. This sign convention makes a round sphere have positive sectional curvature when K(u,v)=g(R(u,v)v,u)/area².
Example: Euclidean space has R=0 even in curvilinear coordinates with nonzero Christoffel symbols.
Prerequisites: Covariant derivative in coordinates; Matrix commutator and Lie bracket

Name: Sectional curvature
Intuition: Each two-dimensional tangent plane has its own curvature measurement. Dividing by the plane’s squared area removes dependence on how its two basis vectors were chosen.
Conditions: u,v are linearly independent real tangent vectors at one point of a Riemannian manifold. R uses ∇X∇Y−∇Y∇X−∇[X,Y]; the denominator is strictly positive.
Example: Every tangent plane of a round sphere of radius R has sectional curvature 1/R².
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Riemann curvature tensor; Gram determinant and volume

Name: Ricci and scalar curvature as traces
Intuition: Ricci curvature summarizes how a chosen direction bends against all perpendicular directions. Scalar curvature adds the directional summaries into one number.
Conditions: e₁,…,eₙ is any orthonormal basis at a point of a smooth Riemannian manifold. R uses the stated sphere-positive convention; both contractions are basis-independent. These are sums, not normalized averages.
Example: An n-dimensional manifold of constant sectional curvature c has Ric=(n−1)cg and Scal=n(n−1)c.

Name: Laplace–Beltrami operator
Intuition: Diffusion on a curved space must account for both directional lengths and local volume. The Laplace–Beltrami operator is divergence of the metric gradient.
Conditions: f is C² and g is a smooth Riemannian metric in a chart; repeated indices are summed. This convention is Δg=divg gradg, giving Σ∂ᵢ² in Euclidean coordinates; some texts use its negative.
Example: On the Euclidean plane in polar coordinates, Δf=frr+(1/r)fr+(1/r²)fθθ for r>0.

Name: Gauss–Bonnet theorem for closed surfaces
Intuition: Local bending accumulates into a global topological invariant. Stretching and reshaping a closed surface can redistribute curvature but cannot change its total unless its topology changes.
Conditions: M is a compact oriented smooth Riemannian two-manifold without boundary, K its Gaussian curvature and χ its Euler characteristic. Boundary and corner versions require extra terms, omitted here.
Example: A sphere has total curvature 4π and χ=2; a torus has total curvature 0 and χ=0.
Patterns: Accumulation; Symmetry and invariance; Boundary and interior
Prerequisites: Gaussian curvature of a surface; Riemann integral; Euler characteristic

Name: Exterior derivative
Intuition: One derivative operation unifies differential, curl and divergence by acting on oriented measurement objects of successive dimensions. Differentiating twice cancels because mixed derivatives are symmetric while orientation is antisymmetric.
Conditions: ω is a smooth k-form in a coordinate chart, dxᴵ=dxⁱ¹∧…∧dxⁱᵏ with increasing multi-indices, and dω is a (k+1)-form. The identity d²=0 holds globally on smooth manifolds.
Example: For ω=x dy in R², dω=dx∧dy.
Prerequisites: Derivative; Wedge product and graded commutativity

Name: Wedge product and graded commutativity
Intuition: The wedge product combines oriented measurements in different directions. Repeating a direction gives zero because it cannot create new oriented volume.
Conditions: α is a k-form and β an ℓ-form over R on the same manifold, or alternating covariant tensors on one real vector space. The wedge product is bilinear and associative.
Example: dx∧dy measures oriented coordinate area, and swapping the axes gives dy∧dx=−dx∧dy.

Name: Pullback of a differential form
Intuition: A form on the destination becomes a measurement on the starting space by first pushing its input directions forward. Differentiation respects this transfer.
Conditions: F:M→N is smooth and ω is a smooth k-form on N; F*ω is a k-form on M. No invertibility of F is required.
Example: If F(u,v)=(2u,3v), then F*(dx∧dy)=6 du∧dv.
Prerequisites: Dual space and pullback of linear functionals; Exterior derivative

Name: Cartan’s formula for the Lie derivative
Intuition: The change of a form under a flow splits into two simpler operations: insert the flow direction and differentiate, or differentiate and then insert. This connects motion with the algebra of forms.
Conditions: X is a smooth vector field and ω a smooth differential form; ιX is contraction with X and LX is the Lie derivative defined through the local flow. For zero-forms take contraction to be zero.
Example: For a function f, the formula gives LXf=ιXdf=X(f).
Prerequisites: Exterior derivative; Pullback of a differential form

Name: Topology by open sets
Intuition: Topology specifies which regions count as open without committing to numerical distances. Arbitrary unions and finite intersections preserve the notion of being locally inside a region.
Conditions: T is a collection of subsets of X; every Uα and Uⱼ lies in T, A is any index set, and m is finite. Infinite intersections are not required to be open.
Example: The intervals (a,b) generate the usual topology of the real line.

Name: Continuity by inverse images
LaTeX: f:X\to Y\text{ continuous}\iff f^{-1}(U)\text{ is open in }X\ \text{for every open }U\subseteq Y
Intuition: A destination neighborhood pulls back to a neighborhood condition on inputs. This captures continuity even when distance and coordinates are unavailable.
Conditions: X,Y are topological spaces and f is any map; f⁻¹(U) denotes a set inverse image and does not require f to be invertible.
Example: Every map from a discrete topological space is continuous because every input subset is open.
Prerequisites: Topology by open sets; Composition of functions

Name: Homeomorphism
LaTeX: f:X\to Y,\quad g:Y\to X,\quad g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X,\quad f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y
Intuition: Two spaces have the same topological shape when a continuous relabeling can be continuously reversed. Length and curvature may change while neighborhood structure is preserved.
