Conditions: Both f and g are continuous maps; the equations make them inverse bijections. A continuous bijection alone need not be a homeomorphism.
Example: An open interval is homeomorphic to the real line, even though its ordinary length is finite.
Prerequisites: Continuity by inverse images; Inverse function

Name: Homotopy of maps
Intuition: A homotopy is a continuous movie deforming one map into another. It formalizes changing shape without jumping or tearing the map.
Conditions: F is continuous for the product topology; f₀,f₁:X→Y are its endpoint maps. For based homotopies, the chosen basepoint is held fixed throughout.
Example: The maps f₀(x)=0 and f₁(x)=x from R to R are homotopic through F(x,t)=tx.
Prerequisites: Continuity by inverse images; Cartesian product

Name: Fundamental group
Intuition: The fundamental group records loops that cannot be deformed into one another while their starting point stays fixed. Its multiplication is following one loop and then another.
Conditions: X is a topological space with basepoint x₀; all loops are continuous and the equivalence is homotopy fixing endpoints. Concatenation gives a group only after passing to homotopy classes.
Example: A disk has trivial fundamental group, while a torus has fundamental group Z².
Prerequisites: Homotopy of maps; Group axioms; Equivalence relation

Name: Fundamental group of the circle
Intuition: A loop around a circle remembers its net number of turns. Continuous deformation can remove detours but cannot change that integer winding count.
Conditions: γ is a continuous loop based at 1 in S¹⊂C; γ̃ is a continuous real lift with e^(iγ̃(t))=γ(t) and γ̃(0)=0. The endpoint difference is an integer multiple of 2π.
Example: The loop γ(t)=e^(6πit) represents the integer 3.

Name: Seifert–van Kampen theorem
Intuition: Global loops can be built from loops in overlapping regions. The overlap supplies exactly the relations needed to identify local descriptions of the same loop.
Conditions: X=U∪V where U,V and U∩V are nonempty path-connected open subsets; choose one basepoint in U∩V. The amalgamated product means the quotient of the free product identifying images of every overlap loop under the inclusion maps; those maps need not be injective.
Example: A figure-eight space has fundamental group the free group on two generators, using suitable overlapping neighborhoods.

Name: Number of sheets and subgroup index
Intuition: Lifting loops moves among the sheets above a point. Loops that return to the chosen starting sheet form a subgroup, and its cosets label all sheets.
Conditions: p:X̃→X is a covering map, X and X̃ are path-connected and locally path-connected, and p(x̃₀)=x₀. The formula is a cardinal equality, allowing infinitely many sheets; p* is injective.
Example: The covering S¹→S¹, z↦zᵐ for m≥1, has m sheets and corresponds to mZ⊂Z.
Prerequisites: Fundamental group; Lagrange’s theorem for finite groups

Name: Oriented simplex boundary
Intuition: A simplex’s boundary is the sum of its faces with compatible orientations. Alternating signs arrange for shared boundaries to cancel when pieces are glued.
Conditions: k≥1 and the ordered vertices form a simplex in a simplicial complex; the hat means omit that vertex. Extend the map linearly to chains over Z or a stated coefficient ring; set ∂=0 on zero-dimensional chains for unreduced homology.
Example: The oriented triangle boundary is [v₁,v₂]−[v₀,v₂]+[v₀,v₁].

Name: The boundary of a boundary is zero
Intuition: An oriented boundary already closes up. Taking its boundary again leaves pairs of equal pieces with opposite signs and therefore nothing.
Conditions: ∂ are the standard boundary maps in a simplicial or singular chain complex, with coefficients in Z or any chosen commutative ring. More abstractly this is the defining condition of a chain complex.
Example: The endpoints of the three oriented edges around a triangle cancel at every vertex.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Conservation and balance

Name: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries
Intuition: Homology records closed chains that cannot be filled by higher-dimensional chains. It ignores the cycles that are merely boundaries of material already present.
Conditions: Use a singular chain complex of X over a commutative coefficient ring R, or a simplicial/cellular complex computing the same homology when applicable. The inclusion im ∂k+1⊆ker ∂k follows from ∂²=0.
Example: For a circle, H₀(S¹;Z)=Z and H₁(S¹;Z)=Z, with higher groups zero.
Prerequisites: The boundary of a boundary is zero; Quotient group

Name: Euler characteristic
Intuition: Euler characteristic balances pieces of alternating dimension. Refining a shape changes the individual cell counts but preserves the total.
Conditions: X is a finite CW complex (including a finite simplicial complex); cₖ is its number of k-cells. The alternating sum is independent of the finite cell decomposition and invariant under homotopy equivalence.
Example: A torus with one vertex, two edges and one face has χ=1−2+1=0.

Name: Euler–Poincaré formula
Intuition: Local chain pieces that cancel as boundaries disappear from the alternating total. What survives is a balance of global homological features.
Conditions: X is a finite CW complex, F any field, and bₖ are finite Betti numbers. The equality follows from its finite-dimensional cellular chain complex.
Example: For a torus, b₀=1,b₁=2,b₂=1, so χ=0.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Euler characteristic; Rank–nullity theorem

Name: Exactness of consecutive maps
Intuition: Exactness says that every obstruction killed by the next map is explained by the preceding map. There is no unexplained information left in the middle.
Conditions: f,g are homomorphisms of abelian groups or linear maps (or module maps); the equality is in B. A sequence is exact when this holds at every indicated position.
Example: For a linear map T, 0→ker T→V→im T→0 is exact.
Prerequisites: Kernel and image of a homomorphism; Linear map

Name: Mayer–Vietoris exact sequence
LaTeX: \cdots\to H_k(U\cap V)\to H_k(U)\oplus H_k(V)\to H_k(X)\to H_{k-1}(U\cap V)\to\cdots
Intuition: To understand cycles in a union, track cycles inside each piece and the ways those pieces overlap. The connecting map records cycles that only close after the two sides are combined.
Conditions: X=U∪V with U,V open; use singular homology with a fixed abelian coefficient group. The first map is induced by (inclusion, minus inclusion), the next by addition of inclusion maps; the sequence is exact. No connectedness assumption is needed.
Example: Cover a circle by two overlapping arcs whose intersection has two components; the sequence detects one independent loop.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Exactness of consecutive maps

Name: Künneth formula over a field
Intuition: A cycle in a product can combine a p-dimensional cycle from one factor with a q-dimensional cycle from the other. Their dimensions add while their independent choices form tensor products.
Conditions: X,Y are topological spaces and F is a field; use singular homology. The cross-product map gives the natural isomorphism. Integral coefficients generally require additional Tor terms.
Example: For S¹×S¹, the two circle factors give b₁=2, and their product gives b₂=1.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Tensor product universal property; Cartesian product

Name: Poincaré duality
Intuition: On a closed oriented manifold, k-dimensional measurements correspond to complementary-dimensional cycles. The ambient dimension creates a global pairing between apparently different degrees.
Conditions: M is a closed (compact without boundary) oriented n-dimensional manifold and F a field; [M] is the fundamental class with those coefficients. Nonorientable manifolds require suitable coefficients or local systems; manifolds with boundary need a relative version.
Example: For a closed oriented surface, b₀=b₂=1 on each connected component, while b₁ records the remaining independent loops.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Dual space and pullback of linear functionals

Name: Degree of a map
Intuition: Degree counts how many times one oriented closed manifold wraps over another, with orientation signs. Composition multiplies wrapping counts.
Conditions: f:M→N is continuous between connected closed oriented manifolds of the same dimension; fundamental classes use integral homology. The composition formula assumes a third connected closed oriented manifold of that dimension.
Example: The circle map z↦zᵐ has degree m, and a reflection of the circle has degree −1.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Group homomorphism

Name: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
Intuition: Any continuous self-map of a closed ball leaves some point fixed. The ball’s topology prevents every point from being shifted away from itself at once.
Conditions: Bⁿ is the closed unit ball in finite-dimensional Euclidean space and n≥1; f maps the entire ball into itself. The theorem guarantees existence, not uniqueness or convergence of iteration.
Example: On [0,1], the map f(x)=1−x has the fixed point x=1/2.

Name: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem
Intuition: Add the action of a map on homology with alternating signs. A nonzero total is an algebraic certificate that the map cannot avoid all fixed points.
Conditions: X is a finite simplicial complex and f:X→X continuous; the rational homology groups are finite-dimensional and vanish in high degrees, so the sum is finite. The converse is false: L(f)=0 does not rule out fixed points.
Example: For a circle map of degree d, L(f)=1−d; therefore d≠1 forces a fixed point.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Trace; Degree of a map

Name: De Rham’s theorem
Intuition: Closed differential forms detect the same real topological information as singular cohomology. Integration is the bridge: a form measures a cycle, while exact forms integrate to zero on cycles.
Conditions: M is a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold; take real smooth forms and real singular cohomology. The isomorphism is induced by integration over smooth singular chains and extends through their equivalence with ordinary singular theory. Integral torsion is invisible to real coefficients. Here k≥0 and Ω⁻¹ is zero.
Example: The circle has one independent degree-one de Rham class, detected by integrating once around it.
Patterns: Duality; Boundary and interior; Algebraic structure
Prerequisites: Exterior derivative; Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Stokes' theorem for curl

Name: De Morgan’s laws
LaTeX:
eg(P\land Q)\iff(
eg P\lor
eg Q),\qquad
eg(P\lor Q)\iff(
eg P\land
eg Q)
Intuition: Negating a combined condition reverses whether all parts or at least one part are required. A failed conjunction needs one failure; a failed disjunction needs both failures.
Conditions: P,Q are propositions in classical two-valued logic. The analogous set identities use complements relative to a fixed universal set.
Example: “Not both numbers are positive” means at least one is not positive.

Name: Negating quantifiers
LaTeX:
eg( orall x\,P(x))\iff\exists x\,
eg P(x),\qquad
eg(\exists x\,P(x))\iff orall x\,
eg P(x)
Intuition: To refute a universal statement, produce one counterexample. To refute an existence statement, rule out every candidate.
Conditions: Classical first-order logic with a specified domain and predicate P; quantifiers bind the same variable over the same domain on both sides.
Example: Negating “every real number has a positive square” produces “some real number has a square that is not positive,” witnessed by zero.

Name: Implication and contrapositive
Intuition: An implication forbids only one situation: the premise holds and the conclusion fails. The contrapositive forbids exactly that same situation from the opposite direction.
Conditions: P,Q are propositions in classical two-valued logic. The converse Q⇒P is generally a different claim.
Example: “If an integer is divisible by 4, it is even” is equivalent to “if it is odd, it is not divisible by 4.”

Name: Cantor’s power-set theorem
Intuition: A list indexed by X can never contain every subset of X. Construct the subset that disagrees with the proposed list at its own index, and it must be missing.
Conditions: X is any set. For every proposed function f:X→P(X), the diagonal subset D is not in its image; an injection X→P(X) exists via singleton sets. No finiteness assumption is needed.
Example: For a finite set with n elements, its power set has 2ⁿ elements; the theorem also distinguishes infinite sizes.

Name: Soundness and completeness of first-order logic
Intuition: Formal derivation and truth in every model agree for classical first-order consequence. The result connects symbol manipulation with semantic meaning.
Conditions: Γ is a set of first-order sentences and φ a first-order sentence in one language, with a standard sound and complete proof calculus. Γ⊨φ means every structure satisfying Γ satisfies φ. This is logical completeness, not the claim that a fixed arithmetic theory proves every true arithmetic sentence.
Example: If Γ contains ∀x(P(x)⇒Q(x)) and P(c), then it both formally proves and semantically entails Q(c).

Name: Compactness theorem for first-order logic
LaTeX: \Gamma\text{ has a model}\iff\text{every finite }\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma\text{ has a model}
Intuition: An infinite first-order specification is consistent with some structure if every finite part can be satisfied. A contradiction cannot require genuinely infinitely many premises.
Conditions: Γ is a set of sentences in classical first-order logic and models use the usual nonempty-domain semantics. The property need not hold for stronger logics such as full second-order logic.
Example: Adding a constant c and requirements c>1,c>2,… to the theory of ordered fields is finitely satisfiable, so it has a model containing an element larger than every standard integer.
Prerequisites: Soundness and completeness of first-order logic

Name: Euler gamma integral
Intuition: A weighted exponential integral extends factorials to a continuous argument.
Conditions: The integral converges absolutely for complex z with Re z>0; t^{z−1}=exp((z−1)log t) for real t>0.

Name: Gamma recurrence and factorial values
Intuition: One integration by parts shifts the argument and extracts its current value.
Conditions: First identity holds for Re z>0 directly, and meromorphically elsewhere; finite values exclude poles. n is a nonnegative integer.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Boundary and interior
Prerequisites: Euler gamma integral; Integration by parts

Name: Euler reflection formula
Intuition: Gamma values on opposite sides of one-half pair into an elementary trigonometric expression.
Conditions: z is complex and not an integer; both sides are interpreted by meromorphic continuation.
Example: At z=1/2 the identity yields Γ(1/2)²=π.

Name: Legendre duplication formula
Intuition: Two half-step gamma factors combine into one factor at doubled scale.
Conditions: Re z>0 is sufficient for the displayed finite identity; it extends meromorphically.

Name: Stirling asymptotic formula for gamma
Intuition: The gamma integral is concentrated near its peak; its local quadratic shape determines the leading factor.
Conditions: x is positive real tending to infinity; ∼ means the ratio tends to one, not exact equality.

Name: Digamma logarithmic derivative
Intuition: The digamma function measures relative change of gamma and turns its multiplicative recurrence into addition.
Conditions: z avoids 0,−1,−2,… for finite values; the recurrence is used where both sides are defined.
Example: ψ(n)=H_{n−1}−γ for positive integer n.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Recursion and iteration

Name: Polygamma reciprocal-power series
Intuition: Higher relative-growth derivatives of gamma are encoded by a convergent lattice sum.
Conditions: m≥1 is an integer and Re z>0; the series converges absolutely and locally uniformly.
Prerequisites: Digamma logarithmic derivative; Termwise differentiation of a function series

Name: Euler beta integral
Intuition: Beta balances two endpoint powers and separates total size from the share assigned to each coordinate.
Conditions: Re a>0 and Re b>0 for the integral; powers use the real logarithm on (0,1).
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Euler gamma integral; Multivariable change of variables

Name: Incomplete gamma decomposition
Intuition: Split the gamma mass at a threshold into accumulated and remaining portions.
Conditions: a>0 and x≥0 are real; these hypotheses ensure convergence and the stated decomposition.

Name: Error function and Gaussian mass
Intuition: The error function records accumulated Gaussian mass on a convenient scale.
Conditions: x is real; Φ is the standard normal CDF. The integral definition extends to an entire complex function.
Example: erf(0)=0 and erf(x)→1 as x→+∞.

Name: Gaussian tail asymptotic expansion
Intuition: Repeated integration by parts peels off successively smaller corrections to a Gaussian tail.
Conditions: x→+∞ on the real axis; (−1)!!=1. The infinite expression is asymptotic and generally divergent; truncate at finite order.
Example: Leading order is erfc(x)≈e^(−x²)/(√π x).
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Recursion and iteration
Prerequisites: Error function and Gaussian mass; Integration by parts

Name: Dawson integral and its differential equation
Intuition: An exponential integrating factor balances a rapidly growing integral to produce a bounded-scale response.
Conditions: x is real; the definition extends to an entire function; F(0)=0 selects the solution.
Example: F′(0)=1 and F is odd.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Integrating factor for a linear ODE

Name: Fresnel sine and cosine integrals
Intuition: Quadratic phase makes the oscillations speed up, causing cancellation without absolute integrability.
Conditions: x is real; as x→+∞, C(x) and S(x) converge conditionally to 1/2.
Example: The curve (C(x),S(x)) is a Cornu spiral.
Prerequisites: Improper integral on a half-line; Euler's formula

Name: Exponential integral E1
Intuition: An inverse-scale weight modifies exponential accumulation into a logarithmic singularity near zero.
Conditions: x>0 real; the displayed derivative follows on that interval. Complex continuation requires a branch choice.
Example: E1(x)=Γ(0,x), using the convergent upper incomplete gamma integral for x>0.

Name: Sine and cosine integrals
Intuition: Inverse-distance weighting accumulates oscillations; cancellation makes the infinite cosine tail converge.
Conditions: x>0 is real; sin(t)/t has continuous value 1 at t=0; the cosine tail is conditionally convergent.
Example: Si(x)→π/2 as x→+∞.

Name: Bessel function of the first kind
Intuition: A factorial-weighted power series provides oscillating functions adapted to radial coordinates.
Conditions: For the stated real-valued convention take x>0 and real ν; reciprocal gamma handles vanishing coefficients at its zeros. The series converges for every such x.
Prerequisites: Euler gamma integral; Taylor series of an analytic function

Name: Bessel differential equation
Intuition: Radial curvature adds a first derivative and an inverse-square angular contribution to an oscillator equation.
Conditions: x>0; ν is real. Jν is one solution; a second independent solution can be taken as Yν.
Example: For ν=0, a regular-at-zero solution is J0(x).
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Bessel order recurrence
Intuition: Neighboring angular orders are coupled by a short algebraic recurrence.
Conditions: x>0 and ν real; standard Bessel first-kind functions are used.
Prerequisites: Bessel function of the first kind

Name: Bessel derivative as neighboring orders
Intuition: Differentiating in radius can be traded for subtracting adjacent orders.
Conditions: x>0, real ν; derivatives use the same first-kind Bessel convention.
Prerequisites: Bessel function of the first kind; Derivative

Name: Bessel modes orthogonal with radial weight
Intuition: Radial eigenmodes are perpendicular when the area-element weight r is included.
Conditions: ν≥0, m,n≥1 integers; jν,n are distinct positive zeros of Jν. The regular radial solution is selected at zero.
Example: For ν=0 these modes represent radially symmetric Dirichlet data on a disk.
Prerequisites: Bessel differential equation; Regular Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville problem

Name: Large-argument Bessel oscillation
Intuition: Far from the origin, radial oscillations resemble cosine waves with an amplitude that decays as a square root.
Conditions: x→+∞ and ν is fixed real; the remainder inside brackets is additive, not relative near cosine zeros.
Example: J0(x) oscillates with phase x−π/4 and amplitude √(2/(πx)).
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Bessel function of the first kind

Name: Modified Bessel first-kind function
Intuition: Removing the alternating signs turns radial oscillation into exponential-type behavior.
Conditions: x>0 and real ν; the convergent series solves the displayed modified Bessel equation.
Prerequisites: Bessel function of the first kind

Name: Modified Bessel decaying solution
Intuition: A continuum of exponentially damped contributions selects the decaying modified radial solution.
Conditions: x>0, real ν. This representation converges and gives Kν=K−ν.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Exponentials and logarithms
Prerequisites: Modified Bessel first-kind function; Improper integral on a half-line

Name: Hankel combinations of Bessel solutions
Intuition: Complex combinations separate the two radial oscillatory phases.
Conditions: x>0, real ν; Jν,Yν use the standard real Bessel normalization. Incoming/outgoing labels depend on the time convention.
Example: For time dependence e^(−iωt), Hν^(1)(kr) has outgoing large-r phase.

Name: Spherical Bessel functions
Intuition: A half-order shift and a radial scale factor adapt cylindrical functions to three dimensions.
Conditions: n≥0 is an integer and x>0; j0 extends continuously to value 1 at zero.
Example: j1(x)=sin(x)/x²−cos(x)/x.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Bessel function of the first kind; Laplacian

Name: Airy equation and normalized solutions
Intuition: Airy functions describe the transition between oscillation and exponential behavior when a linear coefficient changes sign.
Conditions: x is real or complex; the displayed initial values uniquely specify the entire solution Ai. Bi denotes the conventional independent solution.
Example: Ai(x) decays for large positive x and oscillates for negative x.
Prerequisites: Constant-coefficient second-order linear equation; Euler gamma integral

Name: Airy positive-axis decay
Intuition: Integrating the local decay rate √x produces the characteristic x^(3/2) exponent.
Conditions: x tends to positive infinity; ∼ denotes ratio convergence for the decaying Ai solution.
Example: The exponent equals −∫₀ˣ√t dt.
Prerequisites: Airy equation and normalized solutions; Riemann integral

Name: Legendre polynomials by Rodrigues formula
Intuition: Repeated differentiation generates polynomials whose lower-degree moments cancel.
Conditions: n≥0 integer; x real or complex. The normalization is Pn(1)=1.

Name: Legendre orthogonality and normalization
Intuition: Legendre modes separate polynomial information into independent directions on a finite interval.
Conditions: m,n are nonnegative integers; Pn(1)=1.
Example: ∫₋₁¹x²dx=2/3 agrees with P1=x.
Prerequisites: Legendre polynomials by Rodrigues formula; Inner product

Name: Legendre polynomial eigenvalue equation
Intuition: One differential operator organizes every polynomial degree into its own eigenvalue.
Conditions: n≥0 integer; the polynomial identity holds for all x; the Sturm–Liouville interpretation uses −1<x<1 and regular endpoint behavior.
Example: P1=x has eigenvalue 2.
Prerequisites: Legendre polynomials by Rodrigues formula; Regular Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville problem

Name: Generating function for Legendre polynomials
Intuition: A single inverse-square-root kernel stores every Legendre polynomial as a coefficient.
Conditions: For real |x|≤1 and complex |t|<1; the square root is the branch equal to 1 at t=0.
Example: At x=1 the expression reduces to 1/(1−t).
Prerequisites: Legendre polynomials by Rodrigues formula; Ordinary generating function

Name: Relative rounding model
Intuition: Rounding behaves like a small relative perturbation to one exact arithmetic operation.
Conditions: Round to nearest in binary precision p; u=2^(−p); ∘ is +,−,× or ÷ with a finite normal exact result and nonzero divisor. Underflow and overflow are excluded.
Example: Binary64 has unit roundoff 2^(−53).

Name: Relative condition number of a scalar function
Intuition: Conditioning measures how much a small relative input error is magnified by the mathematical problem itself.
Conditions: f is differentiable near real x≠0 and f(x)≠0; this is a first-order local measure.
Example: For f(x)=x^a on x>0, κf=|a|.

Name: Linear-system condition number
Intuition: An invertible map is sensitive when it stretches some directions far more than others.
Conditions: A is an invertible square real or complex matrix; the first norm is an induced operator norm, the second is Euclidean.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Norm of a bounded linear operator; Singular value decomposition

Name: Residual-to-solution error bound
Intuition: A small equation defect certifies accuracy only after accounting for conditioning.
Conditions: A invertible, Ax=b≠0, compatible vector and induced matrix norms.
Example: A residual of 10^(−10) with κ=10^8 may certify only a 10^(−2) relative error.

Name: Normwise backward error of a linear solve
Intuition: Ask how much the input equations must change to make the computed answer exact.
Conditions: Euclidean vector and induced matrix norm; A,b not both zero and denominator positive. This equals the minimal common relative normwise perturbation bound for A and b.
Example: An exact solution has η=0 even if its problem is ill-conditioned.

Name: Horner nested polynomial evaluation
Intuition: Reuse each partial polynomial instead of computing powers separately.
Conditions: p(x)=∑k=0^n akx^k over real or complex arithmetic; the identity is exact before rounding.
Example: 1+2x+3x² becomes 1+x(2+3x).

Name: Bisection root bracketing
Intuition: Keep a sign-changing bracket and halve its uncertainty at every step.
Conditions: f continuous on [a0,b0], f(a0)f(b0)<0; [an,bn] is the bracket after n halvings and r is a root inside it.
Example: Ten halvings reduce a unit bracket to width 1/1024.

Name: Secant root iteration
Intuition: Estimate the derivative from two recent values and follow the resulting line to zero.
Conditions: Denominator nonzero; local convergence of order (1+√5)/2 holds near a simple root for sufficiently smooth f and sufficiently close suitable starting points. Global convergence is not guaranteed.
Example: Applied to x²−2, no derivative evaluation is needed.

Name: Newton iteration for nonlinear systems
Intuition: Solve the local linearized equations, then correct the current point.
Conditions: F:Rⁿ→Rⁿ is C² near a root with nonsingular Jacobian; sufficiently close starts give local quadratic convergence. Each step requires an invertible current Jacobian.
Example: Two intersecting nonlinear curves can be solved by a 2×2 Jacobian system.

Name: Broyden rank-one Jacobian update
Intuition: Repair a Jacobian approximation just enough to match the newest observed displacement.
Conditions: Real nonzero step sk=xk+1−xk; this is the good Broyden Jacobian update for rootfinding. Convergence needs additional local regularity and suitable initialization.
Example: The update satisfies Bk+1 sk=yk exactly.

Name: Polynomial interpolation remainder
Intuition: Interpolation error combines an unknown high derivative with an explicit node-placement factor.
Conditions: Distinct real nodes xj and x lie in an interval where f∈C^(n+1); ξ lies in their convex hull, and pn interpolates f at the nodes.
Example: For linear interpolation the error involves (x−x0)(x−x1)f″(ξ)/2.

Name: Newton divided-difference interpolation
Intuition: Add one node at a time while preserving every previously fitted value.
Conditions: Nodes are distinct; f[xi]=f(xi); the empty product is 1.
Example: Appending a node adds only one new highest-degree basis term.

Name: Barycentric polynomial evaluation
LaTeX: p(x)=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^n w_j f_j/(x-x_j)}{\sum_{j=0}^n w_j/(x-x_j)},\qquad w_j=\prod_{k\ne j}(x_j-x_k)^{-1}
Intuition: Common factors cancel from the Lagrange formula, yielding efficient repeated evaluation.
Conditions: Distinct nodes; x≠xj in the formula and p(xj)=fj by continuity. Exact weights are assumed for the polynomial identity.
Example: Multiplying every weight by the same nonzero constant leaves p unchanged.

Name: Lebesgue constant interpolation bound
Intuition: Approximation quality depends on both the best available polynomial and amplification caused by node placement.
Conditions: Distinct nodes in a compact real interval; f continuous; ℓj are Lagrange cardinal polynomials on that interval.
Example: Large Λn warns that tiny data errors may become large interpolation errors.
Prerequisites: Lagrange interpolation; Norm of a bounded linear operator

Name: Chebyshev root nodes
Intuition: Cluster nodes near interval endpoints to reduce the largest nodal product.
Conditions: j=0,…,n and n≥0; on [−1,1] the monic polynomial 2^(−n)Tn+1 minimizes the uniform norm among monic degree n+1 polynomials.
Example: For n=1 the nodes are ±1/√2.

Name: Natural cubic spline interpolation
Intuition: Join local cubic pieces smoothly rather than forcing one high-degree polynomial across all data.
Conditions: Strictly increasing real knots and real data; these conditions determine a unique natural cubic spline.
Example: For two knots the natural spline is the straight line between them.

Name: Second-order centered derivative formula
Intuition: Symmetric samples cancel the leading one-sided bias.
Conditions: f is C³ near x; h→0 with both sample points in the domain. The claim concerns truncation error before rounding.
Example: The formula differentiates every quadratic exactly.
Prerequisites: Forward finite difference; Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder

Name: Centered second-derivative stencil
Intuition: Compare the center with its neighbors to detect curvature.
Conditions: f∈C⁴ near x, h→0; all three sample points lie in the domain.
Example: For f=x² the stencil gives 2 exactly.

Name: Truncation–roundoff balance for a derivative
Intuition: Smaller steps reduce Taylor error but amplify errors in nearly equal sampled values.
Conditions: Centered first differences with smooth f, function-evaluation errors of magnitude O(u), and problem-dependent bounded constants; the scaling is not a universal step prescription.
Example: Making h arbitrarily tiny can worsen a numerical derivative.
Prerequisites: Second-order centered derivative formula; Relative rounding model

Name: Richardson extrapolation
Intuition: Combine two resolutions to cancel their shared leading error term.
Conditions: A(h)=A+ch^p+O(h^(p+q)) as h→0, with p,q>0 fixed and the same coefficient c for both scales.

Name: Composite midpoint quadrature
Intuition: Use each cell’s central value so the first-order local variation cancels.
Conditions: h=(b−a)/n, n≥1, a<b, f∈C²[a,b].
Example: On [0,1], one midpoint sample of x² gives 1/4 instead of 1/3.

Name: Gaussian quadrature exactness
Intuition: Choose both sample locations and weights to match twice as many polynomial moments.
Conditions: Positive integrable weight w on a finite interval, finite moments and support containing at least n+1 points; xj are zeros of its degree-n orthogonal polynomial.
Example: Two-point Gauss–Legendre integrates every cubic exactly.

Name: Gauss–Legendre nodes and weights
Intuition: Legendre roots and their slopes determine optimal polynomial integration samples on a symmetric interval.
Conditions: j=1,…,n are the distinct roots in (−1,1); Pn(1)=1; the integration interval is [−1,1].
Example: For n=2, nodes are ±1/√3 and both weights equal 1.

Name: Romberg extrapolation table
Intuition: Repeatedly remove even-power errors from nested trapezoidal estimates.
Conditions: 0≤j≤k; T is composite trapezoidal quadrature. Smoothness sufficient for the required Euler–Maclaurin error expansion is needed for predicted orders.
Example: R1,1 is the first Richardson-improved estimate.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Clenshaw–Curtis interpolatory quadrature
Intuition: Interpolate on an endpoint-clustered cosine grid and integrate the resulting polynomial.
Conditions: n≥1, j=0,…,n; In is the degree≤n polynomial interpolant. Exactness holds for all polynomials of degree≤n. Faster convergence needs regularity.
Example: At n=2 the nodes are −1,0,1 and the rule is Simpson’s rule.

Name: Householder elimination step for QR
Intuition: Reflect an entire column tail onto one coordinate axis in one norm-preserving operation.
Conditions: Real nonzero x; use sign(0)=1. Embedded reflectors successively zero entries below the diagonal.
Example: A sequence of reflectors produces QᵀA=R.

Name: Gaussian elimination and pivoted LU
Intuition: Eliminate one column at a time while storing the multipliers for later solves.
Conditions: A is nonsingular square; row pivoting selects a nonzero pivot. L is unit lower triangular, U upper triangular, P records row swaps; the update uses the current pivoted matrix.
Example: Solving Ax=b becomes Ly=Pb then Ux=y.
Prerequisites: Matrix multiplication; Inverse by the adjugate

Name: Dominant-eigenvector power iteration
Intuition: Repeated multiplication suppresses directions whose eigenvalues have smaller magnitude.
Conditions: A is diagonalizable with one simple eigenvalue λ1 satisfying |λ1|>|λj| for j>1; x0 has nonzero component along its eigenvector in the eigenbasis. Direction converges up to sign or complex phase.
Example: For diag(3,1), the second-to-first coordinate ratio shrinks by 1/3 per step.

Name: Shifted inverse eigenvector iteration
Intuition: Invert a shifted operator to make an eigenvalue near the shift become dominant.
Conditions: μ is not an eigenvalue; for convergence assume diagonalizable A, a unique eigenvalue closest to μ, and a nonzero initial component in its eigendirection.
Example: A shift near an interior eigenvalue targets it instead of the largest-magnitude one.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Recursion and iteration

Name: Hermite polynomials in Gaussian weight
Intuition: Gaussian derivatives reproduce the same envelope multiplied by polynomials.
Conditions: n≥0 integer; this is the physicists’ normalization, with weight e^(−x²).
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Hermite orthogonality
Intuition: The Gaussian-weighted inner product separates polynomial degrees.
Conditions: m,n≥0 integers; Hn is the physicists’ Hermite polynomial.
Example: ∫e^(−x²)(2x)²dx=2√π.

Name: Hermite exponential generating function
Intuition: A shifted Gaussian packages all Gaussian derivative polynomials.
Conditions: x,t complex; the series converges for every finite t. Physicists’ normalization is used.
Example: The coefficient of t² is 2x²−1=H2(x)/2.

Name: Generalized Laguerre polynomials
Intuition: Differentiation generates polynomials adapted to a power-weighted exponential on a half-line.
Conditions: n≥0 integer, α>−1, x>0; the expression extends as a polynomial to all x.

Name: Laguerre weighted orthogonality
Intuition: Gamma-weighted polynomial modes separate behavior on an unbounded positive interval.
Conditions: α>−1 and m,n are nonnegative integers.
Example: With α=0 every Ln has squared norm 1.

Name: Jacobi polynomial Rodrigues formula
Intuition: Independent endpoint exponents tailor a polynomial family to unequal endpoint behavior.
Conditions: n≥0 integer, α,β>−1 and −1<x<1; the result extends polynomially to all x.
Example: α=β=0 recovers Legendre polynomials.

Name: Chebyshev polynomials as multiple-angle cosines
Intuition: A cosine coordinate turns oscillation frequency into polynomial degree.
Conditions: n≥0 integer and θ real; the identity uniquely determines a real polynomial.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Chebyshev three-term recurrence
Intuition: Two neighboring polynomials generate the next without expanding large powers.
Conditions: n≥1 integer; x real or complex.

Name: Chebyshev weighted orthogonality
Intuition: The endpoint weight exactly compensates for stretching in the cosine coordinate.
Conditions: m,n≥0 integers; integrals are improper but convergent.
Example: T0 and T1 are orthogonal because the weighted integrand is odd.

Name: Gegenbauer generating function
Intuition: Changing one kernel exponent generates a family that includes Legendre polynomials.
Conditions: λ>0, real |x|≤1, complex |t|<1; the analytic branch equals 1 at t=0.
Example: λ=1/2 gives Cn^(1/2)=Pn.

Name: Christoffel–Darboux kernel identity
Intuition: A long orthogonal-polynomial sum telescopes to its last two modes.
Conditions: pj are orthogonal real polynomials for a positive measure with finite moments, hj=∫pj²dμ>0, kj their leading coefficients; x≠y. The diagonal is the continuous limit.
Example: The kernel reproduces polynomials of degree at most n.

Name: Gauss hypergeometric series
Intuition: A rational ratio between neighboring coefficients unifies many familiar special functions.
Example: 2F1(a,b;b;z)=(1−z)^(−a) on its analytic branch.

Name: Gauss hypergeometric differential equation
Intuition: Three regular singular points organize a large family of second-order equations.
Conditions: a,b,c complex; c avoids nonpositive integers for the standard series solution near z=0.
Example: Legendre’s equation follows from a=−n,b=n+1,c=1,z=(1−x)/2.

Name: Euler integral for the hypergeometric function
Intuition: Hypergeometric evaluation becomes an average of a power function under a beta-shaped weight.
Conditions: Re c>Re b>0 and z lies off [1,∞); use the principal branch for (1−zt)^(−a).
Example: At z=0 the beta normalization makes the result 1.
Prerequisites: Euler beta integral; Gauss hypergeometric series

Name: Gauss hypergeometric summation at one
Intuition: At the boundary argument one, the power kernel merges with a beta endpoint weight.
Conditions: c avoids nonpositive integers and Re(c−a−b)>0; reciprocal gamma interprets zeros where denominator factors have poles.
Example: For a=b=1,c=3 the value is 2.
Prerequisites: Euler integral for the hypergeometric function

Name: Confluent hypergeometric Kummer function
Intuition: Coalescing singularities leaves an entire power-series solution of a simpler hypergeometric equation.
Conditions: a,b complex, b not a nonpositive integer; the series converges for all complex z.
Example: 1F1(a;a;z)=e^z when a avoids forbidden denominator values.

Name: Generalized hypergeometric pFq series
Intuition: Products of rising factors encode many coefficient recurrences in one notation.
Conditions: No bj is a nonpositive integer. For nonterminating series: entire if p≤q; radius 1 if p=q+1; radius 0 if p>q+1. Boundary cases need further conditions.
Example: 0F0(z)=e^z and 0F1 relates to Bessel functions.

Name: Complete elliptic integral of the first kind
Intuition: A trigonometric integral gains a scale factor that becomes singular as the modulus approaches one.
Conditions: 0≤k<1 real; k is the modulus, not the parameter m=k².
Example: K(0)=π/2 and K(k)→∞ as k→1−.

Name: Complete elliptic integral of the second kind
Intuition: The elliptic second-kind integral adds weighted local lengths along an ellipse.
Conditions: 0≤k≤1 real; modulus convention k is used.
Example: An ellipse with semiaxes a≥b>0 has perimeter 4aE(√(1−b²/a²)).
Prerequisites: Arc length of a parametrized curve

Name: Arithmetic–geometric mean evaluation of K
Intuition: Alternating arithmetic and geometric averaging preserves an elliptic quantity while the two values merge rapidly.
Conditions: 0≤k<1; a0=1,b0=√(1−k²)>0; AGM is their common limit.
Example: For k=0 the iteration stays at 1 and K=π/2.
Prerequisites: Arithmetic mean; Geometric mean; Complete elliptic integral of the first kind

Name: Jacobi elliptic sine through inversion
Intuition: Invert elliptic arc accumulation to obtain nonlinear periodic analogues of sine and cosine.
Conditions: 0≤k<1, real u; φ is the continuously chosen real amplitude. Set dn(u,k)=√(1−k²sn²(u,k)).
Example: At k=0, sn(u,0)=sin u and cn(u,0)=cos u.
Prerequisites: Inverse function; Complete elliptic integral of the first kind

Name: Lambert W inverse relation
Intuition: W undoes a variable multiplied by its own exponential.
Conditions: The derivative formula is on any analytic branch away from z=0 and W=−1; W0′(0)=1 by continuation. Real W0 exists for z≥−1/e; W−1 is real on [−1/e,0).

Name: Riemann zeta Dirichlet series
Intuition: Zeta gathers reciprocal powers of every positive integer into one complex function.
Conditions: Re s>1 gives absolute convergence; analytic continuation elsewhere is a different representation and has a pole at s=1.

Name: Completed zeta reflection symmetry
Intuition: Gamma and pi factors reveal a reflection symmetry hidden in the original integer sum.
Conditions: The equality holds meromorphically; Λ has simple poles at s=0 and s=1. It is not a claim that the defining Dirichlet series converges everywhere.
Example: Values on the right half-plane determine continued values on the left.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Exponentials and logarithms
Prerequisites: Riemann zeta Dirichlet series; Euler gamma integral

Name: Zeta values at positive even integers
Intuition: Even reciprocal-power sums are rational multiples of corresponding powers of pi.
Conditions: n≥1 integer; Bernoulli numbers use t/(e^t−1)=∑Bm t^m/m! near zero.

Name: Hurwitz shifted zeta function
Intuition: Shift the integer lattice before accumulating reciprocal powers.
Conditions: a>0 real and Re s>1 for the series; the shift identity continues meromorphically in s.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Polylogarithm power series
Intuition: Polynomially damped geometric coefficients connect logarithms with zeta values.
Conditions: |z|<1 and s complex; the derivative holds there, including its continuous interpretation at zero. Other arguments need continuation and branches.
Example: Li1(z)=−log(1−z).

Name: Jacobi theta Gaussian lattice sum
Intuition: A Gaussian sampled across an integer lattice packages discrete and continuous scales together.
Conditions: t is positive real; the sum converges absolutely and locally uniformly. It equals θ3(0,e^(−πt)).

Name: Jacobi theta scale inversion
Intuition: A narrow Gaussian sampled densely has the same information as its reciprocal-scale Fourier lattice.
Conditions: t>0 real; ϑ(t)=∑n∈Z exp(−πn²t).
Example: At small t, ϑ(t)∼t^(−1/2).
Prerequisites: Jacobi theta Gaussian lattice sum; Fourier transform of a Gaussian

Name: Mellin transform
Intuition: Mellin analysis turns multiplicative scaling into an additive frequency coordinate.
Conditions: Use complex s in a strip where ∫₀∞x^(Re s−1)|f(x)|dx<∞. Outside it, continuation requires separate justification.
Example: The Mellin transform of e^(−x) is Γ(s) for Re s>0.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Improper integral on a half-line; Fourier transform

Name: Regularized incomplete beta function
Intuition: Normalize a partial beta integral to measure a fraction of total endpoint-weighted mass.
Conditions: a,b>0 and 0≤x≤1 real.

Name: Krylov subspace for a matrix action
Intuition: Repeated matrix action builds a small space containing progressively richer polynomial responses.
Conditions: A square real or complex, b nonzero, m≥1; the space may stop growing before dimension m.
Example: If b is an eigenvector, every Krylov space has dimension one.
Prerequisites: Basis and unique coordinates; Matrix multiplication

Name: Arnoldi orthogonal reduction
Intuition: Orthogonalize each new matrix action to represent the large operator by a small Hessenberg matrix.
Conditions: Columns of Qm span a Krylov space; exact arithmetic and no breakdown through step m; Hbar is (m+1)×m upper Hessenberg. At a breakdown the already-built subspace is invariant and a shorter relation applies.
Example: A zero new residual indicates an invariant Krylov subspace.
Prerequisites: Krylov subspace for a matrix action

Name: Lanczos three-term recurrence
Intuition: Hermitian symmetry reduces orthogonal Krylov construction to three neighboring vectors.
Conditions: A Hermitian, normalized start, exact arithmetic, and no breakdown; αj real and βj≥0. Finite precision can destroy orthogonality.
Example: The projected matrix Qm*AQm is tridiagonal.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Recursion and iteration

Name: GMRES minimum-residual iterate
Intuition: Choose the combination of explored directions that best satisfies the equations.
Conditions: A nonsingular square matrix, r0 nonzero until termination, and exact arithmetic; the minimizer is unique over the affine Krylov space. Restarting changes the global minimization property.
Example: Unrestarted GMRES solves the system in at most n steps in exact arithmetic; an earlier Arnoldi breakdown is a successful termination for nonsingular A.
Prerequisites: Krylov subspace for a matrix action

Name: Conjugate-gradient recurrence for SPD systems
Intuition: Use mutually A-orthogonal search directions so new corrections preserve earlier progress.
Conditions: A real symmetric positive definite; r0=b−Ax0,p0=r0; stop when residual is zero. Exact arithmetic gives termination in at most n steps.
Example: For A=I the first correction solves the system.

Name: Preconditioned linear system
Intuition: Change the shape of the equations using an easier approximate inverse.
Conditions: M is nonsingular and its action can be solved efficiently; the equation has the same solution as Ax=b. Convergence depends on more than condition number for general nonsymmetric A.
Example: A diagonal M rescales equations before iteration.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Geometry and distance

Name: Bauer–Fike eigenvalue perturbation bound
Intuition: A poorly conditioned eigenvector basis can amplify small matrix perturbations into large eigenvalue shifts.
Conditions: A complex diagonalizable square matrix, E arbitrary of the same size, μ any perturbed eigenvalue.
Example: For normal A choose unitary V, giving a bound of ‖E‖2.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Geometry and distance

Name: QR iteration for eigenvalues
Intuition: Repeated orthogonal similarities expose eigenvalues while preserving the underlying spectrum.
Conditions: Qk unitary, Rk upper triangular; shifts μk are specified. The similarity identity is exact; convergence needs suitable shifts and assumptions.
Example: For symmetric matrices, practical shifted iterations approach diagonal form.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Recursion and iteration

Name: Iterative refinement of a linear solve
Intuition: Recompute the remaining defect and solve for a correction using the existing factorization.
Conditions: A nonsingular; approximate correction solves are used computationally. Improvement requires sufficiently accurate residuals and controlled solve error relative to conditioning.
Example: In exact arithmetic one exact correction solve recovers the exact solution.

Name: Jacobi stationary linear iteration
Intuition: Update every coordinate from the old iterate using only its own diagonal solve.
Conditions: D has nonzero diagonal; convergence for every start is equivalent to spectral radius ρ(−D⁻¹(L+U))<1. Strict row diagonal dominance is sufficient.
Example: All coordinates can be updated in parallel.

Name: Gauss–Seidel linear iteration
Intuition: Use each freshly updated coordinate immediately in subsequent equations.
Conditions: D+L nonsingular; convergence holds for symmetric positive definite A or strictly row diagonally dominant A. It is not guaranteed for every invertible A.
Example: One sweep solves a lower-triangular system with the previous upper-triangular contribution.

Name: Backward Euler time step
Intuition: Use the slope at the unknown endpoint, trading an implicit solve for stronger damping.
Conditions: ODE y′=f(t,y), h>0. Under standard smoothness/Lipschitz conditions and well-solved implicit steps, the global order is one.
Example: For y′=λy, amplification is 1/(1−hλ).

Name: Implicit trapezoidal ODE step
Intuition: Average initial and final slopes to obtain a second-order implicit step.
Conditions: Smooth Lipschitz f and sufficiently small h for the chosen implicit solve; global order two.
Example: For y′=λy, amplification is (1+hλ/2)/(1−hλ/2).

Name: Explicit midpoint Runge–Kutta step
Intuition: Predict the midpoint, then use its slope for the whole interval.
Conditions: Smooth Lipschitz f; fixed step h; global order two under standard bounded-derivative hypotheses.
Example: For y′=λy, amplification is 1+hλ+(hλ)²/2.

Name: Two-step Adams–Bashforth method
Intuition: Extrapolate the recent slope history instead of evaluating new intermediate stages.
Conditions: Uniform h, fn=f(tn,yn); a second-order accurate starting value and smooth Lipschitz f give global order two.
Example: The negative old-slope weight extrapolates a rising slope trend.

Name: Second-order backward differentiation formula
Intuition: Differentiate a quadratic through recent states at its newest endpoint.
Conditions: Uniform step h; sufficiently smooth Lipschitz problem, accurate start, and solvable implicit equations; global order two.
Example: For a constant solution both sides vanish when f=0.

Name: General Runge–Kutta stage formula
LaTeX: k_i=f(t_n+c_i h,y_n+h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}k_j),\qquad y_{n+1}=y_n+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_i k_i
Intuition: A table of coefficients specifies how trial slopes inform one another and the final update.
Conditions: Finite s and specified real coefficients; ai,j=0 for j≥i makes the method explicit. Consistency and higher order require coefficient conditions.
Example: Classical RK4 is one four-stage explicit tableau.

Name: Embedded Runge–Kutta error estimate
Intuition: Reuse the same stages in two accuracy formulas and let their disagreement suggest a step size.
Conditions: The pair’s difference is assumed O(h^(p+1)); η∈(0,1) is a safety factor; use scaled error norms and practical bounds. The estimate is not a universal rigorous error certificate.
Example: A large estimated error reduces the proposed step.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Absolute stability region of a time integrator
Intuition: A numerical method must avoid amplifying modes that the differential equation damps.
Conditions: Apply a one-step method to y′=λy; R is its amplification function where defined. This linear test does not settle all nonlinear stability.
Example: Forward Euler has R(z)=1+z and stability disk |1+z|≤1.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: A-stability of one-step methods
Intuition: All linearly decaying modes remain nonamplifying regardless of step size.
Conditions: S is the absolute stability region; boundary points are interpreted where the amplification function is defined. A-stability does not guarantee accuracy for large steps.
Example: Backward Euler and implicit trapezoidal are A-stable.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Absolute stability region of a time integrator

Name: Zero-stability root condition
Intuition: Parasitic recurrence modes must not grow as the step size goes to zero.
Conditions: For a fixed-step linear multistep method ∑αjyn+j=h∑βjfn+j with αk≠0, zero-stability is equivalent to the displayed condition on every root of ρ.
Example: A repeated root at ζ=1 causes polynomial growth in the homogeneous recurrence.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Characteristic-root solution of a linear recurrence

Name: Consistency plus zero-stability gives convergence
Intuition: Small local defects accumulate safely only if the recurrence does not amplify them uncontrollably.
Conditions: Fixed-step linear multistep methods for sufficiently smooth well-posed Lipschitz ODE initial-value problems, with convergent starting values.
Example: A locally accurate but zero-unstable scheme may diverge as h→0.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Recursion and iteration

Name: Explicit centered heat-equation scheme
Intuition: Diffusion updates each grid value by averaging it with its neighbors.
Conditions: Uniform one-dimensional grid, κ>0, standard periodic or homogeneous Dirichlet setting; r≤1/2 ensures the usual explicit stability and nonnegative weights.
Example: At r=1/2 the next value is the mean of its two neighbors.
Prerequisites: Heat or diffusion equation; Centered second-derivative stencil

Name: Crank–Nicolson diffusion discretization
Intuition: Average diffusion at the beginning and end of a step to gain second-order time accuracy.
Conditions: Lh is the semidiscrete diffusion matrix with nonpositive real eigenvalues in a stable symmetric spatial discretization. The method is linearly unconditionally stable but may have sign oscillations for stiff modes.
Example: A Fourier mode with eigenvalue λ≤0 is multiplied by (1+Δtλ/2)/(1−Δtλ/2).

Name: First-order upwind advection scheme
Intuition: A positive-speed signal is sampled from the side where information arrives.
Conditions: c>0; uniform grid; 0≤ν≤1 for the convex-combination stability property. For negative speed reverse the spatial direction.
Example: At ν=1 the data shift exactly one cell per step.

Name: CFL numerical-domain condition
Intuition: A numerical stencil must reach every point that can influence the exact solution.
Conditions: This bound is necessary for convergence of explicit nearest-neighbor schemes for constant-speed advection; wider or implicit stencils have different conditions. It is not sufficient for stability by itself.
Example: A physical characteristic cannot cross more than one cell in one such explicit step.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Method of lines semidiscretization
Intuition: Discretize space first and leave time to an ODE solver.
Conditions: A spatial grid and boundary treatment define Dxx; consistency and stability of both discretizations are needed for convergence.
Example: The largest diffusion eigenvalues scale like −1/(Δx)², making fine grids stiff.

Name: Galerkin stiffness system for Poisson
Intuition: Require the residual to vanish against a finite collection of test functions.
Conditions: Linearly independent basis functions φj in H0¹(Ω), bounded Lipschitz Ω, f∈L²; K is positive definite for the Dirichlet Poisson problem.
Example: Piecewise-linear basis functions give sparse couplings between neighboring mesh vertices.
Prerequisites: Weak formulation of the Dirichlet Poisson problem

Name: Céa quasi-optimal Galerkin error
Intuition: A stable Galerkin solution is nearly as accurate as the best approximation in its chosen space.
Conditions: Real Hilbert V; bilinear a bounded by M and coercive with α>0; Vh a finite-dimensional subspace; exact and Galerkin solutions have the same continuous linear right-hand functional.
Example: For the energy norm of a symmetric coercive form the factor can be 1.

Name: Shooting method for a two-point boundary problem
Intuition: Guess a missing initial slope, integrate forward, and adjust until the far boundary is met.
Conditions: A second-order ODE with a well-defined initial-value solution reaching b for candidate slopes; solutions and their sensitivities may be ill-conditioned.
Example: A scalar root solve adjusts s to enforce y(b)=β.

Name: Differentiation matrix on interpolation nodes
Intuition: Differentiate each cardinal basis function once, then reuse the resulting matrix on any data vector.
Conditions: n+1 distinct nodes; pj=p(xj), and ℓj are their degree-n Lagrange basis polynomials. Exactness is polynomial, not arbitrary-data accuracy.
Example: D times the constant vector is zero.

Name: Adaptive Simpson local error estimate
LaTeX: E\approx\frac{S_{\rm fine}-S_{\rm coarse}}{15},\qquad I\approx S_{\rm fine}+\frac{S_{\rm fine}-S_{\rm coarse}}{15}
Intuition: Compare one Simpson panel with two half-panels and spend more samples where they disagree.
Conditions: Smooth integrand in an asymptotic error regime; Sfine uses two half-panels on the same interval. The estimate can miss narrow unsampled features and is not a universal certificate.
Example: A small estimated local error lets a panel remain coarse.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Gaussian quadrature remainder
Intuition: The first missed derivative is multiplied by the squared nodal polynomial’s weighted size.
Conditions: f∈C^(2n)[a,b], positive integrable weight w with finite moments, πn monic orthogonal degree n, and Gaussian Qn; ξ∈(a,b).
Example: For a function with f^(2n)≥0, Gaussian quadrature underestimates its weighted integral.

Name: Clenshaw evaluation of a Chebyshev series
Intuition: Evaluate a whole polynomial expansion backward using its basis recurrence.
Conditions: The backward recurrence runs k=n,…,1; finite coefficients and real or complex x. Formula is exact before rounding.
Example: This avoids expanding Chebyshev polynomials into monomials.

Name: Givens plane rotation for elimination
Intuition: Rotate two coordinates to remove one entry while preserving their length.
Conditions: a,b real and not both zero; use a scaled hypot evaluation numerically to avoid unnecessary overflow.
Example: The pair (3,4) rotates to (5,0).

Name: Differentiation under an integral
Intuition: Differentiate a continuously changing accumulation when one integrable bound controls its local rate.
Conditions: Near t0, f(t,x) is differentiable in t almost everywhere, |∂tf|≤g∈L¹, and f(t0,·)∈L¹. Then the identity holds at t0 if the pointwise derivatives exist there.
Example: Differentiating a gamma integral introduces a factor log x.

Name: Leibniz rule with moving integration limits
Intuition: Accumulation changes because the integrand changes and because its boundaries move.
Conditions: a,b are C¹ and f,∂tf continuous on a neighborhood of the region swept by the limits.
Example: For ∫₀ᵗx²dx, the derivative is t².
Prerequisites: Chain rule; Fundamental theorem of calculus

Name: Faà di Bruno higher chain rule
Intuition: Higher derivatives distribute repeated differentiations among inner-function factors in every possible grouping.
Conditions: n≥1 integer; f and g are C^n on appropriate neighborhoods; each mj is a nonnegative integer.

Name: Euler identity for homogeneous functions
Intuition: A scaling law determines the directional derivative along rays.
Conditions: f is C¹ on an open cone in Rⁿ; homogeneity holds for positive t; k is real.
Example: For a quadratic form, x·∇Q=2Q.

Name: Hessian chain rule for a scalar composite
Intuition: Curvature comes both from the outer function and from bending of the inner coordinates.
Conditions: g:Rⁿ→Rᵐ and f:Rᵐ→R are C² on compatible open domains; all terms are evaluated at x unless indicated.
Example: For affine g the second sum vanishes.

Name: Integral mean-value formula for vector maps
Intuition: The finite change of a map is the accumulated directional derivative along a straight segment.
Conditions: F:C¹(U,Rᵐ), U⊂Rⁿ open, and the entire segment [x,y] lies in U.
Example: A uniform bound ‖DF‖≤L on the segment gives ‖F(y)−F(x)‖≤L‖y−x‖.

Name: Hadamard factorization near a vanishing point
Intuition: A smooth function vanishing at the origin contains one coordinate factor in every term.
Conditions: f is C∞ on a star-shaped open neighborhood of 0 in Rⁿ; each gj is smooth there. C^k versions lose at most one derivative.
Example: In one variable, f(x)−f(0)=xg(x).

Name: Total variation of a real function
Intuition: Count all upward and downward movement, including changes that cancel in the net displacement.
Conditions: f:[a,b]→R; bounded variation means the supremum over finite partitions is finite.
Example: For monotone f, Var f=|f(b)−f(a)|.

Name: Jordan decomposition of a BV function
Intuition: Separate total motion into accumulated upward and downward movement.
Conditions: A real function on [a,b] has bounded variation iff it is a difference of two bounded increasing functions. One choice uses V(x)=Var[a,x]f and g=(V+f)/2,h=(V−f)/2.
Example: A smooth oscillating function splits according to the positive and negative parts of its derivative.
Prerequisites: Total variation of a real function

Name: Absolute continuity and integral recovery
LaTeX: f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x g(t)dt,\quad g\in L^1[a,b]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\in AC[a,b]
Intuition: Absolute continuity means every change is accounted for by an integrable rate, with no hidden singular movement.
Conditions: Real f on a compact interval; in this representation f′=g almost everywhere. Equivalent interval definition requires small total interval length to force small total increments.
Example: The Cantor function is continuous and BV but is not absolutely continuous.
Prerequisites: Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Riemann–Stieltjes integral
Intuition: Accumulate f according to increments of another function rather than uniform coordinate increments.
Conditions: A sufficient setting is f continuous and α of bounded variation on [a,b], with arbitrary tagged partitions.
Example: If α is C¹, ∫f dα=∫fα′dx.
Prerequisites: Riemann integral; Total variation of a real function

Name: Stieltjes integration by parts
Intuition: Exchange which factor supplies increments while keeping the boundary product.
Conditions: A sufficient setting is real continuous f,g of bounded variation on [a,b]. If both may jump, extra conventions or jump corrections are needed.
Example: With g(x)=x the formula recovers ∫f dx+∫x df=[xf].

Name: Hölder continuity seminorm
Intuition: A power law bounds how quickly values can separate across short distances.
Conditions: 0<α≤1 on a metric subset of Euclidean space; α=1 is Lipschitz continuity.
Example: √x is Hölder-1/2 on [0,1] but not Lipschitz there.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Geometry and distance

Name: Almost-everywhere differentiability of Lipschitz maps
LaTeX: f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ Lipschitz}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Df(x)\text{ exists a.e.}
Intuition: A global slope bound forces a genuine linear approximation at almost every point.
Conditions: Lebesgue almost everywhere; local Lipschitz continuity gives the local version. Differentiability means total Fréchet differentiability, not merely coordinate derivatives.
Example: The function |x| fails to differentiate at 0 but differentiates elsewhere.

Name: Egorov almost-uniform convergence
LaTeX: f_n\to f\ \text{a.e.}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists E:\ \mu(E)<\varepsilon,\ f_n\to f\text{ uniformly on }X\setminus E
Intuition: Remove a small exceptional region and pointwise convergence becomes uniform.
Conditions: Measurable finite-valued functions on a finite measure space; convergence almost everywhere. The removed set depends on ε.
Example: On [0,1], xn converges uniformly away from a small neighborhood of 1.
Prerequisites: Uniform convergence; Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Lusin approximation by continuous restrictions
LaTeX: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists K\subset E\text{ compact}:\ |E\setminus K|<\varepsilon,\quad f|_K\text{ continuous}
Intuition: A measurable function looks continuous after removing a set of arbitrarily small measure.
Conditions: E⊂Rⁿ measurable with finite Lebesgue measure; f:E→R measurable and finite almost everywhere, adjusted on a null set if needed.
Example: Even a discontinuous measurable function has continuous restrictions on nearly all of a bounded interval.
Prerequisites: Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Convergence in measure
Intuition: Large errors are allowed, but the region where they occur must shrink in measure.
Conditions: Measurable functions on a fixed measure space; finite-measure assumptions are needed for some relations with almost-everywhere convergence.
Example: The spikes n·1[0,1/n] converge in measure to zero but not in L¹.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Uniform integrability by tail control
Intuition: No member of the family can hide a fixed amount of integral mass in arbitrarily tall spikes.
Conditions: A family of integrable functions on a finite measure space; this tail condition also yields a uniform L¹ bound.
Example: A common L¹ dominating function implies uniform integrability.
Prerequisites: Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Vitali convergence theorem
Intuition: Small bad sets cannot obstruct convergence if they also cannot carry substantial mass.
Conditions: Finite measure space; fn integrable, f finite almost everywhere and measurable. The hypotheses imply f∈L¹.
Example: The spike family n·1[0,1/n] fails uniform integrability, explaining its missing L¹ limit.
Prerequisites: Convergence in measure; Uniform integrability by tail control

Name: Jordan decomposition of a finite signed measure
Intuition: Separate positive and negative mass on disjoint measurable supports.
Conditions: ν is a finite signed measure; ν± are unique finite positive mutually singular measures.
Example: For density g, ν± have densities max(±g,0).
Prerequisites: Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Total variation measure and integral bound
Intuition: Partition mass finely enough that opposite signs cannot cancel each other.
Conditions: ν finite real or complex measure; supremum over finite measurable partitions of E; f integrable with respect to |ν|.
Example: For ν=gμ, |ν|=|g|μ.
Prerequisites: Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Lebesgue decomposition of measures
Intuition: Separate a measure into a density visible to the reference measure and mass on a reference-null set.
Conditions: μ,ν are σ-finite positive measures; f≥0 measurable and νs positive are unique up to μ-null changes of f.
Example: Lebesgue measure plus a point mass splits into continuous density 1 and a singular atom.

Name: Carathéodory measurable-set criterion
Intuition: A measurable set cuts every test set without creating or losing outer mass.
Conditions: μ* is an outer measure on all subsets of X. Sets E satisfying this criterion form a σ-algebra, and μ* restricted to it is a complete measure.
Example: Intervals satisfy the criterion for Lebesgue outer measure.
Prerequisites: Union of sets; Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Completeness of Lp spaces
Intuition: Approximations that become mutually close have a limit inside the same normed function space.
Conditions: Any measure space; functions are identified almost everywhere; the Cauchy condition is as m,n→∞.
Example: An absolutely summable series of Lp norms yields convergence of the function series in Lp.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Lp norm of a function; Cauchy criterion for convergence

Name: Dual representation of Lp functionals
Intuition: Every continuous linear measurement of an Lp function is integration against a conjugate-exponent weight.
Conditions: Real Lp spaces on a σ-finite measure space, 1≤p<∞, 1/p+1/q=1. Complex conventions may insert conjugation. The statement excludes the full dual of L∞.
Example: At p=2 this is Hilbert-space Riesz representation.

Name: Interpolation inequality for Lp norms
Intuition: Control at two integrability exponents supplies control between them.

Name: Baire category theorem
Intuition: A complete space cannot be assembled from countably many closed pieces that are all locally thin.
Conditions: X is a nonempty complete metric space; interiors are relative to X. Equivalently, countable intersections of dense open sets are dense.
Example: R cannot be a countable union of closed sets with empty interior.

Name: Uniform boundedness principle
Intuition: Pointwise bounded responses force a common operator bound when the input space is complete.
Conditions: X Banach, Y normed, and each Tα:X→Y bounded linear; arbitrary indexed families are allowed.
Example: A weakly convergent sequence in a Banach space is norm bounded.
Prerequisites: Baire category theorem; Norm of a bounded linear operator

Name: Banach open mapping theorem
LaTeX: T:X\twoheadrightarrow Y\text{ bounded linear}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T(U)\text{ open for every open }U
Intuition: A surjective continuous linear map between complete spaces cannot flatten every neighborhood arbitrarily.
Conditions: X,Y Banach over R or C; surjectivity is essential.
Example: A bijective bounded linear map between Banach spaces has continuous inverse.
Prerequisites: Norm of a bounded linear operator; Baire category theorem

Name: Bounded inverse theorem
Intuition: An algebraically reversible bounded map between Banach spaces has a stable continuous inverse.
Conditions: X and Y are Banach spaces; both completeness assumptions matter.
Example: A bijective bounded operator has ‖Tx‖≥c‖x‖ for some c>0.

Name: Closed graph theorem
LaTeX: x_n\to x,\ Tx_n\to y\Longrightarrow y=Tx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\text{ bounded}
Intuition: A linear operator defined everywhere is continuous if its graph admits no missing limit points.
Conditions: T:X→Y linear, defined on all of Banach X, with Y Banach. Closed unbounded operators can exist on proper domains.
Example: Differentiation is not bounded on C[0,1] with the sup norm and cannot be an everywhere-defined closed derivative there.

Name: Weak convergence in a Banach space
Intuition: Every fixed continuous linear measurement settles down, even if norm distance does not.
Conditions: X is a Banach space; X* consists of bounded scalar-valued linear functionals.
Example: An orthonormal sequence in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space converges weakly to zero but has norm one.
Prerequisites: Norm of a bounded linear operator

Name: Weak-star convergence of dual functionals
Intuition: Compare functionals only through their evaluations on original-space vectors.
Conditions: ℓn,ℓ∈X*, X normed; weak-star topology is σ(X*,X). It can differ from weak topology on X*.
Example: Bounded linear functionals may converge on every input without converging in operator norm.
Prerequisites: Weak convergence in a Banach space

Name: Banach–Alaoglu compactness
Intuition: A bounded family of linear measurements is compact when observed one input at a time.
Conditions: X normed. Weak-star compactness does not automatically mean sequential compactness; if X is separable, the dual ball is weak-star metrizable and sequentially compact.
Example: Bounded L∞ functions admit weak-star convergent subnets when viewed as the dual of L¹ in the standard σ-finite setting.

Name: Canonical embedding and reflexivity
LaTeX: J:X\to X^{**},\quad Jx(\ell)=\ell(x),\qquad X\text{ reflexive}\iff J(X)=X^{**}
Intuition: A space is reflexive when measuring its measurements introduces no genuinely new vectors.
Conditions: X is Banach; J is an isometric embedding. For 1<p<∞, Lp is reflexive on standard measure spaces; infinite-dimensional L¹ and L∞ need not be.
Example: Every Hilbert space is reflexive.

Name: Norm is weakly lower semicontinuous
Intuition: Weak limits can lose visible norm but cannot acquire more than the limiting lower bound.
Conditions: X normed and weak convergence defined through its continuous dual; sequence formulation shown.
Example: An orthonormal sequence weakly tends to zero, so its norm can drop from one to zero.
Prerequisites: Weak convergence in a Banach space

Name: Adjoint operator between continuous duals
Intuition: Pull an output measurement backward to become a measurement on the input.
Conditions: T:X→Y bounded linear between normed spaces; duals contain bounded linear functionals.
Example: For matrices, dual-coordinate representation is transpose, with complex conjugation under Hermitian identifications.
Prerequisites: Dual space and pullback of linear functionals

Name: Compact linear operator
Intuition: A compact operator turns bounded input families into outputs with convergent subsequences.
Conditions: T:X→Y bounded linear, X,Y Banach; BX is the closed unit ball. In metric spaces this is equivalent to every bounded sequence having an image-convergent subsequence.
Example: An integral operator with continuous kernel on a compact interval is compact on C[a,b].
Prerequisites: Norm of a bounded linear operator

Name: Spectral expansion of a compact self-adjoint operator
LaTeX: Tx=\sum_j\lambda_j\langle e_j,x\rangle e_j,\qquad \lambda_j\to0\text{ if infinitely many nonzero eigenvalues}
Intuition: An infinite-dimensional symmetric compact operator decomposes into orthogonal modes whose strengths fade away.
Conditions: T compact self-adjoint on a Hilbert space; ej form an orthonormal basis of the closure of ran T for nonzero eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity; the sum converges in norm. The inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot and linear in the second.
Example: A compact symmetric integral kernel has such an eigenfunction expansion.
Prerequisites: Compact linear operator; Spectral theorem in finite dimensions

Name: Fredholm alternative for compact perturbations
Intuition: A compact perturbation of identity fails to invert only through finite-dimensional compatibility obstructions.
Conditions: K compact on a Hilbert space; range is closed. If I−K is not invertible, its kernel is nonzero and finite-dimensional.
Example: Solvability of (I−K)u=f requires f to be orthogonal to adjoint null vectors.

Name: Resolvent and spectrum of a bounded operator
Intuition: Probe an operator by asking which shifts can be stably inverted.
Conditions: T bounded linear on a nonzero complex Banach space. In infinite dimensions, spectrum can contain values with no eigenvector.
Example: The unilateral shift has spectral points that are not all eigenvalues.
Prerequisites: Norm of a bounded linear operator

Name: Resolvent identity
Intuition: Changing the spectral parameter factors into two inverse responses and one scalar difference.
Conditions: z,w in the resolvent set of the same bounded operator T.
Example: Taking w→z gives R′(z;T)=−R(z;T)².
Prerequisites: Resolvent and spectrum of a bounded operator

Name: Gelfand spectral radius formula
Intuition: Long-run root growth of operator powers reveals the outer radius of the spectrum.
Conditions: T bounded on a nonzero complex Banach space; any operator norm induced by the fixed Banach norm may be used.
Example: A nilpotent operator has spectral radius zero even if its norm is large.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Recursion and iteration
Prerequisites: Resolvent and spectrum of a bounded operator

Name: Real Stone–Weierstrass theorem
Intuition: An algebra of simple functions approximates every continuous function if it distinguishes points and includes constants.
Conditions: K compact Hausdorff; A a real subalgebra of C(K,R), containing constants and separating every pair of distinct points. Complex versions also require closure under conjugation.
Example: Real polynomials are dense in continuous functions on a compact interval.

Name: Dini monotone convergence theorem
Intuition: On a compact space, monotone continuous approximation to a continuous limit cannot hide a persistent moving error.
Conditions: K compact; pointwise monotone convergence, either decreasing or increasing; all functions and the limit are real-valued continuous.
Example: Continuous monotone approximations to a continuous target on [0,1] converge uniformly.

Name: Hilbert operator norm-square identity
Intuition: The squared size of an operator is encoded by its positive self-adjoint energy operator.
Conditions: T bounded between Hilbert spaces; adjoints use the Hilbert inner product and norms are operator norms.
Example: For a matrix, the largest eigenvalue of A*A is σmax(A)².
Prerequisites: Adjoint of a linear map; Norm of a bounded linear operator

Name: Dirac point-evaluation distribution
Intuition: A point mass is described by what it does to test functions instead of by a finite density.
Conditions: a∈Rⁿ; φ∈Cc∞(Rⁿ). δa is both a positive measure and a distribution; it is not an ordinary integrable function.
Example: Convolution with δ0 leaves a function unchanged.

Name: Cauchy principal-value distribution 1/x
Intuition: Symmetric cancellation extracts a finite response from a nonintegrable singular kernel.
Conditions: φ∈Cc∞(R); the limit is symmetric around zero. It is not an absolutely convergent Lebesgue integral near zero.
Example: The odd singularity cancels against the constant term φ(0).
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Limits and convergence

Name: Derivative of a jump is a delta
Intuition: A sudden unit jump contributes a point impulse to the generalized derivative.
Conditions: Equality is in distributions on R; changing H(0) has no effect.
Example: A piecewise smooth function with jump J at a gains Jδa in its distributional derivative.
Prerequisites: Dirac point-evaluation distribution; Derivative of a distribution

Name: Delta under a smooth scalar map
Intuition: Each simple zero contributes point mass weighted by the reciprocal local stretching.
Conditions: g:R→R smooth; zeros are simple and locally finite on the test-function support. The pullback distribution is defined under this transversality condition.

Name: Convolution of a distribution with a test function
Intuition: Slide a smooth probe across a generalized function to obtain an ordinary smooth response.
Conditions: T∈D′(Rⁿ), φ∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); the result is C∞. More general distribution pairs require support or growth conditions.
Example: δa*φ=φ(·−a).

Name: Schwartz rapidly decreasing functions
Intuition: A Schwartz function and every derivative decay faster than any inverse polynomial.
Conditions: α,β range over all nonnegative multi-indices. The displayed seminorms define the Schwartz topology.
Example: The Gaussian e^(−|x|²) is Schwartz.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Limits and convergence

Name: Tempered distributions
LaTeX: \mathcal S^\prime(\mathbb R^n)=\{\text{continuous linear functionals on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\}
Intuition: Polynomial-growth generalized functions act on rapidly decaying probes.
Conditions: Continuity is with respect to the Schwartz seminorm topology. Every polynomially bounded locally integrable function defines one; arbitrary distributions need not be tempered.
Example: Dirac masses and polynomials are tempered distributions.

Name: Fourier transform on Schwartz space and its dual
LaTeX: \widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)e^{-ix\cdot\xi}dx,\quad\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S,\quad\langle\widehat T,\varphi\rangle=\langle T,\widehat\varphi\rangle
Intuition: Rapid decay and smoothness exchange roles under Fourier transformation, and duality extends the transform beyond functions.
Conditions: The displayed unnormalized negative-phase transform is a continuous automorphism of S; inverse has factor (2π)^(−n). The dual definition uses the bilinear distribution pairing.
Example: With this convention, the Fourier transform of δ0 is the constant distribution 1.

Name: Poisson summation formula
Intuition: Sampling in space becomes periodic frequency sampling on the reciprocal lattice.
Conditions: f∈S(Rⁿ); Fourier convention is fhat(ξ)=∫f(x)e^(−ix·ξ)dx. Both sums converge absolutely.
Example: Applying the identity to exp(−πt|x|²) gives theta scale inversion.
Prerequisites: Fourier transform; Schwartz rapidly decreasing functions
