Name: Sobolev inequality on Euclidean space
Intuition: An integrable gradient forces stronger integrability of the function.
Conditions: n≥2, 1≤p<n, initially u∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); extension holds in the corresponding homogeneous completion or W0¹,p setting.
Example: In dimension 3, an L² gradient controls the L6 norm.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Geometry and distance

Name: Morrey Hölder estimate
Intuition: A sufficiently integrable gradient prevents sharp small-scale jumps and creates a continuous representative.
Conditions: p>n, initially u∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); W¹,p functions have a Hölder representative with exponent 1−n/p.
Example: In one dimension p=2 gives a 1/2-Hölder bound.

Name: Compact Sobolev embedding
Intuition: Derivative control prevents bounded function sequences from shifting or oscillating too freely inside a bounded region.
Conditions: Ω bounded open in Rⁿ, 1≤p<n, p*=np/(n−p). The strict inequality q<p* is essential in general; zero-boundary space is used.
Example: A bounded H0¹ sequence in a bounded three-dimensional domain has an L²-convergent subsequence.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Boundary trace of a Sobolev function
Intuition: A function without pointwise values everywhere can still have a well-defined boundary restriction.
Conditions: Ω bounded with C¹ boundary, 1≤p<∞; trace is the bounded extension of ordinary restriction for smooth functions, with surface measure on ∂Ω.
Example: H0¹ functions have zero trace.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Limits and convergence

Name: Hardy inverse-distance inequality
Intuition: Gradient control limits how much mass a function can place near an inverse-distance singularity.
Conditions: 1<p<n and u∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); the singular point is the origin.
Example: In dimension 3 with p=2, ∫|u|²/|x|²≤4∫|∇u|².
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Geometry and distance

Name: Sobolev chain rule
Intuition: A smooth scalar change of a weakly differentiable function obeys the expected local derivative law.
Conditions: u∈W¹,p(Ω), 1≤p<∞; F∈C¹(R), F′ bounded and F(0)=0. Then F(u)∈W¹,p even when Ω has infinite measure.
Example: F(s)=tanh s preserves W¹,p and has bounded derivative.

Name: Sobolev product rule
Intuition: Multiplication remains compatible with weak derivatives when bounded factors keep all products integrable.
Conditions: u,v∈W¹,p(Ω)∩L∞(Ω), 1≤p<∞; then uv∈W¹,p(Ω). More general exponent versions need separate Hölder conditions.
Example: Products of bounded H¹ functions remain H¹.

Name: Hardy–Littlewood maximal weak bound
Intuition: Test every local averaging scale and control how much space can have a large average.
Conditions: f∈L¹(Rⁿ), λ>0; centered Euclidean balls and Lebesgue measure are used.
Example: A narrow spike may raise nearby averages, but the large-average region has controlled measure.

Name: Marcinkiewicz weak-to-strong interpolation
Intuition: Control of rare large outputs at two exponents yields full norm control between them.
Conditions: T sublinear with weak-type bounds on compatible measure spaces; 1≤p0<p<p1<∞. Lp,∞ denotes the weak norm supλ>0 λ μ(|g|>λ)^(1/p).
Example: The result is a central step in upgrading maximal-operator bounds.

Name: Hilbert transform and its Fourier multiplier
Intuition: An odd singular kernel rotates the phases of positive and negative frequencies in opposite directions.
Conditions: Initially f Schwartz; Fourier convention exp(−ixξ); the transform extends boundedly on Lp(R) for 1<p<∞, not strongly on L¹ or L∞.
Example: On nonzero Fourier modes, applying H twice gives minus the original mode.

Name: Morera integral criterion
LaTeX: f\in C(\Omega),\quad\oint_{\partial T}f(z)\,dz=0\ \forall T\Subset\Omega\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ holomorphic}
Intuition: Vanishing circulation around every small triangle forces complex differentiability.
Conditions: Ω open in C; T denotes every filled triangle contained in Ω with positive boundary orientation.
Example: Uniform limits of holomorphic functions on compact sets satisfy the integral criterion.

Name: Riemann removable-singularity theorem
LaTeX: f\text{ holomorphic on }0<|z-a|<r,\quad |f|\le M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ extends holomorphically to }a
Intuition: A bounded isolated hole contains no genuine analytic obstruction.
Conditions: Boundedness is needed in some punctured neighborhood of a; the extension is unique.
Example: sin z/z extends at 0 with value 1.

Name: Local factorization at a holomorphic zero
Intuition: Near a zero, a holomorphic function is a pure integer power times a nonvanishing factor.
Conditions: f holomorphic near a and not identically zero there; m≥0 is the first derivative order with f^(m)(a)≠0.
Example: z³e^z has a zero of order three at zero.
Prerequisites: Taylor series of an analytic function

Name: Pole order and reciprocal zeros
LaTeX: f(z)=(z-a)^{-m}g(z),\quad g(a)\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1/f\text{ has a zero of order }m
Intuition: A pole is a finite-order zero viewed through reciprocation.
Conditions: m≥1 integer; f holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood, g holomorphic and nonzero at a.
Example: 1/z² has a pole of order two.
Prerequisites: Local factorization at a holomorphic zero

Name: Casorati–Weierstrass density near an essential singularity
Intuition: Near an essential singularity, the values come arbitrarily close to every complex target.
Conditions: f holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood and a an essential singularity; every sufficiently small r>0 is allowed.
Example: e^(1/z) has dense image in every punctured disk around zero.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Geometry and distance

Name: Little Picard theorem
LaTeX: f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\text{ entire nonconstant}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad|\mathbb C\setminus f(\mathbb C)|\le1
Intuition: A nonconstant entire map cannot avoid two complex values.
Conditions: No growth assumption is required; the conclusion is about omitted finite values.
Example: e^z omits zero and shows that one exception is possible.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Great Picard theorem at an isolated essential singularity
LaTeX: f\text{ essential at }a\Longrightarrow f\text{ assumes every value, with at most one exception, infinitely often near }a
Intuition: An essential singularity produces repeated coverage of almost the entire complex plane at every small scale.
Conditions: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a; every smaller punctured disk has the stated property. The meromorphic version has a different omitted-value count on the sphere.
Example: e^(1/z) repeatedly takes every nonzero value near zero.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Casorati–Weierstrass density near an essential singularity

Name: Open mapping theorem for holomorphic functions
LaTeX: f:\Omega\to\mathbb C\text{ holomorphic nonconstant}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(U)\text{ open for every open }U\subseteq\Omega
Intuition: A nonconstant analytic map sends local regions to regions rather than collapsing them into curves.
Conditions: Ω is a connected open subset of C; nonconstancy is essential.
Example: z↦z² maps a small disk around zero to another disk, despite derivative zero at the center.
Prerequisites: Local factorization at a holomorphic zero

Name: Holomorphic local inverse theorem
Intuition: A nonzero complex derivative gives a locally reversible rotation and scaling.
Conditions: f holomorphic near a; inverse exists between sufficiently small neighborhoods and is holomorphic. The statement is local, not global injectivity.
Example: e^z has local logarithmic inverses but no global inverse on C.

Name: Analytic logarithm criterion
Intuition: A global logarithm exists exactly when multiplicative winding disappears around every loop.
Conditions: f is nonvanishing holomorphic on a domain Ω; loops are piecewise C1. The logarithm g is holomorphic; any two choices differ by 2πik for one integer k, and fixing its value at one point makes it unique.
Example: Every nonvanishing holomorphic function on a simply connected domain has a holomorphic logarithm.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Holomorphic nth root on a simply connected domain
Intuition: Divide a continuous logarithmic coordinate to construct a consistent root branch.
Conditions: n≥1 integer, Ω simply connected domain, f holomorphic and nowhere zero. Different choices multiply h by an nth root of unity.
Example: A nowhere-zero analytic function on a disk admits an analytic square root.

Name: Primitive criterion for a holomorphic function
Intuition: A function can be integrated globally without path ambiguity precisely when all loop totals vanish.
Conditions: f holomorphic on a domain Ω; loops piecewise C¹. A primitive is unique up to a constant.
Example: 1/z has no primitive on C\{0}.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Boundary and interior

Name: Contour winding number
Intuition: Count the net number of turns a closed path makes around a point.
Conditions: γ closed piecewise C¹, a not on its image; self-intersections are allowed and orientation affects the sign.
Example: A counterclockwise circle around a has winding number 1.

Name: Residue at a pole of arbitrary order
Intuition: Remove the singular power and extract the Taylor coefficient that becomes a simple-pole term.
Conditions: f has a pole of order at most m≥1 at a; the bracketed product extends holomorphically.
Example: Res₀(e^z/z³)=1/2.
Prerequisites: Residue and the simple-pole formula; Laurent expansion on an annulus

Name: Residue at infinity and global residue balance
Intuition: The point at infinity supplies the final residue needed to balance every finite singularity.
Conditions: For the sum, f is rational, equivalently meromorphic on the Riemann sphere. The definition applies when infinity is an isolated singularity.
Example: For f(z)=1/z the finite residue is 1 and the infinity residue is −1.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Conservation and balance

Name: Jensen formula for zeros in a disk
Intuition: Boundary-average logarithmic size records how many zeros lie inside and how close they are to the center.
Conditions: f holomorphic near the closed disk, f(0)≠0, and no zeros on its boundary; zeros aj are counted with multiplicity.
Example: With no zeros inside, log|f| satisfies the harmonic mean-value equality.

Name: Hurwitz preservation of zero counts
LaTeX: f_n\to f\text{ locally uniformly},\ f\not\equiv0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_D(f_n)=N_D(f)\text{ eventually}
Intuition: Stable analytic approximation preserves zeros inside a boundary where the limit does not vanish.
Conditions: Holomorphic fn on a common open Ω, converging locally uniformly to f; the closure of the Jordan domain D is compactly contained in Ω, with piecewise smooth boundary and no boundary zeros of f. Counts include multiplicity.
Example: A locally uniform limit of nowhere-zero holomorphic functions is zero-free or identically zero.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Montel normal-family theorem
Intuition: Local value bounds give enough derivative control to extract convergent analytic subsequences.
Conditions: F a family of holomorphic functions on a domain Ω; normal here means every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function.
Example: Holomorphic self-maps of the unit disk form a normal family.

Name: Locally uniform limit theorem for holomorphic functions
LaTeX: f_n\to f\text{ uniformly on compacta}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ holomorphic},\quad f_n^{(k)}\to f^{(k)}\text{ locally uniformly}
Intuition: Uniform control on every compact region preserves analyticity and all its derivatives.
Conditions: fn holomorphic on a common open set; k≥0 fixed integer. Pointwise convergence alone is insufficient.
Example: Taylor polynomials converge with all derivatives on smaller disks inside the convergence radius.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Boundary and interior

Name: Riemann mapping theorem
LaTeX: \Omega\subsetneq\mathbb C\text{ simply connected domain}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists f:\Omega\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathbb D\text{ biholomorphic}
Intuition: Every proper simply connected planar domain has the same internal complex geometry as a disk.
Conditions: Ω nonempty, open, connected and simply connected; Ω≠C. Prescribing f(a)=0 and f′(a)>0 determines the map uniquely.
Example: The upper half-plane is mapped to the disk by a Möbius transformation.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Schwarz–Pick contraction
Intuition: Holomorphic disk maps contract the disk’s natural non-Euclidean distance scale.
Conditions: f holomorphic from the open unit disk to itself; z,w in the disk. Equality at distinct points, or derivative equality at one point, forces a disk automorphism.
Example: At w=0 and f(0)=0 the first inequality is Schwarz’s lemma.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Change of coordinates

Name: All conformal automorphisms of the disk
Intuition: Every reversible analytic disk map combines moving one point to the center with a rotation.
Conditions: These and only these maps are biholomorphic self-maps of the open unit disk.
Example: a=0 gives a pure rotation.

Name: Harmonic conjugate construction
Intuition: Rotate the gradient of a harmonic function by a quarter turn to obtain the gradient of its conjugate.
Conditions: u∈C² harmonic on a simply connected planar domain. The conjugate exists globally and is unique up to a real constant.
Example: For u=x²−y² one conjugate is v=2xy.
Prerequisites: Holomorphic functions have harmonic components; Cauchy–Riemann equations

Name: Harnack inequality on a disk
Intuition: Positivity prevents a harmonic function from spiking sharply in the interior relative to its central value.
Conditions: u nonnegative harmonic in a neighborhood of the closed disk of radius R; interior versions follow by slightly smaller radii.
Example: On the half-radius circle, u lies between u(0)/3 and 3u(0).
Prerequisites: Poisson integral on the unit disk

Name: Schwarz reconstruction from the real part
Intuition: Boundary values of one harmonic component determine its analytic partner up to an imaginary constant.
Conditions: f holomorphic in a neighborhood of the closed unit disk; u=Re f and |z|<1.
Example: Constant real boundary data produce a constant real part throughout the disk.
Prerequisites: Poisson integral on the unit disk

Name: Finite Blaschke product
Intuition: Place prescribed zeros inside the disk while maintaining unit modulus on its boundary.
Conditions: N finite nonnegative integer, θ real; multiplicities come from repeated aj. For N>1 the map is generally not an automorphism.
Example: B(z)=z^N has an N-fold zero and winds the boundary N times.
Prerequisites: All conformal automorphisms of the disk

Name: Runge polynomial approximation for a hole-free compact set
Intuition: Analytic functions near a compact set can be built from polynomials when the complement has no holes.
Conditions: K compact in C, C\K connected, and f holomorphic on a neighborhood of K. With holes, rational functions with appropriate pole locations are generally needed.
Example: Analytic functions near a closed disk admit uniform polynomial approximation.

Name: Mittag–Leffler prescribed principal parts
Intuition: Assemble specified local pole behavior into one global meromorphic function.
Conditions: Ω a planar domain; {aj} discrete with no accumulation inside Ω; Pj finite principal parts in negative powers of z−aj. There exists a meromorphic f with exactly those principal parts and no other poles.
Example: Prescribed residues at a discrete set can be realized by suitable simple-pole principal parts.

Name: Weierstrass entire product factorization
Intuition: An entire function is its zeros multiplied by a nonvanishing exponential, with corrections ensuring convergence.
Conditions: f entire and not identically zero; nonzero zeros aj counted with multiplicity have no finite accumulation; pj can be chosen for locally uniform product convergence; g entire, m the zero order at zero.
Example: A polynomial is a finite product version with constant exponential factor.

Name: Euler infinite product for sine
Intuition: Pair opposite integer zeros to reconstruct sine as a convergent infinite product.
Conditions: z complex; convergence is locally uniform on C. Pairing ±n is part of this product convention.
Example: Comparing the z³ coefficient gives ∑n≥1 1/n²=π²/6.

Name: Entire product for reciprocal gamma
Intuition: Reciprocal gamma is rebuilt from its nonpositive-integer zeros with exponential convergence corrections.
Conditions: z complex; γ is Euler’s constant; product converges locally uniformly on C. The reciprocal extends entirely through gamma poles.
Example: At z=0 the reciprocal has a simple zero.

Name: Hadamard factorization for finite-order entire functions
Intuition: A finite growth rate restricts the unknown zero-free factor to the exponential of a polynomial.
Conditions: f entire, nonzero, of finite order ρ=limsup log log M(r)/log r, M(r)=max|z|=r|f(z)|; standard constant/polynomial cases use order zero. Zeros counted with multiplicity; p=floorρ is an admissible canonical-product genus.
Example: Order-one functions such as sine have only a linear exponential factor.

Name: Contour length-times-maximum bound
Intuition: Total contour accumulation is bounded by path length times the largest local contribution.
Conditions: γ rectifiable piecewise C¹ and f continuous on its image; a supremum version works with an appropriate bounded integrand.
Example: A unit-circle integral is bounded by 2π times the maximum modulus on the circle.

Name: Wirtinger derivatives
Intuition: Combine two real derivatives into operators that distinguish analytic from anti-analytic dependence.
Conditions: f is C¹ for first derivatives and C² for the Laplacian identity; z=x+iy.
Example: ∂barz z=0 but ∂barz zbar=1.

Name: Cauchy–Pompeiu formula
Intuition: Failure of boundary data alone to reproduce a function is measured by its anti-holomorphic derivative inside.
Conditions: Ω bounded planar domain with positively oriented piecewise C¹ boundary, f∈C¹ on a neighborhood of its closure, z∈Ω. The area singularity is locally integrable.
Example: If f is holomorphic, the area term vanishes and Cauchy’s formula returns.

Name: Schwarzian derivative
Intuition: The Schwarzian measures local deviation from fractional linear behavior.
Conditions: f locally univalent holomorphic, so f′≠0; a local identity Sf=0 characterizes Möbius transformations.
Example: Every Möbius transformation has zero Schwarzian.

Name: Schwarzian composition law
Intuition: Projective distortion adds under composition after the outer distortion is rescaled quadratically.
Conditions: f and g locally univalent holomorphic on compatible domains.
Example: Postcomposition by a Möbius map leaves the Schwarzian unchanged.

Name: Schwarz–Christoffel polygon map
Intuition: Power factors turn a straight boundary through prescribed polygon angles.
Conditions: A conformal map from the upper half-plane onto a simple n-gon, with one prevertex at infinity; xj are ordered real prevertices, interior angles are παj, and branches are analytic in the upper half-plane. Prevertices and constants must be chosen to match side lengths.
Example: A right-angle vertex contributes exponent −1/2.
Prerequisites: Primitive criterion for a holomorphic function

Name: Picard–Lindelöf local well-posedness
Intuition: A uniform local bound on slope sensitivity prevents two trajectories from splitting at the same initial point.
Conditions: f is continuous near (t0,y0) and locally Lipschitz in y, uniformly on a small time interval. Existence and uniqueness are local, not necessarily global.
Example: For y′=y² and y(0)=1, the unique solution exists only until t=1.
Prerequisites: Picard iteration for an initial value problem

Name: Peano local existence theorem
Intuition: Continuity is enough to assemble at least one local solution, even when branching cannot be ruled out.
Conditions: f maps an open neighborhood of (t0,y0) in R×Rn continuously to Rn. The theorem guarantees a solution on some time interval, with no uniqueness claim.
Example: For y′=2√|y| and y(0)=0, the zero solution and delayed departures coexist.

Name: Finite-time ODE continuation criterion
Intuition: A solution of a globally defined locally Lipschitz vector field can stop in finite time only by escaping every bounded set.
Conditions: Autonomous y′=f(y), f:Rn→Rn locally Lipschitz; (T−,T+) is the maximal existence interval. For a proper open domain, approaching its boundary is another obstruction.
Example: y′=y², y(0)=1 gives y(t)=1/(1−t), which diverges at the finite endpoint.

Name: Bernoulli equation linearizing substitution
Intuition: A power substitution converts a particular nonlinear equation into a linear one.
Conditions: n≠1 is constant; p,q continuous. Work on an interval where the required powers are differentiable and y≠0; any excluded zero solutions must be checked separately.
Example: For y′+y=y², setting v=1/y gives v′−v=−1.
Prerequisites: Chain rule; Integrating factor for a linear ODE

Name: Scalar Riccati to second-order linear equation
Intuition: A logarithmic derivative converts a quadratic first-order law into a linear second-order law.
Conditions: a,b continuous, c continuously differentiable and nowhere zero; u is a nonzero local solution on the interval considered. Zeros of u can produce poles of y.
Example: For y′=y² use c=1 and u′′=0, giving y=−u′/u.

Name: Exact differential equation criterion
Intuition: An exact equation follows the level curves of a potential function.
Conditions: M,N are C1 on an open simply connected planar domain. Equality of cross-partials gives a global potential there; local potentials need only a small disk.
Example: y dx+x dy=d(xy), so solutions lie on xy=C.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Boundary and interior
Prerequisites: Equality of mixed partial derivatives; Fundamental theorem for line integrals

Name: Cauchy–Euler indicial polynomial
Intuition: Power functions play the role that exponentials play for constant coefficients.
Conditions: x>0, a,b real constants; repeated or complex roots require the usual logarithmic factors or real trigonometric combinations in log x.
Example: x²y′′−2y=0 has solutions x² and x^(−1).
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Power rule; Constant-coefficient second-order linear equation

Name: Reduction of order from one known solution
Intuition: One solution supplies the shape; a varying multiplier generates an independent companion.
Conditions: y1 is a nonzero solution of y″+p(x)y′+q(x)y=0 on an interval where y1 never vanishes; p,q continuous.
Example: For y″=0 and y1=1, the formula gives y2=x.

Name: Frobenius series at a regular singular point
Intuition: A power factor captures a singular scale while an ordinary series supplies corrections.
Conditions: For x²y″+xp(x)y′+q(x)y=0, p,q are analytic near 0, p0=p(0),q0=q(0). At least one Frobenius solution exists locally on x>0; resonant roots may require logarithms for the other solution.
Example: The Bessel indicial roots are r=±ν.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Recursion and iteration
Prerequisites: Taylor series of an analytic function; Cauchy–Euler indicial polynomial

Name: Green kernel for the interval Dirichlet problem
Intuition: The inverse of a differential operator is assembled from responses to point loads.
Conditions: L>0, 0≤x,s≤L; u solves −u″=f with u(0)=u(L)=0, for example for continuous f. The derivative of G jumps by −1 across x=s.
Example: For f=1, u=x(L−x)/2.
Prerequisites: Weak formulation of the Dirichlet Poisson problem

Name: Sturm–Liouville nodal count
Intuition: Higher eigenmodes have more internal sign changes.
Conditions: Regular scalar self-adjoint equation −(py′)′+qy=λwy on [a,b], p∈C1 positive, q,w continuous with w>0, and Dirichlet endpoints; yn is a nonzero nth eigenfunction.
Example: For −y″=λy on (0,π), yn=sin(nx) has n−1 interior zeros.

Name: Fundamental solution of minus the Laplacian
Intuition: A radial point-source response is harmonic away from its source and carries one unit of total flux.
Conditions: Distributional identity on Rn for n≥2; |S^(n−1)| is the area of the unit sphere. The sign convention is −Δ.
Example: In three dimensions Φ(x)=1/(4π|x|).
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Boundary and interior

Name: Dirichlet Green representation for Poisson
Intuition: Separate the influence of interior forcing from boundary values using a kernel adapted to the boundary.
Conditions: Smooth bounded Ω, sufficiently regular solution −Δu=f with boundary u=g; G vanishes on the boundary and satisfies −ΔyG(x,y)=δx. The normal is outward.
Example: If f=0, only the boundary integral remains.
Prerequisites: Green's second identity; Fundamental solution of minus the Laplacian

Name: Weak and strong harmonic maximum principles
Intuition: A harmonic function averages its neighbors, so a strict isolated interior peak is impossible.
Conditions: Ω bounded and connected, u∈C2(Ω)∩C(closure Ω), Δu=0; x0 is interior for the strong statement. The minimum version follows by changing sign.
Example: Boundary temperatures between 0 and 1 force an equilibrium temperature in the same range.

Name: Hopf boundary point lemma for harmonic functions
Intuition: A nonconstant harmonic function reaching a boundary maximum must approach it with a nonzero outward slope.
Conditions: Ω has an interior tangent ball at x0; u harmonic in Ω and C1 up to x0, with a strict boundary maximum over the interior. ν is the outward unit normal at a smooth boundary point.
Example: For u=x1 on a ball, the rightmost boundary point has positive outward derivative.
Prerequisites: Weak and strong harmonic maximum principles

Name: Weyl lemma for distributional harmonic functions
LaTeX: u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega),\quad\Delta u=0\text{ in }\mathcal D^{\prime}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=\widetilde u\ \text{a.e.},\ \widetilde u\in C^\infty(\Omega)
Intuition: A very weak harmonic equation automatically repairs the function into a smooth harmonic representative.
Conditions: Ω open in Rn; distributional Δu=0 means ∫uΔφ=0 for every compactly supported smooth φ. Equality is almost everywhere because L1 functions ignore null sets.
Example: A locally integrable candidate with zero distributional Laplacian is an ordinary smooth harmonic function after changing a null set.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Caccioppoli interior energy estimate
Intuition: Interior derivative energy is bounded by function size in a slightly larger region.
Conditions: 0<r<R, concentric balls with closure BR contained in Ω, and u weakly harmonic on BR. Cn depends only on dimension.
Example: A buffer of thickness R−r pays for differentiating a cutoff.
Prerequisites: Weak formulation of the Dirichlet Poisson problem

Name: Interior H2 estimate for Poisson
Intuition: Two weak derivatives become square integrable when the Laplacian has square-integrable forcing.
Conditions: Ω′ has compact closure in a bounded open Ω, f∈L2(Ω), and u∈H1(Ω) is a weak solution. C depends on the domains; this is an interior estimate and asserts no boundary smoothness.
Example: Rough boundaries can obstruct global H2 regularity while this interior conclusion still holds.
Prerequisites: Sobolev norm; Weak formulation of the Dirichlet Poisson problem

Name: Method of images for a Dirichlet half-space
Intuition: An opposite reflected source cancels the potential on a flat boundary.
Conditions: n≥2, x,y in the upper half-space xn>0, and Φ is the fundamental solution of −Δ. This kernel vanishes on xn=0.
Example: Equal distances to y and y* on the boundary make the two terms cancel.
Prerequisites: Fundamental solution of minus the Laplacian

Name: Compatibility and uniqueness for Neumann Poisson data
Intuition: Net interior forcing must balance outward boundary flux; an additive constant remains invisible.
Conditions: Smooth bounded connected Ω and sufficiently regular data/solution. With appropriate regularity the compatibility condition gives a solution unique up to an additive constant; a zero-mean constraint fixes it.
Example: For zero normal flux, the source f must have mean zero.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Heat semigroup Lp contraction
Intuition: A normalized positive smoothing kernel cannot increase the global Lp size.
Example: The sup norm cannot increase because every new value is a weighted average of old values.

Name: Heat-kernel derivative smoothing bound
Intuition: Diffusion pays inverse powers of time to turn rough data into smooth functions.
Conditions: t>0, integer multi-index α, 1≤p≤q≤∞, f∈Lp(Rn); C depends on n,p,q,α. The equation uses diffusivity one.
Example: With p=q, each spatial derivative costs a factor proportional to t^(−1/2).
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Gaussian heat kernel; Young's convolution inequality

Name: Parabolic maximum principle
Intuition: A heat subsolution cannot create a new temperature peak after the initial time without boundary input.
Conditions: Ω bounded, T>0, u continuous on the closed cylinder and C2 in space/C1 in time inside, with ut−κΔu≤0 and κ>0. Boundary values are understood on the parabolic boundary.
Example: Zero initial and boundary data force a heat solution to remain zero by applying the principle to ±u.

Name: Heat flow in Dirichlet eigenmodes
Intuition: Each spatial eigenmode fades independently, with finer modes typically fading faster.
Conditions: Smooth bounded Ω, zero Dirichlet boundary, κ>0, f∈L2(Ω); eigenfunctions form an orthonormal L2 basis. The expansion converges in L2 and attains f in L2 as t↓0. The inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot.
Example: On (0,π), sine mode sin(jx) is multiplied by exp(−κj²t).
Prerequisites: Heat or diffusion equation; Regular Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville problem

Name: Finite speed of wave propagation
Intuition: A disturbance can influence only points reached by a cone of finite slope.
Conditions: Classical solution utt=c²Δu on Rn, c>0, t≥0, with initial displacement f and velocity g compactly supported. The same support result extends to energy solutions.
Example: Data vanishing on Bct(x) cannot influence (t,x).
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Wave equation; Conservation of wave energy

Name: Kirchhoff formula for three-dimensional waves
Intuition: A three-dimensional wave samples expanding spherical shells of its initial data.
Conditions: t>0,c>0, smooth initial f=u(·,0),g=ut(·,0) on R3, for example compactly supported. The measure is area on the unit sphere, whose total is 4π.
Example: Constant f and zero g give the same constant solution.
Prerequisites: Wave equation; Flux through a parametrized surface

Name: Bromwich inversion of the Laplace transform
Intuition: Recover a time function by superposing complex exponentials along a vertical frequency line.
Conditions: For example f is piecewise C1 and of exponential order a on [0,∞), γ>a, and t>0 is a continuity point; symmetric truncation is used. At a jump, suitable one-sided regularity gives the midpoint value.
Example: F(s)=1/(s+a) inverts to exp(−at).

Name: Laplace method at a nondegenerate interior minimum
Intuition: Strong exponential weighting concentrates almost all contribution near the smallest phase value.
Conditions: λ→+∞, finite [a,b], φ∈C2 has a unique minimum at interior x0 with φ″(x0)>0; g continuous and g(x0)≠0. These sufficient assumptions give the leading ratio asymptotic.
Example: For φ=x²/2, x0=0, the leading scale is √(2π/λ).
Prerequisites: Second-order multivariable Taylor expansion; Gaussian integral

Name: One-dimensional stationary phase
Intuition: Rapid oscillations cancel except near a point where phase temporarily stops changing.
Conditions: λ→+∞; a∈C∞c(R), φ smooth and real near its support, with exactly one stationary point x0 there and φ″(x0)≠0.
Example: A positive quadratic phase contributes the phase factor exp(iπ/4).

Name: Watson lemma for endpoint Laplace asymptotics
Intuition: A large Laplace parameter magnifies only the local endpoint expansion.
Conditions: s→+∞ real, α>0, f has the stated asymptotic expansion as t↓0 and is locally integrable with at most exponential growth at infinity. The resulting series is asymptotic, not necessarily convergent.
Example: For f(t)=1/(1+t), the expansion yields 1/s−1/s²+2!/s³−⋯.
Prerequisites: Unilateral Laplace transform; Euler gamma integral

Name: Lebesgue differentiation theorem
Intuition: Zoomed local averages recover an integrable function at almost every point, even when it is discontinuous.
Conditions: f∈L1loc(Rn); balls are Euclidean and the conclusion is with respect to Lebesgue measure. Values on a null set can be chosen arbitrarily.
Example: The density of a measurable set is 0 or 1 at almost every point by applying the theorem to its indicator.
Prerequisites: Integral with respect to a measure

Name: Cumulative distribution function
Intuition: A distribution can be stored as the running total of probability to the left of a moving threshold.
Conditions: X is real valued; a<b. Every CDF is nondecreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 and 1 at the two infinities.
Example: A fair die has F(3)=1/2.

Name: Generalized quantile function
Intuition: Read the cumulative plot sideways: a probability level asks which threshold first reaches it.
Conditions: F is any real CDF and 0<u<1; this generalized inverse also handles jumps and flat intervals.
Example: For an exponential law, Q(u)=-log(1-u)/λ.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Randomness and distribution
Prerequisites: Cumulative distribution function; Continuous uniform distribution

Name: Probability integral transform
Intuition: A continuous observation's own percentile has no preferred location on the probability scale.
Conditions: X has a continuous CDF; atoms require randomized ranks and invalidate this unmodified statement.
Example: Correctly calibrated continuous predictive percentiles should be uniform.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Survival and hazard relation
Intuition: Hazard measures the instantaneous failure rate among those still present; accumulated hazard determines remaining survival.
Conditions: T≥0 is absolutely continuous, S(0)=1, and S(t)>0 on the interval considered; f is its density.
Example: Constant hazard λ gives exponential survival exp(-λt).
Prerequisites: Cumulative distribution function; Exponential waiting time

Name: Density of an order statistic
Intuition: The kth ranked value needs k−1 observations below it and the rest above it.
Conditions: X1,…,Xn are iid with absolutely continuous CDF F and density f; 1≤k≤n.
Example: The maximum of n independent uniform(0,1) draws has density n x^(n−1).

Name: Multinomial distribution
Intuition: One total count is divided among several mutually exclusive outcomes.
Conditions: n independent categorical trials; pj≥0, sum pj=1; nj are nonnegative integers summing to n; use 0^0=1.
Example: Counts of six faces in repeated die rolls follow a multinomial law.

Name: Dirichlet distribution
Intuition: Random proportions share a fixed total; concentration parameters describe both their preferred balance and variability.
Conditions: αj>0; pj>0, sum pj=1; density uses the first k−1 simplex coordinates.
Example: With all αj=1 the distribution is uniform on the probability simplex.

Name: Lognormal distribution
Intuition: Additive Gaussian variation on a log scale becomes multiplicative variation on a positive scale.
Conditions: σ>0 and μ real; logarithms are natural. The mean is exp(μ+σ²/2), not exp(μ).
Example: A geometric Brownian motion at a fixed positive time is lognormal.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Normal distribution; Density under a change of variables

Name: Chi-squared distribution
Intuition: Squared independent standard Gaussian coordinates turn random displacement into random energy.
Conditions: Zi iid N(0,1) and integer ν≥1 for the sum representation; the density defines the law for any real ν>0.
Example: The squared length of a two-dimensional standard Gaussian vector is χ² with two degrees of freedom.

Name: Student t distribution
Intuition: Dividing a Gaussian quantity by an uncertain estimate of scale adds heavier tails.
Conditions: Z∼N(0,1), V∼χ²ν are independent and ν>0; mean needs ν>1 and variance needs ν>2.
Example: At ν=1 this is the standard Cauchy distribution.
Patterns: Randomness and distribution; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: F distribution
Intuition: A ratio of independent estimates of variance measures how unusually large one source of variation is relative to another.
Conditions: d1,d2>0; U,V independent. Both degrees-of-freedom divisors are essential.
Example: The square of a tν variable follows F(1,ν).

Name: Weibull distribution
Intuition: A power-law change of the clock lets failure risk rise, fall or remain constant with age.
Conditions: Shape k>0 and scale λ>0; density is h(t)S(t) for t>0.
Example: k=1 is exponential; k>1 gives increasing hazard.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Pareto distribution
Intuition: A fixed proportional increase in the threshold always removes the same fraction of the remaining tail.
Conditions: xm>0, α>0; displayed moment formula for real r<α. Moments of order r≥α diverge.
Example: Doubling the threshold multiplies the survival probability by 2^(−α).
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Limits and convergence

Name: Cauchy distribution
Intuition: Rare huge observations remain strong enough that averaging does not squeeze the distribution toward a center.
Conditions: Location x0 real, scale γ>0; the ordinary expectation and variance do not exist. Characteristic function uses E exp(itX).
Example: The mean of iid standard Cauchy observations is itself standard Cauchy.

Name: Laplace distribution
Intuition: Two exponential tails meet at a sharp center, making absolute deviations the natural measure of mismatch.
Conditions: μ real, b>0; mean μ and variance 2b². This is a probability distribution, distinct from the Laplace transform.
Example: With fixed b, fitting μ by likelihood minimizes the sum of absolute deviations.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Wishart Gaussian scatter distribution
Intuition: A scalar sum of squares becomes a matrix of accumulated cross-products, recording energy in every direction.
Conditions: Zi iid Np(0,Σ), Σ positive definite, integer n≥1. W is singular almost surely when n<p; no nonsingular density is asserted then.
Example: A centered normal sample's scatter matrix has Wp(Σ,n−1) distribution.
Prerequisites: Multivariate normal density; Covariance under a linear map

Name: Conditional multivariate Gaussian
Intuition: Observing correlated coordinates shifts the best prediction linearly and removes the uncertainty explained by them.
Conditions: (X,Y) jointly Gaussian; ΣYY positive definite. The remaining covariance may be singular; it does not depend on y.
Example: For standard correlated scalars, X|Y=y has mean ρy and variance 1−ρ².

Name: Gaussian integration by parts
Intuition: Multiplication by a Gaussian coordinate can be exchanged for a derivative inside an expectation.
Conditions: f is absolutely continuous, E|f'(Z)| and E|Zf(Z)| finite, with vanishing boundary term f(x)e^(−x²/2) at both infinities.
Example: Taking f(z)=z³ gives E Z⁴=3 E Z²=3.

Name: Wick–Isserlis Gaussian moment formula
Intuition: Every centered Gaussian even moment is assembled by pairing coordinates; no extra higher-order interactions are needed.
Conditions: Xi are jointly centered real Gaussian variables, possibly repeated or degenerate. P2 is the set of pair partitions; odd moments vanish.
Example: E[X²Y²]=Var(X)Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)².
Prerequisites: Multivariate normal density; Gaussian integration by parts

Name: First Borel–Cantelli lemma
Intuition: If the total probability budget of later failures is finite, failures eventually stop almost surely.
Conditions: An are events in one probability space. Independence is unnecessary; the conclusion concerns infinitely many occurrences.
Example: Failure probabilities bounded by 1/n² imply only finitely many failures almost surely.

Name: Second Borel–Cantelli lemma
Intuition: Independent fresh chances with an infinite total probability budget cannot all dry up after a finite time.
Conditions: An are mutually independent events; divergence alone is insufficient for arbitrarily dependent events.
Example: Independent trials with success probability 1/n succeed infinitely often almost surely.
Patterns: Randomness and distribution; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Independence of random variables; First Borel–Cantelli lemma

Name: Kolmogorov zero–one law
Intuition: An event unaffected by every finite initial segment of an independent sequence cannot retain an intermediate probability.
Conditions: Xn are mutually independent. The displayed intersection is the tail sigma-algebra; no identical-distribution assumption is needed.
Example: Convergence of an independent random series is a tail event and has probability zero or one.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Information and uncertainty
Prerequisites: Independence of random variables; Probability axioms

Name: Convergence in probability
Intuition: For any fixed error tolerance, the chance of exceeding it eventually becomes negligible.
Conditions: Xn and X are real random variables on one probability space; this need not give convergence along every sample path.
Example: A Bernoulli sample proportion converges in probability to its success probability.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Randomness and distribution

Name: Convergence in distribution
LaTeX: X_n\Rightarrow X\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\ \text{at every continuity point of }F_X
Intuition: The distributions approach one another even when individual random outcomes cannot meaningfully be paired.
Conditions: Real random variables may live on different probability spaces. CDF convergence is required only at continuity points of the limit.
Example: Standardized binomial sums approach a normal distribution.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Information and uncertainty

Name: Lp convergence of random variables
Intuition: Lp convergence makes the average powered error disappear, so rare errors must also be small enough in magnitude.
Conditions: Xn,X belong to Lp on a common probability space; p is finite. Larger p penalizes extremes more strongly.
Example: Independent sample means with finite variance converge in L² to their common mean.
Prerequisites: Lp norm of a function; Expectation

Name: Continuous mapping theorem
Intuition: A transformation preserves a distributional limit when its discontinuities do not matter to the limiting law.
Conditions: Xn,X are random vectors in Euclidean spaces, g is measurable, and Dg is its discontinuity set.
Example: Squaring an asymptotically standard normal statistic produces an asymptotic χ²1 statistic.

Name: Slutsky's theorem
LaTeX: X_n\Rightarrow X,\ Y_n\xrightarrow{p}c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX,\quad X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c
Intuition: A factor whose uncertainty vanishes can be replaced by its constant limit in a distributional calculation.
Conditions: Real random variables; c deterministic. Division also holds when c≠0. Independence of Xn and Yn is unnecessary.
Example: A consistent standard-error estimate can replace the unknown scale in a CLT pivot.
Prerequisites: Convergence in distribution; Convergence in probability

Name: Lévy continuity theorem
Intuition: Convergence of all oscillatory probes identifies a limiting probability law, provided no mass escapes.
Conditions: φn are characteristic functions on R^d. Their pointwise limit must be continuous at zero; necessarily φ(0)=1.
Example: Multiplying characteristic functions and taking a quadratic limit proves many central limit theorems.

Name: Berry–Esseen bound
Intuition: The central limit approximation has a measurable error budget; heavy third moments make convergence slower.
Conditions: Xi iid, E Xi=μ, Var Xi=σ²>0, finite third absolute centered moment. C is a universal finite constant.
Example: For bounded Bernoulli variables away from p=0 or 1, CDF error is O(n^−1/2).
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Limits and convergence

Name: Lindeberg triangular-array CLT
Intuition: Many unequal small contributions still make Gaussian noise when no large contribution carries a lasting fraction of the variance.
Conditions: Each row contains independent centered variables with finite variances; sn²=sumk Var(Xnk)>0. The displayed Lindeberg condition holds for every ε>0.
Example: Bounded centered triangular arrays satisfy the condition when their maximal magnitude is o(sn).
Prerequisites: Central limit theorem; Variance of a sum

Name: Sub-Gaussian moment bound
Intuition: A variable need not be Gaussian to have fluctuations whose exponential moments are bounded by a Gaussian envelope.
Conditions: X integrable; σ²≥0 is a variance proxy, not necessarily the actual variance. The bound must hold for every real t.
Example: A variable in [a,b] is sub-Gaussian with proxy (b−a)²/4.

Name: Bernstein inequality for bounded sums
Intuition: Small deviations depend on actual variance, while very large deviations also feel the maximum size of one summand.
Conditions: Xi independent, centered, |Xi|≤M almost surely, M>0, t≥0; 0<v<∞. If v=0, the sum is identically zero and its tails can be handled directly.
Example: Rare Bernoulli successes can concentrate more sharply than a range-only Hoeffding estimate suggests.
Prerequisites: Exponential Chernoff bound; Variance of a sum

Name: Bennett inequality
Intuition: A sharper exponential calculation preserves the transition from Gaussian-size fluctuations to rare large upward deviations.
Conditions: Independent centered Xi≤M almost surely, M>0; v=sum E Xi² is finite and positive; t≥0.
Example: Expanding h(u) near zero recovers the variance-controlled Gaussian exponent.

Name: Cantelli one-sided variance bound
Intuition: Knowing which side matters gives a sharper variance-only bound than treating both tails together.
Conditions: E X=μ and Var X=σ²<∞. No independence or density assumptions are needed.
Example: At two standard deviations above the mean, the bound is 1/5.

Name: Paley–Zygmund lower bound
Intuition: A nonnegative quantity with a substantial mean and controlled second moment cannot be tiny almost all the time.
Conditions: X≥0 almost surely and 0<E X²<∞, with E X>0.
Example: A second-moment argument can prove a random combinatorial count is positive with nonzero probability.

Name: Efron–Stein variance inequality
Intuition: A function cannot fluctuate much if independently replacing any one input usually changes it only a little.
Conditions: Xi independent, f(X) square-integrable; X^(i) replaces Xi by an independent copy with its same distribution.
Example: For f=sum Xi, the inequality is an equality and recovers the variance sum.

Name: McDiarmid bounded-difference inequality
Intuition: Many individually harmless inputs cannot easily combine into a large surprise, even when the output is nonlinear.
Conditions: Xi independent; changing only coordinate i changes f by at most ci everywhere on the support; t≥0.
Example: An empirical average of [0,1] values has ci=1/n and exponent −2nt².

Name: Azuma–Hoeffding martingale bound
Intuition: A fair evolving estimate still concentrates when each surprise is bounded, even though the surprises need not be independent.
Conditions: Mi is a real martingale and |Mi−M(i−1)|≤ci almost surely for deterministic ci; t≥0.
Example: An adapted game with bounded fair increments has exponentially unlikely large gains.

Name: Kolmogorov maximal inequality
Intuition: The final variance budget also controls the chance that any earlier partial sum crossed a fixed boundary.
Conditions: Xi independent, centered and square-integrable; t>0. The maximum is over the entire finite sequence of partial sums.
Example: The inequality controls maximal fluctuations in proofs of strong laws.
Prerequisites: Variance of a sum; Chebyshev's inequality

Name: Cramér large-deviation principle
LaTeX: I(x)=\sup_t\{tx-\log\mathbb E e^{tX_1}\},\quad -\inf_{A^\circ}I\le\liminf_n\frac1n\log\Pr(\bar X_n\in A)\le\limsup_n\frac1n\log\Pr(\bar X_n\in A)\le-\inf_{\overline A}I
Intuition: Rare sample means have an exponential cost determined by the cheapest tilt that makes them typical.
Conditions: Xi iid real; their MGF is finite on a neighborhood of zero. A is Borel; infimum of the empty set is infinity.
Example: For N(μ,σ²) observations the rate is (x−μ)²/(2σ²).

Name: Le Cam Poisson approximation
Intuition: Many rare independent opportunities behave almost like a Poisson count; the squared probabilities measure collisions with the rare-event approximation.
Conditions: Bi independent Bernoulli(pi); dTV is supremum over events, equivalently half the L1 probability difference.
Example: Binomial(n,λ/n) has approximation error at most λ²/n.

Name: Wald's random-sum identity
Intuition: A fair stopping rule changes how many increments are collected without changing the expected reward per included increment.
Conditions: Xi iid integrable; N is a nonnegative integer stopping time for their natural filtration and E N<∞. These ensure absolute integrability of the stopped sum.
Example: Expected total reward up to a stopping time equals expected count times mean reward.

Name: Variance of an independent random sum
Intuition: Total uncertainty splits into noisy items and uncertainty about how many items there are.
Conditions: Xi iid with finite second moment; N independent of the entire sequence, nonnegative integer valued, with finite second moment. An empty sum is zero.
Example: For Poisson N with mean λ, variance of the compound sum is λ E X1².
Prerequisites: Law of total variance; Variance of a sum

Name: Sklar's copula representation
Intuition: Separate the shape of each variable from the way their percentiles move together.
Conditions: F is a joint CDF with marginal CDFs Fj. C is a CDF on [0,1]^d with uniform marginals; it is unique when all Fj are continuous.
Example: Independence corresponds to C(u)=the product of the coordinates.
Prerequisites: Cumulative distribution function; Probability integral transform

Name: Fréchet–Hoeffding copula bounds
Intuition: Marginal probabilities alone already restrict how large or small an intersection can be.
Conditions: C is a d-dimensional copula and u∈[0,1]^d. The upper bound is a copula in every dimension; the lower-bound function is a copula only for d=2.
Example: For two uniforms, (U,U) attains the upper bound and (U,1−U) the lower bound.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Conservation and balance

Name: Statistical risk
Intuition: Judge a data-dependent decision by averaging its loss over repeated datasets from a specified truth.
Conditions: A statistical model Pθ, measurable decision rule δ, and nonnegative measurable loss L; risk may be infinite.
Example: With squared error, risk is the estimator's mean squared error.

Name: Bayes action by posterior expected loss
Intuition: After observing data, weight each possible consequence by the posterior and choose the smallest expected loss.
Conditions: A proper prior and well-defined posterior are given; a measurable minimizing action exists. Integrated losses must be defined, possibly nonnegative extended values.
Example: Squared-error loss selects the posterior mean; zero–one loss for a finite parameter set selects a posterior mode.

Name: Bayes classifier and irreducible error
Intuition: At each input, choose the most likely label; the remaining conditional probability is unavoidable classification error.
Conditions: A finite label set, measurable conditional class probabilities, and zero–one loss. Ties can be broken measurably.
Example: If class probabilities are (0.7,0.2,0.1), minimum conditional error is 0.3.
Prerequisites: Conditional probability; Bayes action by posterior expected loss

Name: Quantiles minimize pinball loss
Intuition: Charging underestimates and overestimates differently moves the best prediction from the center to a chosen percentile.
Conditions: X integrable and 0<τ<1. Atoms can give nonunique minimizers; the displayed interval condition handles them.
Example: At τ=1/2 this is half absolute error, so every median minimizes it.

Name: Minimax statistical risk
Intuition: Choose a procedure whose worst supported truth hurts as little as possible.
Conditions: A specified model class Θ, sample experiment and nonnegative loss; the infimum may not be attained. This is a statistical decision criterion.
Example: For one observation Y∼Nd(θ,σ²I) and squared error, the usual estimator has constant risk dσ².

Name: James–Stein shrinkage estimator
Intuition: Several noisy coordinates can borrow strength from a common center, lowering total squared error even when the true means are unrelated.
Conditions: Y∼Nd(θ,σ²I), d≥3, known σ²>0; squared Euclidean loss. Define the estimator arbitrarily at Y=0, a probability-zero event.
Example: With d=5 and ||Y||²=12σ², all coordinates are multiplied by 3/4.

Name: Stein's unbiased risk estimate
Intuition: Training residuals underestimate prediction error; the estimator's sensitivity supplies an exact average correction for Gaussian noise.
Conditions: Y∼Nd(θ,σ²I), known σ²; δ weakly differentiable with integrable derivative terms and squared error, and boundary conditions permitting Gaussian integration by parts.
Example: For δ(Y)=aY, the divergence is ad, giving a directly computable shrinkage-risk estimate.
Prerequisites: Gaussian integration by parts; Statistical risk

Name: Minimal sufficient statistic criterion
Intuition: Two datasets can be compressed together exactly when their relative likelihood carries no parameter information.
Conditions: A dominated model with positive densities on a common support; T measurable. The criterion characterizes minimal sufficiency up to model-null sets.
Example: For iid Poisson data, equal sample sums give parameter-independent likelihood ratios.

Name: Completeness of a statistic
LaTeX: \bigl[\mathbb E_\theta g(T)=0\ \forall\theta\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(T)=0\quad P_\theta\text{-a.s. for every }\theta
Intuition: A complete statistic has no nontrivial function that averages to zero for every possible truth.
Conditions: The implication is required for all measurable g with Eθ|g(T)|<∞ for every θ. Completeness is a property of a family of distributions.
Example: A Poisson count with parameter ranging over all positive values is complete.

Name: Lehmann–Scheffé theorem
LaTeX: T\text{ complete sufficient},\quad \mathbb E_\theta g(T)=\tau(\theta)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(T)\text{ is the unique UMVU estimator of }\tau
Intuition: Once all information is compressed into a complete statistic, an unbiased estimate built from it cannot be improved in variance.
Conditions: T complete and sufficient; g(T) square-integrable for every θ. Uniqueness is up to almost sure equality for every model distribution.
Example: The sample mean is the unique UMVU estimator of a Poisson mean.
Prerequisites: Completeness of a statistic; Rao-Blackwell improvement

Name: Basu's theorem
LaTeX: T\text{ complete sufficient},\quad A\text{ ancillary}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\perp A
Intuition: A complete summary of parameter information is independent of statistics whose entire distribution is parameter-free.
Conditions: A is ancillary, meaning its law is the same for every θ; T is complete and sufficient for the same model.
Example: In a normal location family with known variance, the sample mean is independent of centered residual statistics.
Prerequisites: Completeness of a statistic; Neyman-Fisher factorization

Name: Fisher information under reparameterization
Intuition: Information about a coordinate changes with its units and directions, exactly like a quadratic measurement of small displacements.
Conditions: Differentiable parameter map θ(η) in a model with square-integrable scores; J has compatible dimensions. Invertibility is needed only for a true coordinate change.
Example: For η=log σ, information rescales by (dσ/dη)²=σ² in the scalar case.

Name: Asymptotic normality of a regular MLE
Intuition: Near the true parameter, a smooth likelihood is approximately quadratic and its random slope is approximately Gaussian.
Conditions: Iid data; consistent interior MLE; differentiable score with a CLT, mean zero and positive definite covariance I; normalized Hessian converges locally uniformly to −I.
Example: The exponential rate MLE 1/mean has asymptotic variance λ²/n.
Prerequisites: Maximum likelihood estimation; Central limit theorem; Fisher information

Name: Sandwich covariance for estimating equations
LaTeX: \sum_i\psi(X_i,\widehat\theta)=0,\quad \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)\Rightarrow N(0,A^{-1}BA^{-\top}),\ A=\mathbb E\partial_\theta\psi,\ B=\mathbb E[\psi\psi^\top]
Intuition: Noise in an estimating equation is filtered through its sensitivity on both sides of the covariance.
Conditions: Iid data; E ψ(X,θ0)=0, finite second moments; consistent root; A nonsingular; a locally uniform derivative LLN justifies linearization.
Example: Heteroskedastic regression uses residual score variability between inverse design-sensitivity factors.
Prerequisites: Central limit theorem; Covariance under a linear map

Name: Wald test for smooth restrictions
Intuition: Measure the estimated violation of a hypothesis in units of its own uncertainty.
Conditions: Under g(θ0)=0, sqrt(n)(θhat−θ0)⇒N(0,V); Vhat consistent; g differentiable with derivative G of row rank r and GVGᵀ positive definite.
Example: For one scalar restriction, this is the square of its asymptotic z statistic.

Name: Rao score test
Intuition: Test whether the likelihood still has an unusually strong slope at the proposed parameter.
Conditions: Simple null θ=θ0 in a d-dimensional iid regular model; score CLT and nonsingular information In=nI. Formula has no nuisance parameters.
Example: A Bernoulli success-rate score test compares the observed proportion with the null proportion.

Name: Confidence sets by test inversion
Intuition: Keep every parameter value that its own level-α test would not reject.
Conditions: For each θ, the rejection indicator φθ has Eθ φθ≤α; the inverted set is measurable. Randomized tests require their auxiliary randomization in the sample.
Example: Inverting two-sided normal mean tests yields the usual confidence interval.

Name: Bonferroni familywise correction
Intuition: Divide one overall false-alarm allowance among all the questions being asked.
Conditions: m≥1 tests; every true-null p-value is super-uniform. Dependence among tests is unrestricted; V counts false rejections.
Example: With 20 tests and familywise α=0.05, each threshold is 0.0025.

Name: Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control
Intuition: Allow more discoveries when many p-values are convincing while controlling the expected fraction of false discoveries.
Conditions: Independent p-values with super-uniform true-null p-values; m tests. If the defining set is empty reject none. R is total rejections.
Example: The rule controls an expected fraction, not the chance that every reported finding is true.

Name: Permutation randomization test
Intuition: Compare the observed statistic with values obtained by relabeling data in ways the null model treats as interchangeable.
Conditions: A finite transformation group G leaves the null distribution invariant; the full orbit, including identity, is used. The nonrandomized p-value is conservative with ties.
Example: Under equal iid group distributions, permuting group labels tests a difference in means.

Name: Fisher exact test distribution
Intuition: After fixing row and column totals, count which table allocations remain possible under independence.
Conditions: A is the upper-left cell of a 2×2 table under the null odds ratio 1; margins fixed or conditioned upon. Only feasible integer a are included.
Example: Summing the displayed probabilities over a chosen tail gives an exact one-sided test.

Name: Kolmogorov–Smirnov one-sample statistic
Intuition: Find the largest discrepancy between an observed cumulative curve and a proposed distribution.
Conditions: Iid observations under a fully specified continuous null CDF F0; z>0. Fitting null parameters from the same data changes the reference law.
Example: Testing a fully specified uniform law gives the same null distribution as testing a fully specified normal law.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Empirical distribution function; Probability integral transform

Name: Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality
Intuition: One exponential bound covers the entire empirical cumulative curve, despite infinitely many possible thresholds.
Conditions: Xi iid real with any CDF F; n≥1 and ε>0. No continuity assumption on F is needed.
Example: A confidence band half-width is sqrt(log(2/α)/(2n)).
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Information and uncertainty

Name: Glivenko–Cantelli theorem
Intuition: Repeated sampling eventually learns every threshold probability at once.
Conditions: Xi iid real with CDF F; Fn is their empirical CDF. This is a uniform almost sure statement, stronger than pointwise laws of large numbers.
Example: An empirical CDF converges uniformly even when the true distribution has atoms.
Prerequisites: Empirical distribution function; First Borel–Cantelli lemma

Name: Asymptotic distribution of a sample quantile
Intuition: An empirical percentile is unstable when the cumulative curve is flat near the target.
Conditions: Xi iid; 0<τ<1; qτ is unique; F differentiable near qτ with continuous density f(qτ)>0. qhat is the empirical generalized quantile.
Example: For a standard normal sample median, asymptotic variance is π/(2n).
Prerequisites: Generalized quantile function; Central limit theorem

Name: Unbiased U-statistic
LaTeX: U_n=\binom nm^{-1}\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n}h(X_{i_1},\ldots,X_{i_m}),\qquad \mathbb E U_n=\mathbb E h(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
Intuition: Average the same symmetric calculation over every subset of the required size, spreading information evenly across observations.
Conditions: Xi iid; h symmetric and integrable; integers 1≤m≤n. Terms share data and are generally dependent.
Example: With m=2 and h(x,y)=(x−y)²/2, the U-statistic is the unbiased sample variance.

Name: Jackknife variance estimate
Intuition: Remove each observation in turn and measure how much the estimate reacts to losing one data point.
Conditions: n>1; θhat(−i) fits the same procedure to n−1 observations. Consistency needs smooth asymptotically linear behavior and can fail for nonsmooth statistics such as raw quantiles.
Example: For the sample mean the jackknife variance equals s²/n.
Prerequisites: Unbiased sample variance; Bootstrap estimate of standard error

Name: K-fold cross-validation
Intuition: Let each observation take a turn as an unseen exam question for a model trained on the other folds.
Conditions: Disjoint folds partition the data; each fit excludes its validation fold, including preprocessing and tuning internal to that fit. Iid prediction requires an appropriate sampling split.
Example: Five-fold validation evaluates models trained on roughly 80% of the data.

Name: Leave-one-out shortcut for linear smoothers
Intuition: A point that strongly pulls its own fitted value needs a larger correction when pretending it was held out.
Conditions: Squared loss; ordinary least squares or ridge with fixed penalty and linear hat matrix H; Hii≠1 and each deleted fit exists. Arbitrary data-adaptive smoothers need not obey the shortcut.
Example: High-leverage observations get residual inflation by 1/(1−Hii).

Name: Akaike information criterion
Intuition: Reward fit while charging for the optimism gained by estimating parameters on the same data.
Conditions: Compare likelihoods for the same observations and base measure; k is the number of freely estimated parameters. The 2k optimism justification is asymptotic for regular correctly specified fixed-dimensional models.
Example: Adding one parameter must improve maximized log likelihood by more than one to reduce AIC.

Name: Bayesian information criterion
Intuition: A flexible model spreads prior support over more parameter volume, creating a sample-size-dependent evidence penalty.
Conditions: Same observations and likelihood measure across models; regular fixed-dimensional iid models with locally positive smooth priors and interior nonsingular likelihood peaks for the evidence approximation.
Example: At n=100, one extra parameter costs log(100)≈4.61 BIC units.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Information and uncertainty

Name: Bayes factor
Intuition: Evidence compares each model after averaging over the parameter values it predicted before seeing the data.
Conditions: Proper within-model priors; finite marginal likelihoods with positive denominator; common data measure. Arbitrarily normalized improper priors do not define a Bayes factor.
Example: A Bayes factor of 4 multiplies prior model odds by 4.

Name: Jeffreys prior measure
Intuition: Allocate prior mass by distinguishability of nearby distributions instead of equal numerical parameter increments.
Conditions: Regular identifiable model with positive definite Fisher information. The measure may be improper; posterior propriety and any model-evidence use must be checked separately.
Example: For a Bernoulli probability, the prior is Beta(1/2,1/2).
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Geometry and distance

Name: Dirichlet–multinomial posterior update
Intuition: Observed category counts add to prior pseudo-counts while preserving the same probability-simplex geometry.
Conditions: αj>0, fixed finite categories, categorical sampling conditionally iid given p, and counts sum to n.
Example: The next-label predictive probability is (αj+Nj)/(α0+n).

Name: Gamma–Poisson posterior update
Intuition: Counts add to the evidence numerator, while observation exposure adds to the rate denominator.
Conditions: Gamma uses shape α>0 and rate β>0; exposures ti≥0 known; counts conditionally independent. At ti=0 the count must be zero.
Example: The posterior mean is (α+total count)/(β+total exposure).

Name: Kaplan–Meier survival estimator
Intuition: Multiply the observed survival fractions at successive event times, updating who is still eligible to fail.
Conditions: Independent subjects with noninformative right censoring; tj distinct event times, dj failures, nj at risk just before tj>0. Follow-up supports estimation only over observed risk sets.
Example: If one of ten and then two of eight at-risk subjects fail, estimated survival is (9/10)(6/8).
Prerequisites: Survival and hazard relation; Conditional probability

Name: Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard estimator
Intuition: Add estimated local failure exposure instead of multiplying local survival fractions.
Conditions: Independent subjects and noninformative right censoring; tj event times, dj failures and nj>0 at risk immediately before tj.
Example: When every dj/nj is small, exp(−Hhat(t)) is close to Kaplan–Meier survival.

Name: Cox proportional-hazards partial likelihood
Intuition: At each failure, compare the subject with everyone still at risk; the common baseline hazard cancels from that competition.
Conditions: Independent subjects, proportional hazards, conditionally noninformative right censoring, and no tied event times for this formula. R(ti) is the risk set just before ti.
Example: A unit covariate increase multiplies hazard by exp(β), assuming other covariates fixed.
Prerequisites: Survival and hazard relation; Maximum likelihood estimation

Name: Kernel density estimator
Intuition: Replace each observed point mass by a small normalized bump, then average the bumps.
Conditions: Real observations, h>0, and nonnegative kernel K with integral one. Iid sampling is assumed for standard statistical properties.
Example: A Gaussian kernel creates a mixture of equal-width Gaussian bumps centered at the data.

Name: Kernel density bias–variance bandwidth law
Intuition: Narrow bumps reduce smoothing bias but leave noisy spikes; wide bumps trade detail for stability.
Conditions: Iid real data; h→0 and nh→∞; symmetric bounded compactly supported probability kernel; f has bounded continuous second derivative with f''∈L². R(g)=∫g² and μ2(K)=∫u²K(u)du.
Example: Balancing leading terms gives bandwidth of order n^−1/5.

Name: Nadaraya–Watson regression
Intuition: Predict locally by letting nearby observations vote more strongly than distant ones.
Conditions: h>0, nonnegative kernel K, positive denominator; paired observations. To target E[Y|X=x], use iid sampling with integrable responses and appropriate smoothing conditions.
Example: A box kernel averages responses whose inputs lie in a neighborhood of x.

Name: Quantile regression
Intuition: Fit a conditional percentile surface by charging residuals differently on its two sides.
Conditions: 0<τ<1; finite design and responses; rho is the pinball loss. Minimizers may be nonunique. A linear conditional quantile is a modeling assumption.
Example: At τ=0.5 this is least absolute deviations regression.

Name: Huber loss
Intuition: Treat small discrepancies like Gaussian noise but stop letting one extreme residual exert an arbitrarily large force.
Conditions: δ>0; real residual r. The loss is convex and continuously differentiable but not twice differentiable at ±δ.
Example: A residual ten times the threshold has the same derivative magnitude as a residual twice the threshold.

Name: M-estimation objective and equation
Intuition: Define an estimator by the total discrepancy it minimizes, then balance the resulting forces when differentiability permits.
Conditions: The minimizer exists; the displayed first-order equation additionally assumes an interior differentiable optimum. It is necessary, not generally sufficient, without convexity.
Example: Negative log likelihood, squared error and Huber loss give different M-estimators.

Name: Elastic net regression
Intuition: Combine a preference for sparse coefficients with a preference for sharing weight across correlated directions.
Conditions: Finite real design; λ1,λ2≥0. If λ2>0 the coefficient objective is strongly convex and the minimizer is unique. Intercepts, if exempted, are handled separately.
Example: λ2=0 gives lasso; λ1=0 gives ridge with the corresponding normalization.

Name: Regression hat matrix and leverage
Intuition: Regression projects the response vector onto the span of available predictor patterns.
Conditions: X is n×p with full column rank. Hii is leverage; it depends on the design, not on y.
Example: With only an intercept, every fitted response is the sample mean and each leverage is 1/n.

Name: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell residualization
Intuition: To measure a predictor block's added contribution, first remove everything the other block can already explain.
Conditions: [X1 X2] has full column rank. Residualize both the response and X2 against X1; residualizing only the response is insufficient.
Example: An adjusted slope is obtained by regressing residualized outcomes on residualized predictor values.
Prerequisites: Least-squares normal equations; Regression hat matrix and leverage

Name: Generalized linear model mean–variance structure
Intuition: Keep a linear predictor while allowing response means, distributions and variances appropriate to counts, categories or positive outcomes.
Conditions: One-parameter exponential-dispersion family with regular differentiation of its normalizer; a chosen invertible link g on the mean domain. Observations usually conditionally independent.
Example: Poisson regression uses log μ=xᵀβ and variance μ.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Exponential family and log partition function

Name: Gaussian linear discriminant analysis
Intuition: When classes share the same Gaussian shape, common quadratic terms cancel and only linear comparisons remain.
Conditions: Class-conditional X|Y=k∼N(μk,Σ), shared positive definite Σ, priors πk>0; zero–one classification loss.
Example: For two classes, the decision boundary is a hyperplane normal to Σ^−1(μ1−μ0).
Prerequisites: Multivariate normal density; Bayes classifier and irreducible error

Name: Partial correlation from precision
Intuition: Remove the linear effects of all other variables before measuring how two residuals move together.
Conditions: A random vector has finite second moments and positive definite covariance Σ. The formula gives linear partial correlation; zero implies conditional independence only for jointly Gaussian variables.
Example: A zero off-diagonal precision entry marks a missing conditional-dependence edge in a Gaussian graphical model.
Prerequisites: Pearson correlation; Inverse by the adjugate

Name: F test for nested Gaussian linear models
Intuition: Compare improvement from extra fitted directions with the unexplained variation per remaining direction.
Conditions: Fixed nested full-rank design spaces of dimensions p0<p1<n; q=p1−p0; independent N(0,σ²) errors; the smaller mean model is true under H0.
Example: Testing one additional coefficient gives the square of its t test statistic.

Name: Gaussian regression prediction interval
Intuition: A new outcome is uncertain both because the fitted mean is uncertain and because the new observation brings fresh noise.
Conditions: Full-rank fixed X, n>p; Gaussian iid errors of variance σ²; independent new response at fixed x0 with the same variance; s²=RSS/(n−p).
Example: The leading 1 is omitted for a confidence interval for the conditional mean, not for a new response.
Prerequisites: Student t pivot; Least-squares normal equations

Name: Covariate adjustment for average treatment effect
LaTeX: \mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=\mathbb E_X\!\left[\mathbb E(Y\mid A=1,X)-\mathbb E(Y\mid A=0,X)\right]
Intuition: Compare treatment groups at the same observed background, then average those comparable contrasts over the target population.
Conditions: Binary treatment; consistency Y=Y(A); conditional exchangeability (Y(0),Y(1)) independent of A given X; positivity 0<P(A=1|X)<1 almost surely; integrable outcomes.
Example: Randomization makes exchangeability hold without adjustment when treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes.

Name: Inverse propensity weighting identity
Intuition: Give underrepresented treatment-background combinations more weight so each group represents the same target population.
Conditions: Consistency, conditional exchangeability and positivity as in covariate adjustment; integrable potential outcomes. Finite variance requires stronger overlap and moment conditions.
Example: With treatment probability 1/4, each treated outcome receives weight 4 in its treatment mean.
Prerequisites: Covariate adjustment for average treatment effect

Name: Doubly robust treatment-effect score
Intuition: Start from an outcome prediction, then correct it using weighted residuals from the outcomes actually observed.
Conditions: Under causal identification assumptions, Eψ equals the average treatment effect if either e is the true propensity or both ma are true outcome means; weights and terms must be integrable. Estimated nuisances need additional inference conditions.
Example: If both outcome regressions are correct, each weighted residual has conditional mean zero even with a misspecified positive propensity.
Prerequisites: Covariate adjustment for average treatment effect; Inverse propensity weighting identity

Name: Markov transition kernel
Intuition: One object moves observables backward by conditional averaging and moves probability distributions forward.
Conditions: K(x,·) is a probability measure for each x and K(·,A) measurable for each measurable A; f bounded measurable, μ a probability measure.
Example: A finite transition matrix is the case K(i,{j})=Pij.
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Conditional expectation

Name: Finite Markov chain time-average theorem
Intuition: One long dependent trajectory samples each state in its stationary proportion.
Conditions: Finite irreducible Markov chain with stationary distribution π; any real f and any initial state. Aperiodicity is not needed for this time-average conclusion.
Example: A deterministic two-state alternation spends half its time in each state despite having no pointwise distributional limit.

Name: Finite Markov chain convergence theorem
Intuition: After enough transitions, the distribution forgets the starting state.
Conditions: P is a finite irreducible aperiodic transition matrix; π is its unique stationary distribution. Periodicity can prevent this limit.
Example: Adding a positive chance of staying in each state removes periodic oscillations from an irreducible finite chain.
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Stationary distribution

Name: Total variation distance between laws
Intuition: Measure the largest probability discrepancy that any yes-or-no event can expose.
Conditions: P,Q probability measures on one measurable space; p,q densities with respect to a common dominating μ, such as P+Q.
Example: For Bernoulli(p) and Bernoulli(q), total variation is |p−q|.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Information and uncertainty

Name: Coupling characterization of total variation
Intuition: Try to realize two laws together so their outcomes agree as often as possible.
Conditions: X∼P and Y∼Q on a common standard Borel state space; the infimum is over all joint laws with those marginals and is attained by a maximal coupling.
Example: Coupling two Bernoulli variables with one uniform draw makes disagreement probability |p−q|.

Name: Dobrushin contraction coefficient
Intuition: If every pair of states produces similar next-step distributions, one transition must erase part of the difference between starting laws.
Conditions: P is a finite row-stochastic matrix; μ,ν probability row vectors. α(P)≤1; a strict one-step contraction needs α(P)<1.
Example: Identical transition rows give α=0 and erase all initial information in one step.
Prerequisites: Total variation distance between laws; Markov transition kernel

Name: Total variation mixing time
Intuition: Ask how many steps suffice to make every starting state look stationary to any event-level test.
Conditions: Finite irreducible aperiodic chain; 0<ε<1; t is an integer. Mixing concerns the distribution, not independence of consecutive samples.
Example: An independent sampler with every row equal to π mixes in at most one step.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Information and uncertainty
Prerequisites: Finite Markov chain convergence theorem; Total variation distance between laws

Name: Kac mean return-time identity
Intuition: A state visited during a fraction π(i) of steps has average spacing 1/π(i) between visits.
Conditions: Finite irreducible Markov chain; start at i; return is strictly after time zero. Periodicity is allowed.
Example: A state with stationary probability 0.1 has mean return time ten steps.

Name: Dirichlet form of a reversible chain
Intuition: A Markov step dissipates variation most strongly when connected states carry very different observable values.
Conditions: Finite chain reversible with stationary π; weighted inner product is sum πi fi gi; f real.
Example: Constant observables have zero energy because all edge differences vanish.

Name: Spectral bound on reversible mixing
Intuition: Every nonconstant eigenmode fades at its own rate; the slowest absolute eigenvalue controls the remaining memory.
