Conditions: Finite irreducible aperiodic reversible chain with at least two states; eigenvalues ordered with λ1=1; t≥0 integer.
Example: An eigenvalue close to −1 causes slowly damped alternation, which explains the absolute value.
Prerequisites: Spectral theorem in finite dimensions; Dirichlet form of a reversible chain

Name: Metropolis–Hastings acceptance rule
Intuition: Correct an easy proposal's directional bias so accepted traffic balances under the desired target law.
Conditions: A proper target π known up to a constant; proposal density or mass q with a common reference measure. At π(x)q(y|x)>0 use the formula; zero-target proposals reject. Invariance alone does not ensure mixing.
Example: Symmetric random-walk proposals reduce the ratio to π(y)/π(x).

Name: Gibbs conditional resampling
Intuition: Replace one coordinate by a fresh draw consistent with the others, preserving the whole joint target distribution.
Conditions: A proper joint target with available regular conditional laws. Coordinate updates preserve π; convergence additionally needs irreducibility and appropriate recurrence or mixing conditions.
Example: A bivariate Gaussian sampler alternates draws from its two conditional normal laws.

Name: Integrated autocorrelation and effective sample size
Intuition: Repeated similar samples provide less averaging precision than fresh independent samples; negative correlations can instead improve precision.
Conditions: Stationary real sequence with 0<σY²<∞ and absolutely summable autocorrelations. Effective-size expression assumes τint>0 and is an asymptotic variance comparison, not a count of independent draws.
Example: For an AR(1)-type correlation ρk=r^k, |r|<1, τint=(1+r)/(1−r).
Prerequisites: Autocorrelation of a stationary process; Variance of a sum

Name: Acceptance–rejection sampling
LaTeX: Y\sim q,\ U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1),\quad \text{accept if }U\le\frac{p(Y)}{M q(Y)};\qquad Y\mid\text{accepted}\sim p
Intuition: Generate points under an easy envelope and retain exactly the fraction needed to carve out the target density.
Conditions: p,q normalized densities, p≤Mq almost everywhere with finite M≥1; U independent of Y. Accepted fraction is 1/M.
Example: A uniform envelope can sample a bounded density on a compact interval.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Randomness and distribution

Name: Importance sampling identity and estimator
Intuition: Visit useful regions more often, then discount each visit by how much it was oversampled.
Conditions: p absolutely continuous with respect to q, E_p|f|<∞; Xi iid q. The estimator is unbiased; finite variance additionally requires ∫f²p²/q<∞.
Example: Shift a Gaussian proposal toward a rare tail and compensate with the density ratio.

Name: Self-normalized importance sampling
Intuition: When the target's total mass is unknown, estimate both the weighted quantity and its normalization from the same draws.
Conditions: Xi iid q, target p proportional to nonnegative ptilde supported where q>0; 0<Eq w<∞ and Eq(w|f|)<∞. A positive denominator is required; the estimator is consistent but generally biased at finite n.
Example: Posterior expectations can be estimated without evaluating the evidence normalizer.

Name: Optimal linear control variate
Intuition: Subtract the predictable part of simulation noise using another quantity whose mean is already known.
Conditions: X,Y square-integrable with positive variances; E Y known and c fixed independently of the draws used for the displayed unbiasedness. Data-estimated coefficients require separate bias analysis.
Example: A simulation output strongly correlated with a known analytic approximation can be estimated much more precisely.

Name: Antithetic sampling variance
Intuition: Pair a random draw with its reflected counterpart so opposite errors can cancel.
Conditions: U uniform(0,1), f(U) square-integrable. Variance improves over two independent draws when the covariance is negative; monotone f is a sufficient condition.
Example: For f(u)=u, the paired estimator is identically 1/2.
Prerequisites: Variance of a sum; Continuous uniform distribution

Name: Stratified Monte Carlo and allocation
Intuition: Guarantee representation of each region, then spend extra draws where probability mass and within-region variability are largest.
Conditions: Known finite partition probabilities ph; independent iid samples within each stratum, nh>0; σh² finite. The displayed interior allocation formula assumes phσh>0 for every stratum and minimizes variance for a fixed total under continuous allocation and equal sampling cost.
Example: Proportional allocation removes randomness in how many samples land in each region.
Prerequisites: Law of total probability; Variance of a sum

Name: Sequential importance weights for particle filtering
LaTeX: w_t^{(i)}\propto w_{t-1}^{(i)}\frac{p(y_t\mid x_t^{(i)})p(x_t^{(i)}\mid x_{t-1}^{(i)})}{q(x_t^{(i)}\mid x_{t-1}^{(i)},y_t)},\quad \widehat\pi_t=\sum_i\bar w_t^{(i)}\delta_{x_t^{(i)}}
Intuition: Carry many possible hidden states forward, reward those that explain the next observation, and replicate promising particles when weights become uneven.
Conditions: State-space model with Markov transitions and conditionally independent observations; proposal covers target support. Formula is before resampling; resampling resets ancestor weights as appropriate. Finite particles give an approximation.
Example: Using the transition itself as proposal leaves the new likelihood as the incremental weight.
Prerequisites: Importance sampling identity and estimator; Bayes' rule

Name: Continuous-time Markov generator matrix
Intuition: Replace per-step transition probabilities with instantaneous traffic rates between states.
Conditions: Finite time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain; off-diagonal qij≥0 and finite, row sums zero. Holding time in i is exponential with rate −qii when positive.
Example: A two-state chain has Q=[[-a,a],[b,−b]].
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Exponential waiting time

Name: Kolmogorov equations for a finite chain
Intuition: Local transition rates assemble into a linear differential equation for the full probability distribution.
Conditions: Finite generator Q; P(0)=I and probability row vector p(0). The two matrix equations are backward and forward forms; Q commutes with its own exponential.
Example: A two-state law relaxes exponentially at rate a+b.

Name: Uniformization of a finite Markov chain
Intuition: Run a discrete Markov chain at a common Poisson clock, allowing harmless self-transitions when a state needs fewer real jumps.
Conditions: Finite generator Q and ν>0 with ν≥maxi(−qii), so P is stochastic. The series converges absolutely for every t≥0.
Example: A chain with escape rates at most 5 can be driven by a Poisson clock of rate 5.
Prerequisites: Continuous-time Markov generator matrix; Poisson process increments

Name: Stationary law of a birth–death process
Intuition: Each neighboring pair balances upward and downward traffic, so probabilities are built by successive rate ratios.
Conditions: Irreducible nonexplosive process on nonnegative integers; births λn>0, deaths μn>0 for n≥1 and μ0=0; displayed normalizing sum finite.
Example: Constant birth λ and death μ give a geometric stationary law when λ<μ.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Continuous-time Markov generator matrix; Detailed balance

Name: Stationary M/M/1 queue
Intuition: One server can balance arrivals only when average service capacity exceeds incoming work; delay rises sharply near that boundary.
Conditions: Poisson arrivals rate λ>0, iid exponential service rate μ>λ, independent arrival/service processes, one FIFO server and unlimited waiting room. L counts jobs in the system; W includes service time.
Example: At λ=1 and μ=2, mean population and mean sojourn time are both 1 in their respective units.
Prerequisites: Stationary law of a birth–death process

Name: Little's queueing law
Intuition: Average occupancy equals entry rate times average time spent inside.
Conditions: A stationary stable system with finite admitted-arrival rate λ and finite arrival-average sojourn time W; L is mean number present. Use consistent system boundaries and count the same population in all three quantities.
Example: An arrival rate of 3 jobs/minute and average stay of 4 minutes imply 12 jobs present on average.

Name: Renewal equation
Intuition: After the first renewal, the process restarts and the remaining time contains a fresh copy of the same counting problem.
Conditions: Iid strictly positive interarrival times with CDF F; N(t) counts completed arrivals after time zero. The integral is Lebesgue–Stieltjes.
Example: Exponential interarrivals solve the equation with m(t)=λt.

Name: Renewal reward theorem
Intuition: Long-run reward per unit time is average reward per cycle divided by average cycle duration.
Conditions: Iid pairs (Ti,Ri), Ti>0, 0<E Ti<∞, E|Ri|<∞; N(t) counts completed cycles. Reward and duration may be dependent within a cycle.
Example: Expected working time divided by expected work-plus-repair cycle length gives long-run availability.
Prerequisites: Strong law of large numbers; Renewal equation

Name: Equilibrium residual lifetime
Intuition: An observer arriving at a random time is more likely to land inside a long interval than a short one.
Conditions: Stationary renewal process with positive interarrival T and 0<E T<∞; R is forward time to the next event. The mean formula is extended-valued if E T²=∞.
Example: Equal-probability intervals of lengths 1 and 9 give mean forward wait 4.1, exceeding half the ordinary mean interval 2.5.
Prerequisites: Renewal reward theorem; Tail integral formula

Name: Galton–Watson extinction probability
Intuition: The population dies out exactly when every child's independent descendant population dies out.
Conditions: Start from one ancestor; each individual has iid nonnegative integer offspring K, finite almost surely. q is the eventual extinction probability.
Example: For K=0 or 2 with equal probabilities, q=1; for K identically 1, q=0 despite mean offspring 1.

Name: Galton–Watson mean and normalized martingale
Intuition: Divide out expected population growth and the remaining population size becomes a conditionally fair process.
Conditions: Z0=1; iid offspring K with 0<m=E K<∞; Fn records the first n generations. Convergence need not preserve mean without additional integrability.
Example: Even with m>1, extinction can occur and the normalized limit can be zero.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Recursion and iteration

Name: Doob Lp maximal inequality
LaTeX: \mathbb E\!\left[\max_{0\le k\le n}|M_k|^p\right]\le\left(\frac p{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb E|M_n|^p,\qquad p>1
Intuition: Control the largest excursion of an entire fair process using only a moment of its final value.
Conditions: Mk is a real discrete-time martingale on 0,…,n with E|Mn|^p<∞. The displayed constant requires p>1.
Example: For p=2, the expected squared maximum is at most four times the final second moment.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Limits and convergence

Name: Discrete Doob decomposition
Intuition: Separate each observed change into what was predictable just before it and its mean-zero surprise.
Conditions: Xn is an integrable adapted discrete-time process. M is a martingale with M0=X0; A is predictable. If X is a submartingale, A is nondecreasing.
Example: A random walk with drift decomposes into its linear drift plus a centered martingale.

Name: L1-bounded martingale convergence
Intuition: A fair process with bounded expected magnitude cannot oscillate forever across fixed intervals.
Conditions: Real discrete-time martingale. This alone gives almost sure convergence; L1 convergence and preservation of E M0 require uniform integrability.
Example: Nonnegative martingales converge almost surely but may lose expectation in the limit.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Conservation and balance

Name: Brownian quadratic variation
Intuition: Brownian increments shrink, yet their squared contributions accumulate into a nonzero clock.
Conditions: Standard Brownian motion on [0,t]; deterministic partitions with mesh tending to zero. Almost sure convergence holds along dyadic partitions; arbitrary mesh convergence here is in L².
Example: The sum's variance is 2 sumk(Δtk)², which tends to zero.
Prerequisites: Brownian motion covariance and increments; Variance of a sum

Name: Itô product rule
Intuition: Two rough processes share an extra product change from their simultaneous fluctuations.
Conditions: X,Y continuous semimartingales; [X,Y] is their quadratic covariation. For Itô diffusions driven by the same scalar Brownian motion, d[X,Y]=σXσY dt.
Example: With X=Y=W, d(W²)=2W dW+dt.

Name: Brownian exponential martingale
Intuition: Subtract half the accumulated noise energy to keep an exponentiated stochastic integral fair.
Conditions: On a fixed finite horizon T, H progressively measurable and satisfies Novikov's condition E exp(1/2∫0^T Hs²ds)<∞. Then Z is a true martingale for t≤T.
Example: For constant H=θ, exp(θWt−θ²t/2) has mean one.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Conservation and balance

Name: Girsanov Brownian drift change
Intuition: Reweight whole paths so what looked like systematic drift under one probability law becomes fair Brownian motion under another.
Conditions: W Brownian under P; finite T; θ progressively measurable with E_P exp(1/2∫0^T θs²ds)<∞. Then WQ is Brownian under Q on [0,T].
Example: A constant tilt θ changes Brownian path drift by −θ under the new measure.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Itô–Stratonovich drift conversion
Intuition: Changing how noise increments are sampled changes the deterministic drift needed to describe the same process.
Conditions: Scalar continuous diffusion with sufficiently regular coefficients, b continuously differentiable, and stochastic integrals well defined; displayed coefficients have no explicit time dependence.
Example: dX=X∘dW corresponds to dX=(X/2)dt+X dW and solution X0 exp(Wt).

Name: Strong existence and uniqueness for Lipschitz SDEs
Intuition: A drift and noise rule that do not amplify nearby states too quickly determine a unique path from the given initial state and noise.
Conditions: b,σ measurable in time, globally Lipschitz in state uniformly on each finite horizon and of linear growth; X0 is square-integrable and F0-measurable. There is a unique continuous adapted strong solution.
Example: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck coefficients b(x)=−θx and constant σ satisfy the assumptions.
Prerequisites: Ito isometry; Picard iteration for an initial value problem

Name: Diffusion infinitesimal generator
Intuition: A diffusion acts on observables through local drift plus the curvature-sensitive spreading caused by noise.
Conditions: Time-homogeneous nonexplosive Itô diffusion dX=b(X)dt+σ(X)dW; f is C² and in the generator domain, for example compactly supported with appropriate continuous coefficients.
Example: Standard d-dimensional Brownian motion has generator one-half the Laplacian.

Name: Kolmogorov backward equation for a diffusion
Intuition: Predict a future observable by evolving a function of the present starting state.
Conditions: Time-homogeneous nonexplosive diffusion; f in the generator domain and u sufficiently C1 in time and C2 in space for the classical equation. Without this smoothness use the semigroup formulation.
Example: For Brownian motion, expected future observables solve the heat equation with diffusivity 1/2.
Prerequisites: Diffusion infinitesimal generator; Markov transition kernel

Name: Feynman–Kac representation
Intuition: A linear evolution with local killing can be computed by averaging terminal values over random paths with survival weights.
Conditions: Nonexplosive diffusion with generator L; bounded continuous V,g. Any bounded C1,2 solution whose Itô integral is a true martingale has this representation; the expectation is not automatically a classical solution without regularity.
Example: With V=0 and Brownian X, this is Gaussian averaging for the heat equation.
Prerequisites: Kolmogorov backward equation for a diffusion

Name: Brownian reflection principle
Intuition: Reflect the part of a path after its first boundary hit to pair paths ending below the boundary with paths ending above it.
Conditions: Standard Brownian motion starting at zero, t>0 and a>0. This exact formula is for zero drift.
Example: The running maximum at time t has the same distribution as |Wt|.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Boundary and interior

Name: Brownian first-passage density
Intuition: Reaching a fixed level is almost certain, but occasional extremely long waits make the average waiting time infinite.
Conditions: Standard Brownian motion starting at zero and a>0. τa is finite almost surely yet E τa=∞.
Example: Doubling the target level multiplies the hitting-time scale by four.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Brownian bridge
Intuition: A Brownian path is pinned to a prescribed endpoint by removing the part linearly explained by that endpoint.
Conditions: Standard Brownian W, fixed T>0, 0≤s,t≤T. B is centered Gaussian with B0=BT=0; it is not adapted to W's original past filtration in this construction.
Example: Its variance t(1−t/T) is largest halfway through the interval.
Prerequisites: Brownian motion covariance and increments; Conditional multivariate Gaussian

Name: Tanaka's local-time formula
Intuition: A corner in the absolute-value function accumulates a correction whenever Brownian motion revisits that corner.
Conditions: One-dimensional Brownian W; a real. Local time is normalized by ∫0^t g(Ws)ds=∫g(a)Lt^a da; sign(0) may be set to zero.
Example: At a=0, absolute Brownian motion is a martingale term plus its increasing local time at zero.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Limits and convergence

Name: Lévy characterization of Brownian motion
LaTeX: M_0=0,\quad M\text{ continuous local martingale},\quad[M]_t=t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M\text{ is standard Brownian motion}
Intuition: Continuity, conditional fairness and the correct accumulated noise clock already determine Brownian behavior.
Conditions: Real process adapted to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions; M is a continuous local martingale with quadratic variation exactly t almost surely.
Example: The stochastic integral of a predictable ±1 process against Brownian motion is Brownian relative to the same filtration.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Information and uncertainty

Name: Compensated Poisson martingale integral
Intuition: Subtract predictable arrivals from the counting process; the remaining jump surprises integrate like orthogonal noise.
Conditions: Poisson process of rate λ>0 in a filtration where its future increments remain independent; H predictable with E∫0^t Hs²ds<∞.
Example: For H=1, Var(Nt−λt)=λt.

Name: Campbell moments for a Poisson point process
Intuition: Random point contributions average according to spatial intensity, and independent Poisson placement gives a particularly simple variance.
Conditions: Poisson point process or random measure with intensity Λ; real measurable f with ∫|f|dΛ and ∫f²dΛ finite. Multiplicities are counted.
Example: For an indicator of a finite-intensity region, both mean and variance equal that region's intensity.
Prerequisites: Poisson process increments; Linearity of expectation

Name: Convex set
Intuition: Every straight journey between two allowed points stays allowed.
Conditions: Subset C of a real vector space; the empty set is conventionally convex. The condition concerns all pairs and all t in [0,1].
Example: A Euclidean ball and an affine half-space are convex; a circle's boundary is not.

Name: Epigraph characterization of convexity
Intuition: A function is convex exactly when all the space above its graph forms a convex solid.
Conditions: Extended-real function f:R^d→(−∞,+∞]; its effective domain is included through the inequality f(x)≤t.
Example: Minimizing a convex function can be written as minimizing t subject to (x,t) lying in its epigraph.

Name: Perspective of a convex function
LaTeX: g(x,t)=t\,f(x/t),\quad t>0;\qquad f\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow g\text{ convex}
Intuition: Separate the amount of a resource from its per-unit value while preserving convex tradeoffs.
Conditions: Convex f on a convex domain; g is defined where t>0 and x/t lies in that domain. Boundary t=0 requires a separately specified closed extension.
Example: The perspective of ||x||² is ||x||²/t, a convex quadratic-over-linear function for t>0.

Name: Support function of a set
Intuition: Ask how far the set reaches when viewed in each linear direction.
Conditions: Nonempty C⊆R^d; the value may be +∞ for unbounded sets. The support function is convex and positively homogeneous even when C is not convex.
Example: For the Euclidean ball of radius r centered at zero, σC(y)=r||y||₂.

Name: Extended-real indicator of a constraint
Intuition: Encode a hard constraint as an infinite penalty so that one optimization language handles both.
Conditions: C⊆R^d and the objective is interpreted in extended-real arithmetic. This 0/+∞ indicator differs from a probability event's 0/1 indicator.
Example: The proximal map of δC is Euclidean projection when C is nonempty, closed and convex.

Name: Strong separation of disjoint convex sets
LaTeX: \exists a\ne0,\alpha<\beta:\quad \langle a,x\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\langle a,y\rangle\quad(x\in C,\ y\in D)
Intuition: Two suitably closed convex regions that do not touch can be distinguished by a linear measurement with a positive gap.
Conditions: Nonempty disjoint convex subsets C,D⊆R^d; C compact and D closed suffice. Mere disjointness of arbitrary convex sets need not give a positive gap.
Example: A point outside a closed convex set can be separated using the direction from its closest point in the set.

Name: Farkas alternative for linear feasibility
LaTeX: \text{Exactly one: }\quad \exists x\ge0:Ax=b\quad\text{or}\quad\exists y:A^\top y\ge0,\ b^\top y<0
Intuition: Either nonnegative ingredients build the target, or one linear test proves that no such recipe can work.
Conditions: Real matrix A∈R^{m×n}, b∈R^m; vector inequalities are componentwise. This alternative needs no strict feasibility assumption.
Example: If every column of A has nonnegative first coordinate but b has negative first coordinate, y=e₁ is an infeasibility certificate.
Prerequisites: Linear map; Strong separation of disjoint convex sets

Name: Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation
Intuition: A closed convex function can be reconstructed from every affine lower support it admits.
Conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f:R^d→(−∞,+∞]. For more general functions, the biconjugate may instead describe a closed convex relaxation.
Example: The absolute-value function is recovered by maximizing xy over slopes |y|≤1.

Name: Infimal convolution
Intuition: Split a target into two components and choose the cheapest division of labor.
Conditions: Extended-real functions on R^d for which the displayed sum is defined; convex f,g give a convex result. Finiteness, closedness and attainment require additional conditions.
Example: With f=δC and g=δD, the result is the extended-real indicator of the Minkowski sum C+D.

Name: Conjugate of an infimal convolution
Intuition: A common price makes the two components of a split optimization separate.
Conditions: Proper functions f,g on R^d with their infimal convolution proper; extended-real conjugates are allowed. No claim of primal attainment is needed.
Example: Combining quadratic costs by optimal splitting turns into adding reciprocal-curvature quadratic conjugates.

Name: Moreau envelope and its gradient
Intuition: Allow a point to move a little while charging for distance, producing a smooth version of a possibly sharp objective.
Conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f on R^d and λ>0. The minimizer is unique, the envelope finite and continuously differentiable, and its gradient is 1/λ-Lipschitz.
Example: The envelope of absolute value is a scaled Huber loss.

Name: Moreau primal-dual decomposition
Intuition: A proximal point and a scaled dual proximal residual divide the same vector into complementary roles.
Conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f on R^d and λ>0; prox_h minimizes h plus half squared distance.
Example: For f=||·||₁, soft thresholding plus clipping to the dual ℓ∞ ball reconstructs x.

Name: Firm nonexpansiveness of a proximal map
Intuition: A convex proximal step cannot amplify differences, and its displacement obeys a stronger angle constraint.
Conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f on R^d; λ>0. In particular ||P(x)−P(y)||≤||x−y||.
Example: Projection onto a closed convex set is firmly nonexpansive by taking f to be its extended-real indicator.

Name: Monotone set-valued operator
Intuition: The output never changes in a direction that opposes the change in input.
Conditions: A:R^d⇉R^d may be set-valued. Maximal monotonicity additionally means its graph cannot be enlarged while preserving this inequality.
Example: The subdifferential of a proper closed convex function is maximal monotone.

Name: Resolvent of a maximal monotone operator
LaTeX: J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1},\qquad A=\partial f\Longrightarrow J_{\lambda A}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}
Intuition: Solve one implicit balance equation to convert a possibly multivalued relation into a stable single-valued update.
Conditions: Maximal monotone A on finite-dimensional Euclidean space and λ>0. Its resolvent is everywhere defined and firmly nonexpansive.
Example: For A(x)=Mx with symmetric M≥0, the resolvent is (I+λM)⁻¹x.

Name: Baillon–Haddad gradient inequality
Intuition: For a smooth convex landscape, the gradient's change must align with the displacement strongly enough to control its size.
Conditions: Convex differentiable f:R^d→R with L-Lipschitz gradient and L>0. Lipschitz continuity without convexity is insufficient.
Example: For f(x)=L||x||²/2, equality holds.
Prerequisites: Descent lemma; First-order characterization of convexity

Name: Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient domination
Intuition: A large objective error must leave a detectable slope, so a small gradient certifies near-optimal value.
Conditions: Differentiable f bounded below by attained minimum f*, globally L-Lipschitz gradient and the displayed PL inequality with 0<μ≤L. Rate for xk+1=xk−∇f(xk)/L; convexity is not required.
Example: Rank-deficient least squares can satisfy PL despite lacking strong convexity in every parameter direction.

Name: Projected gradient mapping
LaTeX: G_\alpha(x)=\frac{x-\Pi_C(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))}{\alpha},\qquad G_\alpha(x)=0\iff\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\ \forall y\in C
Intuition: Measure the part of the gradient step that survives the feasibility constraint.
Conditions: Nonempty closed convex C⊆R^d, x∈C, differentiable f and α>0. The zero condition is first-order stationarity; it implies global optimality if f is convex.
Example: At the minimizer of f(x)=x on [0,∞), the ordinary gradient is 1 but the projected gradient mapping is zero.

Name: Nonconvex gradient-descent stationarity bound
Intuition: Repeated decreases cannot consume more objective value than is available, so some iterate must have a small slope.
Conditions: Differentiable f:R^d→R with L-Lipschitz gradient, L>0 and finite infimum. This bounds a gradient norm, not distance to a global minimum.
Example: To find an iterate with gradient norm at most ε, the bound requires K≥2L(f(x0)−inf f)/ε².

Name: Nesterov accelerated gradient scheme
Intuition: Use carefully scheduled extrapolation to make past progress help the next gradient evaluation.
Conditions: Convex differentiable f with L-Lipschitz gradient, L>0 and a minimizer x*. Initialize y0=x0,t0=1. This scheme gives f(xk)−f*≤2L||x0−x*||²/(k+1)² for k≥1.
Example: The worst-case convex objective rate improves from order 1/k for ordinary gradient descent to order 1/k².
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Limits and convergence

Name: FISTA for composite convex objectives
Intuition: Combine a smooth gradient, a nonsmooth proximal correction, and an acceleration schedule.
Conditions: F=f+g; f convex differentiable with L-Lipschitz gradient, g proper closed convex, L>0, and a minimizer exists. Start x0∈dom g,y0=x0,t0=1; objective gap is O(1/k²), but individual values need not decrease.
Example: For least squares plus an ℓ₁ penalty, each accelerated step ends with soft thresholding.
Prerequisites: Proximal gradient method; Nesterov accelerated gradient scheme

Name: Frank–Wolfe conditional gradient
Intuition: Find the best feasible point for a linearized objective, then blend toward it.
Conditions: Nonempty compact convex C, differentiable f on a neighborhood of C, x0∈C and 0≤γk≤1. The formula defines a feasible method; convergence rates additionally need smoothness and suitable step choices.
Example: On a simplex, the linear oracle selects a coordinate vertex, so iterates are sparse mixtures of selected vertices.
Prerequisites: First-order characterization of convexity; Convex barycentric combination

Name: Frank–Wolfe optimality gap
LaTeX: g_{\rm FW}(x)=\max_{s\in C}\langle\nabla f(x),x-s\rangle,\qquad0\le f(x)-f_*\le g_{\rm FW}(x)
Intuition: The largest feasible linearized improvement is a computable upper bound on how much objective value remains to gain.
Conditions: Convex differentiable f on a neighborhood of nonempty compact convex C; x∈C and f*=min_C f.
Example: The same linear oracle that produces a Frank–Wolfe direction also produces its stopping certificate.
Prerequisites: Frank–Wolfe conditional gradient; First-order characterization of convexity

Name: Projected dual ascent
Intuition: Raise the price of violated inequalities and lower prices when constraints are comfortably satisfied.
Conditions: L(x,λ)=f(x)+λᵀg(x), constraints g≤0, λk≥0, αk>0 and an attained finite Lagrangian minimum at each step. Convergence needs additional step-size and regularity assumptions.
Example: If a resource constraint exceeds its budget, its multiplier increases at the next update.
Prerequisites: Lagrangian dual function; Projected gradient method

Name: Augmented Lagrangian for equality constraints
Intuition: Combine constraint prices with a quadratic charge for disagreement, then revise prices using the remaining residual.
Conditions: Equality-constrained problem Ax=b, ρ>0. In the method of multipliers, xk+1 minimizes Lρ(·,λk); convergence is not guaranteed for arbitrary nonconvex problems.
Example: The extra quadratic term penalizes infeasibility while vanishing at every feasible point.

Name: Alternating direction method of multipliers
Intuition: Let two objective blocks solve separate subproblems and use a shared residual to coordinate their agreement.
Conditions: Problem min f(x)+g(z) subject to Ax+Bz=c; fixed ρ>0. Standard two-block convergence assumes proper closed convex objectives, a saddle point and attained subproblem minima; more than two naive blocks need not inherit it.
Example: Splitting lasso with x=z separates a quadratic solve from soft thresholding.
Prerequisites: Augmented Lagrangian for equality constraints; Proximal operator

Name: Douglas–Rachford splitting
Intuition: Reflect through one proximal solution, correct using the other, then average the effect.
Conditions: Proper closed convex f,g on R^d, γ>0, and a solution of 0∈∂f(x)+∂g(x). The shadow pk converges to a minimizer; z itself is an auxiliary variable.
Example: For two closed convex sets with nonempty intersection, the two proximal maps are projections.
Prerequisites: Proximal operator; Resolvent of a maximal monotone operator

Name: Chambolle–Pock primal-dual splitting
LaTeX: \begin{aligned}y^{k+1}&=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\\x^{k+1}&=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^\top y^{k+1}),\\\bar x^{k+1}&=2x^{k+1}-x^k\end{aligned}
Intuition: Alternate primal and dual proximal corrections while a linear operator passes disagreement between their spaces.
Conditions: Minimize f(x)+g(Kx) with proper closed convex f,g on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and an existing saddle point. Set x̄0=x0 and τ,σ>0 with τσ||K||²<1.
Example: Image denoising can place pixel fidelity in f and a gradient penalty in g(Kx).

Name: BFGS Hessian approximation update
LaTeX: B_{k+1}=B_k-\frac{B_ks_ks_k^\top B_k}{s_k^\top B_ks_k}+\frac{y_ky_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k},\quad s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k,\ y_k=\nabla f(x_{k+1})-\nabla f(x_k)
Intuition: Use the observed change in gradient to repair a curvature model along the latest step.
Conditions: B_k symmetric positive definite, s_k≠0 and y_kᵀs_k>0. The update remains positive definite and satisfies B_{k+1}s_k=y_k; convergence claims require further hypotheses.
Example: For a one-dimensional quadratic, one nonzero secant step recovers its exact second derivative.
Prerequisites: Newton step for optimization; Hessian matrix

Name: Exact trust-region subproblem conditions
Intuition: A local quadratic model is optimized only within a radius where it is trusted, including directions of negative curvature.
Conditions: Real symmetric B and Δ>0. A feasible p is a global minimizer exactly when some λ satisfies the displayed conditions; B itself need not be positive semidefinite.
Example: At a saddle with zero gradient and negative curvature, the optimal step can lie on the boundary instead of staying at zero.

Name: Armijo sufficient-decrease condition
Intuition: Accept a step when it earns a specified fraction of the improvement predicted by the local slope.
Conditions: f continuously differentiable, p a descent direction with ∇f(x)ᵀp<0, α>0 and 0<c1<1. Sufficiently small positive steps satisfy this condition; backtracking contracts α by a fixed factor in (0,1).
Example: For gradient descent p=−∇f(x), the required decrease is c1α||∇f(x)||².

Name: Wolfe line-search conditions
LaTeX: \begin{aligned}f(x+\alpha p)&\le f(x)+c_1\alpha\nabla f(x)^\top p,\\\nabla f(x+\alpha p)^\top p&\ge c_2\nabla f(x)^\top p,\qquad0<c_1<c_2<1\end{aligned}
Intuition: Require both enough decrease and enough flattening along a downhill direction.
Conditions: Continuously differentiable f, descent direction p, α>0. If f is bounded below along the search ray, acceptable Wolfe steps exist. These are the weak Wolfe conditions.
Example: With s=αp and y=∇f(x+αp)−∇f(x), the curvature condition guarantees yᵀs>0.

Name: Natural gradient direction
LaTeX: v_{\rm nat}=-I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla L(\theta)=\arg\min_v\left\{\nabla L(\theta)^\top v+\tfrac12v^\top I(\theta)v\right\}
Intuition: Measure the size of a parameter move by how much it changes the probability model.
Conditions: Differentiable objective L and a regular statistical model with finite positive-definite Fisher information I(θ). The tangent direction is invariant under smooth invertible reparameterization; a finite coordinate Euler step need not be.
Example: For a normal location model with known variance σ², the natural gradient scales the ordinary gradient by σ².
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Change of coordinates

Name: Diagonal AdaGrad update
Intuition: Coordinates with a long history of large gradients take smaller future steps.
Conditions: Gradient or subgradient vectors gt, η>0 and numerical safeguard ε>0; this is an unconstrained diagonal version. Regret and convergence guarantees require boundedness and assumptions on the objective sequence.
Example: A rarely active feature keeps a larger effective learning rate than a frequently active coordinate.

Name: Adam moment-corrected update
Intuition: Smooth the gradient and its squared magnitude separately, then use their ratio to scale each update.
Conditions: m0=v0=0, 0≤β1,β2<1, α,ε>0; squaring, square roots and division are coordinatewise. Bias correction removes zero-initialization bias for stationary moments; the formula alone gives no universal convergence guarantee.
Example: At the first step, the bias-corrected estimates are g1 and g1 squared.

Name: Variance-reduced finite-sum gradient
LaTeX:
v_i(x)=
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(\widetilde x)+
abla f(\widetilde x),\quad f= rac1n\sum_{j=1}^n f_j,\quad\mathbb E_i v_i(x)=
abla f(x)
Intuition: Correct a noisy component gradient by subtracting its remembered value and adding back the exact average at that snapshot.
Conditions: Differentiable finite-sum objective, i sampled uniformly from {1,…,n} independently conditional on x and snapshot x̃. This establishes unbiasedness; algorithmic rates require smoothness and step schedules.
Example: When x=x̃, every sampled estimator equals the full gradient at the snapshot, so sampling variance is zero.
Prerequisites: Stochastic gradient descent; Linearity of expectation

Name: Online projected-gradient regret bound
Intuition: Even without knowing future losses, projected gradient updates can approach the performance of the best fixed decision in hindsight.
Conditions: Nonempty closed convex feasible set of diameter at most D>0; convex losses with chosen subgradients gt of norm ≤G>0. Update xt+1=ΠC(xt−ηgt), x1∈C; bound holds for every fixed u∈C.
Example: Average regret is at most DG/√T under the displayed horizon-dependent step size.

Name: Logarithmic barrier and central-path gap
Intuition: Stay inside the feasible region while increasing pressure toward the true objective, with reciprocal slacks acting as prices.
Conditions: Differentiable convex f,gi, constraints gi(x)≤0, strictly feasible domain and an attained stationary barrier minimum for t>0; unconstrained except for these inequalities. The resulting dual certificate yields the gap.
Example: Increasing t tenfold reduces the certified barrier suboptimality m/t tenfold.

Name: Semidefinite programming form
LaTeX: \min_{X\in\mathbb S^n}\langle C,X\rangle\quad\text{subject to }\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i,\quad X\succeq0,\qquad\langle A,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top X)
Intuition: Optimize linearly over matrices that represent nonnegative quadratic energies.
Conditions: Real symmetric data C,Ai; X≽0 means vᵀXv≥0 for all v. This is a convex optimization model; strong duality requires an appropriate qualification such as strict feasibility.
Example: Restricting X to diagonal matrices recovers nonnegative variables in linear programming.

Name: Second-order cone programming form
LaTeX: \min_x c^\top x\quad\text{subject to }\|A_i x+b_i\|_2\le d_i^\top x+e_i,\quad Fx=g
Intuition: Keep Euclidean magnitudes below affine budgets while optimizing a linear cost.
Conditions: Real compatible matrices and vectors. Each constraint is the preimage of a Lorentz cone, so its right side is necessarily nonnegative at feasible points.
Example: Least-squares norm minimization becomes an SOCP by minimizing t subject to ||Ax−b||₂≤t.
Prerequisites: Norm axioms and induced norm; Convex set

Name: Empirical risk minimization
Intuition: Choose a rule by minimizing its average observed loss, hoping that this average represents future cases.
Conditions: Measurable loss and predictors with well-defined expectations; the training sample is usually iid from the target distribution. An exact minimizer must exist for the displayed argmin; empirical success alone does not imply generalization.
Example: Squared-loss empirical risk over linear predictors gives ordinary least squares.

Name: Regularized empirical risk
Intuition: Balance fitting observed examples against a cost for the complexity or size of the fitted rule.
Conditions: λ≥0, specified loss, hypothesis class and penalty; existence and uniqueness depend on them. The numerical meaning of λ changes if the loss is a sum rather than an average.
Example: An ℓ₂ penalty on regression coefficients gives ridge; an ℓ₁ penalty gives lasso.

Name: Finite-class uniform generalization bound
Intuition: Testing many candidate rules costs only a logarithm of their number in the sample-size requirement.
Conditions: A fixed finite nonempty class H, iid sample of size n and measurable losses in [0,1]; ε>0. The class cannot be freely chosen after looking at the same sample.
Example: It suffices that n≥log(2|H|/δ)/(2ε²) to make every empirical risk ε-accurate with probability at least 1−δ.

Name: Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension
Intuition: Count how many sample locations can receive every possible binary labeling from the model class.
Conditions: Class H of binary-valued functions on a set X; A ranges over finite subsets of X. The value is an integer or infinity; shattering concerns existence of a suitable set, not all sets of that size.
Example: Thresholds on the real line have VC dimension 1; intervals have VC dimension 2.

Name: Sauer–Shelah growth bound
Intuition: A class that cannot freely label d+1 points has only polynomially many patterns on larger samples.
Conditions: Binary class H of VC dimension d; ΠH(n) is the largest number of labelings on n points. The first sum uses binomial coefficients zero above n; the final bound requires n≥d≥1.
Example: For line thresholds, the exact growth is n+1, matching the d=1 binomial sum.

Name: VC uniform-convergence bound
Intuition: An infinite model class can behave like a finite collection once restricted to the observed and comparison samples.
Conditions: Binary classification with 0/1 loss, iid sample of size n, ε>0 and a class satisfying the standard measurability condition for the supremum; otherwise use outer probability. Constants here are a conservative classical version.
Example: Combining with Sauer–Shelah gives an error scale of order sqrt((d log(n/d)+log(1/δ))/n) when n≥d.
Prerequisites: Sauer–Shelah growth bound; Finite-class uniform generalization bound

Name: Empirical Rademacher complexity
Intuition: Measure how well the function class can align with random signs on this particular sample.
Conditions: Fixed sample S=(Z1,…,Zn), nonempty real function class and independent symmetric signs. Assume the supremum measurable and integrable; this convention uses no absolute value and a factor 1/n.
Example: A single fixed function has empirical Rademacher complexity zero because its random signed average has mean zero.

Name: Rademacher generalization bound
Intuition: The capacity to fit random noise on the sample bounds how optimistic the sample average may be.
Conditions: Fixed measurable class F of [0,1]-valued loss functions; iid sample size n and 0<δ<1. The displayed simultaneous bound holds with probability at least 1−δ; R(f)=E f(Z).
Example: Two classes of equal parameter count can receive different bounds because their sample-specific Rademacher complexities differ.
Patterns: Randomness and distribution; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Empirical Rademacher complexity; Empirical risk minimization

Name: PAC-Bayes Bernoulli-KL bound
Intuition: A data-chosen distribution over predictors pays for how far it moves from a prior fixed before seeing the data.
Conditions: Finite hypothesis and observation spaces, losses in [0,1], iid sample n≥8, prior P independent of S, 0<δ<1. With probability ≥1−δ the bound holds for all Q≪P; risks average over h∼Q and kl is Bernoulli relative entropy in nats.
Example: A concentrated posterior around a low-loss group can be certified if its KL cost relative to the prior is modest.
Prerequisites: Kullback-Leibler divergence; Entropy variational formula for log-sum-exp

Name: Uniform stability implies expected generalization
Intuition: If replacing one training example barely changes any prediction loss, reusing the training data creates little average optimism.
Conditions: S and S′ have size n and differ in one observation; deterministic measurable learning rule A, iid data and integrable loss. The stated bound is on the expected signed gap, not a high-probability or expected-absolute-gap bound.
Example: Strongly regularized convex learning algorithms often have replacement stability of order 1/n under Lipschitz loss assumptions.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Limits and convergence

Name: Hard-margin support vector machine
Intuition: Choose a separating hyperplane with the widest empty buffer between the two classes.
Conditions: Finite sample xi∈R^d, yi∈{−1,1}, both classes present and linearly separable. The canonical functional margin is fixed at 1; the distance between the two supporting planes is 2/||w||.
Example: Only observations touching the optimal margin need nonzero dual multipliers.

Name: Soft-margin SVM and hinge loss
Intuition: Permit violations of the ideal margin but charge linearly for their size.
Conditions: Finite binary-labeled sample and C>0; the intercept b is unpenalized. This equals the slack-variable program with ξi≥0 and yi(wᵀxi+b)≥1−ξi.
Example: A correctly classified point can still incur hinge loss if it lies within the margin.
Prerequisites: Hard-margin support vector machine; Regularized empirical risk

Name: Kernel soft-margin SVM dual
Intuition: Express the classifier through weighted training examples and pairwise similarities.
Conditions: Positive-semidefinite kernel k, finite labels ±1, C>0, unpenalized intercept and the soft-margin primal. Prediction uses sign(Σi αiyi k(xi,x)+b).
Example: For a linear kernel, w=Σi αiyi xi.
Prerequisites: Soft-margin SVM and hinge loss; Lagrangian dual function

Name: Positive-semidefinite kernel
Intuition: A similarity function is a valid kernel when it behaves like an inner product in some feature space.
Conditions: Real symmetric k on X×X; the quadratic inequality must hold for every finite choice of points and real coefficients. This is equivalent to a Hilbert-space feature representation.
Example: k(x,x′)=(1+xᵀx′)² is the inner product of suitable constant, linear and quadratic features.

Name: Representer theorem
Intuition: Although the hypothesis space may be infinite, an optimum needs only components visible at the training points.
Conditions: Reproducing-kernel Hilbert space H; Φ depends only on the displayed evaluations and Ω is strictly increasing. The implication assumes a minimizer exists; nondecreasing Ω guarantees an in-span minimizer when one exists, not necessarily every minimizer.
Example: Kernel ridge regression searches finitely many coefficients despite using an infinite-dimensional Gaussian kernel space.
Prerequisites: Positive-semidefinite kernel; Orthogonal decomposition and energy split

Name: Kernel ridge regression
Intuition: Fit a weighted collection of data-centered similarities, shrinking unstable directions of the Gram matrix.
Conditions: Real positive-semidefinite kernel, λ>0; objective is n⁻¹Σi(yi−f(xi))²+λ||f||H² with no separate intercept. K+nλI is invertible even if K is singular.
Example: With a linear kernel, this is ridge regression written in sample coordinates.

Name: Gaussian process
Intuition: Specify a random function by requiring every finite list of its values to form a Gaussian vector.
Conditions: Mean function m and positive-semidefinite covariance kernel k; finite-dimensional laws must be consistent, as this construction ensures. Sample-path continuity or differentiability requires additional kernel regularity.
Example: Brownian motion is a zero-mean Gaussian process with k(s,t)=min(s,t) for s,t≥0.

Name: Gaussian-process regression posterior
Intuition: Observed values pull the predicted function through covariance, while subtracting the part of uncertainty those observations explain.
Conditions: Zero-mean GP prior, yi=f(xi)+εi with independent N(0,σ²) noise independent of f, σ²>0. Formulas describe latent test values; predicting noisy observations adds σ²I.
Example: The posterior mean equals kernel ridge prediction when nλ=σ² and the kernel is the same.

Name: Gaussian-process log marginal likelihood
Intuition: A covariance model is rewarded for explaining the data and charged for spreading probability over a large volume.
Conditions: Zero-mean Gaussian-process observations with independent Gaussian noise and positive-definite C. Nonzero means replace y by y−m; kernel parameters affect both the fit and determinant terms.
Example: A very flexible covariance can reduce the quadratic mismatch but pays through its log determinant.

Name: Gaussian radial-basis kernel
Intuition: Two inputs are similar when their distance is small relative to a chosen length scale.
Conditions: x,x′∈R^d, ℓ>0 and σf²≥0. The squared-exponential kernel is positive semidefinite; it is a covariance/similarity function rather than a normalized probability density over x.
Example: Doubling all input coordinates and doubling ℓ leaves every kernel value unchanged.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Positive-semidefinite kernel; Derivative of an exponential

Name: Affine-activation neural layer
Intuition: Mix input features linearly, shift their thresholds, then apply a nonlinear response.
Conditions: Compatible real matrix/vector dimensions and a specified activation σ, usually applied coordinatewise. Stacking purely affine layers without nonlinearities is still an affine map.
Example: Choosing σ(t)=max(0,t) produces a piecewise-affine layer.

Name: Backpropagation through dense layers
Intuition: Pass loss sensitivities backward through each operation, reusing intermediate values from the forward computation.
Conditions: a^(ℓ+1)=Wℓh^(ℓ)+bℓ, h^(ℓ)=σ(a^(ℓ)), and δ^(ℓ)=∂L/∂a^(ℓ). Scalar differentiable loss and differentiable activations at the evaluated points; nonsmooth points require a convention and need not have an ordinary derivative.
Example: A weight derivative is the downstream sensitivity times the upstream activation.
Prerequisites: Multivariable chain rule; Affine-activation neural layer

Name: Rectified linear unit
Intuition: A gate blocks negative input and passes positive input unchanged.
Conditions: Real z; the derivative at zero does not exist. The convex subdifferential at zero is [0,1], and implementations choose a convention for backpropagation.
Example: ReLU(z)−ReLU(−z)=z exactly.

Name: Softmax cross-entropy gradient
LaTeX: p_j=\frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_ke^{z_k}},\qquad L=-\sum_j y_j\log p_j,\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j}=p_j-y_j
Intuition: The learning signal is predicted probability minus target probability.
Conditions: Finite real logits, target vector yj≥0 summing to1, and natural logarithms. The derivative is with respect to logits; one-hot labels are a special case.
Example: For a one-hot correct class c, its gradient is pc−1 while other class gradients equal their predicted probabilities.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Information and uncertainty

Name: Inverted dropout
Intuition: Randomly omit features during training while rescaling the survivors to preserve their conditional mean.
Conditions: Keep probability 0<q≤1, masks independent of h and usually independent across coordinates; the formula uses inverted scaling during training. Nonlinear network outputs need not equal their expectation when masks are removed.
Example: With q=1/2, each retained activation is doubled and each omitted activation is zero.

Name: Mini-batch normalization
Intuition: Put the current batch on a common scale, then learn a useful shift and rescaling.
Conditions: Applied to one feature across a batch of m≥1 observations; ε>0 and learned γ,β. This uses divisor m, not the unbiased sample-variance divisor m−1. Inference commonly uses stored population-moment estimates.
Example: For γ=1,β=0, the normalized batch has mean zero and variance vB/(vB+ε).

Name: Scaled dot-product attention
Intuition: Each query forms a data-dependent weighted average of value vectors using its similarity to keys.
Conditions: Q∈R^{nq×dk}, K∈R^{nk×dk}, V∈R^{nk×dv}, dk≥1; row-wise softmax has finite logits. Masked rows must retain at least one allowed key.
Example: Identical logits in a row give the arithmetic mean of that row's available value vectors.

Name: Sigmoidal universal approximation
Intuition: Enough shifted and tilted copies of one nonlinear response can approximate any continuous shape on a bounded cube.
Conditions: Continuous sigmoidal σ with limits0 at −∞ and1 at +∞; finite-dimensional unit cube, real coefficients and an unrestricted finite width N. The theorem gives existence, not efficient training, sample complexity or an economical width.
Example: The logistic activation satisfies these hypotheses; a single affine layer does not have this approximation property.

Name: k-means distortion objective
Intuition: Represent each observation by its nearest prototype and minimize total squared replacement error.
Conditions: Finite points xi∈R^d and integer1≤k≤n; the centroids are unconstrained real vectors. The objective is generally nonconvex in all centroids together.
Example: For k=1, the unique centroid is the arithmetic mean.

Name: Lloyd assignment-and-centroid iteration
Intuition: Alternate sending each point to its nearest center and moving each center to its group's average.
Conditions: Finite Euclidean data, specified tie-breaking and nonempty updated clusters; empty clusters need a separate reinitialization or retention rule. Each exact block step cannot increase distortion, but global optimality is not guaranteed.
Example: Starting from two centers, each pass alternately changes the partition and the two means.

Name: Finite Gaussian mixture model
Intuition: Choose a hidden group, then draw from that group's Gaussian cloud.
Conditions: Finite k, xi∈R^d and positive-definite covariance matrices for ordinary densities. A mixture of Gaussians is generally not itself Gaussian.
Example: Two separated one-dimensional Gaussian components can produce a bimodal density.
Prerequisites: Multivariate normal density; Law of total probability

Name: EM updates for a Gaussian mixture
Intuition: Use fractional group memberships to compute weighted counts, means and covariance matrices.
Conditions: Positive mixture weights and nonsingular component densities for the E-step; each Nj>0. The unconstrained covariance update may become singular and Gaussian-mixture likelihood can be unbounded, so regularization is often needed.
Example: A point with responsibility0.8 contributes0.8 of an observation to that component's updated mean.
Prerequisites: Finite Gaussian mixture model; Expectation-maximization algorithm

Name: Naive Bayes classifier
Intuition: Add separate pieces of class evidence after assuming the features are independent within each class.
Conditions: Finite classes with positive prior mass and specified conditional feature probabilities/densities; conditional independence Xj⊥Xk given Y is a modeling assumption. Zero factors give log probability −∞ and ties require a rule.
Example: Under Bernoulli feature models, word-presence evidence contributes additive class log odds.
Prerequisites: Bayes' rule; Independence of random variables

Name: k-nearest-neighbor regression
Intuition: Predict by averaging the outcomes of the k observations closest to the query.
Conditions: 1≤k≤n, a specified distance on inputs and deterministic or randomized tie-breaking defining exactly k neighbors. Statistical consistency needs assumptions and a growing k with k/n→0; the formula alone is only an estimator.
Example: For k=n, every query receives the global response mean.
Prerequisites: Arithmetic mean; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Decision-tree impurity decrease
Intuition: A useful split makes each child group more predictable than the unsplit parent.
Conditions: Empirical class proportions in a nonempty parent, two nonempty children and weights equal to child fractions. Here I is entropy in nats; other tree criteria use different impurity functions.
Example: A perfectly separating split has zero child entropy, so its gain equals parent entropy.

Name: AdaBoost exponential reweighting
Intuition: Increase the influence of examples the current weak rule misses and combine the rules with confidence weights.
Conditions: Binary labels and predictions ±1, positive normalized observation weights, and0<εt<1/2 for the displayed positive finite αt. Final classifier uses sign(Σt αtht(x)); the separable εt=0 case needs stopping or a convention.
Example: A mistaken example's weight is multiplied by e^α while a correctly classified example's weight is multiplied by e^−α before normalization.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Exponentials and logarithms
Prerequisites: Weighted arithmetic mean; Exponential family and log partition function

Name: Random Fourier feature approximation
Intuition: Approximate a stationary similarity by averaging a finite collection of randomly chosen oscillations.
Conditions: Continuous real stationary positive-definite kernel k with k(0)=1 and spectral probability law ρ such that k(t)=Eρ cos(ωᵀt). Independent ωj∼ρ and bj∼Uniform[0,2π]; this formula uses angular frequencies.
Example: For k(t)=exp(−||t||²/(2ℓ²)), sample ω∼N(0,ℓ⁻²I).

Name: Autoencoder reconstruction objective
Intuition: Compress each example into an internal representation and train a decoder to reconstruct what matters.
Conditions: Finite Euclidean data and specified encoder/decoder families. A bottleneck, regularization or corruption is needed to prevent an unrestricted identity solution; useful representations do not follow from reconstruction alone.
Example: A linear rank-r encoder-decoder at a global squared-error optimum reconstructs the PCA subspace for centered data.

Name: Bayesian-network factorization
Intuition: Build a joint distribution from local conditional rules arranged without directed cycles.
Conditions: A finite directed acyclic graph and normalized conditional probability tables, or compatible conditional densities/kernels; parent sets follow a topological order. A causal interpretation requires additional assumptions beyond this factorization.
Example: A first-order Markov chain factors as p(x0)∏t p(xt|xt−1).

Name: Sum-product messages on a pairwise tree
LaTeX: m_{i\to j}(x_j)=\sum_{x_i}\psi_i(x_i)\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\!\!\prod_{\ell\in N(i)\setminus\{j\}}\!\!m_{\ell\to i}(x_i),\qquad p_i(x_i)\propto\psi_i(x_i)\prod_{\ell\in N(i)}m_{\ell\to i}(x_i)
Intuition: Each branch sends the rest of the tree a compact summary of all possibilities it contains.
Conditions: Finite discrete variables on a tree with nonnegative unary/pairwise factors and positive finite partition sum. Messages are computed after receiving all other-neighbor messages; the formulas give exact marginals. On loopy graphs, naive iteration is not generally exact.
Example: For a chain, the two message directions are forward and backward marginalization.
Prerequisites: Law of total probability; Bayesian-network factorization

Name: Log-linear Markov random field
Intuition: Score compatible local configurations, add their scores, and normalize the resulting global weights.
Conditions: Finite discrete state spaces and finite real parameters/features on cliques C of an undirected graph. Positivity ensures the equivalence between graph separation and the appropriate Markov factorization theorem; edges need not represent causal influence.
Example: Unary terms favor labels while pairwise terms favor compatible neighboring labels.
Prerequisites: Exponential family and log partition function; Gibbs distribution

Name: Coordinate mean-field variational update
Intuition: Replace a complicated joint posterior with independent factors, letting each factor feel the averaged effect of the others.
Conditions: A normalizable posterior with finite relevant expectations; restrict q to a product family. Each coordinate update is valid when the exponentiated expectation is integrable and normalized. Coordinate optima need not give the global best product approximation.
Example: In conjugate models, averaging sufficient statistics often keeps each updated factor in a recognizable exponential family.
Prerequisites: Evidence lower bound identity; Kullback-Leibler divergence

Name: Pathwise reparameterization gradient
Intuition: Keep the underlying random draw fixed while differentiating how the generated sample moves with the parameters.
Conditions: Base law p0 independent of θ; almost-sure differentiability in a parameter neighborhood and an integrable dominating bound on derivatives justify exchange of gradient and expectation. The derivative on the right includes all direct and pathwise parameter dependence.
Example: For Z=μ+σε with ε∼N(0,1), derivatives can pass through μ and σ while ε remains fixed.
Prerequisites: Multivariable chain rule; Dominated convergence theorem

Name: Likelihood-ratio gradient of an expectation
Intuition: A parameter changes an average both by changing each outcome's value and by changing how often outcomes are sampled.
Conditions: Densities or masses with parameter-independent support, differentiable integrand/density and domination sufficient to differentiate under the integral; score terms integrable. Moving support may add boundary terms. No differentiability in Z is needed.
Example: A constant baseline b can be subtracted from f in the score term because the expected score is zero under the same regularity.

Name: Gaussian denoising score matching
LaTeX: \widetilde X=X+\sigma\varepsilon,\quad \min_s\mathbb E\left\|s(\widetilde X)+\frac{\widetilde X-X}{\sigma^2}\right\|^2,\qquad s_*(u)=\nabla_u\log p_\sigma(u)
Intuition: Learn a field pointing toward likely clean structure by predicting how noise displaced the observations.
Conditions: X∈R^d, independent ε∼N(0,I), σ>0; pσ is the Gaussian-smoothed data density. Minimize over measurable square-integrable fields, with differentiation of the Gaussian convolution justified. The target is the spatial score of pσ, not a parameter score or the unsmoothed density's score.
Example: The optimal denoised mean is E[X|X̃=u]=u+σ²s*(u).

Name: Hellinger distance
Intuition: Take square roots of probabilities and compare them with Euclidean geometry.
Conditions: Probability measures P,Q dominated by a common measure μ, with densities p,q. This normalized convention has0≤H≤1; some references omit the factor1/2. The result is independent of μ.
Example: Distributions with disjoint supports have H=1.

Name: Rényi divergence
Intuition: Change the order to tune how heavily rare or large likelihood ratios contribute to distributional mismatch.
Conditions: Finite alphabet, probability vectors and natural logs. For α>1, pi>0 with qi=0 gives +∞; zero-over-zero terms contribute0. For0<α<1, terms with either mass zero vanish; disjoint supports give +∞.
Example: As α→1, the expression tends to KL divergence; at α=1/2 it is −2log Σ√piqi.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Scaling and homogeneity

Name: Rényi entropy
Intuition: Measure effective diversity while changing how strongly common outcomes dominate the count.
Conditions: Finite probability vector, α>0 with α≠1 in the displayed sum, and natural logs. The value at1 is its continuous limit; zero masses contribute0.
Example: H2(P)=−log Σpi² is negative log probability that two independent draws collide.

Name: Jensen–Shannon divergence
Intuition: Compare two distributions through a common mixture so neither is asked to explain outcomes it assigns no mass to.
Conditions: Probability measures on the same measurable space, KL in nats. This equal-weight convention satisfies0≤JS≤log2 and remains finite for disjoint supports; √JS is a metric.
Example: If a fair hidden coin chooses P or Q, JS is the mutual information between the coin and the observed draw.

Name: Csiszár f-divergence
Intuition: Compare probability laws by applying a convex penalty to their local likelihood ratio.
Conditions: P≪Q, convex f:(0,∞)→R with f(1)=0 and f(0) defined by the right limit; expectation may be +∞. General nondominated laws need an added singular-mass term, which is outside this displayed version.
Example: f(t)=tlog t gives KL; f(t)=|t−1|/2 gives total variation.

Name: Pinsker inequality
Intuition: Small relative entropy guarantees that every event has nearly the same probability under the two laws.
Conditions: Probability measures on the same measurable space, TV=sup_A|P(A)−Q(A)| and natural-log KL; if KL is infinite the bound is vacuous. The factor changes with log base or unhalved variation conventions.
Example: KL≤0.02 nats implies event probabilities differ by at most0.1.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Kullback-Leibler divergence; Total variation distance between laws

Name: Chain rule for relative entropy
Intuition: Total mismatch splits into disagreement about the first variable and remaining disagreement after it is known.
Conditions: Finite or countable joint distributions with PXY≪QXY; conditional laws are evaluated only at x of positive PX. Extended nonnegative values are allowed, with the usual zero-mass conventions.
Example: If the two models share the same conditional law of Y given X, all divergence lies in the X marginals.

Name: Log-sum inequality
LaTeX: \sum_i a_i\log\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge A\log\frac AB,\qquad A=\sum_i a_i,\quad B=\sum_i b_i
Intuition: Combining categories can hide mismatch, but cannot create more of it.
Conditions: Finite nonnegative ai,bi with A,B>0;0log(0/b)=0 and a log(a/0)=+∞ for a>0. Equality holds when ai/A=bi/B for every i.
Example: With A=B=1, the inequality reduces to nonnegativity of KL divergence.

Name: Information density
Intuition: One outcome pair supplies evidence for dependence relative to an independence model.
Conditions: Finite/countable variables, or jointly dominated densities with the corresponding ratio; evaluate on the joint support and use natural logs. Individual information density may be negative although its expectation is nonnegative.
Example: An outcome pair rarer jointly than under independent marginals has negative information density.

Name: Conditional Shannon entropy
LaTeX: H(X\mid Y)=-\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log p(x\mid y)=\mathbb E_Y H(P_{X|Y})
Intuition: Average the uncertainty remaining about X after learning which value Y took.
Conditions: Finite discrete variables; only positive-probability y need conditional laws and0log0=0. Natural logs give nats. This is an average number, not a random conditional entropy function.
Example: If X is determined by Y, conditional entropy is zero; if they are independent, it is H(X).

Name: Entropy rate of a stationary source
Intuition: Count fresh uncertainty per symbol after the past has already been described.
Conditions: Stationary discrete-time process on a finite alphabet; both limits exist and agree. Independence is not required, and ergodicity is not needed for this equality.
Example: For a stationary Markov chain, H̄=−Σi,j πiPijlogPij.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Conditional Shannon entropy; Entropy chain rule

Name: Shannon–McMillan asymptotic equipartition
Intuition: Long typical messages have almost the same exponential probability scale, even when symbols are dependent.
Conditions: Stationary ergodic finite-alphabet process; natural logs and entropy rate H̄. Without ergodicity, the limit can depend on the ergodic component rather than equal one constant.
Example: For an iid source, typical block probabilities are approximately e^(−nH), and roughly e^(nH) typical messages carry most mass.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Information and uncertainty
Prerequisites: Entropy rate of a stationary source; Strong law of large numbers

Name: Binary symmetric channel capacity
Intuition: Each transmitted binary symbol offers one binary choice, reduced by the uncertainty of an independent flip.
Conditions: Memoryless binary channel Y=X⊕N with independent Bernoulli(p) noise,0≤p≤1; capacity in nats per channel use. Divide by log2 for bits.
Example: At p=1/2 the output is independent of the input and capacity is zero.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Capacity of a discrete memoryless channel; Shannon entropy

Name: Binary erasure channel capacity
Intuition: A received symbol reveals its entire binary choice or explicitly announces that the choice was erased.
Conditions: Memoryless binary channel that independently erases each input with probability ε∈[0,1] and otherwise returns it exactly; erasure is a distinct output symbol. Units are nats per use.
Example: Erasing half of the symbols leaves capacity one-half bit per use.
Prerequisites: Capacity of a discrete memoryless channel; Conditional Shannon entropy

Name: Water-filling for parallel Gaussian channels
Intuition: Allocate power to quieter channels until all used channels have the same combined noise-plus-power level.
Conditions: Parallel real memoryless additive Gaussian channels with independent noises of variances Nj>0 and total average input power P≥0. Independent Gaussian inputs attain capacity; ν is chosen to satisfy the budget. Units are nats per vector channel use.
Example: A channel whose noise variance exceeds the water level receives no power.
Prerequisites: Real Gaussian channel capacity; Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions

Name: Rate-distortion function
LaTeX: R(D)=\inf_{P_{\widehat X|X}:\ \mathbb E\,d(X,\widehat X)\le D}I(X;\widehat X)
Intuition: Find the least information a reconstruction must retain to meet an average accuracy requirement.
Conditions: Specified source law, reconstruction alphabet and nonnegative distortion d; infimum over conditional reconstruction laws. For finite-alphabet memoryless sources, its operational meaning is the asymptotic block-compression rate with vanishing excess tolerance.
Example: At a distortion large enough for a constant reconstruction, the rate can be zero.

Name: Gaussian squared-error rate-distortion
Intuition: Precision is logarithmically expensive: every fixed factor of error reduction costs the same extra information.
Conditions: Memoryless real Gaussian source of variance σ²>0, real reconstructions and mean squared error distortion; nats per source symbol.
Example: Reducing mean squared error by a factor4 costs one additional bit per symbol.
Prerequisites: Rate-distortion function; Gaussian maximum entropy at fixed variance

Name: Bernoulli Hamming rate-distortion
Intuition: Retaining only approximate bits saves the entropy associated with the allowed error fraction.
Conditions: Memoryless Bernoulli(p) source, binary reconstruction, distortion1{x≠x̂},0≤p≤1 and natural-log binary entropy h2 with0log0=0.
Example: For a fair source, R(D)=log2−h2(D) until D=1/2; guessing a constant reaches that zero-rate error.

Name: Slepian–Wolf separate-compression region
LaTeX: R_X\ge H(X|Y),\qquad R_Y\ge H(Y|X),\qquad R_X+R_Y\ge H(X,Y)
Intuition: Two encoders can exploit correlation even when they cannot see each other's data, provided the decoder sees both messages.
Conditions: Iid pairs from a fixed finite-alphabet joint distribution; separate block encoders, joint decoder and error probability tending to zero. The inequalities describe the closure of achievable rates in nats per pair.
Example: If X=Y, the total rate need only equal H(X); one encoder can carry the entire description.
Prerequisites: Conditional Shannon entropy; Entropy bound for binary prefix coding

Name: Information bottleneck objective
Intuition: Build a compact summary that forgets details of X while preserving information useful for predicting Y.
Conditions: Fixed finite-alphabet joint law PXY, specified finite representation alphabet T and β≥0. The Markov condition means T is generated from X; predictive relevance depends on the chosen Y.
Example: A summary suitable for identifying a speaker need not be suitable for transcribing the words they speak.

Name: Sanov large deviations for empirical laws
Intuition: An empirical distribution unlike the true one costs an exponential probability governed by relative entropy.
Conditions: Iid observations on a finite alphabet with strictly positive true probabilities p; A is any Borel subset of its probability simplex, using the usual topology. Infimum of the empty set is+∞; matching interior/closure infima yields a limit.
Example: For a Bernoulli sample whose empirical success rate is near q≠p, the exponent is the Bernoulli KL divergence D(q||p).
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Limits and convergence

Name: Chernoff–Stein testing exponent
Intuition: With one error probability held below a fixed tolerance, the other can shrink exponentially at a KL-determined rate.
Conditions: Two distinct strictly positive distributions P,Q on a finite alphabet, iid samples and fixed0<α<1. A is the event of accepting P, so α controls rejection under P and β is erroneous acceptance under Q.
Example: Doubling sample size approximately squares the optimal small type-II error on its leading exponential scale.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Limits and convergence

Name: Chernoff information for symmetric testing
Intuition: Balance both kinds of classification mistake and choose the exponential tilt at which the two models are hardest to distinguish.
Conditions: Distinct strictly positive finite-alphabet distributions, iid samples and fixed positive prior probabilities for the two hypotheses; Pe* is minimum average Bayesian error. Natural logs are used.
Example: Unlike the directed KL exponent, Chernoff information is symmetric in P and Q.
Prerequisites: Exponential Chernoff bound; Neyman-Pearson likelihood-ratio test

Name: Entropy power inequality
Intuition: The effective Gaussian variance associated with entropy grows at least additively when independent noises are added.
Conditions: Independent R^d-valued vectors with densities, finite second moments and finite differential entropies; natural-log h. Equality holds for nondegenerate Gaussian vectors with proportional covariance matrices.
Example: For independent scalar Gaussians, entropy power equals variance and the inequality becomes variance additivity.
Prerequisites: Differential entropy; Variance of a sum

Name: de Bruijn entropy derivative
LaTeX: \frac d{dt}h(X+\sqrt t\,Z)=\frac12J(X+\sqrt t\,Z),\qquad J(Y)=\mathbb E\|\nabla\log p_Y(Y)\|^2
Intuition: The rate at which Gaussian smoothing creates entropy is measured by the roughness of the log density.
Conditions: X∈R^d with finite second moment, independent Z∼N(0,I), and t>0. J is total spatial Fisher information of the smoothed density; natural-log entropy. A statement at t=0 requires additional regularity.
Example: For X∼N(0,σ²I), both sides equal d/[2(σ²+t)].
Prerequisites: Differential entropy; Heat or diffusion equation

Name: I-MMSE identity
Intuition: The extra information gained from a slight increase in signal strength equals half the estimation error still left.
Conditions: Real X with finite second moment, independent standard normal Z and γ≥0, with the right derivative at zero. Mutual information is in nats; the input distribution is fixed while γ changes.
Example: For X∼N(0,σ²), the MMSE is σ²/(1+γσ²), matching the derivative of (1/2)log(1+γσ²).

Name: Mutual information of a Gaussian pair
Intuition: For jointly Gaussian variables, dependence is exactly the reduction in covariance volume from independent to joint uncertainty.
Conditions: Jointly Gaussian vector (X,Y) with positive-definite full covariance ΣXY and marginal covariance blocks ΣX,ΣY. The scalar formula uses correlation |ρ|<1; logs are natural.
Example: Uncorrelated jointly Gaussian variables have zero mutual information and are independent.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Geometry and distance

Name: KL divergence between Gaussian laws
Intuition: Separate distributional mismatch into covariance shape, mean displacement and normalization volume.
Conditions: Two real d-dimensional Gaussian laws with positive-definite covariance matrices; natural-log KL. Singular Gaussian cases require support-aware formulas and may have infinite divergence.
Example: With equal covariance Σ, the divergence is half the squared Mahalanobis distance between means.

Name: Maximum entropy on a half-line with fixed mean
Intuition: With only a nonnegative support and an average size specified, exponential decay spreads uncertainty most.
Conditions: Absolutely continuous law on [0,∞) with mean μ and well-defined differential entropy; equality exactly for density μ⁻¹e^(−x/μ) almost everywhere. Natural logs.
Example: A mean-one exponential variable has maximal entropy1 nat among nonnegative continuous variables of mean1.

Name: Dual of finite maximum-entropy moment matching
Intuition: Find the least-committed probability vector by adjusting prices until model moments match the required moments.
Conditions: Finite real feature vectors Ti, target τ in the relative interior of their convex hull, and natural logs. The minimizing parameter may be nonunique along redundant feature directions, but the maximizing probability vector is unique.
Example: With only normalization and no feature constraints, the optimum is uniform and the value is log m.
Prerequisites: Entropy variational formula for log-sum-exp; Exponential family and log partition function

Name: Local quadratic expansion of KL
Intuition: Very close probability models have a quadratic information distance determined by Fisher information.
Conditions: Finite observation alphabet with strictly positive probabilities that are twice continuously differentiable in a parameter neighborhood; θ interior. Natural logs; I may be singular if parameters are locally redundant.
Example: For a normal location family with known variance, the corresponding exact KL is δ²/(2σ²).
Prerequisites: Fisher information; Second-order multivariable Taylor expansion

Name: Wasserstein p-distance
Intuition: Match the mass of one distribution to the other and minimize the average cost of moving matched mass.
Conditions: Probability laws on R^d with finite pth moments,1≤p<∞; Π(μ,ν) is the set of joint couplings having the required marginals. The infimum is attained and defines a metric.
Example: For two point masses δa and δb, Wp equals ||a−b|| for every p.
Prerequisites: Expectation; Norm axioms and induced norm

Name: Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality
Intuition: The cheapest transport cost equals the largest difference detectable by a function that cannot change faster than distance allows.
Conditions: Probability measures on R^d with finite first moments; real1-Lipschitz functions. Constants cancel, so one may impose φ(0)=0 to make integrability explicit.
Example: For point masses at a and b, a suitable distance-aligned linear function attains ||a−b||.

Name: Sinkhorn scaling for entropic transport
Intuition: Repeatedly fix row totals and column totals of a positive transport table until both marginal budgets agree.
Conditions: Strictly positive probability vectors a,b, finite real cost matrix C, ε>0 and positive initialization; division is componentwise. The transport table converges to the unique minimizer of ΣCijPij+εΣPij(logPij−1) with the stated marginals. At fixed ε this is regularized transport.
Example: Uniform a,b make the scaled table have equal row and column sums.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Information and uncertainty

Name: Finite-alphabet entropy continuity bound
Intuition: Changing only a small fraction of probability mass changes entropy by a controlled amount when the alphabet is fixed.
Conditions: Two distributions on the same finite alphabet of size m≥2, total variation t∈[0,1], natural logs and binary entropy h2. The bound is not uniform over arbitrarily large alphabets.
Example: For binary laws the bound simplifies to |H(P)−H(Q)|≤h2(t).
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Shannon entropy; Total variation distance between laws

Name: Bilateral z-transform
Intuition: Encode a whole sequence by weighting each time index with a power of one complex variable.
Conditions: Complex sequence on the integers; z≠0 at points of absolute convergence. The region of convergence is part of the transform and can be an annulus, possibly with boundary circles; a rational expression alone does not specify the sequence.
