Example: For x[n]=a^n for n≥0 and zero otherwise, X(z)=1/(1−az⁻¹) on |z|>|a|.

Name: Bilateral z-transform shift rule
Intuition: A delay of k samples attaches a factor representing k units of waiting.
Conditions: Bilateral transform and finite integer k; equality holds at every nonzero finite z in the original absolute-convergence region. Behavior at zero or infinity can change. One-sided transforms need boundary terms.
Example: A one-sample delay of the unit impulse has transform z⁻¹.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Change of coordinates

Name: z-transform convolution rule
Intuition: Combining all pairs of time contributions becomes ordinary multiplication of their generating expressions.
Conditions: At a nonzero z where both weighted series converge absolutely, the convolution converges absolutely and the identity holds. The resulting transform can have a larger region after cancellation. This is linear convolution on all integers.
Example: Two causal sequences aⁿ and bⁿ have convolution transform [(1−az⁻¹)(1−bz⁻¹)]⁻¹ in their common outer region.

Name: Discrete-time Fourier transform
Intuition: An aperiodic sequence has a continuous frequency description that repeats every full turn.
Conditions: Absolute summability x∈ℓ¹(Z) gives a continuous2π-periodic transform and the stated inversion. There is also an ℓ²-to-L² extension. Here ω is angular frequency per sample; this is not a finite DFT.
Example: The sequence x[0]=x[1]=1, zero elsewhere, has X(ω)=1+e⁻ⁱω.
Prerequisites: Fourier series and Fourier coefficients; Euler's formula

Name: Exponential eigenfunctions of LTI filters
LaTeX: T_h(e^{2\pi i\xi t})=\widehat h(\xi)e^{2\pi i\xi t},\qquad (T_hf)(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}h(s)f(t-s)\,ds
Intuition: A time-invariant linear filter changes each pure frequency's size and phase while preserving its frequency.
Conditions: Impulse response h∈L¹(R) and real ξ. The bounded complex exponential makes the displayed integral well-defined; it is a generalized frequency mode, not a square-integrable eigenvector on the whole real line.
Example: A moving average suppresses frequencies whose oscillations cancel within its averaging window.

Name: Noncausal Wiener filter for additive noise
Intuition: Keep frequencies in proportion to how much of their observed power is expected to be signal.
Conditions: Zero-mean jointly wide-sense stationary discrete-time signal S and noise N, uncorrelated at all lags, with integrable spectral densities. The formula gives the mean-square optimal noncausal linear estimator in the closed span of all observations. Set H=0 where both spectra vanish. It need not be causal or have an absolutely summable impulse response.
Example: If signal and noise have equal power at a frequency, that frequency is multiplied by one half.
Prerequisites: Wiener-Khinchin relation; Averaging as orthogonal projection

Name: Matched-filter signal-to-noise optimum
Intuition: To detect a known shape in equally noisy coordinates, add the data with weights matching that shape.
Conditions: Nonzero deterministic signal s∈Cⁿ and additive mean-zero noise with covariance E[NN*]=σ²I, σ>0. The criterion is output squared signal divided by noise variance; Gaussianity is unnecessary for this SNR optimum.
Example: For a real pulse with samples(1,2,1), the statistic y1+2y2+y3 collects its energy; convolution implements this with a time-reversed template.
Prerequisites: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality; Covariance under a linear map

Name: Short-time Fourier transform
Intuition: Slide a window across a signal and measure the frequencies visible within each window.
Conditions: f,g∈L²(R), g nonzero, and real τ,ξ. Cauchy–Schwarz makes each displayed integral absolutely convergent. ξ is cycles per unit time. Window choice sets the time-frequency resolution.
Example: A rising chirp traces a rising frequency band in |Vgf|² even though its whole-signal Fourier transform does not record when each frequency occurred.

Name: Continuous wavelet transform
Intuition: Compare a signal with shifted copies of one shape at many zoom levels.
Conditions: f,ψ∈L²(R), ψ nonzero; a∈R\{0}, b∈R. The normalization preserves the template's L² norm. The admissibility condition ∫|ψ̂(ξ)|²/|ξ|dξ<∞ is additionally needed for the usual reconstruction theorem.
Example: A short oscillating feature produces a large coefficient when the template's location and scale fit it.

Name: Hilbert transform and analytic signal
Intuition: Build a quadrature partner for a real signal so the combined complex signal retains only positive frequencies.
Conditions: Real f∈L²(R), with the Fourier transform defined using e⁻²πⁱξt and the Hilbert transform defined by its L² multiplier. The last equality is almost everywhere; a possible value at ξ=0 is irrelevant in L². A principal-value integral needs its own pointwise hypotheses.
Example: In the periodic analogue, H(cos t)=sin t and cos t+i sin t=eⁱt.

Name: Cauchy–Binet formula
Intuition: A determinant of a composite sums the volume contributions from every intermediate coordinate plane.
Conditions: A is m×n and B is n×m over a commutative field, with m≤n; index subsets use increasing order.
Example: For B=Aᵀ, each summand is a squared maximal minor.

Name: Matrix determinant lemma
Intuition: A rank-one change modifies volume by a single scalar factor.
Conditions: A is an invertible n×n real or complex matrix; u,v are n-vectors and * denotes conjugate transpose.
Example: For A=I the new determinant is 1+v*u.

Name: Sylvester determinant identity
Intuition: A coupled transformation has the same nontrivial determinant contribution whether tracked through its input or output space.
Conditions: A is m×n and B is n×m over a commutative field. Neither matrix need be square or invertible.
Example: A tall matrix can reduce a large determinant to one of smaller dimension.

Name: Determinant of a matrix exponential
Intuition: Trace adds infinitesimal expansion rates; exponentiation turns their sum into total volume scaling.
Conditions: A is any finite square complex matrix, including real matrices; no diagonalizability is assumed.
Example: For a trace-zero real matrix, eᵗᴬ preserves oriented volume for every real t.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Conservation and balance

Name: Complex Schur triangularization
Intuition: An orthonormal change of coordinates makes every complex linear map triangular, even when eigenvectors do not form a basis.
Conditions: A is a finite complex square matrix; U is unitary and diagonal entries of T are the eigenvalues with multiplicity. This is an existence statement, not an algorithm.
Example: A defective Jordan block is already triangular but cannot be diagonalized.

Name: Simultaneous diagonalization of commuting Hermitian matrices
LaTeX: AB=BA\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A=U\Lambda U^*,\ B=U M U^*
Intuition: Commuting self-adjoint measurements can be resolved in one common set of orthogonal directions.
Conditions: A,B are Hermitian n×n matrices over C, or real symmetric matrices with orthogonal U; Λ and M are real diagonal.
Example: Two diagonal matrices commute because each coordinate is processed independently.

Name: Eigenvalue interlacing for a principal submatrix
Intuition: Removing one coordinate constrains allowable directions, trapping each new eigenvalue between two old ones.
Conditions: A is n×n Hermitian, n≥2; B is a principal (n−1)×(n−1) submatrix; eigenvalues are sorted increasingly.
Example: Deleting a graph vertex gives an adjacency principal submatrix with interlacing eigenvalues.

Name: Weyl eigenvalue bounds for a Hermitian sum
Intuition: Adding B shifts every ordered eigenvalue by an amount between B’s weakest and strongest quadratic effects.
Conditions: A,B are n×n Hermitian and eigenvalues are indexed increasingly, 1≤i≤n.
Example: If −εI≼B≼εI, every eigenvalue shifts by at most ε.

Name: Schur product theorem
Intuition: Entrywise products preserve positive-semidefinite Gram structure by pairing the feature vectors through tensor products.
Conditions: A,B are Hermitian positive-semidefinite matrices of equal finite size over R or C.
Example: Multiplying two valid covariance-kernel matrices entrywise gives another positive-semidefinite matrix.
Prerequisites: Inner product; Tensor product universal property

Name: Hadamard determinant inequality
Intuition: A parallelepiped has maximal volume when its edge directions are perpendicular.
Conditions: A is a real or complex square matrix with columns aⱼ. A zero column gives equality automatically; when every column is nonzero, equality holds iff the columns are pairwise orthogonal.
Example: Unit-length columns give determinant magnitude at most one.
Prerequisites: Gram determinant and volume; Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization

Name: Pfaffian and skew-symmetric determinant
Intuition: A skew-symmetric determinant is the square of a signed sum over pairings. Pairing is the natural building block of an alternating bilinear form.
Conditions: A is a 2n×2n skew-symmetric real or complex matrix; n≥0 and the empty Pfaffian is 1.
Example: For a 2×2 matrix with upper-right entry a, the Pfaffian is a and the determinant is a².
Prerequisites: Determinant; Wedge product and graded commutativity

Name: Minimal polynomial of a linear operator
Intuition: The shortest monic polynomial relation among powers of A generates every polynomial relation satisfied by A.
Conditions: A is an endomorphism of a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space over a field; mₐ is monic of least positive degree with mₐ(A)=0.
Example: A nonidentity matrix with A²=I in characteristic not two has minimal polynomial dividing (t−1)(t+1).

Name: Rational canonical form
Intuition: A linear map is assembled from cyclic blocks describing how repeated application acts on one starting vector.
Conditions: A is a nonempty square matrix over a field; fᵢ are monic nonconstant invariant factors, C(fᵢ) their companion matrices, and the ordered invariant factors are unique.
Example: A real rotation can be represented by a quadratic companion block without introducing complex eigenvalues.
Prerequisites: Minimal polynomial of a linear operator; Change of basis and similarity

Name: Primary decomposition of a linear operator
Intuition: Coprime polynomial factors separate a linear system into independent invariant parts.
Conditions: V is finite-dimensional over a field; pⱼ are distinct monic irreducible factors of the minimal polynomial and aⱼ≥1.
Example: Over C the pieces are generalized eigenspaces.
Prerequisites: Minimal polynomial of a linear operator; Bézout’s identity

Name: Sylvester rank inequality
Intuition: Composition can lose only the directions sent by B into A’s kernel.
Conditions: A is m×n and B is n×p over a field. A negative lower bound remains true but uninformative.
Example: Two rank n operators on an n-dimensional space have a rank n product.

Name: Vectorization of a matrix product
Intuition: A two-sided matrix action becomes an ordinary linear map on one long column of entries.
Conditions: A,X,B are finite matrices over one field with compatible sizes; vec stacks columns, and T is ordinary transpose even over C.
Example: A matrix-valued linear equation can be regarded as a vector-valued one.

Name: Spectrum of a Kronecker sum
Intuition: Independent additive actions on two factors produce every pairwise sum of their spectral values.
Conditions: A is m×m and B is n×n over C; eigenvalues on the right include algebraic multiplicity. The symbol ⊕ here denotes Kronecker sum, not block direct sum.
Example: A separable grid Laplacian has eigenvalues equal to sums of one-dimensional Laplacian eigenvalues.

Name: Determinant of a Kronecker product
Intuition: Each eigenvalue of one factor pairs with every eigenvalue of the other, multiplying the total volume factors repeatedly.
Conditions: A is m×m and B is n×n over a commutative field.
Example: For A=2I₂ and B=3I₃, A⊗B=6I₆ and both sides equal 6⁶.

Name: Dimension and top action of an exterior power
Intuition: Alternating tensors keep distinct directions without ordering them twice. In top degree, every linear map acts by one scalar: its determinant.
Conditions: V has finite dimension n over a field, 0≤k≤n; T is an endomorphism. Wedges of increasing basis indices form a basis.
Example: In three dimensions the space of oriented area elements Λ²V has dimension three.
Prerequisites: Wedge product and graded commutativity; Determinant

Name: Dimension of a symmetric power
Intuition: Symmetric tensors remember how often each direction is selected, rather than the order of selection.
Conditions: V is n-dimensional over a field, n≥1, k≥0; SymᵏV is the degree-k part of the symmetric algebra, defined as a quotient of the tensor algebra.
Example: Homogeneous degree-three polynomials in two variables have four monomials.
Prerequisites: Tensor product universal property; Stars and bars

Name: Completing the square for a quadratic polynomial
Intuition: Translate a multivariable quadratic to remove its linear term and expose its center.
Conditions: A is a real symmetric invertible matrix; b,x are compatible real vectors and c is real. A positive-definite A gives a unique minimum; an indefinite A need not.
Example: For A=I, the center is −b/2.

Name: Cayley transform of a skew-Hermitian matrix
Intuition: A rational change of coordinates converts an infinitesimal rotation into an exact length-preserving map.
Conditions: A is a finite complex skew-Hermitian matrix, so I+A is invertible. The inverse A=(I−U)(I+U)⁻¹ is defined for unitary U without eigenvalue −1. Real skew-symmetric A gives orthogonal U.
Example: A 2×2 real skew matrix produces a planar rotation by a rational formula.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Adjoint of a linear map; Inverse by the adjugate

Name: Frobenius inner product on matrix space
Intuition: Treat all matrix entries as one Euclidean vector while retaining a basis-independent trace expression.
Conditions: A,B have equal finite size over R or C; singular values include multiplicity. The Frobenius norm differs from the operator norm in general.
Example: An identity n×n matrix has Frobenius norm √n but operator norm one.
Prerequisites: Inner product; Trace; Singular value decomposition

Name: Spectral projectors by polynomial interpolation
Intuition: Build a filter that is one on a chosen eigenspace and zero on every other eigenspace.
Conditions: A is diagonalizable over a field; λ₁,…,λᵣ are its distinct eigenvalues. The Pⱼ need not be orthogonal unless A is normal in an inner-product setting.
Example: For eigenvalues 0 and 1, the projectors are I−A and A.

Name: Second isomorphism theorem for groups
Intuition: Taking a subgroup and then forgetting a normal subgroup removes exactly their overlap.
Conditions: H≤G and N is normal in G. Then HN is a subgroup, H∩N is normal in H, and h(H∩N) maps to hN.
Example: For G=Z, H=2Z and N=3Z, both quotients have order three.

Name: Third isomorphism theorem for groups
Intuition: Forgetting distinctions in two stages agrees with forgetting their total effect at once.
Conditions: N and H are normal subgroups of G with N⊆H. The isomorphism sends (gN)(H/N) to gH.
Example: Reducing integers first modulo 12 and then modulo the subgroup generated by 4 leaves Z/4Z.

Name: Subgroup correspondence for a quotient
LaTeX: \{H\le G:N\subseteq H\}\longleftrightarrow\{K\le G/N\},\qquad H\mapsto H/N,\quad K\mapsto q^{-1}(K)
Intuition: A quotient keeps precisely the subgroups that already contain everything being collapsed.
Conditions: N is normal in G and q:G→G/N is the quotient map. The correspondence preserves inclusion and normality.
Example: Subgroups of Z/12Z correspond to subgroups of Z containing 12Z.

Name: Semidirect product
Intuition: Combine two groups while allowing one factor to change how the other is viewed during multiplication.
Conditions: N,H are groups and φ:H→Aut(N) is a homomorphism. The displayed law is on N×H.
Example: The dihedral group combines cyclic rotations with a reflection that inverts them.
Prerequisites: Direct product of groups; Group action

Name: Commutator subgroup
Intuition: Collect every obstruction to swapping the order of two group operations.
Conditions: G is a group; angle brackets mean the subgroup generated by all displayed commutators. This subgroup is normal.
Example: For S₃ the commutator subgroup is A₃.

Name: Abelianization and its universal property
Intuition: Erase exactly the noncommutative information that no abelian target can detect.
Conditions: G is a group and A is an abelian group; the bijection is induced by composing with G→Gab.
Example: The abelianization of a free group on r generators is Zʳ.

Name: Derived series and solvable groups
LaTeX: G^{(0)}=G,\qquad G^{(k+1)}=[G^{(k)},G^{(k)}],\qquad G\text{ solvable}\iff G^{(r)}=\{e\}\text{ for some }r
Intuition: Repeatedly remove the abelian part and inspect the remaining noncommutativity. Solvability means this process eventually ends.
Conditions: G is any group and r is a finite nonnegative integer. Finite nonabelian groups need not be solvable.
Example: S₃ has derived series S₃, A₃, {e}.

Name: Free group universal property
Intuition: Choose images of generators freely; every word then has a uniquely forced image.
Conditions: S is a set, G a group, and F(S) the group of reduced finite words in symbols s and s⁻¹. The bijection restricts a homomorphism to generators.
Example: The free group on one generator is Z; on two generators it is noncommutative.

Name: Presentation by generators and relations
Intuition: Start with all possible words and identify those forced equal by the declared relations.
Conditions: R is a set of words in the free group F(S); double brackets denote its normal closure. Relations are imposed as words equal to the identity.
Example: A cyclic group of order n has presentation ⟨a∣aⁿ=1⟩.
Prerequisites: Free group universal property; Quotient group

Name: Jordan–Hölder theorem for finite groups
LaTeX: G=G_0\triangleright G_1\triangleright\cdots\triangleright G_r=\{e\},\qquad\{G_i/G_{i+1}\}_{i=0}^{r-1}\text{ unique up to permutation and isomorphism}
Intuition: Different ways of peeling a finite group into simple layers yield the same list of irreducible group factors.
Conditions: Each successive subgroup is normal in the preceding one and each quotient is nontrivial simple; G is finite. The actual subgroups and their order need not be unique.
Example: Any composition series of S₃ has factors C₂ and C₃.

Name: Chinese remainder theorem for rings
Intuition: Independent congruence conditions split one ring into separate coordinate rings.
Conditions: R is commutative with identity; I₁,…,Iᵣ is a nonempty finite family of pairwise comaximal ideals, meaning Iᵢ+Iⱼ=R for i≠j.
Example: Distinct linear factors split k[x]/∏(x−aᵢ) into copies of k.

Name: Prime ideal quotient criterion
LaTeX: R/\mathfrak p\text{ is an integral domain}\iff\mathfrak p\text{ is prime}
Intuition: A prime ideal removes elements without creating zero divisors among the surviving nonzero classes.
Conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity and p is a proper ideal; prime means ab∈p implies a∈p or b∈p.
Example: (x) is prime in k[x,y], since the quotient is k[y].

Name: Gauss’s lemma for primitive polynomials
LaTeX: c(fg)\sim c(f)c(g),\qquad f\text{ primitive}:\quad f\text{ irreducible in }R[x]\iff f\text{ irreducible in }K[x]
Intuition: Common factors in coefficients behave multiplicatively, so factorization over fractions can be cleared back to integral coefficients.
Conditions: R is a unique-factorization domain, K its fraction field, f,g are nonzero polynomials, and c is coefficient gcd up to units. The irreducibility statement assumes f is primitive and nonconstant.
Example: A primitive integer polynomial factors over Q exactly when it factors nontrivially over Z.
Prerequisites: Polynomial division algorithm; Fundamental theorem of arithmetic

Name: Eisenstein irreducibility criterion
LaTeX: p\nmid a_n,\quad p\mid a_i\ (i<n),\quad p^2\nmid a_0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\text{ irreducible over }\mathbb Q
Intuition: Reduction modulo a prime forces every prospective factor to have a highly restricted shape; the constant term prevents both factors from existing.
Conditions: n≥1, all aᵢ are integers, aₙ≠0 and p is prime.
Example: x⁵−2 is irreducible over Q using p=2.
Prerequisites: Gauss’s lemma for primitive polynomials; Congruence modulo an integer

Name: Minimal polynomial and a simple field extension
Intuition: An algebraic number is described by one irreducible polynomial relation; every expression in it reduces to a bounded list of powers.
Conditions: α is algebraic over a field F and mα is its monic minimal polynomial. The isomorphism evaluates x at α.
Example: Q(√2) has basis 1,√2 because the minimal polynomial is x²−2.
Prerequisites: Polynomial remainder and factor theorem; Tower law for field extensions

Name: Primitive element theorem
LaTeX: L/F\text{ finite separable}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L=F(\alpha)\text{ for some }\alpha\in L
Intuition: A finite separable extension with many algebraic generators can be encoded by a single well-chosen element.
Conditions: L/F is a finite separable field extension. Separability is essential over imperfect fields.
Prerequisites: Minimal polynomial and a simple field extension; Fundamental theorem of Galois theory

Name: Repeated-root criterion by a formal derivative
LaTeX: f\text{ has no repeated roots in }\overline F\iff\gcd(f,f^{\prime})=1
Intuition: A repeated zero is detected simultaneously by a polynomial and its rate-of-change polynomial.
Conditions: f is a nonconstant polynomial over a field F; f′ is its formal derivative, including in positive characteristic; gcd is monic.
Example: Over characteristic p, xᵖ−a has zero derivative and is inseparable unless its degree has collapsed.
Prerequisites: Polynomial remainder and factor theorem; Euclidean algorithm

Name: Localization of a commutative ring
LaTeX: S^{-1}R=\{a/s:a\in R,\ s\in S\},\qquad a/s=b/t\iff\exists u\in S:\ u(at-bs)=0
Intuition: Declare a selected set of elements invertible and allow exactly the fractions this requires.
Conditions: R is commutative with identity; S is multiplicatively closed, contains 1 and does not contain 0. Zero divisors may still make R→S⁻¹R noninjective.
Example: Localizing Z at all nonzero integers gives Q; localizing away from a prime gives Z₍ₚ₎.
Prerequisites: Ring structure and distributivity; Modular inverse criterion

Name: Noetherian ring condition
LaTeX: I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N:\ I_n=I_N
Intuition: An indefinitely growing list of algebraic constraints eventually adds nothing new.
Conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity. The displayed ascending-chain condition on ideals is equivalent to every ideal being finitely generated.
Example: Z and polynomial rings in finitely many variables over a field are Noetherian.

Name: Hilbert basis theorem
Intuition: Adding finitely many polynomial variables preserves the ability to describe every ideal using finitely many equations.
Conditions: R is a commutative Noetherian ring and n is a finite nonnegative integer.
Example: Every ideal of real polynomials in three variables has a finite generating list.
Prerequisites: Noetherian ring condition; Polynomial division algorithm

Name: Nakayama’s lemma
Intuition: A finite module cannot be entirely generated by multiples from a universally noninvertible ideal unless it is already zero.
Conditions: R is commutative with identity, M a finitely generated R-module, and I an ideal inside the Jacobson radical, the intersection of maximal ideals.
Example: For a local ring with maximal ideal m, elements spanning M/mM lift to generators of M.
Prerequisites: Noetherian ring condition; Maximal ideals and fields

Name: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID
LaTeX: M\cong R^r\oplus R/(d_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(d_s),\qquad d_1\mid\cdots\mid d_s
Intuition: Separate freely moving coordinates from coordinates constrained by divisibility relations.
Conditions: R is a principal ideal domain, M a finitely generated R-module, r≥0, and dᵢ are nonzero nonunits. Rank and invariant factors are unique, the latter up to units.
Example: For R=Z this describes every finitely generated abelian group, including infinite free parts.
Prerequisites: Structure theorem for finite abelian groups; Quotient ring

Name: Smith normal form
Intuition: Independent invertible row and column changes expose divisibility relations in a matrix over a principal ideal domain.
Conditions: A is an m×n matrix over a PID; P and Q are invertible over that same ring, r is the rank over its fraction field, and nonzero dᵢ are unique up to units. This is a structural theorem.
Example: An integer matrix’s Smith factors describe the torsion of its cokernel.
Prerequisites: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID; Change of basis and similarity

Name: Splitting a short exact sequence
Intuition: If quotient data can be lifted consistently, the middle object separates into the kernel and a complementary copy of the quotient.
Conditions: The sequence is exact in modules over a ring, or abelian groups; s:C→B must be a module homomorphism. The isomorphism sends (a,c) to i(a)+s(c).
Example: Every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits, but 0→Z→Z→Z/2Z→0 with first map ×2 does not.
Prerequisites: Exactness of consecutive maps; Direct product of groups

Name: Snake lemma
Intuition: A compatible pair of exact rows transfers a failed lift into a precise connecting obstruction.
Conditions: Start with a commutative diagram of short exact sequences 0→A→B→C→0 and 0→A′→B′→C′→0 with vertical module maps a,b,c. Then the displayed sequence is exact.
Example: Connecting homomorphisms in homology are constructed by lifting, applying a map, and measuring the remaining class.
Prerequisites: Exactness of consecutive maps; Homology as cycles modulo boundaries

Name: Projective module lifting property
LaTeX: p:E\twoheadrightarrow M,\quad f:P\to M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists\widetilde f:P\to E:\ p\widetilde f=f
Intuition: A projective module can lift its maps across every surjection without getting trapped by relations.
Conditions: P is a module over a unital ring; the property is required for every surjective module map p and every f. Equivalently, P is a direct summand of a free module.
Example: Free modules are projective; a projective module need not itself be free.

Name: Flat module and preservation of exactness
LaTeX: 0\to A\to B\to C\to0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad0\to A\otimes_R M\to B\otimes_R M\to C\otimes_R M\to0
Intuition: A flat module changes coefficients without introducing new failures of injectivity.
Conditions: R is commutative with identity and M an R-module. Flatness means the displayed implication holds for every short exact sequence of R-modules.
Example: Localizations S⁻¹R are flat R-modules.
Prerequisites: Tensor product universal property; Exactness of consecutive maps

Name: Tor from a projective resolution
Intuition: Resolve a module into free-like pieces, then measure the exactness lost when tensoring.
Conditions: R is commutative with identity, M,N are R-modules, n≥0, and P•→M is a projective resolution. The result is independent of the resolution up to canonical isomorphism.
Example: Tor₁^Z(Z/mZ,Z/nZ) is Z/gcd(m,n)Z.
Prerequisites: Projective module lifting property; Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Flat module and preservation of exactness

Name: Ext from a projective resolution
Intuition: Resolve the source before asking for maps into N; higher cohomology measures information ordinary homomorphisms miss.
Conditions: R is a unital ring, M,N are left modules, n≥0, and P•→M is a projective resolution. Hom_R(P•,N) is the induced cochain complex.
Example: Ext₁^Z(Z/nZ,Z)≅Z/nZ; Ext¹ classifies module extensions up to the standard equivalence.
Prerequisites: Projective module lifting property; Exactness of consecutive maps

Name: Universal enveloping algebra
LaTeX: U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/\langle x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\rangle
Intuition: Replace Lie brackets by ordinary noncommutative multiplication, imposing exactly the commutator relations.
Conditions: g is a Lie algebra over a field; T(g) is its tensor algebra and the quotient is by the two-sided ideal generated by the displayed elements.
Example: For an abelian Lie algebra, the enveloping algebra is its symmetric algebra.
Prerequisites: Matrix commutator and Lie bracket; Tensor product universal property; Quotient ring

Name: Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem
Intuition: At the level of highest degree, noncommutative Lie-algebra products behave like commuting polynomial variables.
Conditions: g is a Lie algebra over a field and U(g) carries its filtration by tensor degree. For an ordered basis of g, ordered monomials form a basis of U(g).
Example: For sl₂, ordered products fᵃhᵇeᶜ form a vector-space basis of its enveloping algebra.
Prerequisites: Universal enveloping algebra; Dimension of a symmetric power

Name: Linear representation of a group
Intuition: Turn an abstract symmetry into an invertible linear transformation so its effects can be studied with matrices.
Conditions: G is a group and V a vector space over a specified field; the displayed map is a group homomorphism and sends the identity to I.
Example: Permuting the coordinates of Rⁿ represents the symmetric group Sₙ.

Name: Intertwining map between representations
Intuition: An intertwiner translates vector descriptions while preserving every symmetry operation.
Conditions: ρ:G→GL(V), σ:G→GL(W) are representations over the same field, and T:V→W is linear. Equivalence of representations requires an invertible intertwiner.
Example: A change of basis intertwines a matrix representation with its conjugate representation.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Maschke’s theorem
Intuition: When division by the group order is possible, averaging turns an arbitrary complement into a symmetry-respecting one.
Conditions: G is finite, V is finite-dimensional over a field k, and char(k) does not divide |G|. Without this characteristic hypothesis, invariant complements may fail to exist.
Example: A real representation of a finite rotation group decomposes into invariant irreducible subspaces.
Prerequisites: Linear representation of a group; Orthogonal projection

Name: Schur’s lemma for complex representations
LaTeX: \operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)=0\text{ or consists of scalar multiples of an isomorphism},\qquad\operatorname{End}_G(V)=\mathbb C I
Intuition: An irreducible symmetry system has no nontrivial internal linear adjustment compatible with every symmetry.
Conditions: V,W are nonzero finite-dimensional irreducible complex representations of a group. Hom is zero if they are inequivalent; the scalar endomorphism conclusion uses algebraic closure of C.
Example: An operator commuting with every matrix of an irreducible complex representation is scalar.
Prerequisites: Intertwining map between representations; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

Name: Character of a finite-dimensional representation
Intuition: Take a basis-independent summary of each symmetry matrix. Conjugate group elements receive the same summary.
Conditions: ρ is a finite-dimensional representation over a field; the class-function identity holds generally. Character classification by these values will later use finite groups over C.
Example: The character of a permutation representation counts the coordinates fixed by the permutation.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Information and uncertainty
Prerequisites: Linear representation of a group; Trace

Name: Orthogonality of irreducible characters
Intuition: Irreducible symmetry patterns behave like perpendicular frequency modes under a uniform group average.
Conditions: G is finite and χᵢ are characters of inequivalent irreducible finite-dimensional complex representations.
Example: For a cyclic group, the characters are roots-of-unity exponentials and this is discrete Fourier orthogonality.
Prerequisites: Character of a finite-dimensional representation; Schur’s lemma for complex representations

Name: Sum of squared irreducible dimensions
Intuition: The regular action contains every irreducible representation as many times as its dimension. Their squared sizes fill the whole group algebra.
Conditions: G is finite and Ĝ indexes inequivalent irreducible complex representations.
Example: S₃ has irreducible dimensions 1,1,2, whose squares sum to 6.
Prerequisites: Maschke’s theorem; Orthogonality of irreducible characters

Name: Multiplicity from a character inner product
Intuition: Project a character onto an irreducible character to read off how many copies of that symmetry type occur.
Conditions: G is finite and V a finite-dimensional complex representation. The resulting coefficients are nonnegative integers.
Example: The three-coordinate permutation representation of S₃ is one trivial copy plus one two-dimensional standard copy.
Prerequisites: Orthogonality of irreducible characters; Maschke’s theorem

Name: Averaging projection onto invariant vectors
Intuition: Average every symmetry-transformed version of a vector; all nonsymmetric components cancel.
Conditions: G is finite and ρ a representation over a field where |G| is invertible. Vᴳ consists of vectors fixed by every ρ(g). For a unitary complex representation, Pᴳ is an orthogonal projection.
Example: Averaging all coordinate permutations sends a real vector to its arithmetic-mean constant vector.
Patterns: Averaging; Fixed points; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Linear representation of a group; Orthogonal projection

Name: Complex group algebra decomposition
Intuition: Fourier analysis of a finite group changes convolution into independent matrix multiplications.
Conditions: G is finite; the algebra map sends ∑g a_g g to the family ∑g a_gρ(g). The direct sum is finite.
Example: For a finite abelian group every block is 1×1; for S₃ there are two scalar blocks and one 2×2 block.
Prerequisites: Maschke’s theorem; Sum of squared irreducible dimensions

Name: Induced representation
Intuition: Replicate a subgroup representation over cosets and let the larger group move those copies coherently.
Conditions: G is finite, H≤G, and W a finite-dimensional complex H-representation. G acts by left multiplication on the first tensor factor.
Example: Inducing the trivial H-representation gives the permutation representation on G/H.
Prerequisites: Linear representation of a group; Tensor product universal property

Name: Frobenius reciprocity
Intuition: Extending symmetry on the source and restricting symmetry on the target give the same compatible maps.
Conditions: H≤G are finite groups and W,V are finite-dimensional complex representations of H,G respectively; the isomorphism is natural.
Example: The multiplicity of V in an induced representation can be calculated after restricting V to H.
Prerequisites: Induced representation; Intertwining map between representations

Name: Character of an induced representation
Intuition: Only cosets stabilized by g contribute to the trace, and each contributes the corresponding subgroup action.
Conditions: G is finite, H≤G, W a finite-dimensional complex H-representation, and g∈G. An empty sum is zero.
Example: Inducing the trivial subgroup representation counts fixed cosets of g.
Prerequisites: Induced representation; Character of a finite-dimensional representation

Name: Character of a tensor product
Intuition: Combining two symmetry systems multiplies their character fingerprints point by point.
Conditions: V,W are finite-dimensional representations of the same group over C, with diagonal action ρV(g)⊗ρW(g).
Example: For one-dimensional cyclic characters, tensoring adds their frequency indices modulo the group order.
Prerequisites: Character of a finite-dimensional representation; Tensor product universal property

Name: Dual or contragredient representation
Intuition: Let a symmetry act on measurements so evaluation of a transformed vector by a transformed measurement stays unchanged.
Conditions: V is a finite-dimensional representation over a field and V* its algebraic dual. The transpose here is not a conjugate transpose. For finite complex groups, the dual character is the complex conjugate character.
Example: A rotation acts on linear coordinate measurements by the inverse transpose.
Prerequisites: Dual space and pullback of linear functionals; Linear representation of a group

Name: Frobenius–Schur indicator
Intuition: One average distinguishes whether an irreducible complex symmetry type has a symmetric, skew, or absent invariant bilinear pairing.
Conditions: G is finite and χ is an irreducible complex character. Values +1, −1, 0 correspond respectively to invariant nondegenerate symmetric, alternating, or no nonzero bilinear form on that representation.
Example: The quaternionic irreducible representation of the quaternion group has indicator −1.
Prerequisites: Dual or contragredient representation; Orthogonality of irreducible characters

Name: Character of the regular representation
Intuition: Translate the group’s own elements. A nonidentity translation fixes no basis position, so its trace vanishes.
Conditions: G is finite; this is the left regular representation on the vector space with basis G, over C. The direct-sum statement is as a representation.
Example: A cyclic shift of n coordinates has trace zero unless it is the identity shift.
Prerequisites: Linear representation of a group; Multiplicity from a character inner product

Name: Irreducible characters form a class-function basis
LaTeX: \#\widehat G=\#\{\text{conjugacy classes of }G\},\qquad\operatorname{Cl}(G;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{\rho\in\widehat G}\mathbb C\chi_\rho
Intuition: One independent irreducible character is needed for each independent conjugacy-class value.
Conditions: G is finite and Cl(G;C) is the space of functions constant on conjugacy classes. The irreducible characters form an orthonormal basis in the group-average inner product.
Example: S₃ has three conjugacy classes and three irreducible complex representations.

Name: Invariant inner product by averaging
Intuition: Average the geometry itself until every group symmetry preserves it.
Conditions: G is finite, ρ a finite-dimensional real or complex representation, and ⟨,⟩₀ any positive-definite inner product. The averaged form is positive definite and G-invariant.
Example: Every finite subgroup of GLₙ(R) becomes orthogonal after a suitable change of basis.
Prerequisites: Inner product; Linear representation of a group

Name: Schur–Weyl decomposition
Intuition: Changing vector coordinates and permuting tensor positions commute, and their irreducible structures organize each other.
Conditions: V is n-dimensional over C and d≥0. GL(V) acts diagonally, S_d permutes tensor factors, SλV is the irreducible polynomial GL(V)-representation and Spλ the Specht representation.
Example: For d=2, tensor square separates into symmetric and alternating parts.
Prerequisites: Tensor product universal property; Linear representation of a group

Name: Hook-length formula for standard Young tableaux
Intuition: A partition shape permits some orderings of labels and forbids others; local hook sizes combine into the exact global count.
Conditions: λ is a partition of n≥0; fλ counts fillings of its Young diagram by 1,…,n increasing along rows and columns. h(u) counts the cell u and cells to its right and below.
Example: Shape (2,1) has hooks 3,1,1, hence two standard tableaux.

Name: The Lie algebra sl₂
Intuition: Three basic traceless directions close under commutators: one separates weights while the other two move between them.
Conditions: Over C, take h=diag(1,−1), e with entry (1,2)=1, and f with entry (2,1)=1. Their span is sl₂(C), the traceless 2×2 matrices.
Example: Direct multiplication of these three matrices verifies all three brackets.
Prerequisites: Matrix commutator and Lie bracket; Trace

Name: Finite-dimensional irreducible sl₂ representations
Intuition: All finite-dimensional complex irreducible sl₂ modules arise from homogeneous polynomials in two variables. The degree records their size.
Conditions: Every finite-dimensional irreducible sl₂(C)-module is isomorphic to exactly one V_m. On degree-m polynomials, e=x∂y, f=y∂x and h=x∂x−y∂y.
Example: Degree two gives the three-dimensional representation on x²,xy,y².
Prerequisites: The Lie algebra sl₂; Dimension of a symmetric power

Name: Schur polynomial alternant formula
Intuition: Divide two alternating expressions and the signs cancel, leaving a symmetric character polynomial.
Conditions: λ is a partition of length at most n, padded by zeros. The quotient formula is initially evaluated at distinct complex xᵢ and extends uniquely to a polynomial at coinciding values.
Example: For λ=(1), the result is x₁+⋯+xₙ, the character of the defining representation.

Name: Category axioms
LaTeX: h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad f\circ1_A=f=1_B\circ f
Intuition: Specify objects through the transformations between them, with a consistent rule for composing transformations.
Conditions: f:A→B, g:B→C and h:C→D are composable morphisms. Every object has an identity; composition must be defined on each compatible pair. Hom-collections are sets when the category is locally small.
Example: Groups with homomorphisms, or vector spaces with linear maps, form categories.

Name: Functor laws
Intuition: Translate objects and transformations together so that every way of composing steps remains consistent.
Conditions: F assigns objects and morphisms from one category to another, with matching domains and codomains; both displayed laws hold for all compatible morphisms.
Example: The fundamental-group construction sends based spaces to groups and based continuous maps to homomorphisms.

Name: Natural transformation
Intuition: A systematic comparison between two translations is compatible with every allowed transformation.
Conditions: F,G:C→D are functors; η assigns a morphism ηA:F(A)→G(A) to every object and obeys the displayed naturality square for every f.
Example: The canonical map V→V** is natural in a vector space V.

Name: Opposite category
Intuition: Reverse every arrow while retaining the same objects. Every categorical law then has a corresponding reversed form.
Conditions: C is a category; in the composition formula the right-hand composition is taken in C with the reversed arrow directions.
Example: Linear duality is naturally a functor from vector spaces with arrows reversed.

Name: Equivalence of categories
LaTeX: F:\mathcal C\rightleftarrows\mathcal D:G,\qquad GF\cong1_{\mathcal C},\quad FG\cong1_{\mathcal D}
Intuition: Two mathematical languages describe the same objects and transformations up to consistent isomorphism.
Conditions: F and G are functors, and the displayed isomorphisms are natural isomorphisms. An equivalence need not give a bijection of the raw object collections.
Example: Finite-dimensional vector spaces over k are equivalent to the category with natural-number objects and matrices as arrows.

Name: Yoneda lemma
Intuition: A natural rule acting on every map out of A is completely determined by what it does to A’s identity map.
Conditions: C is locally small and F:C→Set is a covariant functor; A is an object. The inverse sends x∈F(A) to f↦F(f)(x).
Example: For linear maps out of a vector space, a natural transformation can be recovered from its value on the identity operator.

Name: Categorical product universal property
Intuition: Giving one map into a product is exactly giving one map into each component.
Conditions: A product has projections to A and B and a unique pairing map for every compatible pair of arrows from X; the displayed bijection is natural in X. Products are not assumed to exist in every category.
Example: A linear map into V×W is uniquely a pair of linear maps into V and W.

Name: Categorical coproduct universal property
Intuition: Giving a map out of an assembled sum means independently specifying its behavior on each included piece.
Conditions: The coproduct includes A and B and has the displayed natural bijection for every X. It is the product construction in the opposite category.
Example: Sets use disjoint union; groups use free product; vector spaces use direct sum.
Prerequisites: Categorical product universal property; Opposite category

Name: Pullback or fiber product
Intuition: Pair two descriptions only when they agree on their shared observation.
Conditions: The displayed formula is for functions f:A→C and g:B→C in sets. Categorically, a pullback represents pairs of arrows into A,B whose composites into C agree.
Example: Pair two records exactly when their identifiers match.

Name: Pushout universal property
Intuition: Glue two objects along specified copies of a shared piece, requiring maps out to agree on that overlap.
Conditions: The input diagram is A←C→B. The displayed bijection uses precomposition maps into Hom(C,X), is natural in X, and characterizes a pushout when it exists.
Example: In groups, amalgamated free product is a pushout.
Prerequisites: Pullback or fiber product; Categorical coproduct universal property

Name: Equalizer universal property
Intuition: Extract the largest part of a source on which two proposed transformations agree.
Conditions: f,g:A→B are parallel arrows. An equalizer e:E→A has the displayed universal factoring property, natural in X. In sets E={a:f(a)=g(a)}.
Example: For linear maps, the equalizer is ker(f−g).

Name: Coequalizer universal property
Intuition: Make the smallest quotient in which two parallel descriptions become indistinguishable.
Conditions: f,g:A→B are parallel arrows and q:B→Q is universal among arrows identifying them. In sets, quotient B by the equivalence relation generated by f(a)∼g(a).
Example: For module maps, the coequalizer is coker(f−g).

Name: Limit as a universal compatible cone
Intuition: Package every compatible choice across a diagram into one object with no extra choices left over.
Conditions: D:J→C is a small diagram in a locally small category; ΔX is the constant diagram. A limit exists exactly when the cone functor is representable as displayed.
Example: An inverse limit of residues modulo pⁿ stores a compatible residue at every precision.
Prerequisites: Natural transformation; Categorical product universal property

Name: Colimit as a universal compatible cocone
Intuition: Assemble a diagram by identifying every overlap its arrows prescribe, and nothing beyond those required identifications.
Conditions: D:J→C is small and C is locally small. The displayed property defines a colimit when it exists.
Example: An increasing family of subsets has its union as the colimit in sets.
Prerequisites: Limit as a universal compatible cone; Opposite category

Name: Adjunction of functors
Intuition: Move a construction from the source side of a mapping problem to a corresponding construction on the target side.
Conditions: F:C→D and G:D→C are functors between locally small categories; the bijections must be natural in both C and D.
Example: Tensoring by a fixed module is left adjoint to taking module homomorphisms from that module.

Name: Unit, counit and triangle identities
Intuition: A round trip through the two sides of an adjunction cancels in the precise directions where cancellation is allowed.
Conditions: F⊣G has unit η:1C→GF and counit ε:FG→1D. The equations are identities of natural transformations; η and ε need not be isomorphisms.
Example: For free groups, introducing formal generators and then evaluating words returns the original free-group word.

Name: Right adjoints preserve limits
Intuition: A right adjoint transports compatible families without losing their universal description.
Conditions: D:J→D is a small diagram with a limit and F:C→D is left adjoint to G:D→C. The canonical comparison is an isomorphism; dually, left adjoints preserve colimits.
Example: Hom_R(M,−) preserves products of modules.
Prerequisites: Adjunction of functors; Limit as a universal compatible cone

Name: Composition of adjunctions
LaTeX: F\dashv G,\quad F^\prime\dashv G^\prime\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F^\prime F\dashv GG^\prime
Intuition: Two successive translations of a mapping problem compose, with the reverse translations appearing in reverse order.
Conditions: F:C→D, G:D→C, F′:D→E and G′:E→D are the indicated adjoint pairs.
Example: Two successive free constructions can be compared with forgetting their structures in reverse order.

Name: Tensor–Hom adjunction for modules
Intuition: A bilinear interaction can be supplied all at once or one input at a time without changing its information.
Conditions: R is commutative with identity and M,N,P are R-modules; the bijection sends f to m↦(n↦f(m⊗n)) and is natural in all arguments.
Example: Integer-bilinear maps out of M×N correspond to homomorphisms out of M⊗Z N.
Prerequisites: Adjunction of functors; Tensor product universal property

Name: Monad unit and multiplication laws
Intuition: A monad describes how to form structured expressions and how to flatten nested structure consistently.
Conditions: T:C→C is an endofunctor, η:1C→T and μ:T²→T are natural transformations obeying the displayed laws.
Example: The list monad inserts an item as a singleton list and flattens a list of lists.

Name: Algebra for a monad
Intuition: An algebra evaluates formal structured expressions in a way that respects insertion and flattening.
Conditions: (T,η,μ) is a monad on C; A is an object and a a morphism satisfying both equations.
Example: Algebras of the list monad are monoids: evaluate a list by multiplying its entries, with the empty list giving the unit.

Name: Pointwise left Kan extension
Intuition: Extend a functor to a larger context by assembling every existing piece that can map into the requested new object.
Conditions: C is small, D locally small, E cocomplete, K:C→D and F:C→E. The comma category has objects arrows Kc→d and the compatible commuting morphisms.
Example: Inducing group representations is an instance of extending along a subgroup inclusion.
Prerequisites: Colimit as a universal compatible cocone; Functor laws

Name: Exponential object and currying
Intuition: A function of two inputs can be viewed as a function returning a function of the second input.
Conditions: A category has the required products; an exponential Bᴬ represents the displayed natural correspondence. In sets, Bᴬ is the set of functions A→B. Not every category has all exponentials.
Example: A two-argument table can be read as a list of one-argument lookup rules.
Prerequisites: Categorical product universal property; Adjunction of functors

Name: Galois connection between ordered sets
LaTeX: L(p)\le q\iff p\le R(q),\qquad p\le RL(p),\quad LR(q)\le q
Intuition: Translate a constraint in one ordered system into an equivalent constraint in another. Round trips give closure and interior operations.
Conditions: P,Q are posets and L:P→Q,R:Q→P are monotone. This is the monotone adjunction convention; antitone Galois connections reverse one order.
Example: For a function f, direct image and inverse image satisfy f(S)⊆T iff S⊆f⁻¹(T).

Name: Hockey-stick identity
Intuition: Group subsets by their largest element: a diagonal sum becomes one larger choice.
Conditions: Integers 0≤r≤n.

Name: Binomial inversion
LaTeX: b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a_k\iff a_n=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}\binom nk b_k
Intuition: Alternating signs undo a transform that mixes all smaller subset sizes.
Conditions: Sequences in a characteristic-zero field; n≥0.
Example: If b_n=2^n, inversion gives a_n=1.

Name: Unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind
LaTeX: {n\brack k}={n-1\brack k-1}+(n-1){n-1\brack k},\quad x^{\overline n}=\sum_k{n\brack k}x^k
Intuition: A new element either starts a cycle or joins one of the existing cycle positions.
Conditions: n≥1; [0,0]=1; out-of-range values zero; rising factorial x(x+1)…(x+n−1).
Example: [3,2]=3, the permutations of three objects with two cycles.
Prerequisites: Permutations and falling factorials; Ordinary generating function

Name: Stirling change of polynomial basis
LaTeX: x^n=\sum_k S(n,k)x^{\underline k},\quad x^{\underline n}=\sum_k s(n,k)x^k
Intuition: Powers and falling factorials are two coordinate systems for polynomials.
Conditions: n≥0; s(n,k)=(−1)^{n−k}[n,k]; sums from 0 to n.
Example: x²=x(x−1)+x.
Prerequisites: Unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind; Stirling numbers of the second kind; Change of basis and similarity

Name: Eulerian number recurrence
Intuition: Insert the largest label and track whether the number of descents grows.
Conditions: A(n,k) counts permutations of n with k descents; n≥2; A(1,0)=1; outside 0≤k<n values are zero.

Name: Formal Lagrange inversion
Intuition: Implicit recursive objects can be counted without explicitly solving their generating function.
Conditions: Formal power series over a characteristic-zero field; φ(0)≠0, T(0)=0, n≥1; F any formal power series.
Example: T=z(1+T)² gives [z^n]T=(1/n) binom(2n,n−1), the Catalan numbers.

Name: Exponential formula for labeled components
Intuition: A labeled object made of an unordered set of connected pieces exponentiates its connected-piece series.
Conditions: A labeled combinatorial class is uniquely a finite set of nonempty components; C is its component EGF, C(0)=0.
Example: For set partitions C(z)=e^z−1, so the Bell-number EGF is exp(e^z−1).

Name: Pólya cycle-index substitution
Intuition: A coloring fixed by a permutation must be constant on each cycle.
Conditions: Finite permutation group G acting on n positions; q colors; c_i(g) counts i-cycles. Counts colorings modulo G.
Example: Rotating a triangle with two colors gives (2³+2·2)/3=4 orbits.

Name: Rotational necklace count
Intuition: Rotations with the same cycle lengths contribute the same fixed colorings.
Conditions: n≥1 positions, q≥1 colors; only rotations identify necklaces, not reflections.
Prerequisites: Burnside’s orbit-counting lemma; Euler’s totient function

Name: Gaussian binomial coefficient
Intuition: Count ordered independent vectors, then divide out the different bases of each subspace.
Conditions: q is a prime power; 0≤k≤n; counts k-dimensional subspaces of F_q^n. Empty product is 1.
Example: There are [3,1]_2=7 lines in F₂³.
Prerequisites: Finite fields; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Finite q-binomial theorem
Intuition: Selecting terms from a product weights subsets by the sum of their positions.
Conditions: Formal polynomial identity in q,t; n≥0; Gaussian coefficients viewed as polynomials in q.

Name: Euler pentagonal-number identity
Intuition: The reciprocal partition series collapses to a sparse alternating pattern.
Conditions: Formal power series, or complex |q|<1. Every coefficient depends on finitely many factors.
Example: The product begins 1−q−q²+q⁵+q⁷−q¹²−q¹⁵.

Name: Möbius inversion on finite posets
Intuition: Undo cumulative totals on any partially ordered collection.
Conditions: Finite poset, values in a commutative ring; μ(x,x)=1 and sum_{x≤z≤y} μ(x,z)=0 for x<y.
Example: On subsets μ(A,B)=(−1)^{|B\A|}, recovering inclusion-exclusion.
Prerequisites: Möbius inversion over divisors; Inclusion–exclusion principle

Name: Incidence-algebra convolution
Intuition: Compose interval-weighted relations by summing over intermediate stops.
Conditions: Finite poset, or locally finite poset with finite intervals; coefficients in a commutative ring; ζ(x,y)=1 for x≤y, δ is the identity kernel.
Example: For a chain, convolution is upper-triangular matrix multiplication.
Prerequisites: Möbius inversion on finite posets; Matrix multiplication

Name: Lubell–Yamamoto–Meshalkin inequality
Intuition: An antichain can meet each complete nested chain at most once.
Conditions: A is an antichain of subsets of an n-element set: no distinct members contain one another.
Example: All k-subsets attain equality because every complete chain contains exactly one.
Prerequisites: Binomial coefficient; Permutations and falling factorials

Name: Sperner theorem
Intuition: The widest layer of the subset lattice is its middle layer.
Conditions: A is an antichain in the subsets of an n-element set.
Example: For n=4, the six two-element subsets form a largest antichain.

Name: Dilworth chain-decomposition theorem
Intuition: The largest mutually incomparable collection is exactly the number of ordered tracks needed.
Conditions: Finite partially ordered set P; empty P has both values zero.
Example: A disjoint union of three nonempty chains has width at most three, with equality if no cross-chain comparisons exist.

Name: Euler trail criterion
LaTeX: G\text{ has an Euler trail}\iff |\{v:\deg v\text{ odd}\}|\in\{0,2\}
Intuition: Every visit uses an entrance and an exit, except possibly the two endpoints.
Conditions: Finite undirected graph with at least one edge; all vertices incident to edges lie in one connected component. Loops count twice in degree.
Example: A path has two odd endpoints; a cycle has none and admits a closed Euler trail.

Name: Bipartite graph criterion
LaTeX: G\text{ bipartite}\iff G\text{ has no odd cycle}
Intuition: Alternating two colors works precisely when no loop of steps forces a color reversal.
Conditions: Finite undirected graph; a loop is an odd cycle of length one.
Example: A square is bipartite; a triangle is not.

Name: Kőnig matching–cover theorem
Intuition: In a bipartite graph, the largest set of disjoint pairs equals the smallest set of vertices touching all edges.
Conditions: Finite bipartite graph; ν is maximum matching size and τ is minimum vertex-cover size.
Example: For a star with m≥1 leaves, both values are one.
Prerequisites: Hall’s marriage theorem; Max-flow min-cut theorem

Name: Tutte perfect-matching criterion
LaTeX: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff o(G-S)\le |S|\quad\forall S\subseteq V
Intuition: Deleting vertices cannot leave more odd islands than those deleted vertices can pair with.
Conditions: Finite undirected graph; o counts connected components of odd order; G−S deletes S and incident edges.
Example: Two isolated vertices fail at S=∅ because there are two odd components.

Name: Menger vertex-path theorem
Intuition: Independent routes equal the smallest number of internal junctions whose removal blocks travel.
Conditions: Finite undirected graph; distinct nonadjacent s,t; separators exclude s,t.
Example: Two disjoint arcs around a cycle give two routes and require two internal vertex removals.

Name: Turán extremal graph theorem
Intuition: Avoiding a large clique is most efficiently done by dividing vertices into balanced independent classes.
Conditions: Integers r≥1,n≥1; finite simple graphs; T_r(n) is the complete r-partite graph with class sizes differing by at most one.
Example: For triangles, the maximum edge count is floor(n²/4).

Name: Ramsey-number recursion
Intuition: From one vertex, enough neighbors or enough nonneighbors force a smaller unavoidable pattern.
Conditions: s,t≥2; R(s,t) is least N forcing an s-clique or independent t-set in every N-vertex simple graph; R(1,t)=R(s,1)=1.

Name: Erdős–Stone asymptotic extremal theorem
Intuition: At leading quadratic scale, the chromatic number controls how many edges a forbidden pattern permits.
Conditions: Fixed finite simple H with chromatic number r≥2; n→∞. For bipartite H this only states ex(n,H)=o(n²).
Example: For H with chromatic number three, the leading density is n²/4.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Turán extremal graph theorem; Chromatic polynomial deletion–contraction

Name: Laplacian kernel and connected components
Intuition: Zero energy means every edge joins equal values, so each component carries one free constant.
Conditions: Finite undirected weighted graph with strictly positive edge weights; isolated vertices count as components; L=D−A.
Example: A graph with three components has three independent zero eigenvectors.

Name: Normalized graph Laplacian
Intuition: Degree normalization measures variation relative to the local amount of connectivity.
Conditions: Finite undirected graph with positive edge weights and no isolated vertices; D contains weighted degrees.
Example: For a d-regular graph, normalized eigenvalues are ordinary Laplacian eigenvalues divided by d.
Prerequisites: Graph Laplacian; Spectral theorem in finite dimensions

Name: Graph Cheeger inequality
Intuition: A low-frequency graph mode reveals a weakly connected cut, and every weak cut produces a low-energy mode.
Conditions: Finite connected undirected positively weighted graph with at least two vertices; λ₂ of normalized Laplacian; vol is sum of degrees.
Example: A long cycle has a small λ₂ and admits a cut with small boundary relative to its size.

Name: Effective resistance from the Laplacian
Intuition: Inject one unit at one vertex and remove it at another; the required potential difference is resistance.
Conditions: Finite connected undirected graph; edge weights are positive conductances; L⁺ is Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.
Example: One edge of conductance c has resistance 1/c.

Name: Foster resistance identity
Intuition: Edge leverage scores add up to the dimension of nonconstant vertex signals.
Conditions: Finite connected loopless undirected graph with positive conductances; effective resistance between edge endpoints in the full network.
Example: In a tree, every summand is one, and there are n−1 edges.
Prerequisites: Effective resistance from the Laplacian; Trace

Name: Random-walk commute time and resistance
Intuition: Electrical difficulty of travel determines expected there-and-back duration.
Conditions: Finite connected loopless undirected graph with positive conductances; walk transition p_uv=c_uv/d_u; H_uv expected first hitting time; vol(G)=sum d_u.
Example: On one edge, the commute time is two steps and vol·R=2c/c=2.
Prerequisites: Markov chain transition law; Effective resistance from the Laplacian

Name: Weighted spanning-tree edge probability
Intuition: An edge is used often precisely when it contributes strongly to connecting its endpoints.
Conditions: Connected finite loopless undirected weighted graph; tree probability proportional to product of edge conductances.
Example: Every edge of a tree has probability one; each edge of an unweighted triangle has probability 2/3.
Prerequisites: Matrix–tree theorem; Effective resistance from the Laplacian

Name: Rooted forest determinant
Intuition: Adding one root choice per tree component turns the Laplacian determinant into a forest counter.
Conditions: Finite undirected weighted graph; sum over spanning forests together with one marked root per component; k(F) components.
Example: For one edge of weight c, det(tI+L)=t²+2ct: two root choices for the connected tree.

Name: Matroid independence axioms
LaTeX: \varnothing\in\mathcal I,\quad J\subseteq I\in\mathcal I\Rightarrow J\in\mathcal I,\quad |I|<|J|\Rightarrow\exists e\in J\setminus I:I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I
Intuition: Abstract independence keeps the key feature that smaller independent collections can be enlarged from larger ones.
Conditions: Finite ground set E; in the exchange clause I,J∈I.
Example: Independent vector subsets form a matroid; acyclic edge sets form a graphic matroid.
Prerequisites: Basis and unique coordinates; Edges in a finite tree

Name: Matroid rank submodularity
Intuition: New independent information has diminishing returns when more elements are already available.
Conditions: Finite matroid; r(S) is the maximum size of an independent subset of S.
Example: For vectors, rank is dimension of their span; overlapping spans explain the inequality.
Prerequisites: Matroid independence axioms; Dimension of a sum of subspaces

Name: Dual matroid rank
Intuition: What one basis leaves unused becomes a basis of the dual system.
Conditions: Finite matroid M on E; dual bases are complements of bases of M.
Example: For the uniform rank-r matroid on n elements, the dual has rank n−r.

Name: Symmetric matroid basis exchange
LaTeX: e\in B_1\setminus B_2\Rightarrow\exists f\in B_2\setminus B_1:\ B_1-e+f,\ B_2-f+e\text{ are bases}
Intuition: Two complete independent selections can trade a suitable pair without losing completeness.
Conditions: Finite matroid; B₁,B₂ bases. The simultaneous exchange is stronger than the basic augmentation axiom.
Example: Two spanning trees can exchange an edge across the cut created by deleting a tree edge, with an appropriate partner.
Prerequisites: Matroid independence axioms; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Matroid intersection min–max theorem
Intuition: The largest selection obeying two independence rules is limited exactly by the best split of their capacities.
Conditions: Two finite matroids on the same ground set E.
Example: Bipartite matchings are common independent sets of two partition matroids, one for each endpoint class.
Prerequisites: Matroid independence axioms; Hall’s marriage theorem

Name: Tutte polynomial by rank subsets
Intuition: A single polynomial tracks how far each edge set is from spanning and how much cyclic redundancy it contains.
Conditions: Finite matroid M; for a graph r(A)=|V|−c(V,A).
Example: A bridge contributes x; a loop contributes y; a tree with m edges has polynomial x^m.
Prerequisites: Matroid independence axioms; Cycle rank of a finite graph

Name: Tutte duality
Intuition: Duality swaps missing connectivity with excess dependence.
Conditions: Finite matroid M and its dual; for a connected plane graph, the dual matroid is represented by the geometric dual graph.
Example: The cycle of length three has x²+x+y; its three-parallel-edge dual has y²+y+x.
Prerequisites: Tutte polynomial by rank subsets; Dual matroid rank

Name: Chromatic polynomial from Tutte polynomial
Intuition: Proper coloring is one specialization of the universal edge-subset counter.
Conditions: Finite undirected graph; c(G) counts components including isolated vertices; loops make P_G identically zero.
Example: For a tree on n vertices, P_G(q)=q(q−1)^(n−1).
Prerequisites: Tutte polynomial by rank subsets; Chromatic polynomial deletion–contraction

Name: Bases at the center of the Tutte polynomial
Intuition: At the central evaluation, only subsets with neither rank deficit nor redundancy survive.
Conditions: Finite matroid; powers with exponent zero evaluate to one. For a connected graph, bases are spanning trees.
Example: A triangle has T(1,1)=3 spanning trees.
Prerequisites: Tutte polynomial by rank subsets; Matrix–tree theorem

Name: Tutte matrix perfect-matching test
LaTeX: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff\det A(\mathbf x)\not\equiv0
Intuition: Assign each edge its own variable so matching contributions cannot accidentally cancel identically.
Conditions: Finite simple graph; skew matrix A_ij=x_ij on edges for i<j, A_ji=−x_ij, zeros otherwise; polynomial over a field of characteristic not two.
Example: For four vertices, the Pfaffian is x12x34−x13x24+x14x23, omitting nonexistent edges.

Name: Hensel lifting of a simple root
LaTeX: f(a)\equiv0\pmod p,\quad f^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv0\pmod p\Longrightarrow \exists!\alpha\in\mathbb Z_p:\ f(\alpha)=0,\ \alpha\equiv a\pmod p
Intuition: A root with a nonzero local slope can be corrected one p-adic digit at a time.
Conditions: Prime p; f∈Z_p[x]; a∈Z_p. Uniqueness is within the residue class of a modulo p.
Example: x²−2 has two roots in Z₇, lifting 3 and 4 modulo 7.
Prerequisites: p-adic absolute value and ultrametric; Modular inverse criterion

Name: p-adic digit expansion
Intuition: Digits extend toward higher powers because those powers become smaller in the p-adic metric.
Conditions: Prime p; each nonzero x∈Q_p has a unique such expansion with integer v and a_v≠0; x∈Z_p iff v≥0.
Prerequisites: p-adic absolute value and ultrametric; Euclidean division of integers

Name: Product formula for rational absolute values
Intuition: Ordinary size and prime-divisibility sizes exactly balance for a nonzero rational number.
Conditions: x∈Q×; |p|_p=p^(−1), ordinary real absolute value at infinity; only finitely many prime factors differ from one.
Example: For x=12, the product is 12·2^(−2)·3^(−1)=1.
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; p-adic absolute value and ultrametric

Name: Ostrowski classification on the rationals
Intuition: The rationals admit only the ordinary and prime-based kinds of metric size.
Conditions: Absolute values are equivalent when they induce the same topology; p is prime; trivial absolute value excluded.
Example: Completion gives R for the ordinary class and Q_p for the p-adic class.

Name: Euler prime product
Intuition: A product that chooses an exponent for each prime enumerates every positive integer exactly once.
Conditions: Complex s with real part greater than one; both series and product converge absolutely.
Example: At s=2, multiplying geometric prime-power series reconstructs the sum of reciprocal squares.
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Finite geometric sum

Name: Prime number theorem
Intuition: Primes become sparser, with average density near x on the scale 1/log x.
Conditions: x→∞ through positive real values; π(x) counts primes≤x; asymptotic means ratio tends to one.
Example: The estimate for π(10⁶) is about 72,382, compared with its exact value 78,498.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Logarithm laws

Name: Dirichlet character modulo q
Intuition: A character replaces invertible residue classes by multiplicative complex phases.
Conditions: q≥1; χ restricted to (Z/qZ)× is a homomorphism to C×, extended by zero to nonunits.
Example: Modulo four, χ(1)=1, χ(3)=−1 and even arguments have value zero.
Prerequisites: Group homomorphism; Congruence modulo an integer

Name: Dirichlet L-series Euler product
Intuition: Twisting each prime by a character sorts multiplicative arithmetic information into frequency channels.
Conditions: Dirichlet character χ; complex Re(s)>1, giving absolute convergence.
Example: For the principal character modulo q, primes dividing q contribute factors equal to one.
Prerequisites: Dirichlet character modulo q; Fundamental theorem of arithmetic

Name: Character filter for a residue class
Intuition: Average all multiplicative frequencies with the correct phase to isolate one invertible residue class.
Conditions: q≥1; gcd(a,q)=1; n integer; sum over all characters modulo q, extended by zero on nonunits.
Example: Modulo four, odd numbers are separated by the principal character and the sign character.
Prerequisites: Dirichlet character modulo q; Euler’s totient function

Name: Dirichlet theorem on arithmetic progressions
Intuition: Every residue class that avoids an unavoidable common divisor continues to contain primes forever.
Conditions: Integers q≥1 and gcd(a,q)=1. This existence theorem alone does not assert an error term or rate.
Example: There are infinitely many primes ending in each of 1,3,7,9.
Prerequisites: Congruence modulo an integer; Dirichlet character modulo q

Name: Jordan totient function
Intuition: Exclude k-tuples whose coordinates all share a prime divisor with the modulus.
Conditions: Integers n,k≥1; counts tuples in {1,…,n}^k with gcd(a₁,…,a_k,n)=1.

Name: Ramanujan sum
Intuition: Adding only primitive cyclic frequencies unexpectedly produces an integer.
Conditions: Positive integer q; integer n; μ is the arithmetic Möbius function.
Example: For prime p, c_p(n)=p−1 if p divides n and −1 otherwise.
Prerequisites: Möbius inversion over divisors; Euler's formula

Name: Moduli admitting primitive roots
Intuition: One generator produces every invertible residue only for a restricted family of moduli.
Conditions: p odd prime, k≥1; n positive; the unit group for n=1 is taken as the trivial group.
Example: Modulo seven, powers of three generate all six units; modulo eight the unit group is not cyclic.
Prerequisites: Order of a power in a cyclic subgroup; Chinese remainder theorem

Name: Cyclotomic factorization
Intuition: Roots of unity separate into families according to their exact period.
Conditions: n≥1; Φ_n is the monic polynomial whose roots are primitive n-th roots of unity; Φ_n∈Z[x] and is irreducible over Q.
Example: Φ₆(x)=x²−x+1.
Prerequisites: Euler’s totient function; Polynomial remainder and factor theorem

Name: Lucas binomial congruence
Intuition: Modulo a prime, binomial choices split digit by digit in base p.
Conditions: p prime; n,k≥0 with base-p digits n_i,k_i; binom(a,b)=0 when b>a.
Example: binom(5,2)≡binom(1,0)binom(0,1)binom(1,0)=0 modulo two.

Name: Kummer carry theorem
LaTeX: v_p\binom nk=\#\{\text{carries when adding }k\text{ and }n-k\text{ in base }p\}
Intuition: Prime factors in a binomial coefficient are recorded by elementary carrying operations.
Conditions: p prime; integers 0≤k≤n; count every carry between adjacent digit positions.
Example: binom(5,2)=10 has one factor of two; binary 010+011=101 has one carry.
Prerequisites: Prime exponent in a factorial; Binomial coefficient

Name: Two-square criterion
LaTeX: n=a^2+b^2\iff v_p(n)\text{ is even for every prime }p\equiv3\pmod4
Intuition: Primes of one residue type must occur in pairs before an integer can be a sum of two squares.
Conditions: Positive integer n; a,b integers, allowing zero.
Example: 45=3²·5 is allowed and equals 6²+3²; 21 is not.
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Quadratic reciprocity

Name: Pell equation and quadratic units
Intuition: One smallest expanding unit generates all positive Pell solutions by multiplication.
Conditions: D positive nonsquare integer; (x₁,y₁) is the least solution with x₁>1,y₁>0; n≥1 enumerates all x,y>0 solutions.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Continued-fraction convergent recurrence; Exponential addition law

Name: Dirichlet rational approximation
LaTeX: \forall Q\ge1\ \exists p\in\mathbb Z,\ 1\le q\le Q:\quad \left|\alpha-\frac pq\right|\le\frac1{qQ}
Intuition: Two fractional parts among enough multiples must be close, producing a good rational approximation.
Conditions: Real α; integer Q≥1. For irrational α, infinitely many reduced p/q satisfy |α−p/q|<1/q².
Example: An irrational can always be approximated with denominator at most 100 and error at most 1/(100q).

Name: Algebraic integer criterion
Intuition: The correct integers inside a number field are roots of monic integer equations.
Conditions: α is an algebraic number; m≥1; monicity is essential.
Example: √2 is integral; 1/2 is algebraic but not integral.
Prerequisites: Minimal polynomial and a simple field extension

Name: Norm and trace of a field extension
Intuition: Multiplication by one field element is a linear map; its volume factor and diagonal sum become arithmetic invariants.
Conditions: Finite extension L/K; m_a:L→L is K-linear multiplication by a. For separable extensions, norm and trace equal product and sum over K-embeddings.
Example: In Q(√d), the norm of u+v√d is u²−dv² and the trace is 2u.
Prerequisites: Tower law for field extensions; Determinant; Trace

Name: Number-field discriminant
Intuition: The trace pairing measures how an arithmetic basis sits inside all embeddings at once.
Conditions: Number field K of degree n; ω_i a Q-basis. For an integral basis of O_K this is the field discriminant, independent of basis.
Example: For K=Q(√5), the integral basis 1,(1+√5)/2 has discriminant 5.
Prerequisites: Norm and trace of a field extension; Gram determinant and volume

Name: Unique prime-ideal factorization
Intuition: When element factorization fails, ideals restore a unique list of prime building blocks.
Conditions: Nonzero ideal in a Dedekind domain; finitely many nonnegative exponents are nonzero. For nonzero fractional ideals exponents may be integers.
Example: The ring of integers of every number field is Dedekind, so its nonzero ideals factor uniquely.
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic; Quotient ring

Name: Ramification and residue-degree identity
Intuition: A rational prime distributes its degree budget between repeated factors and larger residue fields.
Conditions: Number field K; p rational prime; distinct prime ideals above p; f_i=[O_K/𝔭_i:F_p].
Example: In Q(i), (2) is ramified with e=2,f=1; primes congruent to three modulo four have e=1,f=2.
Prerequisites: Unique prime-ideal factorization; Tower law for field extensions

Name: Ideal class group
Intuition: The class group records the obstruction to describing every ideal with a single generator.
Conditions: Number field K; I_K group of nonzero fractional ideals of O_K; P_K subgroup of nonzero principal fractional ideals.
Example: For Q the class group is trivial; class number one means O_K is a principal ideal domain.

Name: Dirichlet unit theorem
Intuition: Apart from finitely many roots of unity, all units are generated by finitely many independent multiplicative directions.
Conditions: Number field with r₁ real embeddings and r₂ conjugate pairs of complex embeddings; μ(K) roots of unity.
Example: A real quadratic field has one independent fundamental unit; an imaginary quadratic field has only finitely many units.
Prerequisites: Structure theorem for finite abelian groups; Norm and trace of a field extension

Name: Minkowski convex-body theorem
Intuition: A centrally symmetric body larger than a lattice’s fundamental-volume threshold must capture a nonzero lattice point.
Conditions: Full-rank lattice Λ in R^n; measurable convex C with C=−C. Strict inequality suffices; equality also suffices when C is compact.
Example: For Z², an origin-centered square of side greater than two necessarily contains a nonzero integer point.

Name: Minkowski ideal-class bound
Intuition: Every ideal class has a representative below an explicit size, making a global classification finite.
Conditions: Number field K of degree n with r₂ complex pairs and discriminant D_K; each ideal class contains a nonzero integral ideal 𝔞 satisfying the bound; N is ideal index.
Example: For Q(i), the bound is 2/π<1.28, forcing an ideal of norm one in every class, hence class number one.
Prerequisites: Ideal class group; Minkowski convex-body theorem

Name: Integers of a quadratic field
LaTeX: \mathcal O_{\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)}=\begin{cases}\mathbb Z[(1+\sqrt d)/2],&d\equiv1\pmod4,\\ \mathbb Z[\sqrt d],&d\equiv2,3\pmod4.\end{cases}
Intuition: Half-integer coordinates are allowed precisely when they still give integral trace and norm.
Conditions: Squarefree integer d≠0,1; negative d allowed; congruences taken modulo four.
Example: In Q(√5), the golden ratio is an algebraic integer even though its coefficients in 1,√5 are halves.
Prerequisites: Algebraic integer criterion; Norm and trace of a field extension

Name: Tangent vectors as derivations
Intuition: A direction is a rule that differentiates every smooth observable at one point.
Conditions: Smooth finite-dimensional manifold M; derivations are R-linear and satisfy the displayed Leibniz rule at p.
Example: In a coordinate chart, v=sum_i v^i ∂/∂x^i at p.

Name: Lie derivative via a flow
Intuition: Compare a tensor with its transported version under the motion generated by a vector field.
Conditions: Smooth vector field X with local flow φ_t; smooth tensor T; pullback for contravariant slots uses the inverse differential.
Example: For a function f, L_X f=X(f); for a vector field Y, L_XY=[X,Y].
Prerequisites: Pullback of a differential form; Matrix commutator and Lie bracket

Name: Koszul formula
Intuition: Metric compatibility and absence of torsion determine the connection completely.
Conditions: Smooth Riemannian metric; X,Y,Z smooth vector fields; ∇ is the Levi-Civita connection.
Example: For commuting Euclidean coordinate vectors and constant metric coefficients, every connection coefficient vanishes.
