Prerequisites: Riemannian metric; Covariant derivative in coordinates

Name: Hodge star operator
Intuition: A metric and orientation turn a k-dimensional measurement into its complementary-dimensional measurement.
Conditions: Oriented n-dimensional Riemannian manifold; α,β smooth k-forms; real-valued forms and positive-definite metric.
Example: In oriented Euclidean R³, *(dx)=dy∧dz.
Prerequisites: Wedge product and graded commutativity; Riemannian volume element

Name: Codifferential and Hodge Laplacian
Intuition: Reverse exterior differentiation using the metric adjoint, then combine both directions into an energy operator.
Conditions: Oriented n-dimensional Riemannian manifold; δ is the formal L² adjoint of d on compactly supported forms. Δ_H is nonnegative under the L² pairing.
Example: On functions, Δ_H f=−Δ_g f with the atlas convention Δ_g=div grad.
Prerequisites: Hodge star operator; Exterior derivative; Adjoint of a linear map

Name: Hodge decomposition theorem
Intuition: Every differential form splits into a topological residue and two orthogonal derivative parts.
Conditions: Compact oriented smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary; smooth forms; H^k=ker Δ_H. The direct sum is L²-orthogonal.
Example: On a circle, the nonzero harmonic one-form dθ represents the single circulation class.
Prerequisites: Codifferential and Hodge Laplacian; De Rham’s theorem

Name: Poincaré lemma
Intuition: Locally, the only obstruction to being a derivative is the compatibility condition dω=0.
Conditions: Smooth k-form on a star-shaped open subset of R^n; k>0. More generally holds on sufficiently small coordinate neighborhoods.
Example: A curl-free vector field on a ball has a scalar potential.

Name: Gauss equation for a submanifold
Intuition: Intrinsic curvature combines ambient curvature with the way the submanifold bends.
Conditions: Isometric immersion M into a Riemannian manifold; h normal second fundamental form; R(X,Y)Z=∇X∇YZ−∇Y∇XZ−∇[X,Y]Z.
Example: For a surface in R³, K equals the product of principal curvatures.
Prerequisites: Riemann curvature tensor; Shape operator and second fundamental form

Name: Codazzi equation in Euclidean space
Intuition: The bending tensor cannot vary arbitrarily; its derivatives must be mutually compatible.
Conditions: Smooth isometric immersion into Euclidean space; derivative of h uses both the induced tangent and normal connections.
Example: For a plane, h=0 and the equation holds identically.
Prerequisites: Covariant derivative in coordinates; Shape operator and second fundamental form

Name: Jacobi equation for geodesic variation
Intuition: Curvature controls how neighboring geodesics converge or spread apart.
Conditions: Smooth Riemannian manifold; γ a geodesic; J arises from a smooth variation through affinely parametrized geodesics, or is any solution of this linear equation.
Example: On the unit sphere, a perpendicular Jacobi component satisfies j″+j=0.

Name: Riemannian exponential map
Intuition: A tangent arrow becomes a point by following the geodesic it launches.
Conditions: γ_v starts at p with velocity v; v lies where the geodesic exists to time one. Exp is a local diffeomorphism near zero.
Example: In Euclidean space, exp_p(v)=p+v.

Name: Hopf–Rinow theorem
LaTeX: (M,d_g)\text{ complete}\iff M\text{ geodesically complete}\iff\text{closed bounded subsets are compact}
Intuition: For a connected Riemannian manifold, metric completeness, endless geodesics, and compactness of bounded regions coincide.
Conditions: Connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary. Under these conditions any two points are joined by a minimizing geodesic.
Example: Euclidean space is complete; the open unit ball with its Euclidean metric is not.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Geodesic equation; Riemannian length and distance

Name: Bonnet–Myers diameter bound
Intuition: Uniformly positive Ricci curvature forces geodesics to reconverge, limiting the size of a complete space.
Conditions: Connected complete n-dimensional Riemannian manifold, n≥2. It is compact and has finite fundamental group.
Example: The round sphere of radius r attains diameter πr with k=1/r².
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Scaling and homogeneity
Prerequisites: Ricci and scalar curvature as traces; Hopf–Rinow theorem

Name: Cartan–Hadamard theorem
Intuition: Without positive curvature or topological loops, geodesics never create global coordinate ambiguity.
Conditions: Connected complete simply connected Riemannian n-manifold with nonpositive sectional curvature; exp is a diffeomorphism for every p.
Example: Hyperbolic space is diffeomorphic to R^n despite its non-Euclidean distances.

Name: Bochner identity for functions
Intuition: Differentiating gradient energy reveals both second-derivative energy and a curvature correction.
Conditions: Smooth real function on a smooth Riemannian manifold; Δ_g=div grad; curvature convention as in the atlas.
Example: In Euclidean space for harmonic f, half the Laplacian of gradient energy is the squared Hessian norm.

Name: Bishop–Gromov volume comparison
Intuition: A lower Ricci bound prevents balls from gaining volume faster than the constant-curvature comparison space.
Conditions: Complete n-dimensional Riemannian manifold with Ric≥(n−1)k g; V_k(r) is ball volume in the simply connected n-dimensional space form. For k>0 take 0<r<π/√k.
Example: With Ric≥0, Vol(B(p,r))/r^n is nonincreasing and Vol(B(p,r))≤ω_n r^n.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Riemannian volume element; Ricci and scalar curvature as traces

Name: Killing vector-field equation
Intuition: Infinitesimal motions preserve lengths when their local derivative has no symmetric stretching part.
Conditions: Smooth vector field on a Riemannian manifold; indices lowered with g; the local flow consists of local isometries.
Example: Translations and rotations in Euclidean space are Killing fields.
Prerequisites: Covariant derivative in coordinates; Riemannian metric

Name: Bianchi identities
Intuition: Curvature is constrained by cyclic cancellation, both algebraically and after differentiation.
Conditions: Levi-Civita connection; first sum cycles X,Y,Z; second is an identity of endomorphism-valued tensors cycling X,Y,Z.
Example: Both identities are automatic for flat Euclidean space; they constrain nonzero curvature tensors as well.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Riemann curvature tensor; Covariant derivative in coordinates

Name: Curvature of a bi-invariant metric
Intuition: In a group whose metric respects left and right translation, noncommutativity is exactly the source of sectional curvature.
Conditions: Lie group with bi-invariant positive-definite Riemannian metric; X,Y left-invariant and linearly independent. Not every Lie group admits such a metric.
Example: An abelian Lie group with an invariant flat metric has zero brackets and zero curvature.
Prerequisites: Matrix commutator and Lie bracket; Sectional curvature

Name: Symplectic form
LaTeX: d\omega=0,\qquad v\mapsto\omega(v,\cdot)\text{ is an isomorphism }T_pM\to T_p^*M
Intuition: An alternating pairing matches directions with covectors while satisfying a differential compatibility law.
Conditions: Smooth manifold; ω a smooth closed nondegenerate two-form. Dimension is necessarily even.
Example: On R^{2n}, ω=sum_i dq_i∧dp_i.
Prerequisites: Wedge product and graded commutativity; Exterior derivative

Name: Darboux theorem
Intuition: Every symplectic space has the same local form, regardless of global topology.
Conditions: Smooth symplectic 2n-manifold; the coordinates exist near every point. They need not extend globally.
Example: The sphere admits an area symplectic form but cannot have a single global Euclidean coordinate chart.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Symplectic form; Pullback of a differential form

Name: Lagrangian submanifold criterion
Intuition: A Lagrangian submanifold occupies as many directions as possible while the symplectic pairing vanishes within it.
Conditions: Embedded or immersed submanifold L of symplectic M, with inclusion or immersion ι; both conditions are required.
Example: The graph of df in T*Q is Lagrangian for the canonical symplectic form.
Prerequisites: Symplectic form; Pullback of a differential form

Name: Cohomology cup product
Intuition: Cohomology classes can multiply, detecting how topological features interact rather than merely how many exist.
Conditions: Singular cohomology of a space with coefficients in a commutative ring R; graded commutativity holds at the cohomology-class level.
Example: On a torus, two independent degree-one classes have nonzero product in degree two.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Wedge product and graded commutativity

Name: Universal coefficient theorem for cohomology
Intuition: Dualizing homology almost gives cohomology; a torsion correction explains the difference.
Conditions: Space X, abelian coefficient group G; singular homology and cohomology. The sequence splits as groups, generally not naturally.
Example: If H_{n−1} is free, the Ext term vanishes and H^n is Hom(H_n,G).
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Exactness of consecutive maps; Ext from a projective resolution

Name: Long exact sequence of a pair
Intuition: Relative cycles may have a boundary, provided the boundary lies in the designated subspace.
Conditions: Topological pair A⊆X; singular homology with one fixed coefficient group.
Example: H_n(D^n,S^{n−1};Z)=Z, whose generator maps to the sphere boundary class.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Exactness of consecutive maps

Name: Long exact sequence of a fibration
Intuition: A sphere that contracts after projection may leave a nontrivial trace in the fiber.
Conditions: Pointed Serre fibration F→E→B with chosen compatible basepoints; homotopy-group exactness in positive degrees, with the usual pointed-set interpretation at degree zero.
Example: The Hopf fibration S¹→S³→S² yields π₂(S²)≅π₁(S¹)≅Z.
Prerequisites: Fundamental group; Exactness of consecutive maps

Name: Hurewicz theorem
Intuition: At the first possible nontrivial dimension, sphere-based topology and cycle-based topology agree.
Conditions: n≥2; X a path-connected CW complex with π_i(X)=0 for 1≤i<n. The Hurewicz map sends a sphere map to its fundamental homology class.
Example: For S^n with n≥2, π_n(S^n)≅Z.
Prerequisites: Fundamental group; Homology as cycles modulo boundaries

Name: Whitehead theorem for CW complexes
LaTeX: f_*:\pi_n(X)\overset{\cong}{\to}\pi_n(Y)\ \forall n\ge1\Longrightarrow f\text{ is a homotopy equivalence}
Intuition: For spaces built from cells, matching every sphere-based test is enough to recover the whole homotopy type.
Conditions: Continuous map f between connected CW complexes; compatible basepoints. Without the CW hypothesis a weak homotopy equivalence need not be a homotopy equivalence.
Example: A contractible CW complex is homotopy equivalent to a point.

Name: Suspension isomorphism in reduced homology
Intuition: Collapsing the two ends of a cylinder shifts each reduced homology feature up one dimension.
Conditions: Nonempty CW complex X; unreduced suspension ΣX; n≥0; any abelian coefficient group G.
Example: Suspending S¹ gives S² and shifts its Z class from degree one to degree two.
Prerequisites: Mayer–Vietoris exact sequence; Homology as cycles modulo boundaries

Name: Cellular homology chain complex
Intuition: One generator per cell can replace the enormous singular chain complex.
Conditions: CW complex X with skeleta X^n; boundary maps are induced by attaching maps and connecting homomorphisms.
Example: A sphere has one zero-cell and one n-cell, making its cellular homology immediate.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Long exact sequence of a pair

Name: Excision in relative homology
Intuition: Removing a region safely inside the ignored subspace does not change the relative topological information.
Conditions: A⊆X and closure(Z)⊆interior(A); singular homology with abelian coefficients G; map induced by inclusion.
Example: Removing an interior subdisk from the ignored annular region does not affect the corresponding relative group.
Prerequisites: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries; Long exact sequence of a pair

Name: Classification of connected covering spaces
Intuition: A covering space is determined by which loops close after being lifted.
Conditions: X path-connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected; covers unbased, hence subgroups taken up to conjugacy.
Example: Subgroups nZ of π₁(S¹)=Z give the n-sheeted circle covers; {0} gives its universal cover R.
Prerequisites: Number of sheets and subgroup index; Fundamental group

Name: Borsuk–Ulam theorem
Intuition: A continuous assignment of n measurements to an n-sphere must agree at some opposite pair.
Conditions: n≥1; antipodal points on the unit n-sphere; arbitrary continuous real-valued n-component map.
Example: For n=1, some opposite points on a circle have equal scalar measurement.
Prerequisites: Continuity by inverse images; Degree of a map

Name: Euler class and zero counts
Intuition: The topology of the tangent bundle accounts for the total index of unavoidable vector-field zeros.
Conditions: Closed oriented smooth n-manifold; X a smooth tangent vector field with isolated zeros; e(TM)∈H^n(M;Z).
Example: A sphere S² has Euler characteristic two, so a tangent field cannot be everywhere nonzero.
Prerequisites: Euler characteristic; Degree of a map

Name: Chern classes and the Whitney sum law
Intuition: Characteristic classes package the twisting of complex vector bundles into multiplicative cohomology data.
Conditions: Complex vector bundles of finite rank over a CW complex; c_i(E)∈H^{2i}(X;Z), zero above the rank.
Example: For line bundles L,M, c₁(L⊕M)=c₁(L)+c₁(M) and c₂(L⊕M)=c₁(L)c₁(M).
Prerequisites: Cohomology cup product; Direct product of groups

Name: Stiefel–Whitney classes
Intuition: Real bundles carry mod-two twisting indicators that survive without choosing an orientation.
Conditions: Real rank-r vector bundle over a CW complex; w_i(E)∈H^i(X;F₂), vanish above rank. w₁=0 iff E is orientable.
Example: The Möbius line bundle over S¹ has nonzero w₁.
Prerequisites: Cohomology cup product; Topology by open sets

Name: Thom isomorphism
Intuition: An oriented r-dimensional fiber contributes one canonical relative class and shifts cohomological degree by r.
Conditions: R-oriented real rank-r vector bundle E over a CW complex; u its Thom class; D(E),S(E) disk and sphere bundles from a chosen metric; R commutative coefficient ring.
Example: For a trivial bundle over a point, this is H⁰(point)≅H^r(D^r,S^{r−1}).
Prerequisites: Poincaré duality; Long exact sequence of a pair

Name: Chern character
Intuition: Exponentiating formal Chern roots turns bundle sum and tensor product into ordinary ring operations.
Conditions: Complex vector bundles over a finite CW complex; x_i formal degree-two Chern roots under the splitting principle; values in even rational cohomology.
Example: ch(E)=rank(E)+c₁+(c₁²−2c₂)/2+⋯.
Prerequisites: Chern classes and the Whitney sum law; Tensor product universal property

Name: Compact-to-Hausdorff bijection theorem
LaTeX: f:X\to Y\text{ continuous bijective},\ X\text{ compact},\ Y\text{ Hausdorff}\Longrightarrow f\text{ homeomorphism}
Intuition: Compactness prevents a continuous one-to-one relabeling from hiding a discontinuous inverse.
Conditions: Topological spaces as stated; no metrizability needed.
Example: A continuous bijection from a compact interval onto its image in Euclidean space has continuous inverse.

Name: Tychonoff compactness theorem
Intuition: Even infinitely many compact coordinate constraints remain compact in the topology that inspects finitely many coordinates at a time.
Conditions: Product topology; arbitrary family of compact spaces, in standard set theory with the axiom of choice. The box topology need not satisfy the conclusion.
Example: The infinite binary cube {0,1}^N is compact in its product topology.
Prerequisites: Cartesian product; Topology by open sets

Name: Boolean algebra as a Boolean ring
LaTeX: A+B=A\triangle B,\quad AB=A\cap B,\quad A^2=A,\quad A+A=0
Intuition: Logical choices become arithmetic when addition means exclusive-or and multiplication means and.
Conditions: Subsets of a fixed universe; symmetric difference as addition and intersection as multiplication. More generally every Boolean algebra yields a commutative Boolean ring.
Prerequisites: De Morgan’s laws; Ring structure and distributivity

Name: Downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem
LaTeX: A\subseteq M\Longrightarrow\exists N\preccurlyeq M:\ A\subseteq N,\ |N|\le\max(|A|,|L|,\aleph_0)
Intuition: A structure may have a much smaller part that preserves every first-order statement about its own elements.
Conditions: First-order L-structure M; subset A; N is an elementary substructure. Uses the usual choice principles to select witnesses.
Example: An infinite structure in a countable language has a countable elementary substructure containing any chosen countable set.

Name: Tarski–Vaught test
LaTeX: N\preccurlyeq M\iff\bigl(M\models\exists x\,\varphi(x,\bar a)\Rightarrow\exists b\in N:\ M\models\varphi(b,\bar a)\bigr)
Intuition: A substructure is elementary exactly when it never needs to leave home to find an existential witness.
Conditions: N⊆M an L-substructure; the condition holds for every first-order formula φ and all parameter tuples a from N.
Example: A subfield of an algebraically closed field must contain every needed root to satisfy even the polynomial-witness part of this test.

Name: Łoś theorem for ultraproducts
Intuition: A first-order statement holds in the quotient product exactly when it holds on a set of indices deemed large by the ultrafilter.
Conditions: Structures M_i in one first-order language with nonempty domains; U an ultrafilter on the index set; tuples represented coordinatewise; usual choice principles.
Example: An ultraproduct of fields is a field because every field axiom transfers.

Name: Quantifier elimination for real closed fields
Intuition: Existence conditions involving polynomial inequalities can be rewritten as polynomial inequalities without hidden variables.
Conditions: First-order language of ordered rings; φ may contain parameters, retained in ψ; all real closed fields satisfy the equivalence.
Example: Over R, ∃y(y²=x) is equivalent to x≥0.

Name: Compactness of the space of types
LaTeX: [\varphi]=\{p:\varphi\in p\},\qquad S_n(T)\text{ is compact Hausdorff and totally disconnected}
Intuition: A complete type is a fully specified collection of compatible answers about a tuple; finite questions define its neighborhoods.
Conditions: Consistent first-order theory T; S_n(T) complete n-types over T; basic sets [φ] are both open and closed.
Example: For dense linear orders, one-variable types over a parameter set describe consistent positions relative to those parameters.
Prerequisites: Compactness theorem for first-order logic; Topology by open sets

Name: Affine algebraic zero set
Intuition: A geometric shape is the set of simultaneous solutions of a polynomial system.
Conditions: Field k; ideal I⊆k[x₁,…,x_n]. Over non-algebraically-closed fields, distinct radical ideals may have the same k-points.
Example: V(y−x²) is the parabola over R.
Prerequisites: Quotient ring; Polynomial remainder and factor theorem

Name: Coordinate ring of an affine algebraic set
Intuition: Two polynomials represent the same observable on a shape when they agree at every point of it.
Conditions: X⊆k^n an affine algebraic set; I(X) the ideal of all polynomials vanishing on X.
Example: The parabola y=x² has coordinate ring k[x,y]/(y−x²)≅k[x].
Prerequisites: Affine algebraic zero set; Quotient ring

Name: Radical of an ideal
Intuition: Discard algebraic multiplicity while retaining the underlying vanishing constraint.
Conditions: Ideal I in a commutative ring with identity; sqrt(I) is an ideal.
Example: sqrt((x²))=(x) in k[x].

Name: Hilbert Nullstellensatz
Intuition: Over an algebraically closed field, all equations true on a zero set are exactly the power consequences of its defining ideal.
Conditions: k algebraically closed; I ideal in k[x₁,…,x_n]; V uses k-valued points.
Example: The zero set of x² is the origin, whose full vanishing ideal is (x).
Prerequisites: Radical of an ideal; Coordinate ring of an affine algebraic set

Name: Zariski topology
Intuition: Polynomial vanishing sets become the closed sets, making algebraic constraints into a topology.
Conditions: Affine n-space over a field; arbitrary intersections and finite unions of algebraic zero sets are closed.
Example: On the affine line over an algebraically closed field, proper closed subsets are finite.
Prerequisites: Affine algebraic zero set; Topology by open sets

Name: Affine morphisms and ring homomorphisms
Intuition: Mapping points forward pulls observable functions backward.
Conditions: Affine algebraic varieties over an algebraically closed field k; regular morphisms; reduced finitely generated coordinate algebras.
Example: The parabola parametrization t↦(t,t²) pulls x to t and y to t².
Prerequisites: Coordinate ring of an affine algebraic set; Group homomorphism

Name: Prime spectrum of a ring
LaTeX: \operatorname{Spec}R=\{\mathfrak p\subset R:\mathfrak p\text{ prime}\},\qquad V(I)=\{\mathfrak p:I\subseteq\mathfrak p\}
Intuition: Treat every prime ideal as a point, including points that encode an entire irreducible region.
Conditions: Commutative ring with identity; displayed V(I) are its closed sets; the zero ring has empty spectrum.
Example: Spec Z contains (0) and one closed point (p) for each rational prime.
Prerequisites: Prime ideal quotient criterion; Quotient ring

Name: Localization as an open affine patch
Intuition: Making f invertible restricts geometry to the region where f does not vanish.
Conditions: Commutative ring R; localization at powers of f; canonical isomorphism of affine schemes.
Example: Spec k[x,x^(−1)] is the affine line with the origin removed.
Prerequisites: Localization of a commutative ring; Prime spectrum of a ring

Name: Local ring at a geometric point
Intuition: Near one point, denominators are allowed whenever they stay nonzero at that point.
Conditions: Affine variety X over an algebraically closed field; p a closed point; m_p its vanishing maximal ideal; elements are germs of regular functions.
Example: At zero on the affine line, 1/(1−x) belongs to the local ring, while 1/x does not.
Prerequisites: Localization of a commutative ring; Maximal ideals and fields

Name: Zariski tangent space
Intuition: Keep only first-order changes compatible with every defining equation.
Conditions: Affine variety X=V(I)⊆k^n over an algebraically closed field; p a k-point; f lists generators of I; tangent space over k.
Example: For y²=x³ at the origin, both derivatives vanish, so the tangent space has dimension two although the curve has dimension one.
Prerequisites: Jacobian matrix; Dual space and pullback of linear functionals

Name: Jacobian criterion for nonsingularity
Intuition: At a smooth point, the first-order approximation has exactly the dimension the space actually needs.
Conditions: Reduced affine variety over an algebraically closed field; p closed; equivalently rank J_f(p)=n−dim O_X,p. For smoothness over arbitrary fields additional field hypotheses matter.
Example: The parabola y−x² has Jacobian rank one everywhere; the cusp is singular at the origin.

Name: Krull dimension
Intuition: Dimension counts how deeply irreducible subspaces can nest.
Conditions: Commutative ring; dimension may be infinite; chains consist of prime ideals. For affine domains over a field, equals transcendence degree of the fraction field.
Example: dim k[x₁,…,x_n]=n; dim Z=1.
Prerequisites: Prime ideal quotient criterion; Tower law for field extensions

Name: Noether normalization
Intuition: An affine algebraic space admits a finite projection onto a plain affine space of the same dimension.
Conditions: Finitely generated nonzero integral k-algebra A; t_i∈A algebraically independent; d=trdeg_k Frac(A); finite means finitely generated as module.
Example: For k[x,y]/(y²−x³−1), the subring k[x] gives a finite module generated by 1,y.
Prerequisites: Polynomial division algorithm; Tower law for field extensions

Name: Hilbert polynomial of a projective scheme
Intuition: The number of independent homogeneous observables eventually follows a polynomial whose degree records geometric dimension.
Conditions: Nonempty projective scheme X=Proj A over a field, A a finitely generated standard graded algebra; d=dim X; degree depends on the chosen embedding.
Example: For P^n, P(m)=binom(m+n,n).
Prerequisites: Binomial coefficient; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Hilbert–Serre rationality
Intuition: Finite graded algebraic data forces an infinite dimension-counting series to be rational.
Conditions: M finitely generated nonnegatively graded module over k[x₁,…,x_n] with variables of degree one; finite-dimensional graded pieces; Q∈Z[t]. Cancellation may lower pole order.
Example: The polynomial ring itself has H(t)=1/(1−t)^n.
Prerequisites: Ordinary generating function; Finite geometric sum

Name: Projective space
Intuition: A point records a direction through the origin; multiplying every coordinate by the same nonzero scale changes nothing.
Conditions: Field k; λ∈k×; homogeneous coordinates cannot all be zero.
Example: The chart x₀≠0 becomes affine n-space by dividing all coordinates by x₀.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Equivalence relation; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Projective homogeneous zero sets
Intuition: Homogeneous equations remain meaningful when coordinates are only defined up to scale.
Conditions: Homogeneous ideal I in k[x₀,…,x_n]; evaluate homogeneous generators on any nonzero representative.
Example: The projective conic xz−y²=0 includes the affine parabola chart and its point at infinity.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Boundary and interior
Prerequisites: Projective space; Affine algebraic zero set

Name: Bézout theorem for plane curves
Intuition: Projective intersections conserve a total multiplicity, even when points merge or move to infinity.
Conditions: Plane projective curves over an algebraically closed field with no common irreducible component; intersection multiplicities counted.
Example: A line meets a nonsingular conic in two points counted with multiplicity; tangency counts twice.
Prerequisites: Projective homogeneous zero sets; Polynomial remainder and factor theorem

Name: Genus of a smooth plane curve
Intuition: The degree of a nonsingular projective plane equation determines the curve’s intrinsic genus.
Conditions: Smooth geometrically integral projective plane curve of degree d over an algebraically closed field. Singular curves require correction terms.
Example: Lines and smooth conics have genus zero; smooth cubics have genus one.
Prerequisites: Bézout theorem for plane curves; Euler characteristic

Name: Veronese embedding
Intuition: Promote degree-d monomials to linear coordinates, turning certain nonlinear equations into hyperplane sections.
Conditions: Integer d≥1; all degree-d monomials included exactly once; defined over any field.
Example: For P¹ and d=2, [s:t]↦[s²:st:t²], with image xz=y².

Name: Segre embedding
Intuition: A pair of directions becomes one rank-one tensor direction.
Conditions: Projective spaces over a field; image is cut out by all 2×2 minors of the coordinate matrix.
Example: P¹×P¹ embeds as the quadric z00z11−z01z10=0 in P³.
Prerequisites: Tensor product universal property; Projective space

Name: Plücker embedding of a Grassmannian
Intuition: A k-dimensional subspace is represented by its oriented volume coordinate, with overall scale forgotten.
Conditions: Finite-dimensional vector space V over a field; 1≤k≤dim V; v_i any basis of W. Image consists of decomposable nonzero exterior tensors modulo scale.
Example: Gr(2,4) satisfies p12p34−p13p24+p14p23=0 in P⁵.
Prerequisites: Wedge product and graded commutativity; Determinant

Name: Sheaf gluing axiom
Intuition: Compatible local descriptions assemble uniquely into one global description.
Conditions: Presheaf of sets F on a topological space; every open cover U=union U_i; with the restriction identities, this gluing condition defines a sheaf.
Example: Continuous real functions agreeing on overlaps glue to a continuous function on the union.
Prerequisites: Continuity by inverse images; Topology by open sets

Name: Scheme as a locally affine ringed space
Intuition: Glue affine ring-based spaces along open patches while preserving their local functions.
Conditions: Locally ringed space with an open cover by affine spectra and their structure sheaves; this is the definition of a scheme.
Example: Projective space is a scheme covered by n+1 affine n-space charts.
Prerequisites: Prime spectrum of a ring; Sheaf gluing axiom

Name: Fiber product of affine schemes
Intuition: Combining two geometric objects over a shared base combines their coordinate algebras by tensor product.
Conditions: Commutative R-algebras A,B; fiber product in the category of schemes. The tensor ring can have nilpotents even if both factors are reduced.
Example: Base-changing an affine scheme from R to a field k gives Spec(A⊗_R k).
Prerequisites: Tensor product universal property; Pullback or fiber product

Name: Divisors and degree on a curve
Intuition: Zeros and poles balance globally on a complete curve when counted with multiplicity.
Conditions: Smooth projective integral curve over an algebraically closed field; finite divisor sum; f nonzero rational function. Over a general field, degree uses residue-field weights.
Example: On P¹, the coordinate t has one simple zero and one simple pole.
Prerequisites: Polynomial remainder and factor theorem; p-adic absolute value and ultrametric

Name: Riemann–Roch for curves
Intuition: Allowing poles increases the number of independent functions predictably, with a correction from differentials and genus.
Conditions: Smooth projective integral curve over an algebraically closed field; D divisor; K canonical divisor; ℓ(D)=dim{f rational:div(f)+D≥0} including zero; genus g.
Example: On P¹, g=0 and ℓ(m∞)=m+1 for m≥0, the polynomial space of degree at most m.
Prerequisites: Divisors and degree on a curve; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Elliptic curve chord–tangent addition
Intuition: Join two points, find the third intersection with the cubic, then reflect it to define their sum.
Conditions: Nonsingular E:y²=x³+ax+b over a field of characteristic not 2 or 3; 4a³+27b²≠0; displayed formula assumes x₁≠x₂. For doubling use m=(3x₁²+a)/(2y₁) if y₁≠0; opposite points sum to the point at infinity O.
Example: On y²=x³−x, points (0,0),(1,0),(−1,0) each have order two.
Prerequisites: Group axioms; Bézout theorem for plane curves

Name: Hasse bound for elliptic curves
Intuition: A nonsingular cubic over a finite field has close to one point per field element, with square-root-scale fluctuation.
Conditions: Elliptic curve over finite field F_q; count includes the identity point at infinity; q a prime power.
Example: Over F₅, the curve y²=x³−x has eight points, within 6±2√5.
Prerequisites: Finite fields; Elliptic curve chord–tangent addition

Name: Frobenius polynomial of an elliptic curve
Intuition: Repeated Frobenius action satisfies a quadratic law whose trace records the point count.
Conditions: Elliptic curve over F_q; F the q-power Frobenius endomorphism; [m] multiplication by m; equality in End(E). On an ℓ-adic Tate module with ℓ not dividing q, characteristic polynomial is T²−tT+q.
Example: If #E(F_q)=q+1, Frobenius satisfies F²+[q]=0.

Name: Resultant detects common roots
Intuition: A determinant eliminates the root variable and reports whether two polynomial constraints can share a solution.
Conditions: Nonzero polynomials f,g over a field, positive degrees m,n; a_m leading coefficient of f; roots in algebraic closure counted with multiplicity; resultant is the Sylvester-matrix determinant.
Example: For f=x−a and g=x−b, the resultant is a−b.

Name: Buchberger criterion for a Gröbner basis
LaTeX: G\text{ is a Gröbner basis}\iff \operatorname{rem}_G S(g_i,g_j)=0\quad\forall i<j
Intuition: It is enough to resolve every pairwise clash between leading terms to make polynomial reduction globally reliable.
Conditions: Finite set G of nonzero polynomials over a field, generating ideal I; fixed monomial order; S-polynomials cancel least-common-multiple leading terms; reduction remainder means full multivariate division by G.
Example: For G={x−y,y²−1} with lexicographic x>y, the single S-polynomial reduces to zero.
Prerequisites: Polynomial division algorithm; Hilbert basis theorem

Name: Newton's second law
Intuition: A force tells a trajectory how its velocity bends in time. Giving position and velocity turns this second-order rule into an initial-value problem.
Conditions: A classical point particle of constant positive mass m, observed in an inertial frame; the prescribed force must support the desired existence and uniqueness of solutions.
Example: A constant force gives r(t)=r(0)+v(0)t+Ft²/(2m), component by component.

Name: Work–energy theorem
LaTeX: \Delta K=\int_{\gamma}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r,\qquad K=\tfrac12m\lVert\dot{\mathbf r}\rVert^2
Intuition: The part of force aligned with motion changes kinetic energy. Integrating that local energy transfer gives the total work along the actual path.
Conditions: Constant positive mass in Newtonian mechanics, a differentiable trajectory satisfying Newton's law, and an integrable force along it. Path independence requires additional conservative-force assumptions.
Example: A perpendicular magnetic force can curve a trajectory while doing no work and leaving its speed unchanged.

Name: Angular momentum and torque
LaTeX: \mathbf L=\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r},\qquad\dot{\mathbf L}=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F
Intuition: Rotational motion has its own balance equation. Only a force with a lever arm about the origin changes angular momentum about that origin.
Conditions: Classical point particle of constant mass and a fixed origin in an inertial frame. A central force parallel to r has zero torque and conserves L.
Example: Inverse-square gravity is radial about its source, so a planetary orbit stays in the plane perpendicular to its conserved angular momentum.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Newton's second law; Cross product in three dimensions

Name: Hamiltonian as a velocity Legendre transform
LaTeX: p_i=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i},\qquad H(q,p,t)=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L(q,\dot q,t)
Intuition: The same mechanics can be described using either velocities or their conjugate momenta. The subtraction changes which variables are independent while preserving the dynamics.
Conditions: A smooth regular Lagrangian with invertible velocity Hessian locally, so q̇ can be solved from p. Global identification with a convex conjugate additionally requires suitable convexity and domain conditions.
Example: For L=m q̇²/2−V(q), p=mq̇ and H=p²/(2m)+V(q).

Name: Canonical Poisson bracket
LaTeX: \{f,g\}=\sum_i\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q_i}\right)
Intuition: Two observables interact through paired position and momentum directions. The bracket measures how one observable changes along the motion generated by the other.
Conditions: Smooth real observables on a canonical phase-space chart with the standard symplectic structure. The displayed signs use the convention {q_i,p_j}=δ_ij.
Example: For H=p²/(2m)+V(q), {q,H}=p/m and {p,H}=−V′(q).

Name: Evolution of a classical observable
Intuition: An observable changes because its measuring rule changes explicitly with time and because the state moves through phase space. The Poisson bracket accounts for the second contribution.
Conditions: Differentiable f(q,p,t), smooth Hamiltonian H, and a trajectory satisfying canonical Hamilton equations. If f has no explicit time dependence and {f,H}=0, it is conserved.
Example: Choosing f=H gives dH/dt=∂H/∂t, so an autonomous Hamiltonian conserves its own energy.

Name: Canonical transformation criterion
Intuition: A canonical change of coordinates preserves the position–momentum pairing. It can simplify a Hamiltonian without changing the geometric form of its motion equations.
Conditions: A differentiable local diffeomorphism Φ on even-dimensional canonical phase space. The equation preserves the standard symplectic bilinear form; volume preservation alone is weaker in dimension greater than two.
Example: The rescaling Q=a q, P=p/a is canonical for any nonzero real a.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Change of basis and similarity; Hamilton's equations

Name: Liouville's phase-volume theorem
Intuition: A cloud of Hamiltonian initial states can stretch and fold, but its phase-space volume stays fixed. The conservation concerns the whole cloud, even if individual trajectories separate.
Conditions: A C² Hamiltonian in canonical coordinates, a smooth flow Φ_t defined on the region considered, and no dissipative terms. Volume here is dq₁…dq_n dp₁…dp_n.
Example: A harmonic oscillator rotates phase-space ellipses without shrinking their enclosed area.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Boundary and interior

Name: Hamilton–Jacobi equation
Intuition: An action field labels a family of classical trajectories. Its spatial slope supplies momentum, turning trajectory mechanics into a first-order partial differential equation.
Conditions: A smooth Hamiltonian and a differentiable classical action solution S on a region without the singularities being crossed. Nonsmooth viscosity solutions require a separate framework.
Example: For a free particle, S(q,t)=p·q−|p|²t/(2m) solves the equation with constant momentum p.

Name: Action–angle variables
Intuition: An integrable system becomes uniform motion around circles after the right coordinates are chosen. Actions label invariant tori, while angles describe position on each torus.
Conditions: Near a compact connected regular invariant torus of a Liouville-integrable Hamiltonian system with n independent commuting integrals. Angles are periodic modulo 2π; singular fibers are excluded.
Example: For a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, I=E/ω and its angle advances at angular rate ω.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Hamilton's equations; Line integrals of scalar and vector fields

Name: Virial theorem for a bounded mechanical system
Intuition: A bounded system cannot keep increasing its position–momentum correlation forever. Averaging its derivative balances kinetic energy with the way potential energy scales in position.
Conditions: Newtonian particles in a differentiable time-independent potential. The long-time averages exist and G(T)/T→0 for G=Σ r_i·p_i. For homogeneous degree-k V this yields 2⟨K⟩=k⟨V⟩.
Example: A bound inverse-distance potential has degree −1, so 2⟨K⟩=−⟨V⟩.
Prerequisites: Newton's second law; Average value of a function

Name: Inertia tensor
Intuition: The distribution of mass determines the cost of rotating in each direction. A symmetric matrix packages all directional moments of inertia into one quadratic energy.
Conditions: A rigid mass distribution with finite second moments about a fixed reference point. The displayed kinetic energy is the rotational contribution about that point; translation may contribute separately.
Example: For rotation about a unit axis n, the moment of inertia is nᵀIn.

Name: Euler's rigid-body equations
Intuition: In axes attached to the body, angular momentum changes partly because the axes themselves rotate. The cross product corrects the time derivative for that moving frame.
Conditions: A rigid body with constant inertia tensor in its body frame, angular velocity ω, and applied torque about a fixed point or the center of mass with the corresponding balance assumptions.
Example: In principal axes without torque, I₁ω̇₁=(I₂−I₃)ω₂ω₃, with cyclic companion equations.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Inertia tensor; Angular momentum and torque

Name: Maxwell's equations in vacuum with sources
LaTeX:
abla\cdot E=ho/\varepsilon_0,\quad
abla\cdot B=0,\quad
abla	imes E=-\partial_t B,\quad
abla	imes B=\mu_0j+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\partial_t E
Intuition: Charges produce electric flux, magnetic flux has no local sources, and changing fields generate circulating fields. Together these local rules permit self-propagating electromagnetic waves.
Conditions: Classical electromagnetic fields in SI units in vacuum with charge density ρ and current density j. Smooth fields are assumed in the displayed differential form; singular sources require distributions or integral forms.
Example: Taking divergence of the last equation and using the first gives ∂tρ+∇·j=0.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Conservation and balance

Name: Lorentz force
LaTeX: \mathbf F=q(E+\mathbf v\times B),\qquad \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=qE\cdot\mathbf v
Intuition: Electric fields can speed up a charge; magnetic fields deflect its motion perpendicular to velocity. The work relation reveals the difference immediately.
Conditions: Classical point charge q moving at velocity v in prescribed electromagnetic fields, in SI units. Radiation reaction and self-force are excluded from this test-particle law.
Example: With a uniform magnetic field and no electric field, nonrelativistic motion perpendicular to B is circular at constant speed.
Prerequisites: Cross product in three dimensions; Newton's second law

Name: Electromagnetic scalar and vector potentials
Intuition: Potentials represent fields using functions whose derivatives automatically satisfy the source-free magnetic and induction equations. Multiple potential choices can encode the same measurable fields.
Conditions: Sufficiently smooth potentials on a spacetime region. Recovering potentials globally from fields can have topological obstructions; locally the homogeneous Maxwell equations provide the needed compatibility.
Example: In electrostatics with a time-independent vector potential, E=−∇φ.

Name: Electromagnetic gauge transformation
Intuition: Changing potentials by a coordinated derivative adjustment leaves the fields unchanged. The mathematical description contains a redundancy that can be chosen for convenience.
Conditions: A sufficiently smooth scalar χ and commuting derivatives in a common spacetime chart. The relation compares classical potentials for identical local electromagnetic fields; global gauge structure may be richer.
Example: Adding a spatially constant scalar to an electrostatic potential changes no electric field.
Prerequisites: Electromagnetic scalar and vector potentials; Equivalence relation

Name: Poynting's energy theorem
Intuition: Field energy can stay in a region, flow across its boundary, or be transferred to charged matter. The equation is a local energy ledger with all three entries visible.
Conditions: Classical Maxwell fields in vacuum with sources, SI units, and enough regularity for the differential identity. Material media require the appropriate constitutive and energy accounting assumptions.
Example: In source-free space, integrating over a volume says its field energy decreases by the outgoing Poynting flux.
Prerequisites: Maxwell's equations in vacuum with sources; Divergence theorem

Name: Lorentz boost along one axis
Intuition: Observers in uniform relative motion mix space and time coordinates while preserving a spacetime quadratic form. A boost acts like a hyperbolic rotation rather than a Euclidean one.
Conditions: Inertial frames in flat spacetime with relative velocity v along x, |v|<c, aligned transverse axes and coincident origins at t=t′=0. Transverse coordinates y,z are unchanged.
Example: Writing β=tanh η gives γ=cosh η and γβ=sinh η, so collinear rapidities add.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Minkowski spacetime interval
Intuition: Different observers disagree about elapsed coordinate time and distance, but agree on their particular signed combination. Along a timelike path it measures the proper time recorded by an ideal clock.
Conditions: Flat spacetime with the +−−− convention. The proper-time formula applies to timelike displacements; the interval is indefinite and is not a positive distance norm on all four-vectors.
Example: A lightlike displacement satisfies ds²=0 even when the time and spatial displacement are nonzero.
Patterns: Geometry and distance; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Quadratic form; Lorentz boost along one axis

Name: Relativistic energy–momentum relation
Intuition: Energy and momentum are components of one spacetime object. Their invariant quadratic combination determines rest mass across inertial frames.
Conditions: An on-shell isolated particle in special relativity, invariant rest mass m≥0, and the positive-energy branch for ordinary particles. Momentum is relativistic three-momentum.
Example: At rest E=mc²; for a massless particle E=c|p|. For small |p|/(mc), E=mc²+|p|²/(2m)+higher terms.
Prerequisites: Minkowski spacetime interval; Taylor series of an analytic function

Name: Time-dependent Schrödinger equation
Intuition: The Hamiltonian generates motion of a complex amplitude. Its spatial differential terms spread the amplitude while the potential changes the local phase evolution.
Conditions: A nonrelativistic spinless particle, mass m>0, real scalar potential, and a self-adjoint realization of H with suitable boundary conditions. The differential equation is interpreted on its operator domain or in an appropriate weak sense.
Example: An energy eigenstate φ evolves as ψ(t)=exp(−iEt/ħ)φ; its position probability density stays fixed.

Name: Unitary evolution generated by a Hamiltonian
Intuition: A closed quantum system rotates amplitudes while preserving their inner products. The same generator governs short steps and arbitrarily long evolution.
Conditions: A finite-dimensional time-independent Hermitian matrix H. For time-dependent noncommuting H(t), the simple exponential of an integral must be replaced by a time-ordered evolution.
Example: If H=diag(E₁,E₂), each coordinate gains a phase exp(−itE_j/ħ) and its squared magnitude is unchanged.
Prerequisites: Matrix exponential; Adjoint of a linear map

Name: Stationary Schrödinger eigenvalue problem
Intuition: A stationary energy state changes only by an overall phase. Solving the spatial eigenvalue problem identifies these simple building blocks of time evolution.
Conditions: Time-independent self-adjoint Hamiltonian and a normalizable eigenvector φ in its domain. Continuous spectrum may require generalized eigenfunctions and cannot always be represented by a discrete eigenbasis.
Example: In a one-dimensional box of length L with Dirichlet walls, E_n=ħ²π²n²/(2mL²) for n≥1.
Prerequisites: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Time-dependent Schrödinger equation

Name: Born rule for a projective measurement
Intuition: Measurement probabilities are squared lengths of orthogonal components. Different outcomes partition the total probability through a resolution of the identity.
Conditions: Normalized pure state ψ in a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and mutually orthogonal projections P_a summing to the identity. This is the projective-measurement case; general POVMs use positive effects.
Example: For ψ=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2, measurement in that orthonormal basis gives each result with probability one half.

Name: Expectation of a quantum observable
Intuition: The expected measurement result is an ordinary weighted average once the observable's outcomes and their Born probabilities are identified. Operator notation packages that average independently of basis.
Conditions: A normalized state ψ and Hermitian matrix A with spectral decomposition A=Σa aP_a in finite dimensions. The infinite-dimensional formula additionally needs the relevant domain and integrability conditions.
Example: For A=diag(−1,1) and equal outcome probabilities, the expectation is zero even though zero is not a possible measurement result.
Prerequisites: Born rule for a projective measurement; Expectation

Name: Robertson uncertainty inequality
Intuition: The spreads of two observables cannot both be arbitrarily small when their commutator has a nonzero expectation in the state. The obstruction comes from incompatible operator directions.
Conditions: Hermitian matrices A,B and a normalized state ψ; ΔA²=⟨(A−⟨A⟩I)²⟩. For unbounded observables, require the state in suitable common product domains and finite variances.
Example: For Pauli X,Y in a Z-up state, ΔX=ΔY=1 and |⟨[X,Y]⟩|/2=1, so equality holds.
Prerequisites: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality; Expectation of a quantum observable; Matrix commutator and Lie bracket

Name: Heisenberg equation of motion
Intuition: The time dependence can be assigned to observables instead of states. Their commutator with the Hamiltonian plays the same organizing role as the classical Poisson bracket.
Conditions: A differentiable observable family and unitary Schrödinger evolution in finite dimensions. A_H=U†AU and H_H=U†HU. Unbounded operator versions require domain control.
Example: If A has no explicit time dependence and commutes with a fixed H, then A_H is constant.
Patterns: Change of coordinates; Conservation and balance
Prerequisites: Unitary evolution generated by a Hamiltonian; Matrix commutator and Lie bracket

Name: Ehrenfest equations for position and momentum
Intuition: Quantum averages obey balance laws resembling classical motion. The force is averaged over the state, so nonlinear forces generally do not equal the force evaluated at the average position.
Conditions: A nonrelativistic Hamiltonian p²/(2m)+V(q), a sufficiently regular evolving state with finite relevant moments, and boundary/domain conditions allowing the operator identities and integrations by parts.
Example: For a quadratic potential, ∇V is affine, so the mean position follows the corresponding classical oscillator equation exactly.
Prerequisites: Heisenberg equation of motion; Linearity of expectation

Name: Schrödinger probability current
Intuition: Probability moves locally instead of appearing or disappearing. A wavefunction's phase gradient carries its density through space.
Conditions: A sufficiently smooth solution of the scalar Schrödinger equation with real potential and no vector potential. Conserving total probability also requires decay or boundary conditions eliminating net boundary loss.
Example: For a plane wave C exp(ik·x−iωt), j=(ħk/m)|C|². Such a wave is a generalized state on all of space, not a normalizable wavepacket.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Boundary and interior

Name: Density matrix of a quantum state
Intuition: A density matrix collects the predictions of a statistical mixture of pure states. Different mixtures can give the same matrix, so the matrix captures observable information rather than a unique preparation story.
Conditions: A finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, normalized vectors ψ_k and nonnegative weights p_k summing to one. Every positive-semidefinite trace-one matrix admits such a representation.
Example: The qubit state I/2 is the equal mixture of either the two Z-basis states or the two X-basis states.
Prerequisites: Spectral theorem in finite dimensions; Convex barycentric combination

Name: Trace formula for mixed-state expectation
Intuition: One trace simultaneously averages over both preparation uncertainty and measurement outcomes. It is linear in the state and in the observable.
Conditions: A finite-dimensional density matrix ρ and Hermitian observable A. The result is real; for a POVM effect E_a, tr(ρE_a) is the outcome probability.
Example: For the maximally mixed state I/d, every observable has expectation tr(A)/d, the arithmetic mean of its eigenvalues.
Prerequisites: Density matrix of a quantum state; Trace

Name: Reduced state by partial trace
Intuition: Discarding one subsystem means retaining exactly the predictions for all measurements on the other. Partial trace removes the inaccessible subsystem without choosing a particular measurement outcome.
Conditions: Finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space A⊗B and a joint density matrix. The equality for every operator X uniquely specifies ρ_A.
Example: Either subsystem of the Bell state (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 has reduced state I/2, even though the joint state is pure.
Prerequisites: Density matrix of a quantum state; Tensor product universal property; Trace

Name: Purity of a density matrix
Intuition: Purity measures how concentrated the state's eigenvalue weights are. It is highest for a single pure component and lowest when every spectral direction has equal weight.
Conditions: A density matrix on a d-dimensional Hilbert space. Equality at one holds exactly for rank-one states; equality at 1/d holds exactly for I/d.
Example: For a qubit diagonal state diag(p,1−p), purity is p²+(1−p)².
Prerequisites: Density matrix of a quantum state; Trace

Name: Bloch-ball representation of a qubit
Intuition: A qubit state becomes a point inside a three-dimensional ball. Its direction records spin bias and its radius records purity.
Conditions: A two-dimensional complex quantum state and the standard Pauli matrices. The eigenvalues are (1±|r|)/2; pure states lie on the unit sphere, while the center is maximally mixed.
Example: The Z-up projector has r=(0,0,1); I/2 has r=0.
Prerequisites: Density matrix of a quantum state; Basis and unique coordinates

Name: Von Neumann entropy
Intuition: Quantum entropy is the Shannon entropy of the state's eigenvalue weights. It describes uncertainty in the state itself, which differs from uncertainty for a particular measurement basis.
Conditions: Finite-dimensional density matrix, natural logarithms, and 0 log 0=0 by continuity. Pure states have zero entropy, even though some of their measurements remain random.
Example: S(I/d)=log d, while a rank-one projector has S=0.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Change of coordinates
Prerequisites: Density matrix of a quantum state; Shannon entropy

Name: Schmidt decomposition of a bipartite pure state
Intuition: A joint pure state can be expressed using matched orthogonal pairs. The number and weights of these paired terms reveal whether its components can be separated.
Conditions: A normalized vector in a finite-dimensional bipartite tensor product. The u_j and v_j form orthonormal lists. A state is a product state exactly when its Schmidt rank is one.
Example: The Bell state has two Schmidt coefficients 1/√2, so each reduced density matrix has eigenvalues 1/2,1/2.
Prerequisites: Singular value decomposition; Tensor product universal property

Name: Kraus representation of a quantum channel
Intuition: A quantum channel describes a physical transformation when some environmental information is ignored. Its matrix pieces account for alternative environmental records while preserving total probability.
Conditions: A finite-dimensional linear map is a completely positive trace-preserving channel exactly when it admits this representation. The individual terms are not necessarily unitary, and a Kraus representation is not unique.
Example: Dephasing in an orthonormal basis uses the basis projectors as Kraus operators, deleting coherence between different basis states.
Prerequisites: Density matrix of a quantum state; Adjoint of a linear map; Matrix multiplication

Name: Trace distance and optimal state discrimination
Intuition: The distance between two quantum states measures how well one optimal measurement can tell them apart. Identical states force guessing, while orthogonal states can be distinguished perfectly.
Conditions: Two finite-dimensional density matrices presented with equal prior probabilities, one copy available, and arbitrary two-outcome measurements. The trace norm is the sum of singular values.
Example: For orthogonal pure states D=1 and success probability is one; for identical states D=0 and success is one half.
Prerequisites: Singular value decomposition; Density matrix of a quantum state

Name: Harmonic-oscillator ladder operators
Intuition: Raising and lowering operators organize oscillator states into an algebraic ladder. The commutator fixes the spacing and the square-root coefficients that preserve normalization.
Conditions: The one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator, ω>0, with operators on the standard common invariant domain of finite oscillator-state combinations. The commutator cannot hold for finite square matrices.
Example: The normalized ground state obeys a|0⟩=0; applying a† creates successive excited states.
Prerequisites: Matrix commutator and Lie bracket; Stationary Schrödinger eigenvalue problem

Name: Quantum harmonic-oscillator spectrum
Intuition: A quadratic potential produces equally spaced energy levels, with a positive ground-state energy. The state cannot have both perfectly fixed position and perfectly fixed momentum.
Conditions: A one-dimensional nonrelativistic oscillator H=p²/(2m)+mω²q²/2 with m,ω>0 and the standard self-adjoint realization on L² of the real line.
Example: Adjacent levels differ by ħω, while the ground state has energy ħω/2.

Name: Quantum angular-momentum ladder
Intuition: At fixed total angular momentum, a finite ladder shifts the component along a chosen axis. The coefficient vanishes at the top or bottom, closing the representation.
Conditions: An irreducible unitary angular-momentum representation with j a nonnegative integer or half-integer, m=−j,…,j, J±=Jx±iJy, and normalized simultaneous eigenvectors of J² and Jz.
Example: For j=1/2, raising the lower m=−1/2 state produces ħ times the upper state; raising again gives zero.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Recursion and iteration
Prerequisites: Matrix commutator and Lie bracket; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

Name: Canonical thermal partition function
Intuition: The partition function adds the statistical weights of all energy states. Once this single generating object is known, differentiating it extracts many equilibrium quantities.
Conditions: A quantum canonical ensemble at T>0 with a fixed Hamiltonian whose exponential is trace class; eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity. The finite-state case is immediate; classical phase-space ensembles require their own measure normalization.
Example: For two energy levels 0 and ε, Z=1+exp(−βε). Independent subsystems have a product partition function when their Hamiltonian energies add.

Name: Energy and energy variance from log partition function
Intuition: The slope of log Z gives mean energy, and its curvature gives energy fluctuations. One function therefore records both the typical value and the spread around it.
Conditions: A canonical ensemble with a β-independent energy spectrum, finite relevant moments and differentiation justified under the sum or trace. β is inverse energy, equal to 1/(kBT).
Example: For levels 0,ε with excited probability p, mean energy is εp and variance is ε²p(1−p).
Prerequisites: Canonical thermal partition function; Cumulant generating function

Name: Canonical heat capacity–fluctuation identity
Intuition: How strongly energy responds to temperature is controlled by how much energy already fluctuates at equilibrium. Response and noise are two views of the same partition-function curvature.
Conditions: A canonical ensemble at T>0 with fixed volume and particle number, temperature-independent microscopic energies, finite variance and justified differentiation. Other ensembles or temperature-dependent effective Hamiltonians need separate accounting.
Example: A two-level system has C_V=ε²p(1−p)/(kBT²).
Prerequisites: Energy and energy variance from log partition function; Chain rule

Name: Canonical response as a covariance
Intuition: A small field favors states with large B. Another quantity A changes according to how strongly it co-varies with B in the unperturbed weighting.
Conditions: A finite classical state space, h-independent observables A,B, fixed β, and probabilities proportional to exp[−β(H₀−hB)]. The simple covariance formula is not the general noncommuting quantum response formula.
Example: Setting A=B makes the susceptibility β Var(B), which is nonnegative.

Name: Helmholtz free energy from the partition function
Intuition: Free energy balances expected energy against the number of thermally available possibilities. Taking a logarithm converts independent partition-function factors into additive thermodynamic contributions.
Conditions: Canonical equilibrium at positive temperature with fixed volume and particle number; U is mean energy and S is the Gibbs thermodynamic entropy. The same microscopic normalization must be used in Z and S.
Example: For two noninteracting subsystems, Z_AB=Z_AZ_B and F_AB=F_A+F_B.
Prerequisites: Canonical thermal partition function; Shannon entropy

Name: Boltzmann entropy of a microcanonical shell
Intuition: A macrostate can be realized by many microscopic configurations. Entropy measures the logarithmic size of that collection, making independent multiplicities additive.
Conditions: A specified microcanonical shell with Ω equiprobable discrete microstates. Continuous phase-space versions need a prescribed cell size or reference measure; the shell convention matters.
Example: N independent two-state spins with no energy preference have Ω=2^N and S=NkB log 2.
Prerequisites: Maximum entropy on a finite alphabet; Permutations and falling factorials

Name: Fundamental thermodynamic differential
Intuition: Temperature, pressure and chemical potential are slopes of internal energy with respect to entropy, volume and particle number. The differential identifies which quantities are thermodynamically conjugate.
Conditions: A differentiable equilibrium internal energy U(S,V,N) for a simple compressible single-component system, with the convention that p dV is work done by the system. Additional work modes require extra terms.
Example: Holding V,N fixed gives T=(∂U/∂S)_{V,N}; holding S,N fixed gives p=−(∂U/∂V)_{S,N}.

Name: A Maxwell relation from Helmholtz free energy
Intuition: Two seemingly different responses agree because they are mixed derivatives of one state function. Thermodynamics inherits an exact symmetry from multivariable calculus.
Conditions: A simple equilibrium system at fixed particle number with C² Helmholtz free energy F(T,V) in a single smooth phase. Derivatives at singular phase boundaries require separate treatment.
Example: For an ideal gas p=NkBT/V, the relation gives (∂S/∂V)_T=NkB/V.
Prerequisites: Fundamental thermodynamic differential; Helmholtz free energy from the partition function

Name: Clapeyron coexistence slope
Intuition: A phase boundary tilts because the phases differ in both entropy and volume. The slope balances those differences while their chemical potentials remain equal.
Conditions: Two equilibrium phases of one substance along a differentiable first-order coexistence curve, with specific or molar entropy s and volume v using consistent normalization and Δv≠0. The latent heat is ℓ=TΔs.
Example: If the higher-entropy phase also has larger volume, the coexistence pressure increases with temperature.

Name: Classical equipartition for a quadratic mode
Intuition: Every independent unconstrained quadratic degree of freedom contributes the same average energy at classical equilibrium. The stiffness changes its fluctuation size rather than this mean energy contribution.
Conditions: A classical canonical ensemble at T>0, a>0, x ranging over the real line, and the indicated separable quadratic contribution with convergent integrals. Quantum freezing, constraints and nonquadratic modes need other formulas.
Example: Each Cartesian velocity component contributes kBT/2 to a classical ideal gas particle's mean kinetic energy.

Name: Maxwell equilibrium velocity density
Intuition: Thermal equilibrium gives a Gaussian distribution of velocity vectors. Directional symmetry and quadratic kinetic energy make the three Cartesian components independent with equal variance.
Conditions: A nonrelativistic classical ideal gas in equilibrium at T>0, in its rest frame, with particle mass m>0. This is the vector density with respect to d³v, not the speed density, which has an additional 4πv² factor.
Example: Each component has variance kBT/m and the root-mean-square speed is √(3kBT/m).
Patterns: Randomness and distribution; Symmetry and invariance
Prerequisites: Multivariate normal density; Classical equipartition for a quadratic mode

Name: Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac occupations
Intuition: The allowed occupancy of a quantum mode changes its average population. Bosons permit any nonnegative integer count, while a single fermionic mode permits only zero or one particle.
Conditions: Noninteracting indistinguishable particles in grand-canonical equilibrium, β=1/(kBT)>0. Bosonic mode sums require μ<ε for the displayed finite mean; condensate limits must be treated separately. Mode degeneracies are counted explicitly.
Example: For ε−μ≫kBT, both occupations approach exp[−β(ε−μ)], the dilute classical limit.

Name: Planck blackbody spectral energy density
Intuition: Blackbody radiation combines how many photon modes are available at a frequency with how much thermal energy each mode carries. The quantum occupation factor suppresses high-frequency energy.
Conditions: Electromagnetic radiation in thermal equilibrium in a large three-dimensional vacuum cavity at T>0, both polarizations included, frequency ν in cycles per second. u_ν is energy per volume per unit frequency.
Example: For hν≪kBT, the formula approaches the Rayleigh–Jeans density 8πkBTν²/c³.
Prerequisites: Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac occupations; Density under a change of variables

Name: Ising spin Hamiltonian
Intuition: A simple binary variable at each site interacts with its neighbors. Local preferences can collectively produce large-scale order, making this model a bridge between discrete structure and statistical physics.
Conditions: A specified finite graph or lattice with each interacting pair counted once. J>0 favors alignment; h is a uniform field in energy units. Infinite-volume phase transitions require a thermodynamic limit and boundary conventions.
Example: With two sites, h=0 and J>0, aligned states have energy −J and anti-aligned states energy +J.
Prerequisites: Adjacency powers count walks; Gibbs distribution

Name: Ising mean-field self-consistency
Intuition: Replace each neighbor by its average spin and require the predicted average to agree with the one used in that replacement. Collective order becomes a nonlinear fixed-point equation.
Conditions: Uniform ferromagnetic Ising model with coordination number z, β=1/(kBT), and the single-site mean-field approximation. This is not exact for a general finite-dimensional lattice; fluctuations and correlations are neglected.
Example: At h=0 the zero-magnetization solution loses mean-field stability when βJz passes one, producing two symmetry-related nonzero branches.
Prerequisites: Ising spin Hamiltonian; Weighted arithmetic mean

Name: Landau quartic free-energy model
Intuition: A symmetric energy landscape changes shape as its quadratic coefficient crosses zero. One central minimum can split into two equivalent minima, providing a local model of spontaneous order.
Conditions: An analytic phenomenological expansion in a small scalar order parameter with m↦−m symmetry at h=0, stabilized by b>0. Truncation and mean-field treatment are modeling assumptions, especially near fluctuation-dominated critical points.
Example: At h=0, the minimizing m is zero when a≥0 and m=±√(−a/b) when a<0.
Prerequisites: First-order characterization of convexity; Hessian matrix

Name: Composition law for an autonomous flow
Intuition: Running a time-independent system for two consecutive intervals is the same as running it for their sum. A whole family of trajectories therefore behaves like an action of time on states.
Conditions: A uniquely solvable autonomous differential equation. The identities hold whenever the relevant solutions are defined; a complete flow defines an action for every real time, while a forward-only system gives a semigroup.
Example: For ẋ=ax, Φ_t(x)=e^{at}x and the flow law is the exponential addition rule.
Prerequisites: Composition of functions; Constant relative growth or decay

Name: Spectral criterion for linear asymptotic stability
Intuition: Each spectral direction expands or contracts exponentially, with Jordan blocks adding polynomial factors. Strictly negative real parts make all these contributions decay.
Conditions: A finite-dimensional constant real or complex matrix A and continuous-time evolution. Eigenvalues on the imaginary axis require a different test for mere stability and do not give asymptotic stability.
Example: Eigenvalues −1±2i describe decaying oscillation; an eigenvalue +0.1 produces an unstable direction.

Name: Strict Lyapunov criterion for asymptotic stability
Intuition: A positive scalar quantity that always decreases acts as a certificate of local convergence. It can prove stability without solving the trajectories explicitly.
Conditions: An equilibrium f(0)=0 of a locally Lipschitz autonomous vector field, and a C¹ positive-definite function V with strictly negative derivative on a neighborhood excluding the equilibrium. This gives local asymptotic stability; global claims need additional properness and global assumptions.
Example: For ẋ=−x³, V=x²/2 gives V̇=−x⁴, proving asymptotic stability even though the linearization is zero.

Name: Continuous Lyapunov matrix equation
Intuition: A stable linear system admits a quadratic energy that decreases at a prescribed positive rate. Integrating the future cost of a state constructs that energy matrix.
Conditions: A real Hurwitz matrix A and symmetric Q≻0. The integral converges and is the unique symmetric P≻0 solving the equation. Conversely existence of such P,Q implies A is Hurwitz.
Example: For A=−aI with a>0 and Q=I, P=I/(2a).
Prerequisites: Spectral criterion for linear asymptotic stability; Quadratic form

Name: LaSalle's invariance principle
Intuition: If a certificate only stops increasing, trajectories may settle into a whole invariant set rather than one point. The set where the decrease vanishes identifies the remaining possible long-term motion.
Conditions: A locally Lipschitz autonomous system on a compact positively invariant set K, with C¹ V and V̇≤0 on K. M is the largest invariant subset of {x∈K:V̇(x)=0}; the conclusion holds for starting points in K.
Example: For a damped oscillator, mechanical energy has derivative −c v². The only invariant motion with v=0 throughout is an equilibrium under the usual restoring-force assumptions.
Patterns: Conservation and balance; Limits and convergence
Prerequisites: Strict Lyapunov criterion for asymptotic stability; Underdamped harmonic oscillator

Name: Hartman–Grobman local linearization
Intuition: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium, a nonlinear flow has the same local topological orbit structure as its linear part. A continuous change of coordinates can reveal that similarity even when no smooth one exists.
Conditions: A C¹ autonomous vector field near equilibrium x_*, with no Jacobian eigenvalue on the imaginary axis. The conjugacy is local and homeomorphic; the equation applies while the compared trajectories remain in the relevant neighborhoods.
Example: A nonlinear planar saddle remains locally a saddle when its Jacobian has one negative and one positive real eigenvalue.
Prerequisites: Jacobian matrix; Homeomorphism; Spectral criterion for linear asymptotic stability

Name: Floquet decomposition for periodic linear systems
Intuition: A periodic linear system separates into a repeated within-cycle motion and a steady exponential trend. Its stability can be read from what happens after one full period.
Conditions: Continuous T-periodic matrix A, T>0, and an invertible fundamental matrix X. A complex matrix logarithm gives the stated T-periodic factorization; a real factorization may require period 2T. Stability is determined by the monodromy eigenvalues with the appropriate Jordan conditions.
Example: For constant A, choose P=I and B=A. A multiplier of magnitude greater than one gives growth from cycle to cycle.
Prerequisites: Matrix exponential; Variation of parameters for a linear system

Name: Poincaré return map
Intuition: Observe a continuous trajectory only when it crosses a chosen section. A closed orbit then becomes a fixed point of a lower-dimensional discrete map.
Conditions: A smooth flow and a transverse local section near a periodic orbit, with a well-defined positive first-return time τ on the neighborhood considered. Tangencies or missing returns invalidate this local construction.
Example: For an attracting planar limit cycle, nearby intersections with a transverse segment move toward its fixed intersection point.
Prerequisites: Composition law for an autonomous flow; Implicit function theorem

Name: Derivative test for a one-dimensional map
Intuition: An iteration multiplies a small error by its local slope on each step. Slopes below one in magnitude shrink errors, while larger slopes amplify them.
Conditions: A C¹ real map near its fixed point. The unit-magnitude boundary is inconclusive by this test; higher-order terms or other arguments are needed there.
Example: For f(x)=cos x at its fixed point, the derivative has magnitude below one, so nearby repeated cosine iteration converges.

Name: Saddle–node bifurcation normal form
Intuition: Two equilibria meet and disappear as a parameter crosses a threshold. In this orientation the positive branch attracts and the negative branch repels.
Conditions: This scalar normal-form model has real parameter μ. It describes a generic local saddle–node after appropriate smooth reductions and nondegeneracy assumptions, not every possible equilibrium collision.
Example: At μ<0 there is no real equilibrium; at μ=0 one nonhyperbolic equilibrium remains; at μ>0 there are two.
Prerequisites: Quadratic formula; Spectral criterion for linear asymptotic stability

Name: Supercritical pitchfork normal form
Intuition: A symmetric central equilibrium gives way to two symmetric stable choices. The equation turns an unchanged symmetry of the rules into a choice of one asymmetric state.
Conditions: The scalar model with reflection symmetry x↦−x; nonzero real branches exist for μ>0. Generic pitchfork behavior requires a symmetry or another structural constraint and the relevant nondegeneracy conditions.
Example: For μ>0, zero is unstable and the two equilibria ±√μ are locally asymptotically stable.
Prerequisites: Saddle–node bifurcation normal form; Gradient descent

Name: Transcritical bifurcation normal form
Intuition: Two equilibrium branches cross and exchange stability instead of disappearing. The same local state can change from attracting to repelling as the other branch takes over.
Conditions: The scalar normal-form model with real x,μ. At μ=0 the branches coincide and linearization vanishes; the generic transcritical setting requires the structural conditions preserving the crossing branches.
Example: The zero branch attracts for μ<0, while the x=μ branch attracts for μ>0.
Prerequisites: Logistic growth; Spectral criterion for linear asymptotic stability

Name: Supercritical Hopf normal form
Intuition: An equilibrium begins to oscillate at a nonzero frequency as a stable cycle emerges around it. Polar coordinates separate amplitude selection from phase rotation.
Conditions: z is complex, μ real, and ω≠0. This is a supercritical Hopf normal-form model; applying Hopf theory to another system needs a simple conjugate eigenvalue crossing, transversality and a nonzero first Lyapunov coefficient.
Example: For μ>0 the attracting cycle has radius √μ and period 2π/|ω|; for μ<0 the origin attracts.
Prerequisites: Euler's formula; Integration in polar coordinates

Name: Logistic map
Intuition: Repeated growth followed by crowding can produce equilibria, cycles and chaotic behavior depending on one parameter. A simple quadratic update need not have simple long-term motion.
Conditions: The displayed parameter and state ranges keep the unit interval invariant. Discrete time is part of the model; it is not the exact time-one map of the logistic differential equation.
Example: The nonzero fixed point 1−1/r exists for r>1 and attracts for 1<r<3.
Prerequisites: Derivative test for a one-dimensional map; Quadratic formula

Name: Lyapunov exponent along a one-dimensional orbit
Intuition: Small perturbations multiply along an orbit. Taking logarithms turns their average exponential growth rate into an ordinary time average.
Conditions: A C¹ one-dimensional map, orbit x_k=f^k(x₀), nonzero derivatives along it, and existence of the displayed limit. A positive exponent is a sensitivity indicator; by itself it does not supply every definition of chaos.
Example: For the doubling map away from its coordinate discontinuity, each derivative is two and the exponent is log 2.

Name: Van der Pol oscillator
Intuition: The damping changes sign with amplitude: small oscillations gain energy while large ones lose it. This feedback can select a persistent oscillation instead of rest.
Conditions: The standard dimensionless van der Pol model with μ>0. The scalar second-order equation is an autonomous planar system; statements about its limit cycle use the corresponding Liénard theory.
Example: For mechanical energy E=(ẋ²+x²)/2, Ė=μ(1−x²)ẋ², showing gain at small |x| and loss at large |x|.
Prerequisites: Underdamped harmonic oscillator; Poincaré return map

Name: Lotka–Volterra predator–prey equations
LaTeX: \dot x=x(\alpha-\beta y),\qquad\dot y=y(\delta x-\gamma),\qquad I=\delta x-\gamma\log x+\beta y-\alpha\log y
Intuition: Each population changes the other's growth rate, producing coupled feedback. In this idealized model a conserved quantity organizes closed trajectories in the positive quadrant.
Conditions: Positive parameters α,β,γ,δ and positive populations x,y. The invariant I belongs to the basic autonomous model; harvesting, saturation, noise or parameter changes generally destroy it.
Example: The coexistence equilibrium is x=γ/δ, y=α/β; differentiating I along the flow gives zero.
Prerequisites: Logarithmic derivative; Composition law for an autonomous flow

Name: Lorenz system
Intuition: Three coupled variables create feedback between growth, transfer and damping. For suitable parameters the system has irregular sensitive motion despite being deterministic.
Conditions: The classical dimensionless Lorenz ODE with positive σ,ρ,β. Chaotic conclusions depend on parameter choices and a precise invariant-set analysis; the polynomial equations alone do not prove chaos.
Example: Its divergence is −(σ+1+β), so phase-space volumes contract exponentially wherever the smooth flow is defined.

Name: Bendixson divergence criterion
Intuition: A closed trajectory cannot enclose a region whose flow expands or contracts area strictly everywhere. Boundary flux and interior divergence would contradict one another.
Conditions: A C¹ planar vector field on a simply connected open region D, with divergence strictly of one sign throughout D. The criterion as stated does not apply in three dimensions or to regions with holes.
Example: The linear sink ẋ=−x,ẏ=−y has divergence −2 and no periodic orbit.
Patterns: Boundary and interior; Geometry and distance
