Prerequisites: Green's theorem in the plane; Divergence

Name: Poincaré–Bendixson theorem without equilibria
LaTeX: \omega(x)\text{ compact, nonempty, with no equilibrium}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\omega(x)\text{ is a periodic orbit}
Intuition: A bounded planar flow has strong restrictions on its long-term motion. If its limit set avoids every equilibrium, that set must be a closed orbit.
Conditions: A C¹ autonomous vector field on an open subset of the plane, with a positive orbit contained in a compact subset of the domain. The stated conclusion assumes its omega-limit set contains no fixed point.
Example: A compact forward trapping annulus with no equilibria contains a periodic orbit under the planar hypotheses.
Patterns: Limits and convergence; Geometry and distance
Prerequisites: Poincaré return map; Limit of a sequence

Name: Invariant measure for a dynamical map
Intuition: Individual states move while the overall distribution stays the same. Invariance is the bridge from following trajectories to computing averages over a state space.
Conditions: A measurable transformation T of a probability space and measurable sets A. The integral identity holds for integrable f and characterizes measure preservation. T need not have a pointwise inverse.
Example: A rotation of the circle preserves uniform angular measure even though most individual points move.
Prerequisites: Integration against a pushforward measure; Probability axioms

Name: Koopman operator on observables
Intuition: Instead of moving points, move the functions used to observe them. This turns even nonlinear state evolution into a linear action on a typically infinite-dimensional space of observables.
Conditions: A measurable measure-preserving T on a probability space, acting on L² observables. U_T is an isometry; it is unitary when T is invertible modulo null sets. Finite coordinate observables usually do not form a closed invariant subspace.
Example: For uniform circle measure and T(x)=2x mod 1, the observable exp(2πikx) is sent to exp(2πi(2k)x), creating new frequencies.
Prerequisites: Linear map; Composition of functions; Invariant measure for a dynamical map

Name: Birkhoff pointwise ergodic theorem
Intuition: A long time average keeps the information that the dynamics never mixes away. If the only invariant information is trivial, that time average becomes the same space average for almost every starting state.
Conditions: A measure-preserving transformation of a probability space, f∈L¹, and invariant sigma-algebra I. If T is ergodic, the limit equals ∫f dμ almost everywhere. Exceptional starting points can exist.
Example: For an indicator observable, the average is the fraction of visits to a set; in an ergodic system its limit is that set's probability for almost every start.
Prerequisites: Arithmetic mean; Conditional expectation; Invariant measure for a dynamical map

Name: Von Neumann mean ergodic theorem
Intuition: Repeated averaging removes the changing parts of an observable and retains its invariant component. The limiting average is an orthogonal projection, giving a geometric meaning to long-term averaging.
Conditions: A unitary operator U on a Hilbert space and any vector f. The fixed subspace is closed and P is its orthogonal projection. This is norm convergence, not automatically pointwise convergence of a represented function.
Example: For a planar rotation with angle not a multiple of 2π, averaging successive rotated vectors converges to zero because the only fixed vector is zero.
Prerequisites: Orthogonal projection; Orthogonal decomposition and energy split; Koopman operator on observables

Name: Poincaré recurrence theorem
Intuition: In a finite measure-preserving system, almost every state in a region returns to that region infinitely often. The system cannot permanently send a positive fraction of finite volume into endlessly disjoint new regions.
Conditions: A measure-preserving transformation on a finite measure space and a measurable set A. The theorem gives almost-everywhere recurrence, not a uniform return time, an exact return to the same point, or convergence.
Example: A rotation of the circle repeatedly returns almost every point in an arc to that arc; the theorem itself does not estimate the waiting time.
Prerequisites: Invariant measure for a dynamical map; Probability axioms

Name: Topological conjugacy of discrete systems
LaTeX: h\circ f=g\circ h,\qquad h\text{ a homeomorphism}
Intuition: Two systems can display the same orbit structure in different coordinates. A conjugacy translates every iterate consistently rather than matching only a few trajectories.
Conditions: Continuous self-maps f:X→X and g:Y→Y of topological spaces, related by a homeomorphism h:X→Y. Smoothness, metric distances and derivative growth rates need not be preserved by a mere topological conjugacy.
Example: For f(x)=2x, g(y)=8y and h(x)=x³ on the real line, h(f(x))=g(h(x)).

Name: Doubling map on the circle
Intuition: Each step discards the first binary digit and shifts the remaining digits forward. One elementary operation connects expanding dynamics, symbolic sequences and information loss.
Conditions: The circle R/Z with uniform probability measure. Binary expansions need a convention at dyadic rationals, a null set. The map is measure preserving and two-to-one, not invertible.
Example: A point is fixed by T^n exactly when (2^n−1)x is an integer modulo one, giving 2^n−1 distinct fixed points.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Information and uncertainty
Prerequisites: Congruence modulo an integer; Composition of functions

Name: Arnold's cat map
Intuition: A square torus can stretch in one direction and contract in another while preserving total area. Wrapping the stretched image back onto the torus keeps the motion in a compact space.
Conditions: The map on R²/Z² defined by the indicated integer determinant-one matrix. It is an invertible hyperbolic toral automorphism preserving normalized area; the torus identification is essential.
Example: The eigenvalues multiply to one, with one above one and the other below one, giving reciprocal expansion and contraction.
Prerequisites: Determinant; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Quotient group

Name: Expected payoff of mixed strategies
Intuition: Random strategies average the payoffs of pure action pairs. The average is linear in either player's probabilities when the other player's strategy is fixed.
Conditions: A finite two-player normal-form game with payoff matrix A for player one, and independently randomized mixed strategies p,q on their probability simplices.
Example: For matching pennies with A=[[1,−1],[−1,1]], uniform p and q give expected payoff zero.

Name: Best-response correspondence
Intuition: A player chooses the most favorable strategy against the others' current choices. The answer can be a whole set when several actions tie.
Conditions: A finite normal-form game and independent mixed strategies. Payoff is affine in one's own strategy, so all best mixed responses are supported on payoff-maximizing pure actions.
Example: Against a fixed opponent mixture, if two pure actions tie for the highest payoff, every mixture between them is also a best response.
Prerequisites: Expected payoff of mixed strategies; Convex barycentric combination

Name: Nash equilibrium
LaTeX: u_i(\sigma_i^*,\sigma_{-i}^*)\ge u_i(\tau_i,\sigma_{-i}^*)\quad\text{for every player }i\text{ and deviation }\tau_i
Intuition: Every strategy is a best response to the others. No single player can improve by changing alone, although a coordinated change might help several players.
Conditions: A specified finite normal-form game, mixed strategies independently randomized, and expected utility comparison. Nash equilibrium is a mutual best-response condition, not a guarantee of fairness, efficiency or convergence of learning.
Example: Uniform randomization is a Nash equilibrium in matching pennies; neither player can gain by unilaterally biasing their coin against a uniform opponent.
Prerequisites: Best-response correspondence; Expected payoff of mixed strategies

Name: Existence of mixed Nash equilibrium
LaTeX: \text{Every finite normal-form game has some }\sigma^*\in\prod_i\Delta(A_i)\text{ that is a Nash equilibrium.}
Intuition: Allowing randomized strategies fills discrete action sets into compact convex simplices. A fixed-point argument then guarantees at least one mutually consistent strategy profile.
Conditions: Finitely many players, finite nonempty action sets, and real payoff values. The theorem concerns mixed equilibria; a pure equilibrium need not exist and the theorem gives no general efficient algorithm.
Example: Rock–paper–scissors has no pure equilibrium, but its symmetric uniform mixture is an equilibrium.

Name: Support indifference at a mixed equilibrium
Intuition: A player randomizes only among actions that are equally good against the opponents. An action receiving positive weight could otherwise be replaced by a better one.
Conditions: A mixed Nash equilibrium of a finite game. v_i is player i's equilibrium payoff. Equalities on the proposed support are necessary but must be accompanied by inequalities for excluded actions and valid probabilities.
Example: In a two-by-two game with both actions used, an opponent's mixing probability can be found by equating the two expected pure-action payoffs, then checking all inequalities.

Name: Correlated equilibrium inequalities
Intuition: A shared recommendation device can coordinate strategies. After learning their own recommendation, each player prefers to follow it rather than switch to another action.
Conditions: A probability distribution μ over joint actions of a finite game. The displayed unconditional inequalities encode incentive constraints for each recommendation, including those of zero probability without requiring division.
Example: A traffic-light recommendation can correlate which of two players proceeds, creating coordinated outcomes that independent randomization cannot encode in the same way.

Name: Coarse correlated equilibrium
Intuition: Before seeing any recommendation, no player wants to commit to one fixed alternative action. This is a weaker obedience requirement than checking deviations after each recommendation is revealed.
Conditions: A joint action distribution in a finite game; deviations are fixed actions selected before observing a recommendation. Random fixed deviations add no extra constraints by payoff linearity.
Example: Empirical joint play from players whose average external regret vanishes approaches the coarse-correlated equilibrium set in the finite-game setting.

Name: Additive epsilon Nash equilibrium
Intuition: An approximate equilibrium allows only small unilateral improvements. The tolerance quantifies how far the profile is from exact mutual optimality.
Conditions: A finite game, ε≥0 and additive payoff units explicitly fixed. Rescaling payoffs rescales ε, so comparisons normally use a common normalization such as payoffs in [0,1].
Example: An exact Nash equilibrium is the ε=0 case. If the best unilateral gain is 0.02 in normalized payoffs, the profile is a 0.02 equilibrium.

Name: Exact potential game
Intuition: Every player's unilateral improvement changes one shared scalar by exactly the same amount. Individual incentives can therefore be tracked through a common landscape even when payoffs differ.
Conditions: A finite normal-form utility game and a real function Φ satisfying the displayed identity for every unilateral action change. Cost games use the same identity with costs and descent. This is stronger than an ordinal potential.
Example: Any global maximizer of an exact utility potential is a pure Nash equilibrium; any strict better-response path terminates because Φ increases over a finite set.
Prerequisites: Nash equilibrium; Fundamental theorem for line integrals

Name: Rosenthal potential for congestion games
Intuition: For each resource, add the cost of the first user, then the second, and so on up to current usage. This accumulated quantity changes by exactly a switching player's change in cost.
Conditions: A finite unweighted congestion game, with each player selecting an allowed subset of resources and paying the sum of c_e(n_e) on used resources. The formula is an exact cost potential; weighted variants need separate conditions.
Example: If one additional player joins a resource currently used by k players, its potential contribution rises by c_e(k+1), exactly the joining player's new resource cost.

Name: Wardrop equilibrium in nonatomic routing
Intuition: All routes actually used by a population have minimal travel cost for that origin and destination. An infinitesimal traveler cannot improve by changing route alone.
Conditions: A nonatomic routing model with fixed demands and path costs determined by aggregate edge flows. The comparison is among paths for the same origin–destination pair; a single infinitesimal user does not alter aggregate costs.
Example: If two parallel roads both carry positive flow for one demand pair, their equilibrium travel times are equal.
Prerequisites: Nash equilibrium; Support indifference at a mixed equilibrium

Name: Beckmann potential for nonatomic routing
Intuition: Integrate each edge's travel cost over the amount of flow assigned to it. Minimizing the resulting potential balances route costs at a Wardrop equilibrium.
Conditions: A finite network with fixed nonatomic demands, feasible flow polytope F, and continuous nondecreasing separable edge costs. Potential minimizers are Wardrop equilibria. This potential differs from total travel cost Σf_ec_e(f_e).
Example: For c_e(z)=a_ez+b_e, the edge potential is a_ef_e²/2+b_ef_e.
Prerequisites: Riemann integral; Wardrop equilibrium in nonatomic routing; Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions

Name: Price of anarchy for cost games
Intuition: The ratio compares the worst allowed equilibrium with the best coordinated feasible outcome. It measures a possible inefficiency of decentralized incentives under a specified equilibrium concept.
Conditions: A nonnegative aggregate cost C, a chosen equilibrium set E and feasible set F, with a positive finite optimum denominator and a nonempty equilibrium set. Bounds depend on the game class and solution concept.
Example: A price of anarchy of 4/3 means that every equilibrium in the specified class costs at most one third more than the coordinated optimum.

Name: Smoothness bound on equilibrium cost
Intuition: Bound the total cost of everyone separately switching to their part of an optimal outcome. Combining that bound with equilibrium incentives yields an aggregate efficiency guarantee.
Conditions: A finite cost game with C=Σ_i c_i≥0, λ≥0, μ<1, and the displayed smoothness inequality for every relevant pair a,a*. The bound holds for pure, mixed, correlated and coarse correlated equilibria when costs and comparison are interpreted in expectation.
Example: A (λ,μ)=(1,1/4) smoothness proof gives an equilibrium cost factor at most 4/3.
Prerequisites: Price of anarchy for cost games; Coarse correlated equilibrium

Name: Second-price auction payment
LaTeX: i^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i b_i,\qquad p_{i^*}=\max_{j\ne i^*}b_j,\qquad p_j=0\ (j\ne i^*)
Intuition: The highest bidder wins but pays the strongest competing bid. The payment threshold is independent of the winner's own bid above that threshold, making truthful bidding weakly dominant in the standard model.
Conditions: One indivisible item, at least two bidders with nonnegative private values and bids, quasilinear utility, no participation costs or externalities, and a fixed tie-breaking rule. The stated incentive conclusion depends on these assumptions.
Example: With bids 10,7,4, the winning bidder pays 7. A bidder values the item relative to this threshold rather than setting their own winning price.

Name: Vickrey–Clarke–Groves externality payment
Intuition: Choose the outcome with the largest reported total value and charge each participant for the loss they impose on the others. This aligns the participant's utility comparison with the social value comparison.
Conditions: Finite feasible outcomes or attained optima, quasilinear utilities, independent private valuation reports and the standard pivot-payment setup. Truthfulness does not by itself guarantee budget balance or affordability.
Example: For one item, the winning bidder's externality on the others is the next-highest bid, recovering the second-price auction.
Prerequisites: Second-price auction payment; Linearity of expectation

Name: Myerson's single-parameter payment identity
Intuition: A monotone allocation rule determines its truthful payment schedule. The integral is the utility retained by the participant, leaving the remainder as payment.
Conditions: A single-parameter quasilinear environment, opponents' reports fixed, nondecreasing allocation x(v) on v≥0, and zero payment at type zero. For randomized mechanisms x and p are expected allocation and payment; the characterization is truthfulness in expectation.
Example: For threshold allocation x(v)=1 when v≥τ and zero otherwise, the winner pays τ.
Prerequisites: Fundamental theorem of calculus; Second-price auction payment

Name: Shapley value
Intuition: Average a participant's added value over every possible order in which a coalition could form. This credits contributions that depend on who was already present.
Conditions: A finite transferable-utility cooperative game v on all coalitions, with v(∅)=0 and n players. The interpretation assumes that the coalition worth function has been meaningfully specified.
Example: In a two-player game, each player's value is the average of their standalone contribution and their contribution when joining the other player.
Prerequisites: Weighted arithmetic mean; Permutations and falling factorials

Name: Core of a transferable-utility game
LaTeX: \mathcal C(v)=\left\{x:\sum_{i\in N}x_i=v(N),\quad\sum_{i\in S}x_i\ge v(S)\ \forall S\subseteq N\right\}
Intuition: An allocation belongs to the core when it distributes the grand coalition's worth and leaves no subgroup able to secure more on its own. Coalition stability imposes a family of linear inequalities.
Conditions: A finite transferable-utility game with v(∅)=0. The core can be empty; the inequalities express the assumed coalition-blocking model and unrestricted transfer of utility within a coalition.
Example: If two players create value 10 together and can each earn 3 alone, core allocations satisfy x₁+x₂=10 and x₁,x₂≥3.

Name: Nash bargaining solution
Intuition: The solution balances proportional gains above a disagreement outcome. Taking logarithms turns the product of positive gains into a sum with stronger marginal weight on smaller gains.
Conditions: A compact convex feasible utility set, a specified disagreement vector d, and a strictly feasible point giving every participant a positive gain. The standard axiomatic solution uses positive affine utility invariance and other bargaining axioms.
Example: With two players dividing one unit and disagreement at zero, maximizing x(1−x) selects an equal split.

Name: Replicator equation
Intuition: Strategies grow when their payoff exceeds the population's average payoff and shrink when it falls below average. Subtracting the mean keeps the population fractions normalized.
Conditions: A finite symmetric population game with payoff matrix A and a population state in the probability simplex. This is the standard continuous-time payoff-difference convention; some models rescale time by a positive mean fitness.
Example: Summing the right-hand sides gives zero, so total population share stays one and a zero-frequency strategy remains absent without mutation.
Prerequisites: Expected payoff of mixed strategies; Weighted arithmetic mean

Name: Evolutionarily stable strategy condition
LaTeX: x^{\mathsf T}Ax\ge y^{\mathsf T}Ax,\quad\text{and if equality holds, }x^{\mathsf T}Ay>y^{\mathsf T}Ay\quad\forall y\ne x
Intuition: A resident strategy resists a sufficiently small mutant invasion. If a mutant ties against the resident population, the second comparison checks what happens when mutants meet one another.
Conditions: A finite symmetric two-player game with bilinear payoff xᵀAy and mixed strategies x,y. The displayed two-part condition is equivalent to the standard small-invasion ESS definition; ESS is stronger than symmetric Nash equilibrium.
Example: A strict symmetric Nash equilibrium is evolutionarily stable because every distinct mutant already loses in the first comparison.

Name: Turing-machine transition rule
Intuition: A finite local rule updates a control state, one tape symbol, and the head position. Iterating this small rule over an unbounded tape models general symbolic computation.
Conditions: A deterministic single-tape Turing-machine convention with finite state set Q, finite tape alphabet Γ, initial state and halting conventions specified separately. Partial transitions or a stay-put move give equivalent computability models.
Example: A transition can replace a 0 by a 1, move one cell right and enter a new state; an unbounded sequence of such steps is a program execution.

Name: Universal simulation
Intuition: A program can be treated as input data for another program. One fixed interpreter can therefore simulate every machine described in the chosen effective encoding.
Conditions: A standard effective encoding of Turing machines and a universal partial computable simulator U. Equality includes matching divergence when M does not halt; it does not mean simulation has zero time or memory overhead.
Example: The same universal machine can simulate an addition program or a theorem-search program by receiving a different encoded machine.
Prerequisites: Turing-machine transition rule; Composition of functions

Name: Undecidability of the halting problem
Intuition: No total algorithm can correctly predict termination for every program and input. A supposed predictor can be used to build a program whose behavior contradicts its prediction about itself.
Conditions: Unrestricted Turing-computable programs with unbounded possible runtime. The result does not prohibit deciding termination for particular programs or restricted programming languages.
Example: A hypothetical program that loops exactly when a predictor says that it will halt creates a contradiction when supplied its own code.
Patterns: Information and uncertainty; Recursion and iteration

Name: Computable many-one reduction
LaTeX: A\le_mB\iff\exists\text{ total computable }f:\ x\in A\Longleftrightarrow f(x)\in B
Intuition: Translate every instance of one decision problem into an equivalent instance of another. A solver for the target would then solve the source after this translation.
Conditions: Decision languages over finite effective encodings and a total computable transformation f. The equivalence must hold on every source input, not merely on yes-instances or typical examples.
Example: If the halting problem reduces to B, then B cannot have a total decider, because composing that decider with the reduction would decide halting.
Prerequisites: Composition of functions; Undecidability of the halting problem

Name: Rice's semantic undecidability theorem
Intuition: Any nontrivial yes/no property of what a general program computes is undecidable uniformly from its code. The property must depend on its computed function, not merely on its written syntax.
Conditions: An acceptable effective enumeration of partial computable functions and a nonempty proper extensional class A. Equivalent formulations concern nontrivial properties of recognized languages. Particular inputs, restricted program classes and syntactic properties require separate analysis.
Example: Whether a program computes a function defined on every input is a semantic property and is undecidable for arbitrary programs.

Name: Kleene's recursion theorem
Intuition: Every effective transformation of program descriptions has a program whose behavior already matches its transformed version. The fixed point is in meaning, not necessarily in the literal code number.
Conditions: An acceptable numbering of partial computable functions and a total computable map f on program indices. Equality is equality of computed partial functions, including their divergence sets; e=f(e) is not required.
Example: A program can obtain an effective description of itself for use inside its own computation, which underlies formal self-reproducing constructions.

Name: Polynomial-time class P
Intuition: A decision problem is in P when one deterministic algorithm solves every input within a polynomial worst-case time bound. The exponent may depend on the problem but not on the input size.
Conditions: A fixed standard deterministic Turing-machine model and finite encodings; asymptotic time bounds absorb constant factors. Membership is an asymptotic classification and does not by itself ensure a practical small runtime.
Example: Graph reachability is in P because a systematic graph search decides it in time polynomial in the input encoding length.

Name: NP as polynomially verifiable witnesses
LaTeX: x\in L\iff\exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|),\ V(x,y)=1,\qquad V\text{ runs in polynomial time}
Intuition: A yes-answer can be supported by a short witness that is efficiently checked. Finding such a witness is a separate task from checking one that is already supplied.
Conditions: A decision language L, a polynomial witness-length bound p, and a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V. No-instances must have no accepting witness; the definition is worst-case over all inputs.
Example: A satisfying truth assignment is a polynomial-size witness for a Boolean formula's satisfiability and can be checked by evaluating the formula.

Name: Polynomial-time many-one reduction
LaTeX: A\le_pB\iff\exists f\in\mathbf{FP}:\ x\in A\Longleftrightarrow f(x)\in B
Intuition: An efficient translator preserves yes/no answers without hiding an expensive computation in the translation. It lets complexity upper bounds and hardness statements move between problems.
Conditions: A deterministic total polynomial-time transformation f between finite input encodings; FP denotes polynomial-time computable functions. Its output length is therefore polynomially bounded by the input length.
Example: If A≤pB and B∈P, then A∈P by running the translator and then B's solver.
Prerequisites: Computable many-one reduction; Polynomial-time class P

Name: Cook–Levin theorem
Intuition: A polynomially bounded accepting computation can be encoded as a Boolean formula with locally checkable consistency constraints. Satisfiability becomes a common language for all NP verification problems.
Conditions: Boolean satisfiability under standard finite formula encodings and polynomial-time many-one reductions. NP completeness means both membership in NP and the displayed reduction property; it is not a proof that SAT lacks a polynomial algorithm.
Example: A computation tableau uses variables for tape symbols, machine states and head locations, with clauses checking valid neighboring time steps.
Prerequisites: NP as polynomially verifiable witnesses; Polynomial-time many-one reduction; Turing-machine transition rule

Name: Deterministic time hierarchy
Intuition: Sufficiently more computation time permits solving strictly more decision problems. A diagonal simulation separates the larger time budget from all machines constrained by the smaller one.
Conditions: Standard multitape deterministic Turing machines and suitable time-constructible t,T≥n, with the displayed strict asymptotic gap. The logarithmic factor accounts for universal-simulation overhead in this version.
Example: The theorem separates deterministic quadratic time from cubic time under these machine-model conventions.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Recursion and iteration

Name: Polynomial-space class PSPACE
Intuition: A computation can reuse memory even when it takes many steps. Polynomial space allows exhaustive exploration as long as the program stores only a polynomial amount at once.
Conditions: Standard deterministic work-space complexity with a read-only input tape and finite decision languages. The containments do not assert that any displayed neighboring pair is unequal.
Example: A polynomial-size search witness can be enumerated and checked using polynomial memory, even when there are exponentially many candidate witnesses.
Prerequisites: NP as polynomially verifiable witnesses; Polynomial-time class P

Name: Configuration bound for space-limited computation
Intuition: A machine with limited memory has only finitely many distinct instantaneous states. A deterministic halting computation cannot revisit one, or it would repeat forever.
Conditions: A fixed finite-alphabet machine using O(s(n)) work space and a read-only input of length n, with s≥log n; constants absorb finite control and head positions. This counts configurations for a fixed input, not all possible programs.
Example: A deterministic decider using polynomial space can be simulated within exponential time because a longer nonhalting repeated configuration would create a loop.

Name: Savitch's space simulation theorem
Intuition: A nondeterministic path through configurations can be searched by recursively guessing and testing a midpoint. Time may grow enormously, but the same workspace is reused across the alternatives.
Conditions: A standard read-only-input Turing-machine model and space-constructible s(n)≥log n. The simulation trades nondeterministic space for deterministic squared space, not for comparable deterministic time.
Example: Reachability within at most 2^k steps can be checked by trying every possible midpoint and recursively checking two paths of length at most 2^(k−1).
Prerequisites: Configuration bound for space-limited computation; Polynomial-space class PSPACE

Name: Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time
Intuition: An algorithm may use random bits and occasionally be wrong, but it must have a uniform correctness guarantee for every input. Repetition can reduce the error without changing the polynomial-time class.
Conditions: Worst-case polynomial running time, independent unbiased random bits, and a two-sided error bound on each input. Any fixed success threshold strictly above one half gives the same class by amplification.
Example: A one-third error bound can be reduced exponentially by independent repeated runs and majority voting.

Name: Majority-vote error amplification
LaTeX: \Pr(\text{majority incorrect})\le e^{-r/18}\quad\text{if each independent run succeeds with probability at least }2/3
Intuition: Several independent noisy decisions can be combined into a much more reliable decision. The mean fraction of successes concentrates above the majority threshold.
Conditions: An odd number r of independent runs on the same fixed input, each with success probability at least 2/3. Correlated errors may defeat the bound; the guarantee is for majority voting with binary correctness indicators.
Example: Taking r proportional to log(1/δ) makes the error at most δ while multiplying runtime by only that repetition count.
Prerequisites: Hoeffding's inequality; Probability as an indicator expectation

Name: One-sided randomized polynomial time
Intuition: The algorithm can miss a yes-answer but never invent one. Repeating and accepting if any run accepts amplifies detection while preserving that one-sided guarantee.
Conditions: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm for a language L with the displayed per-input bounds. This convention defines RP; reversing which side is error-free defines coRP.
Example: After r independent runs, a yes-instance is missed with probability at most 2^(−r), while a no-instance is still never accepted.
Prerequisites: Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time; Independence of random variables

Name: Adleman's BPP-to-circuits theorem
Intuition: After amplifying correctness enough, some fixed random seed works for every input of a given length. Hardwiring such a seed produces a polynomial-size circuit for that length.
Conditions: Standard polynomial-time randomized computation and nonuniform polynomial-size Boolean circuit families. The proof establishes existence of a good seed for each length, not an efficient uniform method for finding those seeds.
Example: If each of the 2^n inputs fails with probability below 2^(−n), a union bound shows that at least one seed has no failing length-n input.

Name: Finite-automaton acceptance
Intuition: A finite automaton summarizes the entire input prefix by one of finitely many states. Reading the next symbol updates that summary through a fixed transition rule.
Conditions: A deterministic finite automaton with finite states Q, alphabet Σ, start q₀, accepting states F, transition δ, and δ*(q,empty)=q. The number of states is fixed independently of input length.
Example: A two-state automaton recognizes binary strings with an even number of ones by toggling states whenever it reads a one.
Prerequisites: Composition of functions; Congruence modulo an integer

Name: Pumping lemma for regular languages
Intuition: A long enough accepted path in a finite-state machine must repeat a state. The loop between repetitions can be removed or repeated without changing acceptance of the remaining suffix.
Conditions: If L is regular, some pumping length p exists such that every w∈L of length at least p has a decomposition satisfying the formula. The decomposition exists; it is not arbitrary. The lemma's property alone is not sufficient to characterize regularity.
Example: The language {0^n1^n:n≥0} violates the lemma because pumping a forced early zero block breaks equality of the two counts.

Name: Myhill–Nerode equivalence
LaTeX: x\sim_Ly\iff\forall z\in\Sigma^*:\ xz\in L\Longleftrightarrow yz\in L,\qquad L\text{ regular}\iff[\Sigma^*:\sim_L]<\infty
Intuition: Two prefixes are equivalent when no future suffix can distinguish them. The minimal memory needed for recognition is exactly the number of these distinguishable future-behavior classes.
Conditions: A language over a finite alphabet. The equivalence is right invariant, and finite index equals the number of states of the minimal complete deterministic automaton.
Example: For parity of ones, two prefixes are equivalent exactly when they have the same parity, yielding two minimal states.

Name: Number of Boolean functions
Intuition: A Boolean function chooses one output bit independently for every possible input. There are exponentially many truth-table entries and therefore doubly exponentially many possible functions.
Conditions: n labeled Boolean input coordinates and one Boolean output. This counts distinct functions, not different formulas or circuits that may compute the same function.
Example: Two input bits give four input rows and therefore 2⁴=16 Boolean functions.

Name: Counting lower bound for Boolean circuits
Intuition: Short circuits cannot describe every truth table because there are far too few short descriptions. Counting proves that some functions intrinsically require large circuits without identifying a particular hard function.
Conditions: Boolean circuits over a fixed finite complete bounded-fan-in basis; size counts gates. The asymptotic statement concerns existence for sufficiently large n. It is a nonconstructive lower bound and does not establish such a bound for a named explicit problem.
Example: Circuits of size s have at most 2^{O(s log(n+s))} descriptions, which is too small to represent all 2^{2^n} Boolean functions when s is sufficiently below 2^n/n.
Prerequisites: Number of Boolean functions; Pigeonhole principle

Name: Comparison-sorting decision-tree bound
Intuition: Every comparison supplies at most one binary branch in a decision tree. To distinguish all possible input orders, the tree must have enough leaves to label every permutation.
Conditions: Deterministic comparison-based sorting of n distinct keys with binary less-than outcomes. Algorithms exploiting restricted key encodings or additional operations are outside this model; average-case and randomized variants need their corresponding arguments.
Example: Three distinct keys have six possible orders, so a binary comparison tree needs worst-case depth at least three.
Prerequisites: Permutations and falling factorials; Logarithm laws

Name: Plain Kolmogorov description complexity
Intuition: The complexity of a finite string is the length of its shortest effective description in a fixed universal language. A long regular string can have a short description, while an irregular one may need almost all its bits stated explicitly.
Conditions: A fixed optimal universal partial computable description machine U and finite binary programs p and outputs x. This is plain complexity C, not prefix-free complexity K; constants depend on the chosen machine.
Example: A string of n zeros has a description consisting of a short printing routine plus a description of n, so its complexity grows only logarithmically in n up to encoding overhead.
Prerequisites: Universal simulation; Entropy bound for binary prefix coding

Name: Kolmogorov invariance under description language
Intuition: Changing a fixed description language adds at most the cost of an interpreter. This makes algorithmic complexity robust up to an additive constant, even though exact values remain language dependent.
Conditions: U is an optimal universal plain description machine and M is any fixed partial computable description machine. The constant c_M depends on M and U but not on the described string x.
Example: A fixed simulator prefix translates every M-program into a U-program with a bounded extra number of bits.
Prerequisites: Plain Kolmogorov description complexity; Universal simulation

Name: Counting incompressible strings
Intuition: There are too few short programs to compress every string. A uniformly chosen length-n string is unlikely to have a description shorter by many bits.
Conditions: Plain description complexity for a fixed machine U, integers 0≤c≤n, and binary programs. Each halting program has one output; different programs may coincide on an output, which only strengthens the upper bound.
Example: The fraction of length-n strings compressible by more than c bits under this strict threshold is less than 2^(−c).
Prerequisites: Plain Kolmogorov description complexity; Finite geometric sum

Name: Noncomputability of exact description complexity
LaTeX: x\longmapsto C_U(x)\quad\text{is not a total computable function}
Intuition: The shortest possible program length is mathematically well defined but cannot be calculated exactly for every string by one terminating algorithm. Searching programs can improve upper bounds without recognizing that the best one has been found.
Conditions: Plain Kolmogorov complexity for a fixed optimal universal description machine U. This does not prevent computable compression methods, special-case exact results or progressively improving upper approximations.
Example: Dovetailing all programs can eventually find shorter descriptions, but there is no general computable signal that no still-shorter program will ever halt with the same output.
Prerequisites: Plain Kolmogorov description complexity; Undecidability of the halting problem

Name: Pauli matrices and their product algebra
Intuition: Three small Hermitian matrices encode the geometry of a qubit. Their products combine an ordinary dot-product part with an oriented cross-product part.
Conditions: The standard two-by-two complex Pauli matrices, Cartesian indices x,y,z, Kronecker delta δ and right-handed Levi-Civita symbol ε. Physical spin operators are ħσ_i/2, so their units and commutator factors differ.
Example: For real vectors a,b, (a·σ)(b·σ)=(a·b)I+i(a×b)·σ; each individual Pauli matrix squares to I.
Prerequisites: Matrix multiplication; Cross product in three dimensions

Name: Arithmetic mean
Intuition: Replace a collection by one equal value while preserving its total. It is also the balance point and the best constant approximation under squared error.
Conditions: A nonempty finite list of real numbers; n is its length.
Example: For 2, 4, 9 the mean is 5: three copies of 5 preserve the total 15.

Name: Weighted arithmetic mean
Intuition: Give each value a share of the total influence. Normalizing the weights converts masses, frequencies or probabilities into one averaging rule.
Conditions: Finite real x_i, nonnegative real w_i, and sum of weights strictly positive.
Example: Two units at 10 and one at 16 have weighted mean 12.

Name: Geometric mean
Intuition: Average in logarithmic coordinates, then return to the original scale. It preserves the product instead of the sum.
Conditions: Strictly positive real inputs; n >= 1. The product form extends to nonnegative inputs.
Example: Growth factors 2 and 8 have geometric mean 4 because 4 squared equals 2 times 8.
Patterns: Averaging; Change of coordinates; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Harmonic mean
Intuition: Average reciprocals and invert. This is useful when equal amounts are accumulated at different rates.
Conditions: Strictly positive real inputs and n >= 1.
Example: Equal distances traveled at 30 and 60 km/h give overall speed 40 km/h.

Name: Root mean square
Intuition: Average squared magnitudes before taking a square root. Positive and negative signals both contribute to energy.
Conditions: Real inputs and n >= 1.
Example: The values -3 and 3 have mean 0 but RMS 3.

Name: Power mean
Intuition: A single exponent selects a whole family of means. Larger exponents give more influence to large inputs.
Conditions: A finite nonempty list of n >= 1 strictly positive real inputs; p is real. The p=0 value is the continuous limit.
Example: p=-1, 0, 1, 2 give the harmonic, geometric, arithmetic and root mean square means.

Name: Arithmetic–geometric mean inequality
Intuition: For a fixed sum, balancing positive entries maximizes their product. Unevenness creates the gap between arithmetic and geometric means.
Conditions: Nonnegative real x_i and n >= 1; equality iff all inputs are equal.
Example: A rectangle of fixed perimeter has greatest area when its side lengths are equal.

Name: Weighted AM–GM inequality
Intuition: The same balance principle works when entries carry unequal influence.
Conditions: x_i > 0, w_i >= 0, and sum w_i = 1; equality iff inputs with positive weights are equal.
Example: With weights 1/4 and 3/4, 1/4 + 3x/4 is at least x to the power 3/4.
Prerequisites: Arithmetic–geometric mean inequality; Weighted arithmetic mean

Name: Power mean inequality
Intuition: Increasing the averaging exponent shifts attention toward larger values. This orders many inequalities at once.
Conditions: A finite nonempty list of n >= 1 positive real inputs; p and q real with the continuous definition at zero. Equality iff all inputs agree.
Example: H <= G <= A <= RMS is one chain in this theorem.

Name: Quasi-arithmetic mean
Intuition: Choose coordinates in which averaging makes sense, average there, and transform back. This unifies additive, multiplicative and reciprocal averaging.
Conditions: f is continuous and strictly monotone on an interval containing all x_i; w_i >= 0, sum w_i = 1.
Example: The generators x, log x and 1/x give weighted arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means; equal weights 1/n recover their ordinary forms.

Name: Mean as the best constant
Intuition: Any constant other than the mean adds exactly one extra nonnegative error term. The mean is therefore the unique best constant in squared distance.
Conditions: Real finite data, n >= 1, and real a.
Example: For 2 and 6, predicting 4 costs 8; predicting 5 costs 10, an increase of 2 times 1 squared.

Name: Averaging as orthogonal projection
Intuition: Averaging is the operation of projecting a data vector onto the line of constant vectors. The residual contains every deviation from that common level.
Conditions: Euclidean space R^n, n >= 1; 1 denotes the all-ones column vector.
Example: The vector (2,4,9) projects to (5,5,5); its residual (-3,-1,4) has zero sum.

Name: Center of mass
Intuition: A weighted average of positions gives the point at which first moments balance. The same formula works coordinate by coordinate.
Conditions: Points x_i in a finite-dimensional real affine space, nonnegative masses m_i, and positive total mass. The squared-distance interpretation uses a chosen Euclidean inner product.
Example: Masses 1 at position 0 and 3 at position 4 balance at position 3.
Patterns: Averaging; Conservation and balance; Geometry and distance

Name: Online mean update
Intuition: Correct the old average by a shrinking fraction of the new prediction error. No old data values need to be retained.
Conditions: Real finite sequence, n >= 1; exact arithmetic identity, subject to rounding in computation.
Example: An average 10 from four values becomes 12 after observing 20.

Name: Combining group means
Intuition: A mean of means is correct when each group is weighted by its size. Grouping changes the computation but preserves the underlying sum.
Conditions: Nonempty finite groups of real observations, combined by concatenation; n_j is each group's positive size. To represent a dataset without duplicate observations, the groups must form a disjoint partition.
Example: A group of 2 averaging 5 and a group of 8 averaging 10 combine to 9, not 7.5.

Name: Circular mean direction
Intuition: Average unit vectors before recovering an angle. This respects wraparound at a full turn.
Conditions: Real angles, nonnegative weights, positive weight total, and nonzero vector sum; otherwise mean direction is undefined.
Example: Directions 359 degrees and 1 degree average to 0 degrees, rather than 180 degrees.

Name: Weighted squared-error decomposition
Intuition: Weighted averaging and weighted least squares select the same center. The total error separates into irreducible spread and error from choosing the wrong center.
Conditions: Finite real inputs; nonnegative weights with positive total; a real.
Example: Mass-weighted center estimation and frequency-weighted data fitting use the same identity.
Prerequisites: Weighted arithmetic mean; Mean as the best constant

Name: Sum of consecutive integers
Intuition: Pair the first and last terms so each pair has the same sum. A triangular count becomes half a rectangle.
Conditions: Integer n >= 0; the empty sum at n=0 is zero.

Name: Sum of consecutive squares
Intuition: Accumulating a quadratic sequence produces a cubic expression. This mirrors how integration raises polynomial degree.
Conditions: Integer n >= 0.
Example: The first three squares total 1+4+9=14.

Name: Finite geometric sum
Intuition: Multiply the sum by its common ratio and subtract: almost every term cancels.
Conditions: Real or complex r != 1; integer n >= 0. At r=1 the sum is n.
Patterns: Recursion and iteration; Exponentials and logarithms; Accumulation

Name: Binomial theorem
Intuition: Every term records how many times b was chosen from n factors. The coefficient counts all ways to make that choice.
Conditions: Nonnegative integer n; commuting a and b, for example real or complex scalars.

Name: Logarithm laws
Intuition: A logarithm converts multiplication into addition and powers into scaling. This is why growth rates, likelihoods and products often simplify in log coordinates.
Conditions: x,y > 0 and real a; natural logarithm. Complex principal logarithms require branch corrections.
Example: A product of many probabilities becomes a sum of log probabilities.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Change of coordinates

Name: Exponential addition law
Intuition: Adding time or an exponent composes multiplicative growth. This is the basic bridge between additive and multiplicative structures.
Conditions: Real or complex scalar x,y. For square matrices, the analogous identity holds when the matrices commute and can fail without commutation.
Example: Growing for time x and then y has the same factor as growing for time x+y.

Name: Quadratic formula
Intuition: Shift a quadratic to its center, then take a square root. The discriminant tells whether real roots are separated, repeated or absent.
Conditions: Real coefficients and a != 0; real roots require b^2-4ac >= 0. Both complex roots are allowed over C.
Example: x^2-5x+6=0 has roots 2 and 3.

Name: Completing the square
Intuition: Separate a quadratic into a centered square and a constant. Its location, minimum or maximum, and roots become visible.
Conditions: Real or complex a,b,c with a != 0; the minimum interpretation requires real variables and a > 0.

Name: Pythagorean theorem
Intuition: Perpendicular contributions add in squared length. This becomes the template for energy decomposition in inner-product spaces.
Conditions: A Euclidean right triangle with legs a,b and hypotenuse c.
Example: Lengths 3 and 4 at a right angle give diagonal length 5.

Name: Euler's formula
Intuition: A complex exponential packages circular motion into one expression. Multiplication becomes addition of angles.
Conditions: Real theta for the unit-circle interpretation; the identity extends to complex theta.
Example: At theta=pi/2 the exponential is i.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Symmetry and invariance; Composition

Name: Euler's identity
Intuition: Half a turn on the complex unit circle lands at -1. This is one especially recognizable value of Euler's formula.
Conditions: i^2=-1 and the usual complex exponential.
Example: It encodes a rotation of 180 degrees.
Patterns: Exponentials and logarithms; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Pythagorean trigonometric identity
Intuition: Sine and cosine are the coordinates of a unit vector. Their squared contributions always give unit length.
Conditions: Real theta for the geometric interpretation; the algebraic identity extends to complex theta.
Example: At pi/4 both squares are 1/2.

Name: Sine addition formula
Intuition: Combining two rotations mixes their horizontal and vertical components in a precise way.
Conditions: Real or complex alpha,beta.
Example: Choosing alpha=beta gives sin(2 alpha)=2 sin alpha cos alpha.

Name: Cosine addition formula
Intuition: The horizontal component of two composed rotations is the difference of two products.
Conditions: Real or complex alpha,beta.
Example: Choosing beta=-alpha gives cos squared alpha plus sin squared alpha equals 1.

Name: De Moivre's formula
Intuition: Repeated rotation multiplies the angle. Taking roots reverses that process and exposes cyclic symmetry.
Conditions: Integer n and real theta; negative powers are defined because the base is nonzero.
Example: Cube a unit complex number to triple its angle.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Exponentials and logarithms

Name: Complex modulus
Intuition: The modulus measures the stretching part of a complex number. Multiplication combines stretches while arguments combine rotations.
Conditions: Real x,y and complex z,w.

Name: Union of sets
Intuition: Union turns logical 'or' into a construction on sets. Set operations provide a geometric language for logical rules.
Conditions: Sets A and B in a common universe.

Name: Inclusion–exclusion for two sets
Intuition: Add both counts, then remove the overlap counted twice. Corrections for overlap recur in counting and probability.
Conditions: Finite sets A and B.
Example: If two groups have 8 and 7 members with 3 in common, their union has 12.

Name: Cartesian product
LaTeX: A\times B=\{(a,b):a\in A,\ b\in B\},\qquad |A\times B|=|A||B|
Intuition: Make a joint object by choosing one component from each collection. Independent choices multiply the count.
Conditions: The cardinality equation is stated for finite sets.
Example: Three shirts and four trousers give twelve pairs.

Name: Composition of functions
Intuition: The output of one rule becomes the input to another. This gives a common language for processes, transformations and nested models.
Conditions: x must be in the domain of f and f(x) in the domain of g.
Example: If f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=x squared, then g(f(x))=(x+1) squared.

Name: Inverse function
Intuition: An inverse undoes a transformation while recovering every input uniquely. Both existence and uniqueness matter.
Conditions: f:X to Y must be bijective; restricting the codomain to the image suffices for an injective f.
Example: The exponential maps R bijectively to positive reals; logarithm reverses it.

Name: Equivalence relation
LaTeX: x\sim x,\qquad x\sim y\Rightarrow y\sim x,\qquad x\sim y,\ y\sim z\Rightarrow x\sim z
Intuition: Specify which distinctions are irrelevant. The resulting equivalence classes turn many representations into one abstract object.
Conditions: A binary relation on a set; all three axioms must hold for all elements.
Example: Integers equivalent modulo n have the same remainder.

Name: Mathematical induction
Intuition: Prove a starting case and a rule that carries truth to the next case. The finite successor structure then reaches every natural number.
Conditions: P is a proposition about nonnegative integers; both the base and inductive step are required.
Example: The sum-of-integers formula follows by adding n+1 to the n-case.

Name: Telescoping sum
Intuition: Internal changes cancel, leaving only the endpoints. This is the discrete prototype of the fundamental theorem of calculus.
Conditions: Integer m <= n; a sequence in an abelian additive group, such as real numbers.
Example: Summing daily changes gives the difference between final and initial totals.

Name: Forward finite difference
Intuition: Measure change over a finite step. Dividing by the step size connects discrete differences to derivatives.
Conditions: Both function values are defined; h is a chosen nonzero real step when forming a difference quotient.
Example: For f(x)=x squared, the difference is 2xh+h squared.

Name: Discrete product rule
Intuition: A product's finite change splits into two contributions, with a shift in one factor. The shift is essential before taking a limit.
Conditions: All displayed values are defined; scalar-valued f,g.
Example: Subtract f(x)g(x) after inserting f(x+h)g(x).

Name: Summation by parts
Intuition: Move a difference from one factor to the other while recording endpoint terms. This is discrete integration by parts.
Conditions: Integers m <= n and finite scalar sequences with all displayed indices defined; an empty final sum is zero.
Example: It transfers a difficult difference to a factor whose differences are simpler.

Name: Power-law scaling
Intuition: A homogeneous function changes predictably under rescaling. The exponent says how the measured quantity scales.
Conditions: The equation defines homogeneity of degree k on a domain closed under the allowed positive scale factors lambda.
Example: Length, area and volume scale with exponents 1, 2 and 3.
Patterns: Scaling and homogeneity; Symmetry and invariance

Name: Dimensional homogeneity
Intuition: Quantities can be added only when their dimensions agree; multiplying quantities multiplies their units. This constrains candidate equations before calculation.
Conditions: Physical quantities with declared dimensions; these are consistency rules, not a guarantee of a physically correct model.
Example: A distance cannot be added directly to a time, but speed times time has distance units.

Name: Affine combination
Intuition: Combine points in a way independent of the chosen origin. Unlike a convex combination, some coefficients may be negative.
Conditions: Points in a real affine space; real coefficients summing to one.
Example: 2b-a extends the line segment from a through b by the same distance.

Name: Convex barycentric combination
Intuition: Treat coefficients as mass fractions. The result lies inside the convex hull of the contributing points.
Conditions: A finite set of points in a real affine space. Coordinates are unique for an affinely independent simplex.
Example: A triangle's centroid uses weights 1/3 at each vertex.

Name: Cross-ratio
Intuition: A ratio of ratios survives fractional linear coordinate changes. It is a natural measure in projective geometry when ordinary distances are not preserved.
Conditions: Distinct finite real or complex a,b,c,d with displayed denominators nonzero. Invariance holds for invertible fractional linear transformations T(z)=(alpha z+beta)/(gamma z+delta), with alpha delta-beta gamma nonzero. Interpret points at infinity projectively; the displayed finite formula requires finite transformed points.
Example: Perspective images preserve cross-ratios of four collinear points, although lengths change.
Patterns: Symmetry and invariance; Change of coordinates
